COLUMBUS, Ohio—A four-hour legislative committee hearing in June, punctuated by applause and anger, offered a window into the growing backlash against data centers.
The prospect of unchecked development has galvanized a cross-section of Ohioans, urban and rural, Democrat and Republican, alarmed about the spread of the giant computing facilities. Residents are demanding that local governments impose bans and moratoria on data centers while gathering signatures for a statewide ballot measure that could go before voters in 2027.
Leading the push is an eclectic group from rural Southern Ohio, including an outdoor-tourism guide, a lawyer and others who fear that the state’s data center boom is changing their communities faster than they can respond.
“Especially on America’s 250th anniversary it’s your job to make sure there’s life for another 250,” Nikki Gerber, the tourism guide, said at the June 1 statehouse hearing.
Data centers powered by fossil fuels are a rising source of planet-warming emissions. But for many opponents, the concerns are closer to home: they fear that data centers will change the look and feel of familiar landscapes and threaten local air and water.
Resistance to data centers is spreading across the country, especially against the supersize complexes being built to support artificial intelligence. The issue is emerging as a focal point in the November midterm elections, with about 40 local ballot measures in seven states, according to Ballotpedia.
Ohio has the most, with 21, including 10 communities set to vote next month on local restrictions on data centers: Conneaut, Defiance, Granville, Oregon, Pataskala, Piqua, Sunbury, Upper Sandusky, Trenton and Urbana.
The Ohio campaign stands out because the Columbus region has become one of the nation’s data center development hot spots.
If opponents prevail in Ohio, the outcome could reverberate beyond the state.
But Gerber is not thinking about the national stakes. Her focus is the 1.3-gigawatt data center that Amazon Web Services wants to build about 15 miles from her campground. She’s worried about what the project could do to the area’s water levels and biodiversity.
Inside Climate News visited her business, Moondoggie Liveree, tucked into the woods near Ohio Brush Creek, which flows into the Ohio River in Adams County.
Gerber’s office is an open-air shed left behind by a previous owner, with walls covered with knickknacks, bumper stickers and signs. Among the messages: “Watch! 4 Turtles! Caution!” The business rents campsites, canoes and kayaks, and assists hikers.
“Everybody thinks Ohio’s flat,” she said. “But it’s not, and it’s a really, really special area out here.”
Gerber is a local leader in promoting Adams County—one of Ohio’s poorest counties based on median household income—as a destination for outdoor tourism. She’s worried that the proposed data center could open the door to more projects, transforming the rustic landscape into an industrial zone.
She bought her property after working for years as a medical assistant. During the offseason, she builds rental cabins around the region.
After learning about the proposed Amazon data center early this year, she grew frustrated by what she saw as a lack of details from the local government. Adams County officials did not respond to requests for comment for this story.
In neighboring Brown County, also one of the poorest counties in the state, attorney Austin Baurichter left his job at a law firm office in Cincinnati, partly because he didn’t want to work on behalf of data center developers. He opened his own practice and connected with Gerber and others looking for answers about the projects.
They seem to have little in common. Gerber spends most of her day outdoors in flip-flops and shorts, while Baurichter is an early-career lawyer, usually dressed in a suit and tie. But they share a dedication to the cause.
Gerber is “the living embodiment of the sparkle emoji,” Baurichter said, interviewed by phone from his home office. He praised her energy and optimism.
The two are among the half-dozen people at the core of Conserve Ohio, the organization leading a statewide campaign for a data center moratorium.
Baurichter has grown frustrated with local governments, which he says are becoming more hostile toward data center opponents. He argues that some officials “got bamboozled” by developers early on, sometimes signing nondisclosure agreements and supporting projects without understanding the ramifications.
He approaches his activism with intensity, bringing his legal skills into the fight, filing public-records requests and questioning officials at public meetings.
In late September, he was there when the Ohio General Assembly voted on a temporary pause in the state’s gasoline tax. Data center opponents, along with Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton, a former director of the state health department, urged lawmakers to pass a measure pausing data center development that day. Majority Republicans declined to take up the issue.
Ohio political blogger D.J. Byrnes, who writes The Rooster newsletter about Ohio politics, captured video of Baurichter speaking on the sidelines with state Rep. Bride Rose Sweeney, a Cleveland-area Democrat. Baurichter admonished her for not doing more.
“We would rather you fight for our honor than for scraps that are being offered by people who know what they’re offering [is] scraps,” he said.
His conversations at the statehouse underscored his sense that leaders are not listening.
“It’s exhausting, like throwing your energy down a black hole,” he said soon after.
Dramatic Change and Anxiety
The legislature responded to public concerns last spring by creating the Select Committee on Data Centers. The panel has met five times, including the June 1 hearing, and has gathered feedback from local officials, data center companies and the public.

f13bfd65471a.text:
Three years ago, hydrogen seemed poised for a long-awaited breakthrough. The Biden administration announced $7 billion in federal funding for seven hubs to produce the fuel across the country, and Pennsylvania was set to be a major player in the emerging industry.
Hydrogen has long been heralded as a potential skeleton key to emission reductions: able to power commuter vehicles and mass transportation, as well as hard-to-decarbonize industries like shipping and steel production.
During a 2023 speech at Philadelphia’s Tioga Terminal, President Joe Biden assured the crowd that Pennsylvania’s two hubs—the Mid Atlantic Regional Hydrogen Hub and the Appalachian Hydrogen Hub, commonly known as MACH2 and ARCH2 —would be transformational. The hubs would connect a vast network of hydrogen producers, users, and researchers across Pennsylvania, Delaware, New Jersey, West Virginia and Ohio. They were backed by a bipartisan coalition and designed to bring economic opportunity to red states, with support in Pennsylvania from both Gov. Josh Shapiro and Sen. Dave McCormick. In 2023, Shapiro said the hubs would “ensure Pennsylvania continues to be an energy leader for decades to come.”
MACH2 promised to bring over 20,000 jobs to the Delaware Valley region alone and lead the way in green hydrogen, produced entirely from clean energy, with a $750 million award from the Department of Energy. ARCH2 would receive $925 million to manufacture blue hydrogen, produced via fossil fuels, with emissions sequestered by carbon capture technology. ARCH2 would be centered on Western Pennsylvania’s steel industry.
Today, that momentum has all but disappeared, one of many clean energy investments facing an uncertain future under the Trump administration. ARCH2 has gone totally dark, with former partners denying involvement or stonewalling media requests, and MACH2 has entered a holding pattern. Experts with knowledge of the hubs say that the federal government has been playing a game of “will they, won’t they”—changing their minds from week to week.
Community groups who initially opposed the hubs say they’ve heard nothing about the projects for months, although Manny Cintron, CEO of MACH2, told Inside Climate News via email that the hub’s “award is active,” but partners “continue to proceed cautiously in light of the current budget uncertainty.” In other words, no one wants to move forward with investment until they have a sense of whether the federal government will continue to fund the hub. As of late September, MACH2 was still circulating a request from January for potential partners to join the hub. The Department of Energy did not respond to repeated requests for comment.
“Until I see significant evidence to the contrary, I just don’t think the hubs are happening,” said Tom Torres, chief of staff at the Ohio River Valley Institute, a think tank focused on Appalachia.
This outcome is exactly what the hydrogen industry feared in the wake of the 2024 election. Losing the funding is going to “harm Pennsylvania,” Shapiro told Axios last year. “It’s going to mean we’re producing less energy. I have no idea why the president of the United States would want to do that.”
Even before Donald Trump took office, the hubs were facing an uphill battle, held up by a long lobbying fight over who would qualify for the 45V tax credits, which offered producers up to $3 per kilogram of hydrogen produced. Oil and gas proponents wanted more carve-outs for blue hydrogen hubs, like ARCH2; environmentalists wanted to ensure that the subsidies went to hubs running solely off of clean energy, rather than pulling from Pennsylvania’s gas-heavy grid. The debate dragged on nearly until Biden left office, delaying investment and leaving the projects in limbo.
To complicate matters, green hydrogen, which involves using clean energy to produce a different kind of clean energy, is notoriously difficult to produce cost effectively. The fuel is created through a process called electrolysis—essentially, running an electrical current through water, which separates the hydrogen and the oxygen. If you hook a solar panel up to an electrolyzer, about 30 percent of the energy from that panel will be lost just in the process of isolating the hydrogen. By the time you compress it into a fuel cell or liquefy it for transport, then convert it back into electricity, about 70 percent of the energy generated by that original solar panel is gone. And even once you’ve managed to produce it, hydrogen is exceedingly leaky—the smallest element in the periodic table, able to escape even from sealed steel vats.
This is part of why the hubs drew so much pushback from environmental groups, who decried the fuel as a false solution when Biden’s plans were first announced. The United States currently produces about 10 million metric tons of hydrogen per year, almost all of which are made using oil and gas. Clean hydrogen is significantly more expensive, and even with subsidies, experts have warned that it will never be a practical or cost-competitive fuel for public transit, personal vehicles or commercial and residential heating.
But it is critical when it comes to replacing carbon-intensive chemical feedstocks that create products like ammonia, which is used to make fertilizer. Ammonia production alone accounts for roughly 2 percent of global energy consumption and 1.5 percent of greenhouse gas emissions. Green ammonia could also aid in decarbonizing global shipping, which produces another 3 percent of global emissions.
Under the Biden Administration, MACH-2 made a show of partnering with SEPTA, Philadelphia’s public transit system, to test hydrogen-powered buses. In the hub’s application, though, it was made clear that the main offtakers for MACH2 would, at least initially, be area oil refineries—a tough sell for community and environmental justice groups, who were already concerned about hydrogen’s high flammability and its potential to serve as an indirect greenhouse gas, ma

A merchant ship has sunk after drones hit two vessels off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast, Prime Minister Rumen Radev has said.
He indicated Russia was suspected of the attacks and that he had called in its ambassador.
One of the ships went down 17 nautical miles (31km) east of Krapets and one crew member was saved, he said. The other, Ukrainian-owned vessel was hit by three drones 18 nautical miles from the town of Byala and all 15 crew were rescued, he added.
The drone attacks come a week after two other commercial ships were hit by sea and aerial drones in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone. One of the ships, the Alfa Watan, sank and all 10 crew, including nine Syrians, are presumed dead.
Radev convened an emergency meeting on Tuesday and said he had summoned Russian envoy Eleonora Mitrofanova. Although there was no conclusive evidence of blame on "either side... the logic suggests that the outcome benefits the Russian Federation", he said.
Bulgaria is a Nato member and the prime minister said he would speak shortly to secretary general Mark Rutte. Radev had earlier asked Nato and the EU for technical assistance in investigating the 6 October attacks, indicating it was unclear whether Russia and Ukraine were behind them.
Radev came to office during the summer and has since rejected suggestions that he is "pro-Russian".
Ukraine has directly blamed Russia for the latest attacks and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen spoke on Tuesday of the Black Sea becoming "another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine. This is unacceptable".
Russia's military has not publicly commented on the issue. It has recently intensified its strikes on vessels in the Black Sea, particularly the western side, as part of its war against Ukraine.
The same day that two ships were targeted off Bulgaria last week, Ukraine hit an oil tanker in the Russian Black Sea port of Sochi.
Moscow says it is targeting ships delivering weapons and dual-use cargo to Ukrainian ports - and cited attacks in the ports of Mykolaiv and Chornomorsk last week, along with one in the Black Sea.
However, Kyiv and its European allies say merchant vessels carrying grain and other civilian cargo are being attacked.
Meeting with his security chiefs on Tuesday, Bulgaria's prime minister said: "Another attack on merchant ships in the immediate vicinity of Bulgarian territorial waters is absolutely unacceptable".
Radev identified one of the hit vessels as the Maltese-flagged Chelsea 3, which is registered in Ukraine's Odesa, saying that five its crew members were being treated for minor injuries. He gave no further details about the vessel that had sunk.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said "Russia's latest attack on commercial vessels near Bulgaria's territorial waters... once again demonstrates Moscow's deliberate disregard for civilian lives and maritime security in the Black Sea.
"The Black Sea is a lifeline for global food security. Russia is attacking it to weaponise hunger and hold the world hostage. This must be met with strength," he added.
Both Russia and Ukraine are major grain-exporting countries and Turkey has called on both countries to halt attacks in the Black Sea.
Moscow has repeatedly rejected calls by the US and Europe for a naval ceasefire in the Black Sea, blaming Ukraine for attacking Russian merchant ships in the area.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.

Emergency calls from botched Christa Pike execution released to US media
A series of newly-released calls made after the failed execution of US death row inmate Christa Pike reveal emergency services were delayed by confusion among first responders and Tennessee prison officials.
The recordings, first obtained by the Associated Press, show that minutes passed as officials and responders attempted to confirm whether the request for emergency help in the execution chamber at Riverbend Prison was legitimate.
The first call was released only in a written transcript by the Nashville Department of Emergency Communications (DEC). "We've been carrying out an execution tonight. We've administered 10 grams of pentobarbital. The person is not yet deceased. That started approximately 1 hour ago. And we're calling for an ambulance," the caller told the dispatcher.
The dispatcher asked the caller for a verification code, which the caller did not have.
The DEC also released other calls between the agency and other departments, including the police and highway patrol.
"We are trying to find out if that is an actual thing that is happening and we need to send an ambulance and, or if you need police assistance or if this is someone that is just basically prank calling or, like, swatting us," one dispatcher can be heard saying during a call.
Another recording shows Kelly Gleason, Christa Pike's defence attorney saying: "She is still alive and breathing and needs immediate life-saving care."
Pike, 50, was sentenced to death after murdering Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend in 1995. She survived two injections of the drug pentobarbital on 30 September and was taken to hospital in a critical condition.

Leaders of India's Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) were detained early on Tuesday after they entered a heavily-guarded protest site and chanted slogans demanding the country's election chief resign over a controversial revision of electoral rolls.
Party founder Abhijeet Dipke shared a video showing Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das being taken away by police from Jantar Mantar, a historic Delhi observatory popular for protests.
Footage showed the two - along with others - climbing over police barricades before chanting slogans while holding the Indian flag.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi's opponents allege the voter list revision benefits his party, a charge it and the Election Commission reject.
There have been days of protests demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation.
Police have stepped up security across Delhi as demonstrators challenge restrictions on where protests can be held.
Early on Tuesday, Dipke, Das and Ranka all shared videos showing Das and Ranka entering Jantar Mantar.
"You cannot denotify the resistance," Dipke wrote on X.
Das also posted a message declaring that the site had been "reclaimed" and that they were being detained.
It was not immediately clear where police had taken the leaders.
Ranka later appeared on an Instagram live broadcast from a police bus alongside other detainees where they appeared cheerful and said they would not back down.
The detentions came a day after the federal home ministry announced that Jantar Mantar, long associated with public protests in Delhi, would no longer be a designated protest venue. Authorities instead identified three alternative locations where demonstrations can be held with permission.
Before the decision, the CJP had met Delhi Police officials to seek permission for a peaceful protest at Jantar Mantar and had warned that it would announce further demonstrations if it received no response.
"30 mins after we went to Delhi Police asking for a date when we can go to Jantar Mantar, Jantar Mantar was de-notified as a protest site," Ranka had earlier posted on X.
Most of the party's leadership has been in Delhi in recent days. Dipke, however, had travelled to his hometown in Maharashtra after the death of his grandmother. He was among several CJP leaders detained ahead of a planned demonstration on Saturday and was released the next day.
The CJP had called for a protest at Jantar Mantar on Saturday, but authorities imposed extensive security restrictions across the capital to prevent demonstrators from reaching the site.
Several metro stations were closed, train services were disrupted and thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were deployed.
Over the weekend, the police detained and released thousands of people, including several journalists. Some videos and photos from the protest show police dragging people, including women, by force and pushing them into buses.
Separately, opposition parties held a march in Delhi on Monday from Connaught Place - a major shopping district in the heart of the capital - to the Supreme Court.
The Congress, India's main opposition party, also petitioned the Supreme Court on Monday, challenging the Election Commission's voter revision exercise, which has resulted in tens of millions of names being removed from electoral rolls.
Critics say the exercise risks excluding eligible voters and making it harder for them to prove their eligibility.
Anger over the revision exercise intensified after The Indian Express reported that Kumar had disregarded concerns raised by the two other election commissioners over changes to voter registration. The Election Commission has said its decisions were unanimous.
The current protests follow student-led demonstrations earlier this year over exam irregularities and demands for education reforms.
The CJP led weeks of action that culminated in the resignation of federal Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
The group began as online satire after India's Chief Justice Surya Kant compared some unemployed young people to cockroaches during a court hearing in May. He later said his remarks had been misinterpreted, but the comments had already become a rallying cry for young people seeking change.
After the summer protests, the CJP evolved into a pressure group, tapping into wider anger over unemployment, exam irregularities and government accountability.

Fly-tippers in Cornwall could face fines of up to Â£5,000 if they are caught illegally disposing waste.
The threat is a part of Cornwall Council's new push to quash the crime after it recorded 17,500 fly-tipping incidents in the past five years.
It has introduced the use of covert cameras to catch unlicensed waste carriers in the act, and is also encouraging residents to submit evidence if they catch anything on camera. Households who are found to have employed fly-tippers also face fines.
Cornwall Council said there was "no excuse" for the offence, and that it would hold fly-tippers to account.
"We work hard to identify those responsible for illegal dumping and will hold offenders to account wherever possible," said Sarah-Jane Brown, group leader for community protection at Cornwall Council.
"We're asking people to play their part and work with us to prevent fly-tipping, and to share any information that may help us trace those responsible for dumping rubbish."
Councillor Thalia Marrington, council cabinet member with responsibility for community safety and public protection, said: "Fly-tipping can cause serious harm to our communities, the environment and wildlife.
"It also costs councils and landowners huge amounts of money to clear up."

Groups trying to protect red squirrels are being invited to bid for funding from a Â£250,000 pot.
The Red Squirrel Recovery Network (RSRN) said it hoped to "engage people from all backgrounds" with grants of up to Â£500 available for smaller activities to Â£5,000 to support ideas with a wider reach.
The project, which started in 2025, works with conservation partners and volunteer groups across Northumberland, Cumbria, Manchester, Lancashire, Merseyside and southern Scotland to raise awareness of the endangered species.
In May, animal welfare group Save Our Reds said the species "still clings on" across Cumbria, Northumberland and the North Pennines but could disappear within 25 years.
Red squirrel populations across Britain have dramatically declined and have been estimated at about 287,000, the RSRN said.
According to Natural England, external, causes for the decline include the introduction of grey squirrels from the USA and Canada from 1876 spreading the squirrelpox virus, which is fatal to the red squirrels only.
Save Our Reds said habitat loss and weak enforcement of existing protections were adding to the problem.
Heather Harris, from the RSRN, said the project - which is funded by the National Lottery Heritage Fund - aimed to "remind everyone of why red squirrels are so important to our heritage".
"There are many older generations who remember red squirrels, but we'd also would love to hear from younger people where nature isn't as accessible for them or who haven't had the experience of seeing red squirrels," she said.
The network said it wanted to support plans which helped local communities celebrate red squirrels and reconnect with nature, such as themed walks or improving spaces linked to conservation.
RSRN programme manager Mike Denbury said: "From introducing children to red squirrels for the very first time to delivering larger habitat protection projects, we're keen to hear your ideas on inspiring action for nature."

This story contains details of sexual violence which some readers may find upsetting
"Get out of the car!" screams a woman, accusing a driver of exposing himself and making obscene comments as she walked by. She is filming the scene in a busy Baghdad street on her phone, and the camera captures him resisting her attempts to open the door as she confronts him.
The video can be seen, with others like it, on the Instagram page of Iraqi women's rights activist Sarah Jassim. She posts them on behalf of women who complain about sexual abuse and harassment by Iraqi men and boys.
"Your camera is your weapon," she tells the BBC. "It's a way to document evidence in case a woman decides to sue her harasser, or at least it is a means to shame him."
One of the videos she posted led to the arrest of the alleged perpetrator, a policeman accused of harassing schoolgirls, she says.
Jassim says posting the videos is risky both for herself and for the women concerned. We have spoken to numerous victims of sexual abuse in Iraq who say that society often blames the victim.
"I have received death threats, and I have also been threatened with acid attacks," Jassim says. "I have been accused of inciting public indecency, because I encourage women to speak in a society that expects us to be silent."
She now barely leaves home, for her own safety, and instead spends hours playing with her dog.
There is a need for stricter laws, she argues, including laws that explicitly criminalise "harassment" and "gender-based violence" - terms that are currently absent from the penal code.
"Recognising the problem is the best way to address it," she says. "We need protection, abusers have to be deterred."
'No-one will hear if I kill you'
Many Iraqi women have told the BBC they felt failed by the justice and police systems. Pursuing legal action against a harasser or a rapist is a long path in Iraq, with complicated procedures, and uncertain results, according to a number of activists and lawyers we have spoken to.
Violence against women and girls in Iraq is "widespread and under-reported," according to a report in May by a UN committee on discrimination against women, which called for stronger legislation.
Among dozens of recommendations, it urged the authorities to repeal "discriminatory" laws that exonerate rapists if they marry their victims, and allow reduced sentences for murder in cases where a perpetrator was carrying out a so-called "honour killing".
Amal - not her real name - has been battling in court for about five years. She accuses her ex-husband of repeatedly raping their daughter - who was under 18 at the time - at gunpoint.
She recalls her daughter's harrowing account of the incident, when she says the father walked into the girl's room and laid his weapon on her bed. She says he told her: "No-one will hear you if I kill you."
Sexual abuse has long been seen as a taboo subject in Iraq. I have been in touch with many survivors who say that they prefer to hush it up, because of a potential family backlash. Others told us they were afraid to go to the police, for fear of social stigma and possible harassment. But Amal was determined to seek justice and rushed to police to report the incident.
"She had lots of bruises around her wrists, as he held her hands tight. Whenever she tried to scream, he would cover her mouth with his hands," Amal says.
Amal showed me medical documents, including DNA evidence, which support her account.
A further demonstration of her ex-husband's cruelty came, Amal says, when she heard him tell a family member to "wash off our disgrace" if he was arrested. The expression is used in Iraq to refer to so-called honour killings - carried out in the belief that a woman has compromised a family's reputation.
Amal says she believes the father threatened to put an end to his daughter's life "so the medical report would not be released and the assault would not be proven".
She says her ex-husband is on the run and the court case remains open.
"I fought all alone," says Amal, bursting into tears as she says her ex-husband hired several lawyers but she could not afford legal representation, and her family turned a blind eye to the situation.
She no longer has any faith that a court ruling will come in her favour. "I just want him to stay out of my way forever," she says, with a sigh of despair.
For more on this story, you can watch Sally Nabil's report on YouTube, external.
Activist killed
Amal's daughter is more fortunate than some women who have experienced domestic sexual abuse in Iraq, as she has a safe place to live.
Many survivors have no independent income and nowhere to go. Iraq has very few shelters for abused women.
Those we know of were established by an organisation co-founded by Yanar Mohammed, an internationally recognised women's rights advocate. Last March she was murdered outside her house in Baghdad by armed men. The perpetrators are still unknown.
Experts working for the UN Human Rights Council wrote in April that Mohammed had been receiving death threats and online abuse for years, which were "believed to come from extremist religious militia".
Activists repeatedly told us that targeted attacks on their colleagues have been on the rise in recent years.
Hanaa Edwar, another prominent women's rights activist, says she saw Mohammed just two days before she was killed. She says she has also been threatened.
"There are no laws, no protection, and no justice for women in Iraq," she tells me.
"The problem in Iraq is not that women stay silent. It is that when they speak, very little in the system is built to listen, Mustafa Saadoon, head of the Iraqi Observatory for Human Rights, tells the BBC.
"A woman who reports sexual violence has to get past her family first, then a police station, then a court, and at every one of those doors someone is likely to tell her to settle it quietly."

- Published
Americans head to the polls on 3 November to decide how the rest of Donald Trump's presidency will play out.
Thousands of races are taking place across the US, at different levels of government. But the main event for voters will be electing members of the House of Representatives and the Senate, the two chambers that make up Congress.
Both of them are currently controlled by the Republicans, the president's party. The success or failure of Trump's final two years in office could rest on the outcome.
Here's our visual guide to where the battle for power will be won and lost - from approval ratings, to key races and issues and the huge amount of money being spent.
Midterms come at bad time for Trump
One of the reasons the opposition Democrats have a chance to take back Congress is the president's low approval rating, which is a good indicator for how well his party could perform.
He began his second term as president with an approval rating of just over 50%, according to polling resource website Silver Bulletin, but it quickly fell into the 40s.
It was hovering around 42% when Trump decided to launch air strikes with Israel against Iran at the end of February this year but it fell below 40% shortly afterwards. It is currently sitting at about 37%.
Eight years ago, Trump's approval rating was significantly higher at this point in his first term, at 43%. Joe Biden's at the same point in his term was at 40%. In both cases, the sitting president lost control of the House in the midterms but kept hold of the Senate.
But Trump's poor ratings help explain why Democrats are hopeful of winning both chambers of Congress and why they are setting their sights on states that Republicans have won consistently in recent years.
The battle for the House
The current Republican majority in the House of Representatives, the lower chamber, is as thin as it gets - they have 218 representatives, which is the exact number needed to have control, plus one independent who votes with them.
Members of the House serve a two-year term so all 435 seats are up for election in November.
But most districts are not considered competitive because the party that holds them has such solid support that there is only one likely winner.
The Cook Political Report, which analyses campaigns and elections, suggests that just 21 districts are "toss-ups" that could be won by either party.
Of those 21 toss-ups, 15 are currently held by Republicans and six by Democrats. If the Democrats win five of those on top of 28 districts classed as likely or leaning Democratic, they will win the House.
Historically, the midterms see a high number of seats changing hands in the House, usually in a protest against the White House. The average number lost by the president's party is 27, according to data, external going back to 1934. Of those 23 elections, the president's party has only made gains in three.
The battle for the Senate
The Republicans have a slightly stronger hold on the Senate. They hold 53 of the 100 seats while the Democrats have 45 and two independents who also vote with them.
Members of the Senate serve six-year terms so roughly a third are up for election every two years.
Thirty-five seats are up for grabs in November but analysis by the Cook Political Report suggests that only seven of them are toss-ups that could go either way.
Of those toss-ups, six are currently held by Republicans and one by Democrats. The Democrats would need to win four of those seats, plus the four classed as likely or leaning Democratic, to hit 51 and take control of the Senate.
But winning a majority is no easy task for the Democrats.
They need to keep hold of their seat in Michigan, where polls suggest the race is tighter than Democrats would like between Abdul El-Sayed, a left-wing political outsider, and his Republican rival Mike Rogers, a Trump ally and former FBI agent.
And they would also need to pick up seats in states that Trump won by double-digits in 2024, including Alaska, Iowa and Ohio.
But polls suggest they have a chance, even in Texas where former teacher James Talarico could become the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the state since 1988 if he defeats Ken Paxton, the current state attorney general and close Trump ally.
What are the key issues for voters?
Trump pledged to "end inflation and make America affordable again" in his 2024 election campaign but the cost of living crisis is proving to be the key issue for voters.
The president proudly declared that gas was "now below $2.30 [Â£1.74] a gallon in most states" in his State of the Union address on 24 February. But the war with Iran began four days later, disrupting Middle Eastern energy supplies and causing gas to hit $4 (Â£3.03) in the US.
The war became increasingly unpopular as its consequences reverberated around the world and ultimately hit American consumers in the pocket. One poll carried out in August found 63% of respondents disapproved of Trump's handling of the situation.
Other issues that voters say are important to them include healthcare and immigration.
Trump has recently touted his policies around immigration as a big success, citing significantly lower border-crossing figures than in recent years.
Many Democratic candidates are focusing on the high costs of US health insurance and the impact of Trump's legislation on access to the healthcare system.
Can Trump defy political gravity?
Most signs point towards a successful midterms for the Democrats, but it wouldn't be the first time that Trump and his party have outperformed polls if they do win more seats than expected.
One of the few things in their favour is their huge financial advantage.

Ukraine has stabilised the front line and "broken Russia's ability to advance" by killing so many of its men, Ukraine's former commander-in-chief has said in an interview with the BBC.
Gen Oleksandr Syrskyi made the comments in an exclusive interview, his first since he was dramatically forced from his post in the summer.
He addressed his sacking, disagreeing with his critics who declared him too "old school" to command Ukraine's new, technologically advanced forces.
He also pushed back against allegations made by soldiers who previously served under him, who told the BBC they were ordered to remain at their positions even when they were almost surrounded by Russians, leading to high losses.
Syrskyi said that Moscow's overall losses in the war were six times higher than Ukraine's. "If you count only dead, then it's up to 11 times," he added.
Neither Russia nor Ukraine officially release the numbers of their dead. Ukraine's military says it inflicted record losses this year on Russian soldiers in September, although that cannot be verified.
UK intelligence chiefs estimate Russia has lost around half a million men killed in Ukraine since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022. The US-based Center for Strategic and International Studies meanwhile believes, external Ukraine has lost up to 150,000 troops killed by June 2026.
He says this difference in death toll â as well as technological advances, and a strategy of attacking weak points in Russia's lines while containing their advances in other parts â accounts for the current stalemate at the front.
In the first six months of 2026, Russia managed overall to seize 61 sq km, the general said. "It's an indication that the front line has been stabilised."
The Institute for Study of War (ISW) has also confirmed this trend. One of its recent reports, external says that in September 2026, Moscow lost more territory than it took.
Syrskyi was appointed Ukraine's commander-in-chief in 2024. He had previously won praise for defending Kyiv at the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, and for leading the successful counteroffensive east of Kharkiv in the autumn of that year.
But President Volodymyr Zelensky fired Syrskyi this summer, amid a major disagreement with then-defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov.
Fedorov had said that instead of adapting to the realities of the changing war, the army under Syrskyi had blocked his initiatives.
Zelensky initially fired Fedorov, as tensions burst into the open between the two men. But mass street protests then forced the president to also fire Syrskyi, replacing him with Maj Gen Mykhailo Drapatyi, 43.
Syrskyi told the BBC that he had "disagreements" with Fedorov because the latter "didn't take into consideration the interests of the army" when procuring weapons and supplies.
Fedorov had created an "imbalance" in supplies, Syrskyi said. He had prioritised drones while overlooking key front-line kit such as unmanned ground vehicles, pick-up trucks and motorbikes. Even with drones, Syrskyi said, there were shortages as the army got only half of what they needed.
Fedorov was a popular young minister who was known for his digital and technological initiatives. Many contrasted him with Syrskyi, who critics thought was not fit to lead the new technological arms race with Russia.
But Syrskyi disagrees with such criticism. It was during his time the use of drones reached this new, unprecedented level, including deep strikes more than 2,000km (1,200 miles) behind enemy lines, he said. Ukraine was the first country to create the Unmanned Systems Forces as a separate branch of armed forces, under his command: now, he said, drones account for 80% of Russia's losses.
Under his military leadership, however, Ukrainian troops undertook chaotic withdrawals from the eastern cities of Avdiivka and Vuhledar, and from around Pokrovsk.
Soldiers who spoke to the BBC in the past complained that they were ordered to remain at their positions at any costs. By the time they were told to pull back, it was often too late as they were almost surrounded by Russian troops.
Syrskyi does not deny that such situations occur on the front line. But he told the BBC that Ukraine was fighting against a far more powerful army.
In 2025, the ratio of jets and bombs was 18 to one in Moscow's favour, he said. In the same year, Russia had two-and-a-half times more artillery pieces and shells than Ukraine. And with four million militarily trained men who they can mobilise, Russian forces can create chances to push through, he argued.
One of Syrskyi's most famous operations was an incursion into Russia's Kursk region that started in August 2024. It ended with a dramatic retreat the following spring, which some soldiers described as "catastrophic". Syrskyi, however, insisted that the Kursk operation was "a necessity".
"In the summer 2024, Russian forces were pushing along all main directions on the front line with up to six times more troops than we had," he explained.
The Kursk incursion disrupted Russia's offensive and forced Moscow to redirect troops, giving Ukraine a respite and a chance for its stretched brigades in the east and south to recover, Syrskyi said.
He also had strong words for European allies who doubt that Russia may have territorial ambitions beyond Ukraine. He advised European partners to start preparing for the war now and "drop all illusions that [it] will not come".
He also said he believed Ukraine's war was going to become even more technological. There will be more robots, automated systems and artificial intelligence (AI). "Even ordinary weapons now get an AI-based control system to enhance their capabilities," he said.
Such technologies can give a new life to conventional weapons like tanks. Both Russia and Ukraine were now racing to develop "active systems of defence" to protect armoured vehicles, Syrskyi said.

A five-time US giant pumpkin contest winner tells the BBC he'd "love" to break the world record for a second time.

Army plans ‘rodeo’ to round up supply-chain problems
The service’s “biggest acquisition program” is fostering new companies, acting secretary says.
The U.S. Army is planning a "rodeo" to round up problems that slow the deployment of new weapons, and rope in new ways to improve supply chains and make parts in more places, the service’s acting chief said today.
The “Manufacturing Rodeo,” planned sometime in 2027, will serve as a sort of public competition to expose where the industrial base is failing to meet demand and where new players are providing innovative approaches.
“We need to strain the nation's larger industrial base. We're going to stress-test the supply chain, the manufacturing processes, and see where it breaks,” Adam Telle said at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual conference in Washington, D.C.
Production bottlenecks and a lack of suppliers for many key parts have plagued the Army for decades. The Government Accountability Office, among others, has detailed many breaking points. But, Telle said, those reports don’t capture how bad the problem could become as the Army seeks new drones and counterdrone weapons with components made by companies far from the service’s control.
For instance, he said, the Army needs to “make millions” of one-way attack drones.
“It may look simple, but it's a flying supply chain. If somebody else controls one part, they can break the whole thing,” the acting chief said.
Parts for such drones are largely made in China, which uses its market dominance to help other autocratic states like Russia and Iran attack U.S. forces and partner militaries in Europe.
Telle, who did not name any adversary, said that “an economy that's an extension of the national-security apparatus” can be “ruthlessly efficient” in deploying weapons.
“Over there, you flip a switch, and by law, by design, the economy is nationalized,” he said.
The acting Army chief listed steps the Pentagon has taken to overcome bureaucratic sluggishness in developing and deploying new technologies, such as pushing more acquisition authority down to battalion-level commanders, getting more self-sustained power on U.S. bases, and introducing a program to allow private companies to test new weapons on U.S. Army ranges. New private ranges, such as Second Bend Labs, are also renting time and space to defense startups eager to gain a foothold.
Telle said fostering new companies is more important than any single program.
“When someone tells you the Army's biggest acquisition program is this tank or that helicopter or this missile system, tell them they're wrong. The biggest acquisition program in the Army is building a system of seamless, frictionless, symbiotic relationship with American ingenuity.”

Shares in dating app Bumble soared by almost 50% on Monday following reports it is in advanced takeover talks valuing the business at $1bn (Â£757m).
Ithaca Holdings, a technology investment firm, could announce a deal to buy the Texas-based company as early as this week, according to the Wall Street Journal.
The jump in Bumble's shares pushed its stock market valuation to over $580m but that is still far below a peak of more than $14bn it reached after listing on the Nasdaq in 2021.
Bumble is one of the world's most downloaded dating apps, operating in a crowded market where growth has slowed. The BBC has contacted Bumble and Ithaca for comment.
Bumble was launched in 2014 by Whitney Wolfe Herd, who was also a co-founder of dating app giant Tinder.
Wolfe Herd built Bumble's brand around a distinctive feature that only allowed women to initiate conversations with matches.
It recently abandoned that rule, prompting debate among users over whether the app had lost what set it apart from rivals.
"Today, our community is asking for more flexibility, less pressure, and more opportunities to create real, meaningful connections and that is what this new experience provides," Wolfe Herd said in August.
Dating apps like Bumble have come under pressure in recent years as some younger users have grown disillusioned with browsing for dates.
Bumble said in 2025 that it would cut almost a third of its workforce as the industry grappled with what Wolfe Herd described as an "inflection point" in online dating.
Investments in other dating companies have also soured as apps have struggled to convince users to pay for their services.
Match Group - which owns apps including Tinder, OkCupid and Hinge - has also seen its shares fall sharply from their peak in 2021.
According a report by media watchdog Ofcom in 2025, adults in the UK were spending less time on dating apps compared to three years earlier.
Some single people are instead turning to board game get-togethers, book clubs and other group activities in the hope of finding a partner.

Before dawn breaks over Mumbai, Mansi Kadam begins preparing vada pav, a savoury snack synonymous with the western Indian city, for the day's customers. One ingredient is non-negotiable: Tata salt.
When asked whether she would ever consider switching brands, her reply is a reminder of an old Hindi ad jingle, "If it's salt, it has to be Tata."
She knows little about the developments unfolding in the boardroom of the Tata group, one of India's oldest and most influential business empires that makes everything from salt to software.
But her instinctive loyalty points to a question confronting the group: Can one of India's most trusted brands remain insulated from a public battle over power, governance and control?
A recent public disagreement between the board of Tata Sons, the holding company of the Tata group and Tata Trusts, its principal shareholder, has put a spotlight on the conglomerate.
At the centre of the dispute are two issues - the proposed public listing of Tata Sons and the reappointment of chairman N Chandrasekaran. Most of the Tata Sons board, including its biggest minority shareholder SP Group, supported the decisions.
But Noel Tata, chairman of majority shareholder Tata Trusts, has opposed both resolutions. He maintains that a public listing would dilute the group's philanthropic ethos and is likely to get both decisions overturned at its annual general meeting.
"When we say this is a governance crisis, it's a misalignment of interests between the board [of Tata Sons] and the shareholders [Tata Trusts]," Shriram Subramanian, head of independent corporate governance firm InGovern Research, told the BBC.
While he does not expect the brand's image to be affected immediately, he flags concerns over the leadership's ability to navigate the challenges.
Disagreements within the Tata Group have been simmering since the death of former chairman Ratan Tata - Noel Tata's half-brother who designated him successor after his death - in 2024. For many Indians, Ratan Tata's philanthropy and leadership had become inseparable from the brand. His death triggered widespread mourning and experts say it left a leadership void in the group's image with the public.
The Tata group has topped India's most valuable brand list by valuation consultancy Brand Finance since 2018, according to the group's website.
Tata Sons, the business entity, is described by the group as the "fastener keeping the many disparate elements of the whole together".
Tata Trusts, which represents seven philanthropic trusts that own the majority stake in the group, is widely regarded as its moral compass, guiding the businesses on social impact and philanthropy.
For many Indians, both the entities together make up what most companies cannot buy - trust.
Now with these entities in rival corners, that is coming under strain.
"Once upon a time, there was a unified audience which said the Tatas are good people with good governance. Today, the opinion is divided," said Harish Bijoor, business and brand strategy consultant.
While most consumers appear unfazed, the dispute has polarised other stakeholders including business partners, investors and employees. Some view it as corporate power politics, others as a genuine governance debate, but few agree on which side is right, Bijoor said.
"This conflict has brought the Tatas into conversations everywhere, which is not good as they have always liked to be out of it," he says.
The group has traditionally preferred being low profile about philanthropy and conflict resolution.
The Tata group did not respond to BBC's email with detailed questions.
Founded by Jamsetji Tata in 1868, the Tata group expanded under JRD Tata who transformed it into a professionally managed conglomerate. Ratan Tata drove its global ambitions through acquisitions.
Tata group, which has a combined market value of more than $260bn (Â£195.6bn) and employs hundreds of thousands of people in more than 100 countries, is not new to controversies.
The conglomerate has faced protests over industrial projects, scrutiny of its Indian telecom business during a spectrum allocation controversy, a high-profile dispute with Japan's Docomo and, more recently, questions over Air India's performance.
Some of its business decisions have also drawn attention, particularly Tata Steel's troubled Corus acquisition, though other overseas bets such as Tetley and Jaguar Land Rover were successful and helped expand the group's global footprint.
Its biggest controversy was in 2016 when the Tata Sons board abruptly removed Cyrus Mistry as chairman and brought back Ratan Tata as interim head. Mistry, heir to the SP Group, was chosen by a team led by Ratan Tata himself. It led to a long battle which ended in 2021 with the Supreme Court ruling in the Tatas' favour.
Last month, journalist Sucheta Dalal wrote in her column for Moneylife magazine that the Tata group has "weathered serious governance storms" and enjoys "special privileges available to no other business group [referring to a tax exemption granted to Tata Trusts for holding shares in Tata Sons]" because of a reputation built over decades.
Most Tata watchers agree.
In an email interview, Morgen Witzel, a fellow at Exeter Centre of Leadership who wrote a book on the brand in 2010, cited several examples on the group's connection with people.
At Jamshedpur in Jharkhand state, where the group set up India's first integrated steel plant and an industrial city, it provides healthcare and education to people in hundreds of villages. Watchmaker Titan supports employees who want to leave and start their own businesses. Tata Motors at Pune has supported thousands of female entrepreneurs, he points out.
"It is the concatenation of all of these things that builds trust because people see that, by and large, Tata is there to serve their needs rather than just take their money," Witzel said.
But while the group has weathered other storms, this time, the divide is within.

"Water! Water!" the crowd shouted as it stormed a compound with data centres, armed with empty plastic bottles and jerry cans.
There were about 300 of them, all residents on the Indonesian island of Batam, and they were furious that the taps at home had run dry, while the data centres in the new Nongsa Digital Park seemed to have enough water to protect their machines from overheating.
"Not a single drop has come through our taps for the last three months... Our water supply had been reliable until the data centres came," Dewi Susanti, one of the protesters, told the BBC.
People in her village, Bakau Serip, were now depending on tanker trucks that dispensed "dirty, cloudy and smelly" water, she said.
Batam's water utility told the BBC it was working to improve supply, but did not comment on whether the disruption was linked to demand from the data centres.
But BP Batam, the agency overseeing trade and industry, blamed it on a prolonged dry spell and denied allegations from locals that water meant for homes was being channelled to data centres.
This is not the first such protest in Batam, whose shrinking reservoirs find themselves under more pressure as the island tries to transform itself into a digital hub.
Following protests in August and September, authorities told the firms opening data centres in Batam that they must build their own desalination plants instead of relying on reservoirs for freshwater.
But locals say they are increasingly concerned that they must now compete with servers for water.
"Reliable data on data centre water use in Indonesia remains scarce, partly because companies treat it as proprietary information," says Agus Hasan, a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology.
"We should build [data centres] rationally, transparently, and responsibly, and insist on seeing the numbers... [Otherwise] those kept in the dark while their taps run dry will push back, and rightly so," he adds.
A backlash has been building against data centres across the world, from the US to the UK to parts of Asia, as tech companies pour billions into AI infrastructure.
People are worried about how the huge, windowless buildings might change their neighbourhoods, the constant hum of machines, the security lights that could stay on all night, and the pressure this puts on water and energy resources.
While electricity powers the centres, the water keeps the servers from frying - engineers deploy elaborate cooling systems, which consume a lot of water.
Research in the US suggests a typical data centre consumes around 300,000 gallons of water a day, or about as much as 1,000 US households. A larger, 50MW facility could take as much water as 2,200 households per day, and enough electricity to power 22,000 homes, according to Malaysia's central bank.
It's unclear how much water or electricity the data centres in Batam are consuming.
But the island routinely faces water shortages, and the levels are worse this year, possibly because of a historic "super" El NiÃ±o.
Devoid of natural freshwater sources, Batam's 1.3 million people rely on rainwater collected in six artificial reservoirs.
Nongsa reservoir, which supplies water to Bakau Serip, where Dewi lives, would dry up over the next month with no rainfall, simulations by local environmental non-profit group Akar Bhumi Indonesia suggest.
"The water shortage is affecting our livelihoods... Money that should be used to buy rice is now spent on water drums," Dewi says. "My husband has to wait up overnight to get water, and then go straight to work the next morning."
Batam's water utility had earlier said that it would consider measures like cloud seeding should the water shortage continue. When asked about the recent protests, they pointed us to earlier statements.
Authorities in Batam have approved 10 data centres, six of which will be located in Nongsa Digital Park. Two are up and running, while a third is under construction. At least six more are currently under review for approval, BP Batam told the BBC.
Official figures put investment in data centres on the island at more than $6.7bn (Â£5.1bn) as of mid-2026, spurred in part by demand from Singapore, which is just an hour away by ferry.
Singapore paused construction of data centres in 2019, citing land and energy constraints. It lifted the ban in 2022 after introducing new efficiency standards, which prompted investors to look elsewhere.
Singapore has long been promoting the Riau Islands, which includes Batam, and the Malaysian state of Johor as "complementary" regions.
Quick to absorb the spillover, Johor approved data centre projects worth tens of billions. But this soon drew the ire of residents frustrated with noise, dust and water shortages. The state has since tried to regulate how much water and electricity data centres consume.
Across the strait, Batam is just as attractive to investors - from the US, China, Australia, Singapore - because of relatively low operating costs, proximity to Singapore and connections to major subsea cable routes.
Nongsa is home to a 13,000-sq-m data centre by Hong Kong-based private equity firm Gaw Capital and Indonesian developer Sinar Primera. In April, Singapore's DayOne signed a deal with an Indonesian state utility to build one of the country's largest data centres - around 450MW capacity, enough to power 350,000 average households. In June, DayOne, chip maker Nvidia and Australian AI start-up Firmus Technologies announced a 360MW "AI factory".
By 2030, power demand from data centres in Batam is expected to cross 1,100MW, which is enough to power nearly a million homes, according to the official estimates.
The BBC has contacted DayOne, Sinar Primera and Gaw Capital for comment.

Born with autism and nonverbal, he would bite and scratch himself in frustration when someone couldn't understand his needs. Therapy through a state-subsidized program gave him a voice: using a picture system he's learned from his providers in Houston, he's now able to convey his desires. But Texas wants to eliminate the state program, which allows some families to pay nothing for services, because of state budget cuts. In its budget request to the Legislature for the 2028-2029 biennium, the Texas Health and Human Services Commission (HHSC) proposed eliminating funding for the Children's Autism Program (CAP) entirely, stunning advocates, providers and parents. WATCH: New focus on autism fuels debate over splitting the spectrum "If the doors just completely close to access that at all, you just feel like it's all caving in on you, like 'how am I going to get some help?'" said Israel's mother Elizabeth Solis, who has another son who obtains services through a CAP-funded program at the University of Houston-Clear Lake's Center for Autism and Developmental Disabilities; she pays nothing for their services. CAP, which started in 2008, contracts with 16 providers across Texas to provide focused applied behavior analysis (ABA) therapy to autistic children at a reduced cost based on their families' incomes and insurance coverage. Children are eligible for up to 720 hours of ABA therapy, which advocates consider the gold standard for autism treatment, over their lifetime. Over the last two years, the state spent $13.7 million on the program, and this year even expanded the program, extending eligibility to those up to 21 years old and removing a cap on yearly hours. In fiscal year 2026, the state autism program funded treatment for 583 children, but contractors report there are at least 1,000 more children on waitlists statewide. "We were really shocked to see nothing, and it's just blank where the line item should be," said Jacquie Benestante, executive director of the Autism Society of Texas. "We're used to having to fight for funding, but to actually have a program just slashed and canceled is pretty shocking." In July, Gov. Greg Abbott, Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick and House Speaker Dustin Burrows directed state agencies, appellate courts and universities to cut spending by 3% in the next biennium. In response to questions about why HHSC chose to eliminate the program, officials pointed to HHSC's 3% budget reduction summary, which says the agency "focused reductions on the lowest direct service impact to clients and minimizing impacts to federal funding." But, in HHSC's budget request proposing to axe the program, officials explicitly acknowledged the acute need for autism therapy. "The demand for services exceeds the availability of qualified providers especially in rural parts of the state," per the request. "While private and public insurance now provide coverage for treatment services there are often not providers available in all parts of the state." If the Legislature agrees to eliminate the program, children would still receive services through the end of August 2027, HHSC said. Many of Texas' public programs are funded with federally matched dollars. Jeff Miller, a senior policy specialist at Disability Rights Texas, said CAP, as a solely state-funded program, may have seemed like an easy way to cut costs without endangering federal funding. Complexities around Medicaid coverage for ABA therapy may also be partly to blame. In 2022, Medicaid benefits started covering ABA therapy for people 20 years old and younger, making the state's autism program appear redundant. But relying solely on Medicaid could still leave many without access to ABA therapy, said Jolene Pohl, advocacy director for the Coalition of Texans with Disabilities. First, those Medicaid benefits don't apply to families without insurance or who are on self-funded insurance plans, which aren't required to cover ABA therapy. Second, Medicaid, despite the new benefits, is far from a guarantee for accessing ABA therapy: due to low reimbursement rates, it's difficult to find providers willing to take Medicaid clients. CAP is an avenue for families that fall through these gaps to still access ABA therapy, Pohl explained. "It would make more sense to increase the funding and get those kids off the waitlist and give them the services that they need," Pohl said, "because eventually it's going to cost the state more if we don't provide the services to these eligible families in a timely manner." For instance, to help address Lila's meltdowns when tablet time ended, therapists used something fun, like slime, to redirect her so that she associated the transition with a positive outcome. Why it matters: The decision to turn to Vladimir Putin in an attempt to ease the diesel crunch is piling onto Republican headaches ahead of the midterms and fueling fresh friction between the U.S. and Ukraine. What they're saying: The deal "will not achieve just ends, nor will it benefit Americans," the senators warned, urging Trump to withdraw from it and ramp up the economic pressure on Russia as called for in a sanctions bill named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham that he signed into law last month. While record-shattering diesel and gas prices are squeezing key industries and American households, the lawmakers argued that "allowing Russian-origin diesel into global markets will offer limited to no relief to Americans." Analysts have expressed doubt that the levels Trump pitched will meaningfully sway prices, Axios' Ben Geman reports . However, the lawmakers argued that it will "undoubtedly finance" Russia's war "and advance its security cooperation with China, Iran, and North Korea." The fine print: The signers are Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Thom Tillis (R-NC), Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), Susan Collins (R-Maine), Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), Alan Armstrong (R-Okla.), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), Jack Reed (D-RI), Chris Coons (D-Del.), Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) and John Cornyn (R-Texas). The White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Zoom out: That bipartisan coalition has fellow dissenters on the Hill, including members of the president's party who swiftly condemned the deal. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) vowed over the weekend to force a vote to block Russian oil purchases, predicting that "it will pass overwhelmingly." Retiring Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) told Axios' Andrew Solender he "already agreed" to sign the petition. Friction point: As lawmakers sound the alarm, the agreement reignited tensions between Kyiv and Washington. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told A xios' Barak Ravid the deal "looks like a happy birthday present for Putin." But Axios also reported that Trump decided to make the deal after Ukraine continued its highly effective attacks on Russian oil refineries , which contributed to spiking prices, despite the U.S. requesting for them to halt such strikes. What we're watching: The administration's deadline to implement the sanctions law honoring Graham is Oct. 18 — but the legislation allows the president to waive key provisions. Go deeper: Trump's Russia deal leaves GOP candidates with a Putin problem

2880876fc571.text: The amount of AI-related infrastructure exposed to the public internet jumped 63% in nine months, according to new Censys data shared first with Axios. Why it matters: The AI boom isn't just creating new models and chatbots. It's creating a sprawling layer of software that companies will also need to inventory, patch and secure. Threat level: Many of these tools connect AI applications to sensitive corporate data and other services, creating potential entry points for hackers looking to access company systems. "It's a little bit beyond just like the tool itself, but these [tools] talk to some really sensitive systems," Emily Austin, a principal researcher at Censys and co-author of the report, told Axios. The big picture: Censys identified nearly 268,000 internet-facing systems running 44 different AI-related products as of July, up from roughly 164,000 in October 2025. These include the software used to connect AI models to databases, corporate applications and other services. Between the lines: The ease of building and hosting AI applications is making it harder for companies to keep track of what software employees are using and whether it's secure. Censys CEO Zakir Durumeric told Axios that companies were already struggling to keep track of their existing software even before employees started building their own AI applications. These new AI apps can often connect to sensitive company information, such as emails, financial records and internal databases. Zoom in: The most widely exposed product was n8n, a workflow automation platform that can connect AI agents to other applications and services. Censys found nearly 114,000 internet-facing deployments of n8n, including roughly 77,000 running software versions affected by at least one recently disclosed critical vulnerability. Researchers also found more than 54,000 exposed control panels for OpenClaw, an open-source AI agent that users can connect to personal accounts and other services. Yes, but: The findings don't establish whether those deployments are actually vulnerable to exploitation, but they highlight the risks of exposing software that can access sensitive company systems. The bottom line: Companies need to treat AI infrastructure like any other software they deploy, Austin said, including regularly reviewing, updating and securing the systems. Go deeper : Shadow AI creates new headaches for company IT teams

Watch: Inside Katie Zacharia's very brief White House briefing
That was fast!
The briefest White House briefing the BBC's North America editor Sarah Smith has ever seen happened when new US press secretary Katie Zacharia took questions from only three journalists.
She gave reporters some big news on Kimberly Guilfoyle being asked to resign as the US ambassador to Greece.
