Missiles and drones have been intercepted over Riyadh after the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen struck a fuel depot near the Houthi-controlled capital, Sanaa, its spokesperson says.
Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki said several projectiles targeting the Saudi capital and other cities were intercepted after the coalition carried out a strike on the Yemen Petroleum Company's al-Sabaha facility on Tuesday night.
The Houthis warned they would target the airport and Aramco refinery in Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh, and Aramco's headquarters in the eastern city of Dammam.
Al-Maliki later said missiles targeting cities including Dammam had been intercepted, while shrapnel had fallen in a residential area in Dhahran.
An Armaco administration building in Dhahran was also targeted, resulting in "limited fire", Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Energy said in a statement.
No casualties were reported, the statement said.
It came as the Saudi cabinet, chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, said the Iran-backed group would "bear the consequences" of its recent deadly attacks on the kingdom.
Thirteen people were killed when a missile hit King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday, while another person was killed in a similar attack there the following day.
On Tuesday, the coalition said its forces had destroyed three drones north of Riyadh.
The Houthis have said they are targeting airports, oil and gas facilities, and military bases in Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones in response to deadly Saudi strikes on territory that they control in western Yemen, including Sanaa.
The Saudi-led coalition has been providing air support for Yemeni pro-government forces mounting an offensive on Yemen's Red Sea coast and several other front lines.
A correspondent for AFP news agency reported that queues formed at petrol stations in Sanaa on Tuesday afternoon following the coalition's warning of an impending operation against the al-Sabaha oil facility, with many residents worried about shortages.
The Yemen Petroleum Company, which is run by the Houthis, issued a statement that sought to reassure them, saying the facility "does not contain any stock of petroleum products".
The company also said it had "taken all necessary precautionary measures to address any emergency, ensuring the stability of the supply situation and the continued meeting of citizens' needs in a normal manner".
After al-Maliki confirmed the strike, first reported by Houthi media, explosions were heard over Riyadh and other Saudi cities, with al-Maliki reporting four missiles and two drones had been intercepted near the capital.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.
The conflict escalated in September after the Houthis seized part of Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for global shipping. Their advance contributed to a rise in oil prices following six months of war between the US, Israel and Iran.
US President Donald Trump said on Truth Social on Tuesday the Houthis were "behaving very badly... and purposefully trying to drive up Oil Prices".
Speaking to reporters, he did not answer a question on whether he'd made a decision to help the Saudis retaliate against them, but said he "might" ask Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan to intervene.
Last week, pro-government forces said they had regained control of territory overlooking Bab al-Mandab after launching a major counter-offensive with the support of Saudi air strikes.
Hundreds of people have reportedly been killed in Yemen since August. The UN's human rights office says they include at least 54 civilians, half of them children.
More than 216,000 people have also been displaced across the country, and suspected cholera cases have tripled in three weeks, rising from 217 to 647, according to the UN.

1edfeb38365c.text: By — David Fischer, Associated Press David Fischer, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/florida-executes-a-prisoner-who-killed-his-cellmate-in-hopes-of-getting-a-death-sentence-its-the-states-17th-execution-of-the-year Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Florida executed a prisoner who killed his cellmate in hopes of getting a death sentence. It's the state's 17th execution of the year Nation Oct 13, 2026 6:27 PM EDT STARKE, Fla. (AP) — A Florida prisoner who said he killed his cellmate specifically to get on death row was executed Tuesday, nearly 18 years after the attack. James Robertson, 63, declined to offer any last words before receiving a three-drug injection and was pronounced dead about 10 minutes later. It was a stark contrast to the failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee two weeks ago, where she was rushed to the hospital after surviving two lethal doses of pentobarbital. WATCH: Botched execution reignites debate surrounding death penalty Robertson's execution, the first in Florida since Pike, comes at a time of escalating attention on the death penalty in the United States. The Pentagon said last week that it would livestream the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan, drawing criticism from both Republican and Democratic lawmakers. "Florida has a sound lethal injection process and protocol," Jordan Kirkland, a state Department of Corrections spokesperson, said at a news conference before the execution. Although he couldn't speak to Tennessee's lethal injection procedure, he said Florida would make sure its process was "humane and dignified." Florida executes people by injecting them with a sedative, a paralytic, and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections. Robertson wanted to be executed Robertson had pleaded guilty to first-degree murder for strangling Frank Hart while he slept in 2008, and waived all appeals. He told investigators that he did it so he wouldn't have to live out his days in prison. Hart was killed just eight days before he was due to be released, his daughter, Rebecca Hart, told reporters at Florida State Prison. She stressed that her father was not just a piece of Robertson's story. "When someone you love is taken from you in such a violent way, the world keeps moving, even when a part of yours feels like it has stopped," she read. "Other people go on with their lives, but you carry your loss into every tomorrow." Robertson was 17 years old when he went to prison in 1980 for burglary and assault. Years of convictions for escape, battery and weapons while in prison kept adding time to his total sentence. Hart had been sent to prison in 2003 following a sexual battery conviction. A rare reprieve leaves another Florida prisoner on death row Robertson was supposed to be one of two executions carried out by Florida on Tuesday, but Gov. Ron DeSantis withdrew a death warrant last week for William Lee Thompson. The Republican governor did not provide a reason but had temporarily stayed the execution last month pending a psychiatric evaluation. Records show this was the first time DeSantis withdrew a death warrant. Thompson, 74, will remain on death row, and a new death warrant could be signed in the future. His attorneys say he has dementia and failing health, and they want him transferred to a medical facility. DeSantis is the third Florida governor to sign a death warrant for Thompson. Bob Graham and Bob Martinez both scheduled executions for Thompson in the 1980s, but years of appeals and stays allowed him to avoid the electric chair, the state's method of execution at the time. Thompson was convicted of first-degree murder, kidnapping and sexual battery in the 1976 killing of 23-year-old Sally Ivester. Florida has the nation's busiest death chamber DeSantis oversaw 19 executions in 2025, more than any other Florida governor in a single year since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. Robertson was the state's 17th execution of 2026, with two more already scheduled, not counting Thompson. DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has made few public comments about the unprecedented number of executions but explained previously that his goal is to bring justice to victims' families who have waited decades for the death sentences to be carried out. William Reaves, 77, is scheduled to be executed on Oct. 20, followed by Jesse Guardado, 64, on Nov. 5. Reaves was convicted of fatally shooting a deputy after dropping a gun in front of the law enforcement officer in 1986. Guardado was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004. A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. in 2025. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half the 31 total executions in the U.S. so far this year. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Schools closed. The internet partially shut. Roads blocked by shipping containers. And the army arriving in town.
Imran Khan's party stronghold, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, is under a state of emergency, his party's provincial government suspended. It's another dramatic escalation in the standoff between the former prime minister's supporters and Pakistan's state - and one that some fear could lead to more instability, not less.
According to the federal government this step, allowed by the constitution, was needed to provide protection for the province's population from the threat of terror.
"The PTI KPK government was hand in glove with the terrorists," Attah Tarrar, federal information minister, told journalists on Sunday. He did not elaborate or provide evidence, but promised to do so soon.
Two days later there had still been no update from him - but schools had reopened in Peshawar and most parts of the province, and internet services had been restored.
While police would not confirm any detentions, there is clearly a crackdown under way to prevent protests. Most PTI leaders in the province have gone into hiding.
On Tuesday dozens of PTI supporters took to the streets in Bara, Khyber district, hometown of provincial Chief Minister Sohail Afridi. There were reports of tear gas shelling in the area.
To many observers, the timing of Sunday's announcement of emergency rule is not coincidental.
For the last week, thousands of Imran Khan's supporters have marched through Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where the PTI have been in power for 13 years, demanding Khan's release.
"The charitable response would be to say that it sounded disingenuous," says Farzana Sheikh, associate fellow at Chatham House.
"I do not see the link with terrorism," says Arifa Noor, journalist and commentator. "I'm not even sure if it was the long march itself [that led to this]. Perhaps it was the last straw or perhaps it's just a case of saying, we don't want to deal with the government being in the hands of an opposition party."
The protests were led by Chief Minister Afridi, whose whereabouts are still a mystery. His party says he has been arrested; the government says that he is in protective custody.
Before the march had begun, there had been a crackdown. Three of Khan's sisters were arrested in September, accused among other things of mobilising supporters, and have been detained ever since.
Khan has barely been seen by his family or lawyers in the last year; two of his sisters saw him in August, one in prison, another as he was checked over at a hospital visit after concerns were raised by the Supreme Court about his health, before he was returned behind bars again where he has been held for more than three years.
The PTI leader, who is widely believed to have lost power because of a rift with Pakistan's powerful military, has been imprisoned since August 2023. He is convicted in several corruption cases which he says are politically motivated.
With the party already weakened, why this reaction from the authorities?
"The PTI rank and file has been becoming increasingly restless in recent months amid growing concerns about Imran Khan's health," says Michael Kugelman, senior South Asia fellow at the Atlantic Council.
"There is a sense that perhaps now is the time to send a very strong message to the party and make it more difficult for them to be able to put pressure on the government."
The government has previously argued that Khan was going against jail rules by using his meetings to discuss politics.
Tarar has said of the state of emergency: "There was no political agenda. They could have gone on with their march," and pointed to the talks the two sides had in the run-up to the decision as an indicator that they did try discussion.
But others see this as just another attempt to restrict Khan and his party.
"The government has less and less space for disagreements or dissent and they do not want to negotiate their way out of any kind of conflict," Noor says.
Zahid Hussain, Islamabad-based author and defence analyst, is clear about who is behind the decision.
"The balance of power is completely shifted to the military establishment," he says.
Sheikh thinks that Pakistan's military is feeling confident because it believes it has a good relationship with the White House, its international credentials burnished by their role in the US-Iran peace talks.
"The mode is very much, this is the moment, let's seize it," she says. "There is a sense that, we have all the cards in our hands. We can ride this out internationally."
But Pakistan has plenty to contend with. Militancy is rising. The country was ranked number one in the Global Terrorism Index 2026 as the country which had been affected most.
The country is at loggerheads with two neighbours; it has repeatedly hit Afghanistan with air strikes accusing the Afghan Taliban government of harbouring militant groups, a claim it denies. It would take little to reignite its long-running simmering conflict with India.
Meanwhile, it has promised to help Saudi Arabia defend itself against attacks as the conflict against the Houthis has become increasingly dangerous.
Short of solving one problem, some have warned this state of emergency could lead to more challenges. It risks increasing political instability, with Islamabad taking responsibility for a province without a buffer - the provincial government - they can blame.
"I would argue that this could actually backfire," Kugelman says. "You're playing with fire because if this move ends up adding to the anger and the discontent among so many there, then you have a very big problem on your hands."
"It is reckless, given the challenges, multiple challenges the country is facing," Hussain says. He fears that more of these powers could be used across Pakistan.
Attempts to combat militancy with more active army operations could come with its own perils too, Sheikh argues.

"The biggest difficulty really was the loneliness. Sometimes, if I wanted to talk to someone I'd talk to the TV."
Yang, 91, lives on the outskirts of China's bustling capital Beijing. Following the death of her husband, she was so lonely that she says she even considered the possibility of voluntary euthanasia.
"I asked my son about it but he told me it was banned. I told him that if it ever becomes legal I want to do it - I didn't want to live any longer."
Suffering glaucoma, with failing eyesight, she was unable to even do basic things like adjust the controls on her air conditioner.
Cases such as Yang's have become increasingly common in Chinese cities which Associate Professor Teresa Kuan, from the Chinese University of Hong Kong, says is "exacerbated by the structure of society and the modes by which people interact".
There are many causes of isolation in China. Most of it happens when rural migrants pursue economic opportunities, leaving behind close-knit support networks for urban centres where loneliness and uncertainty can be difficult to overcome, or when graduates uproot themselves chasing employment on the other side of the country.
But now a growing "loneliness industry" has emerged to try to fill these gaps in people's lives.
Yang says her life has been transformed by one of these services - Wang Yingwei and his electric scooter delivery team - who started coming over twice a day with hot meals but whose help extends far beyond that.
"We see ourselves as community children," Yingwei told the BBC. "It means putting yourself in the shoes of older people and carefully considering their needs.
"For example, they may be drinking tap water which can be cloudy and contain a lot of lime. I can fix this problem with a filtered water tank. Such a small thing can make them much happier. Maybe they can't shower because their equipment is broken. I'll buy a part, replace it and their shower is fine."
"The elderly treat us like their children, and we treat them like our own parents," he added.
Yingwei's services cost less than half the price of employing a caregiver.
The former mobile phone salesman says he started his company to help seniors remain at home without having to move into retirement facilities. He was inspired to do this after his own father-in-law, who had developed Alzheimer's, had to go into a nursing home. Yingwei said he felt that the conditions there were so sub-standard he wanted to make sure others could stay out of institutions like this for as long as possible.
His small business currently employs four people but he says there is a possibility he will expand as demand grows.
There is still a shortage of solid data on the size of this sector â which operators say has exploded in recent years â but securities company Sinolink valued it at around $7.4 billion in 2025. And this is only expected to grow given the trajectory of modern lifestyles.
Zheng Ruizhi, another client of Yingwei's who lives in Beijing's northern outskirts, welcomed him at the door with a big smile.
"After retiring, I don't have much opportunity to hang out with others," the 75-year-old, whose son lives two hours away from her, told the BBC.
She was recovering from a recent injury which she said was making everyday tasks more difficult.
But the arrival of Yingwei â who she calls her "dear boy" â lightened her mood.
"I call you 'dear boy' because I am so fond of you. I genuinely like you from the bottom of my heart. I also admire and trust you. When you help me out, I don't have a single worry or fear," she told him.
Yet the services offered by those in this sector are not limited to home visits.
Twenty-three-year-old Liu Yanyan, for instance, works as a "medical escort". She acts as a friendly face taking clients to see the doctor, or picking up their test results or medication from city hospitals, which can be intimidatingly large and bureaucratic.
"Some of my customers are people in their 20s who came to Beijing to build a career. They might not have friends here or feel awkward asking colleagues to accompany them because of the concept of social reciprocity in Chinese culture," she said. "If I accompanied you to a doctor's appointment for free, you might feel obligated to buy me a meal or a movie ticket afterwards."
She said that, because of this, there are many people in modern Chinese society who tend to keep to themselves.
"So, they hire someone like me to accompany them to the hospital. If they had to go alone, they could feel scared or anxious."
At the core of many businesses catering to loneliness in China is a simple offering: human connection.
Teresa Kuan said that some people prefer the option of pouring their hearts out to a complete stranger for a fee.
"If there is a companion you have paid for, the relationship is not exactly equal. It is a service relationship, so you don't have to deal with the unpredictability of a standard relationship. The thing about friendship is that it can be unpredictable. You don't know when someone might disappoint you. But, in a service relationship, you have a better idea of what to expect."
Wang Zhoutao runs a hiking business to help people who want to climb China's famous mountain Huangshan in Anhui Province.
"We provide emotional support, like cheering them up, taking their photo or telling jokes. It's really a service based on companionship," he said.
The former soldier added that he normally hikes up the mountain with clients 10 to 15 days a month. When fully booked, this could be as many as 30 times a month.
He gave an example of a young woman he once accompanied who felt ostracised at work. "She felt useless and wanted to prove something to herself," he said.
"We started climbing but it was a tough trek as the weather was really hot and we were sweating a lot. There were moments she wanted to give up but I told her, 'If you quit now and can't get over this mountain how will you handle anything else in life?'. I kept encouraging her."

As Indonesia battles its worst wildfire season in a decade, a toxic smog is choking millions of residents in the region.
The air on the islands of Kalimantan and Sumatra have turned an ominous amber, with air quality recorded at hazardous levels.
The smog - also known as the haze - has also drifted beyond Indonesia's borders to neighbouring countries, raising public health concerns. It has obscured Singapore's skyline and forced some schools to close in Malaysia.
Now, anger is mounting at the companies accused of burning farmland - as well as the authorities who have struggled to stop them.
The annual dry season wildfires have been especially intense this year because of an unusually strong El NiÃ±o - a natural climate phenomenon which changes weather patterns around the world.
According to independent forest monitoring platform Nusantara Atlas, 1,043,377 wildfire hotspots have been recorded in Indonesia, burning a total of 900,000 hectares of land.
Slash and burn
Many of these fires in Indonesia's forests and peatlands are caused by the razing of vegetation to clear land - a practice known as "slash and burn".
This is an agricultural method that has traditionally been employed by farmers in Indonesia to create nutrient-rich soil for new crops.
But today, many of these fires are associated with commercial farming and are taking place on a much larger scale - and are harder to control. Activists and government investigations have repeatedly accused some companies of using fire as a cheap way to clear large swathes of land.
While slash-and-burn farming is illegal in Indonesia, enforcement of a ban has long proven tricky.
But persistent haze this year has prompted Indonesian authorities to step up efforts to punish offenders.
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has called for tougher sanctions against slash-and-burn farming, describing the practice as "ecological terrorism".
Last month, Indonesian authorities announced they had suspended the operating licences of 26 companies linked to the wildfires and launched investigations into others. Cases involving criminal elements would be taken to court, officials vowed.
But it's not just Indonesian companies that have been embroiled in controversy amid the haze problem.
A Greenpeace report published this month identified businesses based in Singapore and Malaysia which are linked to plots of land in Indonesia where wildfires are burning.
This includes First Resources, a Singapore-based palm oil company. Between August and September more than 30 haze source points were recorded on land managed by its two Indonesian subsidiaries, according to Greenpeace.
First Resources told the BBC in a statement that it maintained a "strict zero burning policy across all planting activities and implement robust fire prevention, monitoring and firefighting measures throughout our operations".
Greenpeace also named Malaysian plantation group Kuala Lumpur Kepong, whose subsidiary PT Menteng Jaya Sawit Perdana managed land in Indonesia where 19 haze source points were recorded.
Kuala Lumpur Kepong said in a statement that a "majority" of the fires originated from beyond its concession area and had all been extinguished.
"We do not condone or permit the use of open burning for land preparation or any other purpose across our operations," it said.
'When there is no smoke, we send oxygen'
It remains to be seen how effective governments can be in sanctioning offending companies.
In 2014, Singapore passed the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act which allows the government to take action against local and foreign firms found to be contributing to the haze.
The following year when Singapore saw a bad bout of haze, authorities issued summonses to several Indonesian companies thought to have cleared land by burning, in a bid to prosecute them under the new law.
But that drew sharp ire from Jakarta, which said the move harmed bilateral ties. And with Indonesia refusing to cooperate, Singapore authorities said they could not obtain information about the suspected companies.
Also in 2015, Indonesia's then-Vice-President Jusuf Kalla angered Singaporeans when he said that "for 11 months, they enjoyed nice air from Indonesia and they never thanked us... they have suffered because of the haze for one month and they get upset".
Similar tensions surfaced again last weekend when Syahganda Nainggolan, who leads Indonesia's government communications agency, said the raging wildfires were beyond human control and added that the oxygen in neighbouring Singapore and Malaysia "also comes from our forests".
"When there is no smoke, we send oxygen," he added, in a video that has been widely circulated on social media, triggering criticism and ridicule from Malaysians and Singaporeans.
But Indonesia has in the past also apologised to its neighbours for causing the haze.
This year, Indonesian officials have thanked Singapore and Malaysia for offering to help tackle the wildfires - though it has not officially requested international support.
In Indonesia, there have been efforts by civil society to force the government to take action.
In Pontianak in the West Kalimantan province, several groups have filed a class action lawsuit against the Indonesian government and Prabowo, accusing them of "gross negligence" over recurrent toxic haze.
They want the government to declare the haze a national disaster, which would allow for recovery measures such as the coverage of healthcare costs.
A similar case was filed last year in South Sumatra, but it was dismissed.
Meanwhile, on the ground in Kalimantan and Sumatra, air pollution levels have remained at dangerous levels for weeks.
There are many who have no choice but to brave the toxic smog every day.
"I'm short of breath and have a headache breathing air now. But I still have to work," Imrayedi, a 63-year-old motorcycle taxi driver in Pekanbaru city, on Sumatra island, told BBC Indonesian last week.

Susie Walker-Munro is one of a handful of tea growers in Scotland.
She says the acidic soil creates ideal conditions for the perfect artisan brew.
Costing about Â£40 per packet for her most expensive product, it's not going to replace the supermarket brands any time soon.
Droughts, intensive downpours and diseases have created challenges for tea growers across the world as they deal with the impact of a warming planet.
But some experts believe Scotland's relatively settled climate could give the tea industry here a helping hand.
As the picking season draws to a close, Susie plucks the last few leaves before proudly pouring me a small glass of her Kinnettles Gold, which is grown in a walled garden on the family farm near Forfar.
She believes Scotland's latitude â sitting 57 degrees north - will always be a bar to having a year-round crop like those countries close to the equator.
But she says wetter weather could help boost production.
"Our yields are never, never going to be high," she says.
"Maybe with climate change they might come up a bit, it depends if we get enough rain. Scotland could be absolutely ideal."
Susie isn't convinced tea will ever be a major crop for Scotland.
But others say it could be one of a numbers of options in the future, as farmers are forced to diversify and adapt to a changing climate.
Rethinking the way we farm the land might be one way to extend the range of crops produced.
Countries like the Netherlands are already embracing glass houses, which could become more commonplace in Scotland. Susie says they would be a good way of growing more tea.
They would also allow Scotland to produce more Mediterranean vegetables like tomatoes, cucumbers, aubergines, and even melons, according to Pete Ritchie from campaign organisation Nourish Scotland.
He says an abundance of renewable energy from wind farms later in the century will make heating them relatively cheap and will cut down on air miles.
"We're going to be able to produce those plants with a lower carbon footprint and provide secure all-round jobs for people on brownfield sites in the cities and also on the islands and remote parts of Scotland," he says.
The James Hutton Institute already has a large number of glass houses â but it is going even further by artificially creating the sort of conditions that may exist in 75 years.
Climate modelling shows that Scotland can expect hotter, dryer summers and milder, wetter winters by the end of this century.
The institute's new advanced plant growth centre is effectively a climate simulator.
It's able to control plants' light, water and nutrient intake to test how they cope with stresses - and then select species which are likely to fare best against all that climate change can throw at them.
For the past three months they have been experimenting with fava beans, which are photographed daily so scientists can monitor their progress.
Dr Robert Hancock says they need to switch from breeding crops for specific environments, such as hot or dry climates, towards ones which are more generally resilient.
"We need to start breeding those crops now and start understanding what Scottish farming's going to look like," he says.
"Farmers need time to plan, we need to get those crops out to the farmers and registered.
"Ultimately it's about what those guys do in the fields that matters, not what we do inside a climate simulator."
The farmers of the 22nd Century are probably only a generation away from those starting out in the industry today.
That means the current crop of young farmers will have to give the closest consideration to the businesses they hand on to their own children.
And that means more precision farming, more artificial intelligence, and automation.
Modern tractors and combine harvesters are so high in technology such as GPS steering that it's no longer such a leap to consider autonomous harvesting.
But the chair of the Scottish Association of Young Farmers, David Murdoch, believes traditional skills will always be important.
"There's no point in doing it if you don't know your cattle, but embracing the technology is what keeps us competitive.
"Working with larger herd numbers and larger machinery to keep us producing more with less people - that's the way the world's going," says David, who farms dairy with his father at Beith in North Ayrshire.
But it's not just food production that will drive future changes in farming.
Protecting and enhancing nature, offsetting carbon emissions, and renewable energy production are already shaping the farms of tomorrow.
Health innovations may also play a growing role, with obesity drugs already showing a demand for proteins and nutrient-dense foods.
Soya, flax and legumes could become a more common sight as conditions for growing them become more favourable and that desire to grow them locally continues.
Prof Wayne Powell - the principal of Scotland's rural college, the SRUC - predicts that Scotland will become "the bread basket of Europe".
That title is currently used to describe Ukraine, because of its abundance of fertile agricultural land and exports of crops including wheat, maize and barley.
"Climate change is redrawing the farming map of Europe and Scotland could become one of Europe's most important climate resilient food regions," he says.
"The possibility of access to cheap renewable energy could also transform the economics of Scottish farming from irrigation, refrigeration, food processing, so that we can capture more value from our land and food."
Scotland's rural communities have seen major changes over the past 75 years which have resulted in far fewer people working the land.
Pressure to keep food affordable for consumers while farms remain profitable will be a key driver of innovation.
The changing climate and the continued destruction of our nature prevent that being a simple equation to calculate.

The stark assessment years ago from Nancy Pelosi echoed anew after Trump's surprise announcement last week that he struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import tons of Russian diesel to the U.S. as a way to ease sky-high prices at the pumps for Americans ahead of the midterm elections. Trump's diesel deal with Putin has been criticized by both Republicans and Democrats as fueling Russia's war against Ukraine, violating existing U.S. laws and drawing the U.S. closer to Russia. It joins a growing list of instances in which the Republican president has sided with Putin, often at the expense of Ukraine — and America's own standing. "The harm to the Ukrainians is real," said William Taylor, a former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine, now a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, in an interview Monday. "And the cost to us, the United States, is high." It's not at all clear the Trump-Putin deal will deliver the supply boost the president is seeking to bring down prices. Energy experts have said the flow of Russian diesel is unlikely to lower prices in the U.S., which have escalated largely due to disruptions from the U.S. war against Iran. But the agreement underlines a message at home and abroad that Trump is an unreliable ally as Ukraine battles Russia. A bipartisan group of six senators urged Trump over the weekend to reverse course, saying the U.S. "should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline." Trump, however, held fast to his deal with Putin and lashed out, blaming Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for America's high diesel costs and asserting he should step aside — something Ukraine's leader has no intention of doing. "Anything that could help our farmers, our ranchers, I like," Trump said Monday outside the White House. Asked about Republican criticism of the Russia deal, Trump said they "can't really be serious." But a dozen senators weighed in with a letter to Trump on Tuesday. The six Republican and six Democratic senators said allowing Russian diesel into global markets would have a negligible impact on fuel prices while the revenue Russia gets will "undoubtedly finance its desired war of attrition" and advance its security cooperation with China, Iran and North Korea. WATCH: How the diesel price spike is rippling through nearly every part of the economy "It will also endanger servicemembers operating overseas in support of Operation Epic Fury," they wrote. Trump also insisted that an energy ceasefire is in place for Ukraine and Russia, despite Zelenskyy saying that Moscow continued to strike his country's energy sites. An AP-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll published Oct. 1 found that Americans disapprove of Trump's handling of the Iran war and blame him for higher prices. Congress voted to halt Russian imports, but Trump has other plans Congress swiftly approved legislation at the outset of the Russian invasion of Ukraine in spring of 2022 to ban the import of Russian energy products, which are widely viewed as providing the financial fuel for Putin's military assault on Ukraine. The bill passed the House on an overwhelming 414-17 vote and the Senate without a single senator opposed. The law says the president can seek to lift the prohibition if an agreement has been reached to withdraw Russian troops from Ukraine and cease military activity. Such a proposal would need to be reviewed by Congress and to have been "accepted by the free and independent government of Ukraine." "Trump is directly violating that law," said Rep. Lloyd Doggett, D-Texas, the bill's chief sponsor, in a statement Monday. He said Trump "illegally rewards his pal Putin while once again blaming Zelenskyy for not capitulating to Putin." More recently, Congress last month approved a sweeping Russian sanctions bill, named after the late GOP Sen. Lindsey Graham, that would slap tariffs on countries that continue importing Russian oil. Trump signed the bill into law. The bulk of the law's provisions go into effect Oct. 18, the end of the administration's 30-day review period. But such action now appears to be in question since Trump's diesel deal with Putin will allow the flow of Russian energy. In a letter to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Senate leaders from both parties last week said the most urgent priority for the U.S. must be to tackle the "shadow fleet" of tankers that Moscow is using to transport oil and bypass America's sanctions. But that was before Trump announced his deal with Putin, which he said would unleash hundreds of tons of diesel. A Saudi national has been charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's offices in California, federal prosecutors announced.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked at the AI firm as an engineer, was charged federally with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.
OpenAI said it had discovered a "sophisticated recording device" hidden in their San Francisco office and alerted the FBI. The company said it used its AI models to track that it had been planted by an employee.
Prosecutors say the device, wrapped in toilet paper, was found inserted in a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room.
OpenAI, the maker of the popular chatbot ChatGPT, said that it has no indication that source code, model weights or customer data were inappropriately accessed or taken in the incident. It said the employee has been fired.
According to the complaint, Alfozan "allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement.
Patel said that the alleged goal was to capture information about the company's AI product.
Alfozan has been working as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, prosecutors say.
On 30 September, OpenAI employees discovered the device - two days after prosecutors say it had been installed. The device was encrypted, prosecutors said.
OpenAI said they were able to use their AI models "to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier".
According to the FBI, the suspect used a "productivity tool" and a "chatbot" to research sensitive locations at OpenAI and how to secretly place audio equipment.
Chatbot prompts that he is alleged to have searched include "building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device", prosecutors allege.
He is also accused of using the chatbot to ask about "'build[ing] a continuous audio recorder,' 'customiz[ing] Wi-Fi . . . connectivity,' 'improv[ing] audio and live listening,' and 'encrypt[ing] the SD card'".
On 5 October, prosecutors say he allegedly returned to inspect the device in the office room. Prosecutors used CCTV camera footage to link him to the scene.
That same day, Alfozan left a bag unattended in a different part of the building. A security team for OpenAI opened it to find his wallet and ID, as well as another recording device that was similar to the one found in the office conference room, prosecutors said.
Alfozan appeared in court on Tuesday. It's unclear whether he has legal representation.
If found guilty, he faces up to five years in prison and a fine of $250,000 (Â£187,000).

35a5e553cd13.text: By — Alanna Durkin Richer, Associated Press Alanna Durkin Richer, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/cvs-agrees-to-pay-315-million-to-settle-justice-department-case-over-opioid-prescriptions Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter CVS agrees to pay $315 million to settle Justice Department case over opioid prescriptions Nation Oct 13, 2026 5:02 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — CVS Pharmacy Inc. and various subsidiaries have agreed to pay $315 million to resolve a Justice Department case alleging it unlawfully dispensed medically unnecessary prescriptions of highly addictive opioids, officials said Tuesday. The settlement resolves a lawsuit brought in 2024 that accused the healthcare giant of providing massive amounts of opioids and other controlled substances "to fuel its own profits at the expense of public health and safety." WATCH: Leading researcher explains how viewing addiction as a brain disorder improves treatments It's the latest effort by the federal government to hold accountable companies that officials have alleged helped fuel the U.S. addiction and overdose crisis. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "Today's settlement is a significant milestone in the Justice Department's efforts to combat the opioid epidemic by cracking down on pharmacies who unlawfully fulfill prescriptions for controlled substances," Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward said in an emailed statement. WATCH: Opioid crisis renews focus on expanding access to methadone treatment CVS said in a statement that its pharmacists were trained "in the safe and appropriate use of all medications" and that it had implemented "best-in-class" programs to help them "make the best decisions on behalf of patients." The company said it strongly disagreed with the claims made in the lawsuit and that the settlement admits no wrongdoing. The company said in 2024 that pharmacists were being held to "vague, undefined, and ever-changing standards of practice" when it comes to filling prescription opioids. READ MORE: CVS, Walgreens announce opioid settlements totaling $10 billion The lawsuit filed under President Joe Biden's administration accused CVS of violating the Controlled Substances Act by filling illegitimate prescriptions for high doses of potent opioids that "fed dependence and addiction." The Justice Department alleged it dispensed large quantities of opioids based on prescriptions from known "pill mills," or providers that hand out prescriptions for drugs without a legitimate medical purpose. It alleged that poor staffing levels coupled with performance metrics and incentive compensation policies implemented by the company led to pharmacists racing to fill prescriptions without confirming they were legitimate. The prescriptions were often billed to and reimbursed by Medicaid and other federal healthcare programs, the lawsuit says. Under the settlement, CVS must also "implement additional safeguards to ensure that prescriptions for opioids and other controlled substances are dispensed only when medically appropriate," Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate, who leads the Justice Department's Civil Division, said in a statement. Over the last decade, drugmakers, wholesalers, pharmacies and other companies have agreed to settlements with governments in the U.S. totaling over $50 billion. Most of the money is intended to go to address the crisis, which has been linked to more than 100,000 deaths in the U.S. some years, though the numbers have fallen sharply recently. Most of the settlements -- and dollars -- have been with state and local governments, but the U.S. has reached several deals, including in the last two years with the pharmacies Walgreens and Walmart. 70c1d9fad782.text: U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro said her office is probing Rep. Ilhan Omar's (D-Minn.) financial disclosures, the day after federal agents searched the congresswoman's Washington, D.C. home. The big picture: It's another example of the administration's escalating fight with the progressive lawmaker, who has clashed with the White House over its immigration crackdown — and whom President Trump has labeled as "crooked." Driving the news: Asked about a prior ethics probe into financial filings from the Office of Congressional Conduct, which her office said cleared Omar, Pirro said Tuesday on Fox News' "America Reports" that "is subject of an investigation as well." "It doesn't matter what the House does. It doesn't matter, you know, what this agency or that does. We're looking at the facts. Based upon the facts, we'll follow them wherever they take us," she said, and confirmed her office is handling the probe. Catch up quick: Federal agents searched Omar's home before dawn Monday as part of a separate immigration probe, Axios' Ben Berkowitz reported. Omar described the search in an X post as "an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement." Trump has repeatedly lashed out against Somali immigrants, including Omar — who he described in a post last year as "always wrapped in her swaddling hijab" and "the worst 'Congressman/woman'" in our Country." Zoom out: Omar's office pointed Axios to The Wall Street Journal's reporting last month that the Office of Congressional Conduct recommended that the House Ethics Committee dismiss allegations that she possibly violated House rules or law by reporting false or incomplete information in her financial disclosures. A disclosure filed last year listed Omar and her husband's assets as ranging from $6 million to $30 million. She later amended the form to reflect a much lower range, the Journal first reported, citing what her team said were accounting errors. Pirro's office did not respond to Axios's request for comment. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

New York City Council is expected to outlaw horse-drawn carriages starting in June 2028, a ban that also has the support of the mayor.
The legislation follows the death of a teenager who fell off a horse-drawn carriage in Central Park this year, and ongoing concerns about inhumane treatment of the horses.
The teenager's death led to Speaker of New York City Council Julie Menin's support of the bill, which she said will come before the council for a vote on 22 October.
"Horse-drawn carriages have long been part of New York City's history, but in an increasingly busy Central Park, this tradition has become a growing public safety liability," Menin said in a statement to the BBC.
"Next week, the Council will take decisive action by voting on [this bill] to protect New Yorkers, visitors, and the horses themselves."
The bill - called Romanch's law for the teenager who died - has support from a council majority, a spokesperson for the speaker said.
A Mamdani official said the mayor, who also supports banning the industry, is constructing a plan to transition those in the horse-drawn carriage business.
"We have been working closely with the City Council, union partners, carriage drivers, animal welfare advocates, and community leaders to deliver a just transition that protects workers while ending horse-drawn carriages in Central Park once and for all," a spokesperson said.
The latest version of the legislation includes an "industry transition framework" including potential job placement, training, career counseling, and financial compensation for those involved in the business. The bill does not allow the horses to be sold for slaughter or for the same purpose.
It is not the first time officials have pushed to end the industry, which is a longtime New York tourist attraction. Former New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio announced soon after his inauguration in 2014 that he wanted to ban the carriages in Central Park, citing poor treatment of the horses, and proposed a fleet of vintage electric cars to replace them.
In the end, he implemented new rules restricting where carriages can pick up tourists.
In June, Romanch Mahajan, who was visiting New York from India, was riding in a carriage when the horse pulling it bolted, causing the 18-year-old to fall and die.
His father, Deepak, later told the city council he could not "properly describe to you the real, true fear inside that carriage".
Also this year, a carriage horse named Dennis died in Central Park from eating a toxic plant.
Some workers' groups, including the Transport Workers Union - which says it represents 300 horse-carriage drivers and owners - have pushed back against legislation banning the industry. The Transport Workers Union argues the horses are treated well and that the industry employs hundreds of people.
Last year, the Central Park Conservancy, the nonprofit group that manages the park, said it was supporting legislation to ban the practice.
"We do not take this position lightly," the conservancy's president, wrote in a letter, "but with visitation to the park growing to record levels, we feel strongly that banning horse carriages has become a matter of public health and safety for park visitors".

8b8b2c785bf6.text: By — Will Weissert, Associated Press Will Weissert, Associated Press By — Becky Bohrer, Associated Press Becky Bohrer, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-heads-to-alaska-in-a-sign-of-how-close-its-senate-race-may-be Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump heads to Alaska in a sign of how close its Senate race may be Politics Oct 13, 2026 4:42 PM EDT WASILLA, Alaska (AP) — It's a long way from Washington, has a small population and hasn't backed a Democrat for Senate in nearly 20 years. Yet President Donald Trump on Tuesday will devote a big chunk of his dwindling time ahead of crucial midterm elections to head all the way to Alaska — attempting to bolster a Republican incumbent senator in another sign of GOP fears about retaining control of Congress after Election Day on Nov. 3. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Trump is headlining a rally for Sen. Dan Sullivan in Wasilla, about 45 miles (72 kilometers) north of Anchorage — famous for being the hometown of former Republican vice presidential nominee Sarah Palin and the headquarters of the Iditarod sled dog race across the state. Trump's stop is part of a western swing also taking him to rallies in Arizona and Montana on Wednesday. "I'm right now going to Alaska to try and help Dan Sullivan. That's a long way away," Trump told reporters as he left the White House for the trip on Tuesday. "I would only do it if I thought he was good. And he's very good. And so, I'm going to Alaska to help Dan Sullivan, and then I'm stopping in numerous places." Watch the clip in the player above. Democrats last won a Senate seat in Alaska in 2008, and the state hasn't elected a governor from that party since 1998. The only time Alaska didn't vote Republican for president was during Lyndon B. Johnson's landslide 1964 reelection. Yet high gasoline prices from the Iran war and persistently elevated inflation have damaged Trump's approval ratings enough to leave Democrats dreaming of Alaska upsets. Trump and Vance have been trying to boost Sullivan repeatedly Seeking his third Senate term, Sullivan faces Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman running to put "Alaska First," emphasizing cost-of-living issues. Alaska pollster Ivan Moore said he's seen a decline in Trump's support statewide that mirrors the president's falling approval ratings nationally — meaning the Senate race may be decided by Trump 2024 voters who are now unsure they still back him. "The visit is certainly appropriate. Whether the visit will be effective or not is another matter," said Moore, who said when he first heard that Trump would visit Alaska, he didn't believe it would actually happen. READ MORE: How the phrase 'Lower 48' became a fixture in Alaska's high-stakes Senate race The Trump administration has prioritized the opening of more of Alaska to oil and gas drilling. Vice President JD Vance already campaigned in Fairbanks for Sullivan. The senator also recently joined Trump in the Oval Office where the president announced a $54 billion investment by South Korea's government into an Alaska natural gas project. That's despite South Korea saying the deal, and its total value, haven't been finalized. Still, Trump trekking four time zones west to get to Sullivan's home turf — an unusually long trip so close to the midterms — is his strongest show of support. The Scoop
Lenders are feeling maxed out on data-center debt.
When Volta, an AI infrastructure company, went out recently to raise $5 billion for a data center in Norway, the deal didnât seem that different from the more than $450 billion in AI-related debt deals done so far this year.
But as Voltaâs bankers at JPMorgan and Goldman Sachs went out to sell it, some investors pushed back, saying theyâre full up on data-center debt and demanding more security and a higher interest rate. The deal is expected to price later this week with a rate of at least 11%, unusually high for a data-center project, anchored by a $1.5 billion order from Apollo, people familiar with the matter said.
Commitments for the deal are due this week and lenders are still in discussion about allocations, so details about the financing could change.
Voltaâs deal is a pulse check on the AI-financing world. Deals are still getting done, but less smoothly than they were earlier this year, with higher rates and more heavily negotiated terms, investors and bankers say.
Volta was founded in February and the Norway data center is its first significant project. Some investors balked at its lack of a track record, while others were unnerved by Voltaâs reliance on Anthropic to buy much of the data centerâs compute. Anthropic doesnât share much financial information with lenders and the exact level of its obligations struck some investors as unsettled.
The deal includes an unusual provision to overcome that skittishness: The interest rate charged to Volta will decrease if Anthropic can get an investment-grade credit rating, some of the people said. The Financial Times reported last month that Anthropicâs and OpenAIâs IPO advisers were lobbying credit-rating agencies for blue-chip status, which would be almost unheard-of for companies as unprofitable as both AI labs are.
JPMorgan and Goldman Sachs have also underwritten a $1.3 billion term loan to Volta.
JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs and Apollo declined to comment. Volta didnât respond to a request for comment. Anthropic didnât respond to requests for comment.
Know More
September has been the second-lowest month this year for issuance for AI financings, as regulatory and political challenges weigh on data center construction, according to a report from Morgan Stanley. The fourth quarter is expected to slow down further, the analysts said.

88c7916b35c7.text: By — Joseph Wilson, Associated Press Joseph Wilson, Associated Press By — Manu Fernández, Associated Press Manu Fernández, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/in-first-visit-to-ceuta-spains-king-asks-for-good-faith-from-morocco-after-migration-crisis Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter In first visit to Ceuta, Spain's king asks for 'good faith' from Morocco after migration crisis World Oct 13, 2026 4:29 PM EDT CEUTA, Spain (AP) — King Felipe VI delivered a staunch message of support for Ceuta as being an integral part of Spain on Tuesday when the monarch visited the North African territory amid a protracted migration crisis that has strained relations with Morocco. His visit with Queen Letizia came with the city of 84,000 residents still grappling with the mass crossing of nearly as many migrants from Morocco in July. The crossing left at least 140 migrants dead and shook the city perched on the Mediterranean coast. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. While Spain's government has defended Rabat's role in helping the return of the majority of the 80,000 who entered Ceuta, many in Spain, including police and some lawmakers, doubt that Rabat could not have known about the mass movement of people. Some, including Ceuta's mayor, called it an "invasion." "Ceuta is Spain. Therefore its frontier ... is a European border, and any threat to it is a threat to the European Union," Felipe said in a speech that was wildly applauded at a gathering of figures from Ceuta's civil society. In his only mention of Morocco, Felipe said that Spain and the EU want healthy relations with Rabat, but that they must be based on "good faith." "That relationship," he said, "must be based on trust, mutual respect and the goal of promoting stability, peace and regional security. Making that possible demands good faith from both sides." Large crowds gathered to greet the royals and shake their hands at Ceuta's central Plaza de Africa when they arrived. Some broke into the familiar sports chant, "I am Spanish, Spanish, Spanish." Church bells rang as people waved Spanish flags. Felipe received the key to the city from Ceuta's top elected official, Juan Jesús Vivas, who called for the expulsion of all migrants who remained after the mass crossing. "Thank you for coming to boost our morale, to resist and to see the light at the end of the tunnel," Vivas told the royals. The royal couple will stay overnight in Ceuta before traveling on Wednesday to Melilla, Spain's other North African exclave. The trip marks the first visit by a Spanish monarch to the two cities since Felipe's father, Juan Carlos I, toured them in 2007. Morocco does not recognize Spanish sovereignty over the two small territories, which have been under Spanish control for centuries. Diplomatic observers in Spain will be watching closely for Rabat's response to Felipe's visit. Morocco's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment about the royal visit to the Spanish exclaves. Royals pay respect to dead migrants at cemetery Felipe and Letizia were accompanied by religious authorities from Ceuta's four main religions — Roman Catholic, Islam, Judaism and Hinduism — at the Sidi Embarek cemetery, where they paid their respects to dozens of unidentified migrants who died in the crossing. The royals also visited a school. The city has a history of religious coexistence, but the border crisis has strained relations between its Christian and Muslim communities. Later, during his speech, Felipe said it was "important and necessary that once again we express our sympathy for all the people who died in such a tragic and senseless manner." Felipe also demanded that the estimated 15,000 migrants who remain two-and-a-half months later in Ceuta be treated with respect. During a recent visit to Ceuta, The Associated Press found many underage migrants still living on the streets. Some migrants have also reported abuse. The Spanish government is investigating allegations detailed in an Amnesty International report of mistreatment and torture by Spanish soldiers. One migrant said soldiers beat him so badly he needed staples to close wounds to his head. Many of the remaining migrants, including minors, have had to sleep in poor conditions or now-demolished makeshift camps. Their presence has fueled social tensions in Ceuta and become a political issue across Spain, where opposition parties hope to use migration concerns to unseat the progressive government in next month's elections. Ceuta and Melilla the focus of complex relations with Morocco Juan Carlos' visit to Ceuta and Melilla nearly 20 years ago triggered a diplomatic crisis. Morocco recalled its ambassador to Spain, and Moroccans protested outside Spanish consulates and near the border. King Mohammed VI, Morocco's highest authority, condemned that visit as a "nostalgic act from a decidedly bygone era." Asked whether the Spanish government feared a similar response this time, spokesperson Elma Saiz insisted on what she called "fluid" communication with Morocco during the migration crisis. "This is a historic trip, but it is happening within the absolute normality of the visit of Spain's majesties to two Spanish cities," Saiz said. "As you all know, the days of July 29 and 30 were days of extraordinary tension where the communication with Morocco was fluid and constant." Haizam Amirah-Fernández, director of the Madrid-based Center of Contemporary Arab Studies, is among the analysts who believe Morocco, even if not directly involved, was likely aware of the buildup of people spurred by social media to cross into Ceuta. He described the mass crossing as an "assault" on Spain's sovereignty. A Spanish Defense Ministry intelligence report

5afb7842aa81.text: Pope Leo has been diagnosed with lung cancer, the Vatican said Tuesday. Why it matters: The Vatican disclosed the pontiff's health news just hours after he underwent surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung . What they're saying: "The surgery was completed successfully, within the expected timeframe and as planned, and the holy father has returned to his room," per a Holy See Press Office statement published Tuesday. The office said in that statement it would provide more information shortly, and later followed up with news of Leo's diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, which they said tests "conducted beforehand" had led them to suspect. Driving the news: The first American pontiff was admitted to Rome's Agostino Gemelli University Hospital on Tuesday afternoon for surgery. "The Pope was in the operating room approximately three hours, while the operation itself lasted about 90 minutes. The doctors said it was successful and there were no complications," the statement said. The Catholic Church leader carried out his usual duties Monday and was greeted by supporters and patients at the hospital, according to the Vatican statement. Zoom in: Adenocarcinoma is the most common subtype of lung cancer, per the Cancer Center. It forms when the cells lining the outside of the lungs become cancerous. Its symptoms include persistent cough, shortness of breath and chest pain, amongst other things. Patients with adenocarcinoma don't always experience symptoms early on, and it is often detected during a scan for a medical reason unrelated to lung cancer. The big picture: Doctors discovered the nodule during routine medical checkups. Leo said Sunday that the nodule "was detected at a very early stage and is well localized." He thanked his supporters for their "spiritual closeness" and said he was entrusting himself to their prayers. Go deeper: Pope Leo to have "nodule" removed from lung Editor's note: This story has been updated with information about Leo's diagnosis.

The Health Ministry reported 9,066 confirmed cases and 4,381 deaths, with the death toll approaching half the number of confirmed cases. Please check your inbox to confirm. The rising death toll has alarmed health workers and authorities, with a large share of recorded deaths occurring outside treatment centers. The outbreak has created new hot spots as it spreads to more communities, with 65 health zones across seven provinces now affected. Officials say the confirmed cases account for only a third of all cases, with many going undetected. The outbreak involves the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment. Army re-evaluating munitions procurement goals as Iran war continues
Buying more Patriot missiles is a top priority, the Army’s fires acquisition boss said.
The Army’s procurement goals for critical munitions could be shifting, officials said Tuesday in a break from the U.S. government’s typical reticence to talk about the enormous expenditure of weapons during the Trump administration's war on Iran.
Increasing annual production of Patriot air defense missiles, particularly the PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement, is high on the priority list, Gen. Frank Lozano, the Army’s fires portfolio acquisition executive, said during a panel at the AUSA annual meeting in Washington, D.C.
“Our goal has always been to get to 2,000, and we've had a lot of discussions about even more interceptors,” he said, “but when we start talking about overall missile output and we start looking at numbers—is it 4,000, is it 6,000, is it 8,000—we're looking at a diverse set of capabilities. Because we have to address the threat, and we need to address the threat in a complementary way, meaning we need to fight on a cost curve that's affordable for the U.S. Army to maintain and sustain that warfighting capability abroad.”
Lozano addressed reports of depleted stockpiles by repeating the government’s insistence that all is well.
“We have to win everywhere, and so when you have to win everywhere, you need to really make sure that from a foundational aspect of the joint force, you have enough depth within your magazine, from from a varying perspective of capabilities, that you're able to contribute to that joint fight in a meaningful way,” he said. “I will continue to double down and echo what our department leadership has stated: we have the capabilities we need to have to fight and win, but it's our job to ensure that victory is achievable in the future inside of any dynamic environment, scenario, fight we might find ourselves in.”
The Army is also “looking into” buying PAC-2 Guidance Enhanced Missile-Tactical, he said.
“Should we buy GEM-Ts? Because they're being produced,” Lozano said. “And so, if it's an effector that's available now, and GEM-Ts are a really good missile in the battle space [in which] they operate…so if we have the opportunity, it's probably something we should take advantage of, and we’re looking into doing that.”
The Army’s ability to scale some of these procurement programs will depend on funding from Congress, said Brent Ingraham, the Army’s civilian acquisition chief.
“We are looking every day, depending on where the budget lands, what a top line looks like, whether it's a reconciliation or not,” Ingraham said. “We have prioritized the missions that we truly need, we think about today and the near future…and so, depending on where the budget ends up, we will have to do some work to reprioritize our systems to focus on those key initiatives.”

Former gang boss Duane "Keffe D" Davis has been sentenced to at least 40 years in prison for orchestrating the murder of Tupac Shakur.
A jury found Davis, 63, guilty in September of one count of murder with a deadly weapon for the rap superstar's death in a drive-by shooting in Las Vegas on 7 September 1996. He has said he will appeal the verdict.
Prosecutors argued that although Davis did not fire the gun himself, he was the ringleader of the group that committed the murder. He admitted in his memoir that he had provided the gun used in the crime.
Davis' conviction was the first in a cold case that has intrigued hip-hop fans for nearly 30 years.
Prosecutor Marc DiGiacomo argued during Tuesday's sentencing hearing that Davis spent years "publicly grandstanding" and bragging about his role on Shakur's death, which he said, "had wide-ranging effects upon the world".
Shakur's sister, Sekyiwa Shakur, told the court: "The loss of Tupac, for a long time, crippled my family."
"He had so much promise, intentions for a better world," said adding that her brother had hoped to help his local community.
Sekyiwa Shakur asked the judge to give Davis the maximum sentence, telling Davis he will sit in prison and "contemplate what you've done to the world, not just to me".
Shakur's brother, Maurice Shakur, also addressed the court, asking the judge for "the longest possible sentence".
Davis was asked by Judge Carli Kierny if he had anything to say, to which he replied: "I'm good. I'm gonna appeal this case for sure."
Before handing down the sentence, Kierny told him: "You don't get to take a man from his family.
"You don't get to take his very life, his whole future from him, and just walk away from it. Especially when that man is Tupac Shakur. The world never forgot about him and his death."
The key evidence in the case were Davis' own words, in which he repeatedly and publicly acknowledged being inside the white Cadillac from where the deadly shots were fired.
In exchange for being shielded from criminal prosecution, he told authorities about his role in Shakur's death during a secret 2008 police interview relating to the death of fellow rapper Notorious B.I.G., real name Christopher Wallace, who was killed in a shooting just months after Shakur.
Davis elaborated further on his role in his 2019 memoir, Compton Street Legend, which led to publicity and media interviews.
But the book and interviews he offered elaborating on his role in Shakur's killing voided a protective agreement he had established with authorities that had blocked any criminal charges from being filed. A judge then allowed his police interview to be used in the murder trial against him.
Shakur was 25 years old and at the height of his career as one of rap's most influential voices at the time of his death. He has sold more than 75 million records worldwide.
For three decades, the investigation into his killing remained one of America's most famous cold cases, spurring countless conspiracies - until the conviction of Davis last month.
Throughout the trial, Davis' defence team tried to persuade jurors that his comments were fiction - bravado and exaggeration intended to sell books and make money.
Prosecutors argued that although Davis, a former leader of the South Side Compton Crips street gang, did not himself fire the gun, he ordered the shooting and supplied the gun that his nephew Orlando Anderson used to open fire.
Anderson died in an unrelated shooting in 1998, having denied involvement in the killing of Shakur.

163f81572e6d.text: By — Bernard Condon, Associated Press Bernard Condon, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/republicans-face-midterm-backlash-from-factory-workers-over-trumps-tariffs Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Republicans face midterm backlash from factory workers over Trump's tariffs Economy Oct 13, 2026 3:43 PM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — Nelson Vandermeer voted Republican for decades but balked at supporting President Donald Trump, fearing that the Republican's plan for tariffs on imports would hurt workers more than help. Last year, Vandermeer's premonition came true in a very personal way. The 62-year-old lost his job as a product designer at Howard Miller, a clockmaker that relied on parts produced overseas. After a century in business, the company in Zeeland, Michigan, closed its factory, sold off its inventory and brand name and laid off nearly 200 workers. "So much for bringing jobs back," Vandermeer said. Next month, he plans to vote straight Democrat in the midterms. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. As if an unpopular war with Iran and persistent inflation were not enough trouble for Republicans, they are confronting a backlash over the tariffs that Trump made a cornerstone of his economic agenda. He promised that charging higher taxes on imports would spur a factory renaissance in the United States, but that has not come to pass. Although the country has added manufacturing jobs so far this year, the sector has fewer employees than when Trump returned to the White House in January 2025. White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers insisted that a factory boom is underway, citing increases in manufacturing output and more work in certain nonresidential construction trades. "Factory construction jobs of today mean more manufacturing jobs down the road once those factories come online," she said. Even before the tariffs, Howard Miller struggled as Americans lost their taste for fancy timepieces such as its signature grandfather and mantel clocks. So the company broadened its offerings years ago to include bar carts, cabinets and consoles. But those products also depended on glass and other parts from abroad, and diversification did not ensure survival. "I could still have a job, but now I don't because of tariffs," Vandermeer said. "It was like taking a knife to the back." Job losses pile up in battleground states Rolled coils of steel sit in the yard at the ArcelorMittal Dofasco steel plant in Hamilton, Ontario, in August. Photo by Nick Iwanyshyn/The Canadian Press via AP Vandermeer lives in Michigan's 4th Congressional District, which is represented by Republican Bill Huizenga, who is running for a ninth term in the Nov. 3 election. Before Trump implemented his broadest set of tariffs last year, on what the president called "Liberation Day," Huizenga was supportive. "Is it going to be easy? Not necessarily. Is it the right thing to do? Absolutely it is," he told reporters at the time. A spokesperson for Huizenga said last week that the congressman "sees a potential role for tariffs" for boosting domestic manufacturing "while recognizing the need to address their broader economic effects." His Democratic opponent, state Sen. Sean McCann, has criticized the incumbent for opposing legislation that would rein in tariffs that Trump imposed unilaterally. There are similar issues in competitive races in Kansas, Iowa and Ohio, where Republican acquiescence could hurt the party on Election Day as their constituents face factory layoffs, farm foreclosures and higher prices. Tracy Chew, 55, voted for Trump in 2016, then for Democrat Joe Biden in 2020 and Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024. She used to work for Case, a backhoe manufacturer, but the company announced before the tariffs that it would close its plant in Burlington, Iowa. She lost her job in April, as did her daughter, followed by husband and son-in-law over the next few weeks. Chew is leaning toward voting for Democrats again this year, feeling that Trump let them down. "I'm furious he isn't doing enough," she said. "Tariffs are not targeting the right companies, the right amount." Layoffs in Iowa have piled up elsewhere. Winnebago Industries, which produces recreational vehicles like campers, cut 200 jobs last year after the cost of importing aluminum, steel and electronics increased by tens of millions of dollars. "It's a day to day battle," said Michael Happe, the company's chief executive. In the tight race for an open U.S. Senate seat in Iowa, U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson faces Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek. There is a close contest, too, in Kansas, where Democrat Adam Hamilton, the pastor of the largest United Methodist Church in the U.S., is trying to unseat Republican Roger Marshall. Cole Hoppock, chief executive of appliance maker Vornado Air in Wichita, Kansas, said Trump's tariffs "impacted virtually everything." The company known for its retro household fans laid off more than 70 factory workers in February, blaming higher prices for imported parts. Trump's trade policy could force cutbacks soon at another Kansas employer, Canadian jet manufacturer Bombardier. Trump has threatened to ban the company's sales in the U.S. if Bombardier does not start making all its planes in the U.S. Bombardier said it buys parts from 2,800 companies in 47 states, including in Kansas, where it employs more than 1,000 people Trump's approach to trade is unpopular Trump has spent years complaining that other countries are ripping off the U.S. when it comes to trade. Most economists say he is wrong and that his remedy — broad universal tariffs — would cause more pain than help.
