3f484287ac43.text: By — Jessica Hill, Associated Press Jessica Hill, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/duane-keffe-d-davis-gets-40-years-to-life-in-prison-for-orchestrating-tupac-shakurs-murder Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Duane 'Keffe D' Davis gets 40 years to life in prison for orchestrating Tupac Shakur's murder Nation Oct 13, 2026 3:28 PM EDT LAS VEGAS (AP) — Duane "Keffe D" Davis was sentenced Tuesday to 40 years to life in prison for orchestrating the murder of rap icon Tupac Shakur who was gunned down off the Las Vegas Strip over 30 years ago. Davis, 63, was convicted in August of first-degree murder with the use of a deadly weapon. He is the only person ever charged in the death of Shakur, whose popularity was peaking at age 25. Prosecutor Marc DiGiacomo said Tuesday that whatever sentence the court imposes, Davis is "guaranteed to die" behind bars. "It's not just about losing a family member," DiGiacomo said as Shakur's sister Sekyiwa "Set" Shakur nods her head in the audience. The killing went unsolved for years until Davis, a former leader of the South Side Compton Crips, gave interviews and published his role in the shooting in his 2019 tell-all memoir. DiGiacomo said Davis was trying to profit off a killing that he committed, and for that he does not deserve the minimum sentence. "In my mind he deserves the maximum possible sentence," DiGiacomo said. Davis spoke briefly in court, telling Judge Carli Kierny he wants items back that police took from his house, including his pictures. Asked if there was anything else he wanted to say, Davis said: "No I'm good." Davis' lawyer, Michael Sanft said he plans to appeal the verdict. Sanft said prosecutors waited too long to bring the case. READ MORE: Forensic pathologist details Tupac Shakur's fatal wounds in Duane 'Keffe D' Davis trial On the night of Sept. 7, 1996, Shakur was in the passenger seat of a black BMW with music mogul Marion "Suge" Knight when a white Cadillac pulled up at a red light, and shots erupted. Shakur was shot multiple times and died six days later, while Knight survived. Shakur is considered one of the most influential and versatile rappers of all time and had a burgeoning film career as an actor at the time of his death. His legend has only grown since. His songs still resonate among fans with themes of hardship, love and Black struggles. In his memoir, Davis explained how Shakur and his entourage beat up Davis' nephew hours before the shooting in Las Vegas. He said he sought retaliation, and that he was in the passenger seat of the Cadillac and passed the gun to the backseat, where shots were fired. Davis had spoken to detectives years before but avoided prosecution because of an agreement he made with law enforcement. During the weekslong trial, prosecutors relied on Davis' own statements he made to law enforcement and documentarians. They argued Davis orchestrated the shooting and provided the gun used in Shakur's death, which was the result of a rivalry between the South Side Compton Crips and Mob Piru. Davis' defense attorney pointed to a lack of physical evidence that connected his client to the 30-year-old crime, and he portrayed Davis as a liar who was trying to make money. After nine days of hearing testimony in August, the jury deliberated for three hours before turning over the guilty verdict. Shakur was an icon, a brother Shakur's family spoke at the sentencing, including his siblings Maurice "Mopreme" Shakur and Sekyiwa "Set" Shakur. Following the verdict, prosecutor Binu Palal said that to many people, Shakur was an icon or an idea, "but to the family, Tupac Shakur was a brother, a son, a cousin, a loved person ripped from them 30 years ago." Palal said the family had to sit through years of Davis "bragging about killing someone they loved." "They loved that man. And the arrogance that Mr. Davis had in expressing his joy in killing that man ultimately was his undoing," Palal said. Prosecutors say they have insufficient evidence to charge anyone else Davis is the only person to be charged and convicted in the killing of Shakur. The three other people who allegedly were in the Cadillac — including Davis' nephew Orlando "Baby Lane" Anderson who Davis said was the one who pulled the trigger — have died. Sean "Diddy" Combs and his alleged role were brought up often throughout the trial. Witnesses testified Combs used members of the South Side Compton Crips for security for Bad Boy Records. In his book and public statements, Davis alleged Combs offered him money to kill Shakur and Knight. Combs, who is serving a four-year prison sentence after being convicted of prostitution-related offenses, has repeatedly denied any involvement in the death of Shakur. Clark County District Attorney Steve Wolfson has said his office doesn't believe it has sufficient evidence to charge anyone else. "But like any other case, if we come into more information, more evidence, we can always consider filing additional charges," he said following the guilty verdict. "But today, we don't believe that's the appropriate move to make." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. President Donald Trump's administration has asked Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign from her position as US ambassador to Greece, according to White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia.
Guilfoyle, a former Fox News host, was facing mounting scrutiny over reports she allegedly asked a Trump donor to pay her hefty credit card bill in exchange for access to the administration and behaved inappropriately while in Athens.
Trump said on Tuesday that she had done a good job, but will "not be there" in Greece any longer. "I didn't like what I read," he said.
Guilfoyle vowed to defend herself, calling the claims false, and said the ambassadorship had been the "honour of a lifetime".
Zacharia announced during her first - and unusually short - media briefing that Guilfoyle "had been asked to resign" without providing more details.
"She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well," she said.
Guilfoyle, the 57-year-old ex-wife of California Governor Gavin Newsom, was first nominated as envoy to Athens in December 2024, a month before Trump returned to the White House as president.
Around the same time, news broke that she had broken up with Donald Trump Jr, to whom she was engaged.
In a lengthy post on X on Tuesday, Guilfoyle thanked President Trump, said she would always be a loyal supporter and denied any wrongdoing.
"I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity," she wrote, adding she will "not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service".
Her position had become increasingly tenuous as allegations of improper behaviour mounted over the past week.
A series of text messages seen by the BBC - and first reported by The Wall Street Journal - appear to show Guilfoyle asking for the money from Eric Deters, a long-time Trump ally.
"It won't show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express," she wrote in one Signal message.
In another message - dated just days before her US Senate confirmation hearing last July - Guilfoyle wrote: "Honey please I need you to get this done for me today."
Guilfoyle's lawyers disputed the authenticity of the messages and said she was asking for money owed to her for speeches and consulting work conducted on behalf of Deters before she became ambassador.
Audio recordings obtained by the Wall Street Journal reportedly include Guilfoyle bragging about her connections to prominent Greek business tycoons who she said bankrolled luxury travel and flights on private jets.
According to the newspaper, she also boasted to an official in Athens that the US could topple the Greek government.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who was pictured alongside Guilfoyle during a trip to Athens last week, also had reportedly become unhappy with the allegations.
Following the news that Guilfoyle was being asked to leave, Deters told the BBC that "it's a great day for American diplomacy".
Deters, who said he did not ultimately pay Guilfoyle, also said it was a "complete lie" that he owed her money for speaking and consulting fees and said he is planning to take legal action against her.
Guilfoyle was a longtime political ally of Trump's and was for years in a relationship with Trump Jr. They became engaged in 2018 and broke up in late 2024.
Trump said on Tuesday that "she, I guess, dated my son a long time ago" but was not like a family member.
The US president said he did not speak with Guilfoyle before she was asked to resign.
"She went to Greece, she was doing a good job, but we didn't like what we were reading," Trump said.
The president also said he thought Zacharia was "very good" in her first White House press briefing.
Zacharia, a longtime conservative commentator and Trump supporter, only answered a handful of questions during the 14-minute briefing.
For the first eight minutes, she read a list of what the administration saw as policy achievements. Then Zacharia answered questions about Guilfoyle, Ukraine, her family, and administration policies towards non-traditional media outlets.
She said she viewed her job as working to "amplify, multiply and expand upon President Trump's incredible agenda".

28a25df02727.text: By — Nicholas Riccardi, Associated Press Nicholas Riccardi, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/what-to-know-about-the-search-of-democratic-rep-omars-home Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter What to know about the search of Democratic Rep. Omar's home Politics Oct 13, 2026 3:19 PM EDT Federal agents searched Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington, D.C. home on Monday, only three weeks before the frequent target of President Donald Trump's criticism stands for reelection in her congressional district in Minnesota. Here's what to know: Is this political retribution? Trump has not been shy about wanting to use federal law enforcement to target his perceived political enemies. He's pushed prosecutions of former FBI Director James Comey and New York's Democratic Attorney General, Letitia James, following earlier probes the two launched against him. Omar, a left-wing firebrand, has been a longtime target of Trump and Republicans in general. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Omar was born in Somalia and is a naturalized U.S. citizen. Trump has especially targeted Somali immigrants in Minnesota, posting on social media last week that the people of the state must "fight back" against them. The state has reeled from several federal fraud cases sometimes involving Somali-run nonprofits in Minnesota. Many of those cases were filed by former President Joe Biden's Department of Justice. Omar is not involved in them. Omar has long criticized Trump, and the president has likewise gone after her repeatedly over the years. Trump late last week alluded to possible action against the congresswoman. At a rally in Tennessee on Saturday, Trump referred pejoratively to Omar as coming from a country of "crime and squalor" and suggested that Vice President JD Vance "and our people" were investigating her. Watch the clip in the player above. Justice Department protocol has long been to avoid legal action against politicians in the final weeks before their election. The Trump administration's violation of that added to Democratic criticism that this is simply political payback. "For years, Donald Trump and far-right extremists have relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Omar with vile personal attacks and baseless accusations," said a joint statement issued from House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and other top congressional Democrats. "Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family." Asked about the search, Trump deferred to the Justice Department, saying "that has nothing to do with me." "I've always found her to be very crooked, personally," he said. Is this about immigration? The agents who searched Omar's home, pursuant to a federal search warrant, were Homeland Security investigators, indicating the investigation regards immigration issues. Several Trump officials have suggested that is how they intend to pursue Omar. Vance has suggested before that Omar committed immigration fraud. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin last month cited an "ongoing investigation" that he suggested was examining potential fraud on her family's immigration paperwork. "Something's going to happen," he said at the time. The Department of Justice on Monday was typically tight-lipped, giving few details about the case other than saying it was a criminal investigation. Omar became a U.S. citizen in 2000 when she was 17 years old, five years after she arrived with her family after obtaining asylum in the United States. What happens next? The election is in 20 days. Omar's district in Minneapolis is deep blue and she's in little actual peril on Nov. 3. We don't know enough about the next steps in the investigation. It's likely, however, that conservatives will continue slamming Omar. Now, however, she has one more way to hit back — by arguing she's being persecuted by her political opponents. In a statement on X on Monday, Omar called the search an "attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement." "For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation," she said. "I will not be silenced." Instead, it's focused on the unprecedented parental challenge of handling the near-certain prospect that children will hear of or see footage of the Dec. 3 U.S. execution by firing squad of Nidal Malik Hasan if the Trump administration follows through with plans to livestream the event. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The danger stretches beyond the broadcast itself, because history shows graphic video from the event could be clipped, copied and pushed into children's social feeds even if the original stream is restricted. Experts suggest that grownups who care about children start by setting aside matters of politics and public policy — like the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections and the debate over capital punishment. Focus instead on how witnessing someone's death by firing squad might land with young viewers — and how best to reassure and protect them. Here are some guidelines that might help. Keep empathy for kids in mind — and facts at hand Mis- and disinformation reach children, too. It's important for parents to have credibility with them, especially because their real, unspoken question might be: Are we safe? Have in hand some basic facts about the case and state them gently. "It will be easier to have a position, share your family's values, and discuss things with a potentially overwhelmed child once you've taken the time to gather accurate, up-to-date info and assess your child's needs," according to Common Sense Media, which advises parents on entertainment and technology. Trump approved Hasan's execution by firing squad Dec. 3 at Fort Hood. A few days later, the Pentagon announced the event would be livestreamed. "People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told Real America's Voice, a conservative outlet. WATCH: Vance says he's 'not going to be watching' livestream of Fort Hood shooter's execution Hasan, an Army psychiatrist, was convicted of killing 13 people there in 2009 when he walked into a medical building where soldiers were getting checkups and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun. He said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims. He made almost no effort to defend himself at trial. The U.S. military has not carried out the death penalty since 1961. The last widely recognized public execution took place on Aug. 14, 1936. Kentucky, the last state to permit them, outlawed the practice in 1938. Stay updated on the plans Also, experts suggest, parents should stay updated on how a livestreamed execution would unfold. Many questions remained unanswered, such as whether the moment of death and its aftermath will be shown, whether any age restrictions will apply, and whether there will be a broadcast delay or a threshold for stopping the feed. Be informed about the technology involved. While the government often uses YouTube to carry its livestreams, including those embedded within government websites, YouTube prohibits content that is "violent or gory" and "intended to shock or disgust viewers," and doesn't allow livestreams that show someone holding, handling or transporting a firearm. YouTube does make exceptions in select cases for content it deems to be in an educational, documentary, scientific or artistic context or that it determines to be in the public's interest. In such cases, the content may be age-restricted. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment regarding how its policies relate to the execution. But the danger to kids spills beyond the live broadcast to unexpected exposure on social media in the form of memes, for example. It's unclear whether the Trump administration is considering children in its decision-making. Emails over two days asking White House spokespeople for thoughts from the president and first lady Melania Trump on the prospect of children seeing the execution went unanswered. Trump said that he'll soon make a decision on the plan to livestream the event. Assume kids will at least hear about the execution, if not see it From the old-fashioned grapevine to social media, grisly news has a way of reaching school-aged children, experts agree. Consider their need for calm and age-appropriate guidance, they suggest. "With young kids, parents should keep it short and focus on reassurance over explaining the events," said Jill Murphy, chief content officer at Common Sense Media. "Reassure them that they are safe. With teens, ask honestly what they have heard first, then ask whether they need to watch it." Remember you are your child's parent, not their friend — and don't overexplain, advises Dr. David Rosenberg, chair of psychiatry and behavioral neurosciences at Wayne State University School of Medicine in Michigan. Answer the questions children ask, and don't be afraid to assert parental authority by, for example, restricting or banning a child's access to the footage. "It's okay to say, 'I don't have all the answers. But here's what we know, you're safe, you're secure, this is what we believe,'" Rosenberg said. 6b47d9320578.text: By — Leah Willingham, Associated Press Leah Willingham, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/cornell-suspends-fraternity-parties-gives-state-police-role-in-investigating-campus-assault-reports Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Cornell suspends fraternity parties, gives state police role in investigating campus assault reports Nation Oct 13, 2026 2:49 PM EDT Cornell University is suspending parties and other social events at fraternity houses for the rest of the academic year and will give the New York State Police a role in investigating sex crimes on campus, university officials announced Tuesday, amid mounting outrage over its handling of allegations that a female student was sexually assaulted at a fraternity house in 2024. The measures announced by Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff include a suspension of all parties and social events at Interfraternity Council houses through the end of the 2026-27 academic year and a new "zero tolerance" policy for violations that would result in the immediate emergency suspension of a chapter. "These measures will provide time for a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue," Kotlikoff wrote in a letter to the campus community. Cornell has more than 20 active fraternities affiliated with its Interfraternity Council. The council did not immediately respond to an email request for comment. The university president said the school would begin conversations with students and faculty experts about "the development of safe social alternatives" to Greek life party culture and invest money to get those initiatives off the ground. He also committed to adding a case manager to the school's Office of Civil Rights to help those who report sexual misconduct on the Cornell campus navigate the process, and to working with the New York State Police to allow its criminal investigators — who are independent of Cornell — to investigate allegations. Crimes reported on Cornell's campus are generally investigated by campus police, a department that has full law enforcement powers but is controlled by the university. The campus police force operates independently from municipal police in Ithaca, New York, where the university is located. Its officers investigated the 2024 gang rape allegations and presented their initial findings to the Tompkins County district attorney, who declined to prosecute within weeks of the woman making her first report to police. WATCH: What the Cornell case reveals about how sexual assault allegations are handled In a lawsuit filed in September, the woman alleged that she was drugged and sexually assaulted by multiple fraternity members after attending a party at the Chi Phi house in October 2024. She said she was pressured to use drugs and that other men entered the room while she was incapacitated. She also alleges that messages describing her as sexually available to anyone at the house circulated among fraternity members on Snapchat without her knowledge. Cornell closed the fraternity chapter and disciplined several students following an internal investigation, but no criminal charges have been filed. New York's governor removed the district attorney from the case this month after a public outcry over the lack of charges. The investigation is now being led by New York Attorney General Letitia James, while Cornell has hired former Deputy U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates to conduct an independent review of the university's response. New York State Police sometimes handle major crime investigations for small municipal police agencies, bringing in expertise that isn't available locally. Kotlikoff's announcement came a day before Cornell's faculty senate was to take up a proposed resolution expressing no confidence in the administration's ability to effectively address sexual assault on campus. Kotlikoff acknowledged that sexual violence extends beyond fraternities, saying Cornell must also confront a campus culture of excessive drinking and drug use and expand education about students' responsibility to intervene when others are at risk. Cornell also plans to add victim advocates and expand sexual violence prevention programs, including education aimed at encouraging bystanders to intervene, he said, calling the various actions announced Tuesday "first steps toward systemic change on our campus." "We will take all necessary steps to address the conditions that led to Jane Doe's experiences, and those of other survivors," he said. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 118abdefe6df.text: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and President Trump last week discussed the possibility of launching a major new operation against Iran before the Israeli and U.S. elections, according to two U.S. officials, one Israeli official and a fourth source with knowledge of the matter. Netanyahu said during the call that he was concerned about Israeli intelligence indicating Iran was taking troubling steps to reconstitute its nuclear program, according to the Israeli official. The Israeli leader's call with Trump about the possible attack took place before Trump said he would not strike Iran ahead of the midterms. Why it matters: Resuming major combat operations in Iran would inject a volatile new issue into the Oct. 27 Israeli elections and the U.S. midterms a week later. But the Israeli and U.S. militaries are still on alert and concluding preparations to be ready in case he changes his mind, sources said. " Bibi seems to want to go in again. He has talked to the president about it a couple times, and the president has said, 'Well, you know, Bibi, go ahead and get ready.' But there's really no commitment. 'Go ahead and get ready' is maybe now, maybe later, maybe never," a U.S. official said. A White House official said it's "false" that Trump and Netanyahu discussed resuming the war. "The President has said that we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections," the person said. Netanyahu's office said that "the prime minister maintains regular contact with President Trump and senior U.S. administration officials and does not comment on the content of their conversations." Driving the news: Netanyahu has had several calls with Trump over the last two weeks about returning to major combat operations in Iran. According to the sources, Netanyahu and Trump spoke about a potential joint U.S.-Israeli operation that would hit military and nuclear targets. Netanyahu expressed concern about steps Israel believes Iran is taking to reconstitute all of the various parts of its nuclear program. Israel is especially concerned about Iran potentially operating Pickaxe Mountain as a uranium enrichment site. Trump's top cabinet members huddled for hours at Camp David on Oct. 2 to discuss next steps in the war and the possibility of resuming strikes. Behind the scenes: An Israeli official said Trump initially seemed to be leaning toward resuming attacks, but then grew more hesitant. A U.S. official said Trump has been going back and forth on the issue. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the leadership of U.S. Central Command are the strongest backers of resuming strikes in Iran, a source familiar with the discussions said. But most of Trump's advisers favor keeping up economic sanctions and other forms of pressure for now. "They claim this economic choking is working better and better. Let's keep it up," the second U.S. official said. Between the lines: Renewed strikes would carry major political implications for both leaders. Resuming the war could dramatically affect the Israeli elections, since Iran would likely fire hundreds of ballistic missiles at the country in retaliation. Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir spoke last week with Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine and discussed the possibility of resuming full-scale fighting against Iran within the next three weeks, according to a source briefed on the call. Zamir said that restarting the war in that timeframe could cause the Israeli elections to be postponed, given that Iran would probably retaliate, the sources said. Caine's spokesman, Joe Holstead, declined to comment. It's a big dilemma for Zamir because a strike ahead of the elections could be seen as a political ploy by Netanyahu that would erode public trust in the military, which is largely viewed as apolitical. The intrigue: The White House is aware of Netanyahu's domestic political considerations. "Bibi's got an election before the midterms. He believes his strength is being a wartime prime minister," one of the U.S. officials said. In meetings with his security and intelligence chiefs in recent days, Netanyahu claimed it was Trump, not him, who initiated the discussion about possibly hitting Iran before the elections, an Israeli official said. According to this account, Trump asked Netanyahu if Israel would join. Resuming the war before the U.S. election could backfire on Trump by reminding voters of the unpopular conflict and potentially sending gas prices higher. The big picture: Qatari mediators are still waiting for Iran to respond to the latest U.S. counterproposal to end the war, which includes demands for nuclear concessions. "The negotiations are not really dead, but they're not really alive. We're just here, piling on the pressure and there's a belief that smarter heads will prevail over there," a U.S. official said. "The Iranians thought this president would back down because of the pressure and the midterms. He has shown them the error of their ways," the official added. Trump repeated a familiar refrain Tuesday, telling reporters that "Iran is a failed country" and "we will make a decision on Iran very soon."

da249d524a91.text: By — Seth Borenstein, Associated Press Seth Borenstein, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/pacific-hurricane-region-sets-record-for-big-long-lasting-storms Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Pacific hurricane region sets record for big, long-lasting storms Science Oct 13, 2026 2:40 PM EDT The drumbeat of monster hurricanes in the Pacific has broken a record for nasty long-lasting storms east of the international date line, turbocharged by nature's supersized El Niño, scientists said. "Since September 20th, when Odalys formed, it's been berserk," said Colorado State University researcher Phil Klotzbach, who forecasts and studies storm activity. "This year just everything that forms is just lasting a long time and getting really powerful." One of the key measurements meteorologists use to judge hurricane seasons is called accumulated cyclone energy, or ACE, which includes a storm's wind speed and longevity. On Sunday, a section of the Pacific east of the date line, which brews storms headed for Hawaii, Mexico and the U.S. West Coast, passed the old mark set in 2018. The area is still going strong with Hurricane Simon and appears on the verge of spawning another one that will really ramp up in strength, Klotzbach said. On Tuesday, the Pacific will tie a record for most days with a hurricane spinning and is likely to break it soon after that, Klotzbach said. "It feels like almost everything that can spin up does spin up," said University of Arizona atmospheric scientist Kim Wood. El Niño and warm water are boosting Pacific hurricanes Several meteorological factors have come together to supercharge the Pacific, chief among them the El Niño, Klotzbach and other hurricane researchers said. An El Niño weakens and shifts the high altitude vertical winds that otherwise can dampen or even decapitate storms. In the Pacific, that wind shear runs east to west, generally with the direction storms travel, so it's like riding a bicycle with a tail wind, Klotzbach said. Meanwhile, the weather pattern has dampened hurricanes in the Atlantic, where the ACE is less than 18% of what's normal for this time of year. El Niño makes the wind shear in the Atlantic like riding into a headwind, he said. Another factor is warm water, which serves as hurricane fuel. By definition El Niño is a warming of the equatorial Pacific that changes weather worldwide. In the Pacific storm basin, it's several degrees Fahrenheit warmer than normal, said Kristen Corbosiero, a professor of storm atmospheric sciences at the University at Albany in New York. WATCH: How a super El Niño is fueling extreme weather patterns Usually in the Pacific, the extra warm storm-friendly water doesn't run as deep as it does in the Atlantic. So when one storm goes over a patch of water, it brings up cold water and makes it hard for a subsequent storm in the same area to stay alive, Wood said. But not this year. Hurricane Rachel, whose remnants swamped Las Vegas over the weekend, didn't suffer as it went over, churned up by Category 5 Hurricane Polo, Wood said. She said the waters are warm from both El Niño and climate change from the burning of coal, oil and gas. Another factor in recent storms was a counterclockwise atmosphere spin over Central America — called a gyre — that spits out seeds of stormy weather that can form into hurricanes. It spit out both the Atlantic's Isaias and the Pacific's Simon at about the same time, Corbosiero and Klotzbach said. Five major hurricanes in a row The last five Pacific hurricanes — long-lasting Nolo, Odalys, Polo, Rachel and Simon — have all reached major status with winds of at least 111 mph (178.6 kph). Nolo, Odalys and Simon hit Category 4, while Polo set the record for time spent at Category 5 at two-and-a-half days. When Klotzbach made those calculations on the record-breaking activity of the eastern and central Pacific, he looked at all storms east of the date line. That's a slightly different approach from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, which breaks that broad area into two regions. Neither NOAA-defined region is quite at record levels for ACE yet; put together they are. Part of that is because often when one of those subregions is more active, the other isn't quite as crazy, but in 2026 they both are hyperactive, Wood said. "This is the first year that both sides have been this active together," Wood said. "Usually it's kind of focused more on one or the other, so that speaks to just the wide extent across this region of where there's been that lower shear, those warmer waters, and that higher moisture." Off the Mexican coast is a disturbance that the National Hurricane Center gives a 90% chance of becoming Tropical Storm Trudy, which then could power up to something big, Klotzbach and Corbosiero said. "It seems like that area is just one after another. So I would not be surprised to have another storm," Corbosiero said. "This year, because of the El Niño, we do have very favorable conditions. So as long as there's some sort of the seeds either from the gyre or from remnant ends of cold fronts, it seems like this is going to continue for a bit." a57139199750.text: By — Sam McNeil, Associated Press Sam McNeil, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/why-saudi-arabias-military-has-struggled-to-defend-the-country-against-houthi-attacks Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Why Saudi Arabia's military has struggled to defend the country against Houthi attacks World Oct 13, 2026 2:28 PM EDT Saudi Arabia has one of the world's most expensive and sophisticated arsenals, filled with American warplanes, missile defenses and other cutting-edge technology. But in recent days it has appeared helpless in the face of barrages of missiles and drones fired by the Houthi rebel group from neighboring Yemen. The attacks have struck Saudi airports, killed at least 14 people and forced schoolchildren and businesspeople to stay indoors and work from home. The Iran-backed Houthis, once seen as little more than a ragtag militia, have grown into a formidable fighting force. They have inflicted damage on the region's top oil producer, threatened critical supply routes in the Red Sea and now risk reigniting a full-scale war on the Arabian Peninsula that displaced millions and killed tens of thousands. The Houthis are attacking Saudi Arabia because it supports government forces in Yemen the rebels seek to overthrow. As Saudi Arabia investigates how its air defenses failed to stop the Houthis' attacks, it must also consider how to respond and what the rebels might do next. Here's what we know and don't know about the Saudi and Houthi conflict: Saudi Arabia has a vast arsenal of US weapons Saudi Arabia is the world's top purchaser of American weapons, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. It says the Saudis received 12% of all U.S. arms exports from 2021-2025. Over the years, the Saudis have purchased American F-15 warplanes, Patriot air defense systems, as well as advanced radars and offensive missile systems, according to the think tank, which tracks global arms transfers. Saudi Arabia's annual budget for 2026 listed $83 billion for military expenditures. Earlier this year, it struck a $9 billion deal with Washington for 730 Patriot missiles. But it has a huge area to defend The Houthis have been able to exploit Saudi Arabia's large size. Vulnerable energy, civilian and military assets are scattered across the country's sparsely populated territory roughly three times the size of Texas. Its border with Yemen stretches more than 1,300 kilometers (800 miles) through rugged desert areas. "Expecting a country the size of Saudi Arabia to intercept every missile is simply unrealistic. No defense can guarantee complete protection," Ali Shihabi, a Saudi analyst, said in a post online Monday. At the same time, regional officials say that Saudi Arabia is running low on interceptors and has reached out to allies for help. Saudi Arabia recently struck a joint defense pact with Pakistan and Turkey. But so far, the two countries appear to be largely staying on the sidelines or limiting their support. President Donald Trump said this week he is evaluating whether the U.S. should join Saudi strikes on the Houthis. But he has not yet announced a decision. Houthi weapons and tactics are battle-tested Like their patron Iran, the Houthis have deployed asymmetric warfare for the 21st century by capitalizing on their strengths — primarily drones and missiles. For the Houthis, success on the battlefield doesn't require toppling Saudi Arabia; disrupting the Saudi economy and sowing fear within its society may be enough to give the Houthis leverage in any possible negotiations to end the fighting. READ MORE: Saudis probe how defense systems failed to stop deadly Houthi attack on Riyadh airport The Houthis have a large arsenal capable of striking targets well over 1,000 miles (1,600 kilometers) away. Some warheads change direction during flight and pose an extra challenge to air defenses. The group has fired hundreds of drones and missiles at Israel since its war in Gaza erupted in October 2023. While most were intercepted, a handful managed to land, in one case killing an Israeli man. Another strike hit an Israeli airport last year. Andreas Krieg, a professor at King's College London, said this experience in challenging Israel's cutting-edge air defenses has given the Houthis confidence and expertise as they now strike Saudi Arabia. "They've learned how to over-saturate the radars," he said. The Houthis, working with allied militias in Iraq, have also targeted Saudi oil installations, including a vital pipeline used to export oil through the Red Sea while movement through the Strait of Hormuz is limited. The Houthis have also seized territory in Yemen near the Bab el-Mandeb, a key Red Sea waterway, putting additional pressure on Saudi oil exports. Saudi Arabia appears to have miscalculated Michael Ratney, a former U.S. ambassador to Saudi Arabia, says the kingdom assumed the Houthis wouldn't strike civilian targets like airports. Doing so marked "a paradigm shift," he said. Ratney, now an adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said the Saudis now find themselves in a position where they have to respond while also trying to prevent the fighting from spinning out of control. "They can't not strike back — they were attacked in a very brutal way by their archenemies," he said. "They need to exert military pressure on the Houthis and then find a way to kind of deescalate." Rather than sending troops into Yemen, the Saudis will likely launch airstrikes against the Houthis and ramp up support of nationalist forces, several analysts said. "It will be surrogate warfare," Krieg said. The Houthis are now a formidable force While the Houthis don't have the firepower of Saudi Arabia, they have grown into a fearsome force controlling roughly one-third of Yemen thanks to help from Iran. Cornell University is banning all parties at fraternity houses as the school faces backlash over its handling of an alleged sexual assault on campus two years ago.
Last month, a woman known as Jane Doe filed a lawsuit alleging she was plied with drugs and raped by several men in 2024 at a party at a Cornell fraternity house.
In a statement on Tuesday, Cornell's president, Michael Kotlikoff, announced a series of measures responding to the alleged assault, including the end to fraternity parties for the rest of the school year.
"I am deeply sorry for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024, and appalled that this act of sexual violence occurred within our Cornell community," he said.
"It is clear that women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe. We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action," he added.
Fraternities have existed at university campuses across the US for decades and function as all-male social clubs where the students live, study and socialise. Over the years, the groups have become notorious for binge-drinking, partying and dangerous hazing rituals.
In a statement, a lawyer representing Doe said she filed a civil lawsuit "to achieve her aim of improving Cornell and its response to abuse claims".
"While the steps announced today are helpful to achieve this goal, they are too late to protect Ms. Doe," said lawyer Thomas Giuffra.
Cornell's president said anyone who violated the new fraternity party policy at the New York university would be suspended.
The school also said it planned to improve support for survivors of sexual assault, including more staff to help people report sexual misconduct and navigate other support systems as well.
Through Title IX, the federal law that governs how universities handle sexual assault claims, schools are required to provide measures of support to help survivors stay in school after assaults. Doe's lawyer has said she dropped out after the alleged assault.
The president said the school will allow New York State Police's trauma-informed officers to investigate allegations of sexual assault on its campus.
These officers will interview survivors who want to pursue criminal charges and prepare "comprehensive investigative summaries for the appropriate law enforcement agency", Kotlikoff said.
Cornell has faced criticism over the information shared with the local district attorney's office about Jane Doe's allegations.
Out of hundreds of documents that US media outlets have obtained from Cornell's investigation into the assault, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said that in 2024, his office received only a six-page statement signed by the victim as well as Snapchat messages in which the men at the fraternity party advertised a free sexual encounter with Doe.
State officials have also criticised Van Houten's decision not to bring charges or interview victims and witnesses himself. New York Governor Kathy Hochul has appointed the state's attorney general, Letitia James, to investigate the case.
Kotlikoff said Cornell would be bringing in national sexual violence prevention experts to examine "the factors leading to campus sexual violence and strategies to promote responsible sexual citizenship".
He said the steps were the first toward "systematic change" on campus.

f5240877dc28.text: By — Jessica Hill, Associated Press Jessica Hill, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/ai-data-centers-are-coming-for-federal-land-and-roiling-nevada-governors-race Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter AI data centers are coming for federal land and roiling Nevada governor's race Politics Oct 13, 2026 2:20 PM EDT BOULDER CITY, Nev. (AP) — Janelle Sorenson loves the clear night skies in Boulder City, less than an hour's drive from the bright lights of the Las Vegas Strip. It's a small, quiet town, and she thinks an artificial intelligence data center would ruin the community and scar the desert landscape. So over the summer, she joined with other residents to successfully oppose plans for one of the giant computing warehouses that have popped up around the country. But their victory was short-lived. The developers withdrew their application and instead sought adjacent land owned by the federal government — and the U.S. Bureau of Land Management signed off. "Not only did we not get to decide anything or have a say," Sorenson said, "we were just really kept in the dark." The Townsite data center was the first in the country to be approved on federal public land, though construction is stalled after a judge ruled that the government couldn't use an old environmental review from when the project was intended to be a solar farm. Tech companies are eager for vast tracts to build data centers that can be as large as 70 football fields, and Townsite could set a precedent for similar projects on federal property with more than a dozen others in the planning stages. President Donald Trump has been a steadfast supporter of the artificial intelligence industry, which he views as a source of economic growth and part of a global competition with China. However, data centers have been unpopular in many communities as voters worry about higher electricity bills, declining water supplies and other impacts. In Nevada, where 80% of the land is owned by the federal government, Townsite and other projects have become a dominant issue in the battleground state's closely watched governor's race. Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo, one of his party's most vulnerable incumbents, doesn't outright oppose building data centers on public lands, as long as they have community support. He recently signed an agreement with Trump's Republican administration to streamline infrastructure projects, which could include data centers on federal lands. Democratic nominee Aaron Ford, the state attorney general, has pledged to oppose data centers on public lands, saying affordable housing should be the priority. Both say the projects, whether on public or private land, must follow state rules, such as requiring data centers to cover their own energy costs and protecting water supplies, or they would lose eligibility for state tax abatements. Voters across the political spectrum unite against data centers Sorenson, the Boulder City resident, considers herself to be liberal, but she said her conservative neighbors are on the same page as she is. "We're all aligned on this," she said. Autumn McGrath-Shook, who lives in the same town, said she recently left the Republican Party and registered with the Green Party over data centers, though she still identifies as conservative. Worried about the environmental impact on wildlife, she joined forces with "these crazy libs" to oppose the project. Data centers have quickly become a "catalyzing issue" in the midterms, catching many politicians flat-footed, said David Damore, a political science professor at the University of Nevada Las Vegas. Some state leaders who were previously supportive of data centers have rushed to respond. For example, Republican Texas Gov. Greg Abbott paused data center approvals until audits are completed, and Democratic Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro signed an executive order removing data center proposals from a fast-track permitting process and requiring them to receive local approval before seeking state approval. READ MORE: Data center controversies have transformed midterms. Here's where different groups stand In August, Ford announced his plan to pause new tax abatements for data centers while an audit is conducted to see if the projects have fulfilled promises about producing tax revenue and economic benefits. In September, Lombardo, who has said data centers provide enormous economic opportunity for Nevada, signed an executive order placing more guardrails on data centers and requiring them to pay more taxes to support schools. The two have successfully "muddied the waters" on their data center positions, Damore said. Lombardo criticized Ford for co-sponsoring 2015 legislation that created the state's tax abatement program for data centers, a measure that received bipartisan support. Ford criticized Lombardo for giving more than $200 million in tax breaks to data centers, which is connected to the legislation that Ford co-sponsored. Ford told The Associated Press that he would use "every tool" at his disposal to prevent data centers from skirting state guardrails, including withholding tax abatements and pursuing litigation. Lombardo, whose campaign declined to make him available for an interview, has a similar pitch. His office said he would not hesitate to confront the federal government to advocate for Nevadans. But that's not good enough for McGrath-Shook, who is on the fence in the governor's race. She thinks Ford is soft on crime, but she views Lombardo as more pro-data centers. "I would much rather vote for Lombardo than Aaron Ford in a normal world," she said. "But with the looming data centers, it really changes the landscape — and literally." cabf53a560c0.text: By — Angela Charlton, Associated Press Angela Charlton, Associated Press By — Dee-Ann Durbin, Associated Press Dee-Ann Durbin, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/cyberattacks-disrupt-refrigeration-systems-at-european-supermarkets Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Cyberattacks disrupt refrigeration systems at European supermarkets World Oct 13, 2026 2:08 PM EDT PARIS (AP) — Cyberattacks have disrupted European supermarket chains, affecting refrigeration systems at hundreds of stores in France and forcing a major grocer to shut down websites serving customers in Europe and the United States. French Finance Minister Roland Lescure told Parliament on Tuesday that about 700 of the country's 10,000 supermarkets were affected. He said there was no risk to France's food supplies but acknowledged that the attack "touches the heart of our food security." "It was a wake-up call for everyone," he said. The Paris prosecutor's office said Tuesday that its cybercrime unit was investigating the large-scale attack, including the extent of damage caused by spoiled food and reports of fires. French supermarket group Groupement Mousquetaires, which operates more than 4,000 stores across Europe, said 300 of its Intermarché and Netto stores were impacted. Some refrigerated and frozen food display cases remained out of service Tuesday. Dominique Schelcher, CEO of French grocery chain Cooperative U, said 80 of the company's 2,000 stores were affected. Most managed to prevent disruptions to refrigeration, but some had to discard food, he said in a post on X. "Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products is an attack on the French food supply chain. It is unprecedented, extremely serious, and unacceptable," Schelcher said. Carrefour and Monoprix supermarkets were also impacted. WATCH: What we know about the cyberattacks on water systems in 7 states Danish technology company Danfoss, which supplied the refrigeration management software, said Monday that most affected systems were older products that no longer received software or security updates. "Danfoss has long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware, as well as to operate behind a firewall," the company said. Danfoss said it was working with affected customers to limit the damage. Separately, Dutch supermarket giant Ahold Delhaize said Tuesday it was working to restore systems it had shut down following what it described as a security issue. The company, which operates Albert Heijn in the Netherlands, Delhaize in Belgium and Stop & Shop in the United States, declined to provide further details. Websites for several of its brands, including Stop & Shop, Food Lion and Albert Heijn, remained offline Tuesday, although stores were open and serving customers. Ahold Delhaize said it had no evidence that customer or employee data had been stolen. "Protecting our infrastructure in the best interest of our customers, associates and partners is a top priority," the company said. "We apologize for any inconvenience this issue may have caused customers and partners." Durbin contributed from Detroit, Michigan. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. d1656610c928.text: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth plans to livestream the December execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan by using a firing squad, one of the rarest forms of capital punishment in the United States. Why it matters: The planned livestream would mark the first public U.S. execution in roughly 90 years, but it has already drawn scrutiny , with President Trump expressing doubt it'll happen. Catch up quick: Hegseth said Oct. 8 that Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people in the 2009 shooting , will be executed in December, and the execution will be livestreamed. Trump has expressed apparent uneasiness despite giving his initial endorsement , Axios' Marc Caputo reported. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) expressed some concerns, too, while Vice President Vance said he wouldn't watch if it were aired. Zoom out: Execution by firing squad is rare, with only six since capital punishment resumed in 1977, per the Death Penalty Information Center. . The U.S. military last executed someone by firing squad in 1945, when it executed Pvt. Eddie Slovik for desertion in France, per NPR . The military's last execution was in 1961, when it hanged John A. Bennett . How a firing squad works State of play: The Pentagon hasn't disclosed its firing squad procedures for Hasan's execution and didn't respond to Axios' request for comment Tuesday. Past executions offer a glimpse of what the method typically involves. How it works: The procedure typically begins with a prisoner strapped to a chair placed before a wall and surrounded by sandbags to absorb blood. A medical professional will typically mark a target over the prisoner's heart, while a black hood covers the prisoner's head. The shooters fire simultaneously, aiming at the heart, from a set distance away from the prisoner. If shooters miss the heart, the prisoner can still die from blood loss. Zoom in: States have different approaches to the firing squad method. For example, Utah uses five shooters, one of whom has a blank round, while South Carolina has three shooters, all with live ammunition. Hasan uses a wheelchair, potentially complicating how the execution would be carried out at Fort Hood. Yes, but: Firing squads don't always work as intended. Last year, prisoner Mikal Mahdi was executed in South Carolina by firing squad. An autopsy later found that only two bullets struck him and missed his heart. Where firing squad is legal The method is legal in Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah, according to the DPIC . It is the main execution method in Idaho as of this past summer. The only authorized method for capital punishment in Texas is lethal injection. Yes, but: State laws don't govern military executions. Data: Death Penalty Information Center ; Note: New Hampshire abolished the death penalty but retains one prisoner on death row; Map: Erin Davis/Axios What we know about the execution livestream Few specifics are known about the livestream execution, where it would streamed, or how people would watch it. It will happen on Thursday, Dec. 3, at 1pm CT, in Fort Hood. It's unclear if the execution would stream on social media or a website. TikTok and Kick said the event would violate their policies. What we're watching: The Army. Army Regulation 190-55 assigns the Army responsibility to choose the method, date and location of the execution.

8ce06f5cf1c2.text: By — Michael Kunzelman, Associated Press Michael Kunzelman, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/supreme-court-to-consider-if-nigerian-man-who-cooked-for-terrorist-leaders-is-ineligible-for-asylum Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Supreme Court to consider if Nigerian man who cooked for terrorist leaders is ineligible for asylum Nation Oct 13, 2026 1:54 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court agreed on Tuesday to consider if a Nigerian man is ineligible for asylum because he cooked meals at a camp for leaders of a group that the U.S. government considers to be a terrorist organization. The high court, granting a request by President Donald Trump's administration, will hear arguments on whether Izuchukwu Ozurumba's cooking job for leaders of the Unknown Gunmen qualifies as providing "material support" for a terrorist group. The Justice Department asked the Supreme Court to review a decision by the Richmond, Virginia-based 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to vacate Ozurumba's removal order. The Republican administration says the 4th Circuit decision conflicts with rulings by at least three other circuits and, if upheld, will hamper the government's ability to deport immigrants with terrorism ties in many other cases. "Providing meals to a terrorist organization's members is no less a material form of support than providing gasoline for its vehicles," they wrote. Ozurumba testified that he didn't know the true purpose of the camp until after he started working there. The Unknown Gunmen is believed to be a group of separatists operating in southern Nigeria. Ozurumba's lawyers say the group's leaders forced him to work without pay and repeatedly threatened him after he escaped from the camp. His attorneys further argued that there is no circuit split for the Supreme Court to resolve. "No federal court has adopted the government's rule, under which any interaction with a terrorist organization, no matter how attenuated or inconsequential, qualifies as 'material' support," they wrote. READ MORE: Supreme Court sides with Trump administration in lawsuit seeking records on Elon Musk's DOGE Ozurumba fled the camp near his home in Lagos, Nigeria, and traveled to Venezuela before entering the U.S. illegally in July 2023 and surrendered to Border Patrol. Several months later, an immigration judge ordered Ozurumba to be deported to Nigeria. A divided 4th Circuit panel decided that Ozurumba's work at the camp didn't constitute material support of terrorism. The majority opinion says it appears that he was "simply a captive laborer" whose work had nothing to do with terrorist activities. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 815b8f4933f5.text: By — Nicole Winfield, Associated Press Nicole Winfield, Associated Press By — Colleen Barry, Associated Press Colleen Barry, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/pope-leo-undergoes-surgery-to-remove-lung-nodule-at-romes-gemelli-hospital Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Vatican says the pope has lung cancer and the lower lobe of his right lung was removed Health Updated on Oct 13, 2026 4:21 PM EDT — Published on Oct 13, 2026 1:45 PM EDT ROME (AP) — Pope Leo XIV underwent surgery Tuesday that confirmed that he has lung cancer, and doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung, the Vatican said Tuesday. The tests confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican said in a medical bulletin after the surgery. It said the diagnosis had been suspected by preoperative tests and was confirmed during surgery. The 71-year-old was in the operating room for about 3 hours, the statement said. The surgery itself lasted approximately 90 minutes. "The surgery was successful, and there were no complications," the statement said. Leo had walked into Rome's Gemelli hospital through the main entrance earlier in the day and waved to dozens of well-wishers who had gathered to greet him. The Vatican said the surgery would be performed by a team led by Gemelli's chief thoracic surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora. The American pontiff has offered a rare level of transparency about the first publicly disclosed major health problem of his 17-month papacy. He revealed the discovery of the small, localized nodule during his Sunday noon prayer and announced that he would have it removed. Oncologists said prior to the operation that even if the nodule turned out to be cancerous, Leo's prognosis is "excellent" since it will have been removed at an early stage. The Vatican on Monday canceled all Leo's audiences through Oct. 20. While Gemelli has a specific papal apartment that past popes have used, complete with a private chapel on the 10th floor, Leo will actually be staying in a nearby room since the papal apartment is currently undergoing renovations, according to the Vatican press office. The Argentinian government has begun legal action seeking to stop the exploration of oil and gas fields north of the Falkland Islands in an escalating row with the UK.
Buenos Aires said in a statement the request lodged with the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea aimed to block activity authorised "illegally" by the UK.
The claim comes a fortnight after Argentinian President Javier Milei demanded the scrapping of the Sea Lion oilfield project, a joint venture between Israeli and British companies.
UK Foreign Office minister Uma Kumaran criticised the "escalating campaign" from Argentina against companies operating in the Falklands, while announcing new protections for them.
The developments heighten tensions between the UK and Argentina over the sovereignty of the self-governing British territory, known in Argentina as Las Malvinas, more than 40 years after a British military task force ejected Argentinian forces which had invaded the territory.
Earlier last month Milei also threatened to impose economic sanctions on firms exploiting oil close to the Falkland Islands.
Uma Kumaran accused the Argentinian government of "economic coercion" against the people of the Falkland Islands.
"We will do whatever it takes to support them," she told the House of Commons on Tuesday.
The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles (209 km) from the Falkland Islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil.
The Falkland Islands government extended exploration licences last month and the field is expected to start pumping in 2028, potentially generating huge revenues for the roughly 3,500 inhabitants of the islands.
Two oil companies â Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum â have insisted they have valid licences issued by Britain.
The Argentinian government claims the marine environment of disputed maritime areas is protected by international law.
Its application "seeks to preserve Argentina's sovereign rights over its continental shelf and prevent activities authorised unilaterally and illegally by the United Kingdom".
In a post on X, Argentinian Foreign Affairs Minister Pablo Quirno said the government was requesting the tribunal make a number of orders against the UK, including halting new exploration permits.
But the UK government insists Sea Lion is lawful, located on the Falkland Islands shelf and regulated by the islands' government.
While the Falkland Islands government grants exploration licences, they must be signed off by the UK Foreign Secretary.
Kumaran said the tribunal application "does not invalidate licenses issued by the Falkland Islands government, alter the islands' regulatory authority, or require lawful hydrocarbon development activities to cease".
The tribunal that will consider the dispute is an independent judicial body based in Hamburg which is responsible for the fair application of the United Nations' Convention on the Law of the Sea.
FCDO officials have made clear the UK will engage with the tribunal but resist Argentina's claim firmly.
They said the aim was not to escalate the dispute but respond firmly to Argentina's latest move, and defend what the UK sees as legitimate economic activity.
They also hope to provide reassurance to businesses fearful of Argentine retribution. That is why they are introducing measures under the Protection of Trading Interests Act that would protect firms from any extra-territorial impact of Argentine laws following Milei's sanctions threats.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said: "Argentina's attempts to intimidate businesses and individuals engaged in legitimate commercial activity are unacceptable. Companies should be free to make lawful commercial decisions without the threat of political coercion."
The latest move comes after Milei roundly criticised the UN in his speech at the General Assembly late last month for failing to act over the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands.
He said the UN had become "a useless organisation" which only serves "arrogant parasites dressed up as well-intentioned bureaucrats".
On Tuesday Kumaran described Milei's remarks at New York as "inflammatory".
Despite its defeat in 1982, Argentina has always maintained its right to the Falkland Islands. But over the years successive governments have pressed their claim with varying degrees of aggression and diplomacy.
UK officials believes the current Argentine leadership is deliberately picking a fight ahead of elections next year.

Warning: This story includes distressing content
A man has died after falling from a rollercoaster at a Six Flags amusement park on Monday in the US state of Georgia.
The man, Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, 42, was found dead under the ride after being ejected and hitting other people on it, according to police.
An investigation is under way and few details have yet to be released about what happened. Six Flags, the largest amusement park operator in North America, has temporarily closed nine rides across the US and Canada as a precaution.
Here's what we know so far about the incident.
What happened?
The Cobb County Police Department said the incident at the Six Flags Over Georgia park happened just before 16:00 local time (20:00 GMT) on Monday.
"Officers working at the park responded to an incident involving a male guest on a roller coaster," it said in a statement on Tuesday.
"Preliminary information gathered through witness and employee interview indicates Kariem was ejected from the ride and struck other patrons before falling beneath the attraction."
The ride involved has not been specified but aerial footage from news helicopters showed the Goliath rollercoaster stopped midway, and multiple witnesses have identified the ride as the one involved in the incident.
The office of the state's insurance and fire safety commissioner, which enforces amusement park safety rules in Georgia, is also conducting a review.
Officials have not held a news conference on the incident.
The Goliath ride opened in 2006, and it has an elevation of 200ft (60m), a 170ft plunge, a 540-degree spiral, and a speed of up to 70mph (112km/h), according to the park website. On its "thrill scale", Six Flags ranks Goliath at level four out of five.
The company said in a statement that it was "deeply saddened by the guest incident" and that "our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest's family, friends, and loved ones".
Witnesses recount 'traumatic' moments
Nick Mendenhall said he witnessed the fatal moments in disbelief, watching the man come out of his seat and then fall into another cart on the ride before falling to the ground.
"It was just super, super bizarre, traumatic. I mean, it took me a couple of seconds, I feel like, to process what was going on," he told the AP. "I cant believe that I just saw that."
He said his mind instantly went to the trauma of all of those impacted by what he witnessed, including the man's loved ones and everyone who was on the ride with him.
One witness told NBC affiliate WXIA that the incident was captured in souvenir photos that were automatically taken of the rollercoaster while it was in motion. The BBC has not been able to verify this statement.
Connor Thompson told the BBC's US partner CBS News that he was in line for the ride when everyone started "yelling, clearly distressed".
"Everyone was kind of confused at first, and then there was someone who was yelling, 'Call 911! Someone fell out!" he said. "At first it was almost like I didn't believe it because I thought that was like impossible for something like that to happen."
He said he saw the cart come into the hub where others were waiting in line and could see the restraint was unlatched.
Another witness, CiCi Nelson, told CNN she, too, was in line to ride the Goliath when the rollercoaster returned and she saw an empty seat with a loose safety bar and a female covered in blood.
Nelson described a scene of hysteria, adding that one man was "freaking out, saying someone fell off".
Brittany Landry, who believed she saw Kariem ejected from the rollercoaster, told Fox News she was in tears.
"I broke because we were just on there," she said.
Who is the victim Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem?
Kariem's family said he was a father, passionate educator and had survived two bouts of cancer.
His family told WXIA that he had survived cancer twice - the last stint in 2018 - and was in a car crash with his 10-year-old daughter three weeks before his death.
He lived in the nearby city of Atlanta and worked for Wesley International Academy, a public charter school, for more than 12 years as an IT manager, technology teacher and robotics coach.
"Mr. Kariem was deeply loved and respected, and his absence will be felt throughout our school community," the school said in a statement posted to its Facebook account.
"His love for Wesley, dedication to our students, and commitment to our school community were evident in everything he did."
Outside of work, Kariem enjoyed creating products with his laser engraver and 3D printers, as well as cooking, watching anime and spending time with family and friends, according to his profile on the school's website.
Has this happened before?
The death at Six Flags Over Georgia is at least the seventh there, according to the Doan Law Firm, which tracks amusement park accidents and represents victims.
According to the firm, this includes two people who had medical emergencies, two who were in restricted areas when they were struck by a ride, two who died in car-related accidents and one who died months after using the park's pool.
Six Flags operates 20 amusement parks, 14 water parks and nine resorts across Canada, the US and Mexico.
In the last 15 years, two deaths caused by falling from the park's rollercoasters led to lawsuits and settlements. One in 2011 involved an Iraq War veteran who was ejected from a ride in New York and hit his head on the car. In the other, in 2013, a woman slipped from her restraints on a rollercoaster in Texas and fell 75 feet.
In September, the Six Flags Magic Mountain park in California announced it was closing its X2 rollercoaster after more 100 people alleged that they had suffered brain injuries from the ride.
With additional reporting by Brandon Drenon

2312131de9cb.text:
Army converts Futures and Concepts Command to Futures and Autonomy Command
Officials released more details about its component organization under the Defense Department’s new Autonomous Warfare Command.
When Lt. Gen. Mac McCurry woke up Tuesday morning, he was the commander of the Army’s Futures and Concepts Command. By the afternoon, the service had announced that his outfit will become the recently announced Futures and Autonomy Command.
FASCOM will be the Army’s component organization within the Defense Department’s planned Autonomous Warfare Command, it announced Oct. 1.
“You know, we did decide to keep the patch, because that's honestly one of the hardest things to do,” McCurry said of his command’s uniform insignia, at the AUSA annual meeting in Washington, D.C. “If we can get the patch, we can get autonomy. I haven't ruled out Optimus Prime 6 as my future callsign.”
FASCOM’s commander will also become the Army’s first Portfolio Acquisition Executive for autonomy, with authority over the full procurement effort for autonomous systems.
“We are incorporating autonomous and unmanned systems at every single echelon, across the formation, with the force structure to match, including introducing UAS and robotics military specialties to integrate these technologies at the point of need,” Gen. Christopher LaNeve, the acting Army chief of staff, said Tuesday during a speech at the AUSA annual meeting.
FASCOM will function much the way Army Cyber Command and Army Special Operations Command support U.S. Cyber Command and U.S. Special Operations Command, with an Army mission and force structure that also reports to the joint combatant command.
The point of the larger autonomy project is not to start fully automating existing warfighting functions, said Alex Miller, the Army’s chief technology officer.
Autonomous systems will compile information and help commanders make decision, but there will be “appropriate levels of human judgment” before weapons are fired.
“Things like counter-battery fire, things like air and missile defense, things that happen at a superhuman speed and scale—want to have humans on the loop for decisions, but then we cannot be limited by you know the 20 watts that have up here,” Miller said, pointing to his head. “If we are taking thousands of drones or hundreds of rounds, we can't put that on a human. We want to enable them to be a crew chief for superintelligence and autonomy.”
The service secretaries and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth are slated to discuss more details about AUTOWARCOM on Wednesday during a panel at the final morning of AUSA’s annual meeting.

A weather system containing the remnants of Hurricane Isaias is forecast to send gales, heavy rain and a surge of warm air to parts of the UK this week.
The centre of the low, and its most significant impacts, will stay hundreds of miles from UK shores but north-west Scotland will see a spell of gales.
A Met Office yellow warning has been issued for parts of the Highlands and Western Isles with the risk of gusts touching 70mph (113km/h) in places.
Heavy rain will also affect parts of Scotland and Northern Ireland but much of England and Wales will remain largely dry with spells of sunshine.
The area of low pressure will also send a renewed surge of warm air across the country bringing above-average temperatures for many.
Hurricane remnants
Hurricane Isaias was the first Atlantic hurricane of the season and made landfall in the southern United States last Friday.
It weakened rapidly and ceased to be a hurricane but its remnants threw heavy rain across the eastern side of North America.
Since then, the leftovers have emerged over the Atlantic and been scooped up by a powerful jet stream.
This has developed a new area of low pressure that has been undergoing what meteorologists describe as explosive cyclogenesis, also referred to as a weather bomb.
The jet stream is steering the centre of the storm hundreds of miles away from our shores, passing close to Iceland where it will bring the threat of blizzards.
Wind gusts over the sea between Iceland and the Faroe Islands could exceed 110mph but nothing this severe is expected in the vicinity of the UK.
Where will the strongest winds be in the UK?
The far north-west of Scotland will bear the brunt of the winds.
A Met Office yellow weather warning is valid on Wednesday from 10:00 until 19:00 BST, and warns of a high risk of moderate impacts including disruption to rail, air and ferry transport, delays on roads and bridges - especially for high-sided vehicles - and possible short-term power cuts.
Widespread gusts of 50-60mph are likely with 70mph possible for exposed coasts and hills around the middle of the day.
Outside the warning area, Shetland is also anticipated to see 50mph gusts - although the risk of disruption here is less - and 40mph gusts are possible in other parts of Scotland, Northern Ireland, northern England and north-west Wales.
After a mainly dry start, outbreaks of rain are expected to arrive in many parts of Scotland and Northern Ireland by the end of the day, with heaviest rain in the north and west.
Some patchy rain may also spread into north-west England and north Wales, but most of both countries will stay fine with sunny spells after any early mist has cleared.
Surge of warmth to spread across UK
The deep area of low pressure is set to send warm south-westerly winds across the UK.
Temperatures will widely climb into the mid to high-teens Celsius, possibly peaking at 20C in a few locations in southern England.
This will leave most places 2-4C above the mid-October average.
This warmth will linger in many parts of England and Wales on Thursday with temperatures expected to peak at 22C in East Anglia.
However, a weather front will move slowly southwards taking rain across Scotland, Northern Ireland, northern England and north Wales and behind it things will start to turn cooler.
Those chillier - and eventually drier - conditions will then spread southwards across the UK through Friday and over the weekend.
Temperatures will fall much closer to the seasonal norm with brisk winds accentuating the colder feel around some eastern coasts and the chance of overnight frost in places.
Computer models suggest that high pressure will then settle close to the UK which should keep Atlantic low pressure systems at bay for the time being, bringing long spells of dry weather for many.
You can check your local weather prospects on the BBC Weather website and app.
