Four years after one of the most dramatic acts of sabotage in modern European history, a Ukrainian man goes on trial in Hamburg on Wednesday accused of blowing up Russia's Nord Stream gas pipelines to Germany.
Serhii K, as he is identified by German prosecutors, is accused of plotting with other Ukrainian military personnel to destroy the pipelines and stop Russia financing its war with gas revenue.
The case is highly sensitive in Germany, seen as one of Ukraine's closest allies since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, seven months before the attacks took place.
Serhii K, extradited to Germany last year, will become the first suspect to go on trial for the blasts.
He denies the charges, as does a second suspect who is fighting extradition from Croatia.
In the months after explosives destroyed three of the four gas pipelines in the Baltic Sea off the island of Bornholm on 26 September 2022, Western suspicion looked towards Moscow without directly apportioning blame.
Russia had already shut off the flow of gas to Germany in Nord Stream 1 weeks before the attack, and Nord Stream 2 had never been turned on. Berlin had frozen the multi-billion dollar project shortly before the invasion and there were reports of suspicious Russian naval movements before the blasts.
As investigators from Sweden, Denmark and Germany tried to find out who carried out the attack, Russia's Vladimir Putin accused the US and its UK allies, blaming "the Anglo-Saxons" - which they denied.
Eventually, after Denmark and Sweden shut down their inquiries, German prosecutors focused on a group of deep-sea divers who had rented a yacht called the Andromeda in the northern German port of Rostock.
They said later that "traces of subsea explosives were found in the samples taken from the boat".
Despite the strain on relations with Kyiv, German prosecutors pressed ahead with the case, and in January 2025 the German federal court of justice ruled that it fell within German territorial jurisdiction, external and prosecutors had a responsibility to act as it involved "undermining [Germany's] internal security".
Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky has always maintained that Ukraine had "nothing to do with [the Nord Stream blasts]", although in their indictment German prosecutors allege the saboteurs conceived the plot "acting by order of Ukrainian state agencies".
They say the case falls under Germany's code of crimes against international law as a war crime" as an attack by military means against civilian objects".
The case has highlighted differences of opinion on the trial in Kyiv and Berlin.
Oleksandr Merezhko, who chairs the Foreign Affairs Committee in the Ukrainian parliament, points out that the blasts took place during a time of war with Russia and "Nord Stream 2 was nothing but a tool used by Russia in order to get prepared for the war".
He told the BBC they had no confirmation of the German account: "It's one of the versions."
However, Stefan Meister, of the German Council on Foreign Relations, says successive chancellors in Berlin have done their best to remove the politics from the case.
"They tried to make not a big story out of it, not to give it too much attention, to give it to the institutions, to the judiciary that they will deal with it. This is not a political case. So they tried to depoliticise it," he explained.
In August 2025, Serhii K was arrested after checking into a hotel near the Italian Adriatic resort of Rimini, by police acting under a European arrest warrant issued by federal prosecutors in Germany.
After several weeks of court battles fighting extradition, Serhii K - identified in court documents as Serhii Kuznetsov - was transferred to Germany late last year.
German prosecutors allege that in 2022 he was a serving officer in the Ukrainian army, external, and he had led a group of professional divers, a boat captain and an explosives expert.
While his legal fight was going on in Italy, another Ukrainian man called Volodymyr Zhuravlov successfully challenged Germany's extradition bid in a Polish court.
In a ruling very different from Italy's Supreme Court, the Polish judge ordered Zhuravlov's release in October 2025, stating that the attack on the pipelines was not unlawful, and if Ukraine had organised an armed mission it was "justified, rational and just".
Although he was released by the court in Warsaw, he was arrested last August in Croatia on suspicion of being a suspect who "participated in the dives necessary" for the sabotage.
Last month, Croatia approved his extradition, although it is not clear when that will happen, and if his case could become part of the Hamburg trial.
Despite the difficult nature of the case for Kyiv and Berlin, Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko does not believe it will spoil relations as "it's in the best national interests of Germany to continue to support us".

f52073d57c5f.text: By — Madison Czopek, PolitiFact Madison Czopek, PolitiFact Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/does-a-russian-lab-workers-death-carry-pandemic-risk-experts-say-its-unlikely-with-one-caveat Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Does a Russian lab worker's death carry pandemic risk? Experts say it's unlikely, with one caveat Health Oct 13, 2026 7:32 PM EDT This article originally appeared on PolitiFact. It sounded familiar: Pneumonia reported near a lab studying infectious pathogens in a country where the government is known to conceal unfavorable information. Conflicting reports and unanswered questions about a potential pneumonic plague death in Russia on Oct. 2 returned memories of COVID-19's early days. READ MORE: What we know so far about a Russian lab worker's death and pneumonic plague A laboratory worker at an anti-plague research lab in Siberia died of an illness, and a local official initially reported the woman had died "possibly from the plague." The earliest reports sounded like the death followed an accidental lab exposure to pneumonic plague, the World Health Organization reported. Dozens of people had been quarantined or isolated. The WHO confirmed the woman's death followed her hospitalization with "severe pneumonia," but the exact pathogen that caused her illness has not been announced or independently verified. Adding to the confusion: Russian authorities reported no recent case of plague in Irkutsk Oblast, an administrative region in east-central Russia, where all this was said to have happened. Despite some of the situation's parallels to the coronavirus news of late 2019 and early 2020, virology and health security experts told PolitiFact's Well Informed they don't see signals this is a precursor to another pandemic crisis. The caveat, however, could be significant: Russian authorities' actions didn't align with their public statements. Although the government's official statement was that the lab worker had pneumonia of undetermined origin, Russia responded by putting 200 contacts under observation, quarantining a hospital and flying its top disease control leader to Irkutsk. "That is not how you respond to garden-variety pneumonia — and it isn't really how you'd respond to ordinary plague either, which has been curable with cheap antibiotics for decades," Dr. Amesh Adalja, senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security, said. Even without confirmation of the pathogen, however, the shape of spread is the most important factor to watch. "Pandemic potential shows up as a growing chain of human-to-human transmission, and that is not what we're seeing," he said. Adalja said no cluster of severe illness had developed among nearly 200 people who The Moscow Times reported were placed under medical observation. Hayley Anne Severance, deputy vice president for the Nuclear Threat Initiative's global biological policy and programs, said she needed more information before providing a global health risk assessment. "I am still in 'wait-and-see' mode," Severance said. "We need to know more about laboratory test findings, the treatments provided and her reaction to them, and any other potential exposure factors. We do not have confirmation of the causative agent, or if there even is an infectious agent involved, so we are flying in the dark here." Experts are watching Russian authorities, local media for reports of more cases Currently, about 10 days after the researcher's death, there have been no secondary cases confirmed in connection with the lab worker's death. "If this were a fast-spreading cluster, the window in which we'd expect to see it has basically passed," Adalja told Well Informed on Oct. 8. WATCH: Understanding pneumonic plague after Russian lab worker's death Other concerns would include expanding quarantine measures and Russian authorities refusing outside investigators or blocking a WHO team, Adalja said. Local media reports could also offer clues, Severance said. "I would be concerned if I begin to see reports from independent news outlets in Russia that there are unreported cases or deaths ongoing in the region that are not being acknowledged or confirmed by official Russian sources," she said. Standard pneumonic plague isn't a significant pandemic threat Pneumonic plague occurs when someone inhales respiratory droplets that contain the bacteria Yersinia pestis — or when the bacteria causing bubonic or septicemic plague spreads to the lungs. It can be treated with antibiotics. Without prompt treatment, pneumonic plague has "a nearly 100% case-fatality rate," according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. It is the only plague that can spread person to person, usually with prolonged contact. Measures such as masking could decrease disease spread. Pneumonic plague's incubation period is short — about one to four days — so it's less likely infected people would spread disease unknowingly, Severance said. "In past pneumonic plague outbreaks, on average, each infected person spread to between one and two others," and that dropped quickly with isolation measures, Severance said. Experts worry about information obstruction WHO officials said the illness that caused a lab worker's death in Russia presents a "very low" risk to people outside of Russia, based on available information. But more answers are needed. "A trained worker inside a plague research institute died of something still unexplained, and we're relying on the word of a government with a documented history of concealment on biosecurity," Adalja said. Ian Jones, a virology professor at the University of Reading in the United Kingdom, said it was "almost unbelievable" that scientists hadn't identified the cause of the lab worker's pneumonia given modern testing capabilities. Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using artificial intelligence (AI) to write his short story, which won this year's Caine Prize for African Writing.
His statement comes a week after he scooped the Â£10,000 ($13,000) award and a recent article in The Atlantic said AI-detection software Pangram had shown his work about a boy whose family falls on hard times was entirely AI generated.
"For the avoidance of doubt, I wrote The Blue Fighter," he posted on X, external.
The accusation has caused an uproar on social media and Caine Prize chair Ellah Wakatama told the BBC she was shocked that the US magazine had not waited for a full investigation before publishing.
"I do wish The Atlantic had spent more time investigating this so that alongside Pangram, they did have evidence of real human investigation of it before tainting the prize and tainting this winner," Wakatama told the BBC's Front Row programme.
The chair of the Caine Prize's board of trustees said she had been contacted on Friday about the allegation and Vauhini Vara's article - Yet Another Prizewinner Seems to Be AI, external - had been published on Sunday.
It follows rows over other literary prizes this year, in particular the Commonwealth Short Story Prize, which was won by Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir despite allegations that he had used AI, and the withdrawal of Canadian-Haitian author ThÃ©lyson OrÃ©lien from France's top literary award, the Goncourt, over allegations he used AI for his first novel, which he denies.
Vara, who quoted Wakatama in her article, said her wariness of Silicon Valley was "well founded and reasonable" but she said Pangram's internal research showed its assessments were rarely wrong.
The backlash to the article on social media has included comments from African writers with suggestions that such accusations are primarily being made against non-white writers.
Wale Lawal, the Nigerian founder of The Republic magazine, called out The Atlantic article for being "crazy, racist and wildly unethical", external.
Zimbabwean writer Joe Ruzvidzo, whose novel Welcome to Anywhere came out last year, said he stood by Kundizeza and that it was time "to fight this literary stop-and-frisk", external.
Nigerian publisher Modupe Daramola said it was necessary to discuss how "these AI allegations are targeting Black and African writers" and how they were often disproportionately scrutinised.
"There's something incredibly sinister about this," the Noisy Streetss Limited publisher posted on X, external.
"Pangram is itself AI-powered. Why should its assessment be treated as definitive?" she added.
Wakatama said as part of an internal investigation for the Caine Prize Kundizeza would be sending in documentation about his various drafts and there were ongoing conversations with all the judges and The Shallow Tales Review, the publication that first published The Blue Fighter in 2025, external.
In his statement, Kundizeza said had "a concrete, documented history" about the story's inspiration and he set out the chronology of its development.
Wakatama, who is also editor-at-large at Canongate Books, said Caine Prize submissions, which are all previously published, were not checked for AI, but writers vouched that their work was original.
She added that she was not against using AI per se to check entries, but she was "against is it being used as a final arbiter in this case".
I am not happy for the work of writers, and in this case especially black writers, to form the testing ground for something that is at best still rough and ready"
Wakatama said it was also important to remember Pangram was "not yet tested".
"I am not happy for the work of writers, and in this case especially black writers, to form the testing ground for something that is at best still rough and ready."
Research has found that AI detectors can wrongly flag human writing as AI generated. Vara conceded that any AI-detection product, "including one as good of Pangram" was "not going to be 100% accurate".
In her article, as well as citing Pangram research she also quoted a recent paper by researchers at Free University of Brussels, external, which said it had found zero cases of Pangram, and two other AI-detection tools, getting it wrong when it came to English-language writing by non-native English speakers.
The study notes that tools like Pangram should be considered "as an initial flag for further investigation".
Vara told BBC's Front Row programme that she had also used her own judgment "to suss out these things" and that every other previous Caine Prize winning story she had put through Pangram "came out as 100% human".
"I also found an earlier 2021 story by the same author. I ran that through Pangram. It also came out as 100% human. And what struck me was that was a really good, interesting story. And tonally, it's so different from this story, as if the same person hadn't written both."
In response Kundizeza wrote: "To suggest that a writer cannot write in different styles or genres, or improve his writing substantially after five or more years fundamentally misunderstands the craft of writing."
For Vara, one of the stylistic issues that stood out about The Blue Fighter was that it had used sentence constructions using "X but Y", which she says is common in AI-generated texts.
"Not with anger, but with the quiet resignation of someone who had known all along this moment would come," is an example she gave from the story that described the character of the mother.
"The proliferation of those struck me," Vara told Front Row, adding that the story also had a lot of metaphors, also prevalent in writing generated by AI.
The day after winning the Caine Prize, Kundizeza told the BBC he was inspired after hearing a poem read by South African Vangile Gantsho at an event in Ghana last year about her father's obsession with building fish tanks.

An emotional scene of an elephant carrying a deceased calf has earned Italian photographer Federico Veronesi the title of Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026.
While tracking elephants in Namibia's Huab River Valley, Veronesi spotted an unusual trail of drag marks across the sand of a dry riverbed.
Following the tracks, he came across a female elephant carrying a dead calf, its leg wedged between her tusk and trunk.
Initially, Veronesi assumed the elephant was the calf's mother. But after sharing his photographs with an elephant research project working in the area, he learned that this wasn't certain.
Researchers recognised the elephant as a female who had lost a calf several years earlier and said she had previously picked up dead calves belonging to other females.
For Veronesi, the encounter was deeply significant. "Of all the 20 years I've done photographing animals, this is the most heart-wrecking and fascinating and dramatic," he said, describing it as "revealing of the depth and complexity of the emotions, the feelings of the animals."
He hopes the image will encourage people to look beyond animals' physical appearance and recognise them as individuals with their own relationships, memories and emotions. "It's a small window that opens just a crack into the complexity of their world," he said.
The competition's annual exhibition, external opens at the Natural History Museum on Friday 16 October 2026. Keep scrolling to see more award-winning images.
Labour of love
Category: Young Grand Title and 11 to 14 Years
Photographer: Oscar Whitfield, Zimbabwe/UK
Location: Zambezi National Park, Zimbabwe
Only by lying in the dust and capturing the beetle at eye level could Whitfield show how much strength its task required.
While on a family game drive in Zimbabwe, near his home in Victoria Falls, he spotted the dung beetle struggling to push a ball of dung uphill through the sand, with a trail of flies following closely behind. After experimenting with different angles and compositions, he captured a moment that reveals the extraordinary effort involved in this seemingly simple task.
"I hope that when people look at the photograph, they can see too, and maybe appreciate how much can be happening in a small moment in the natural world," says Whitfield.
Flight of the Bumblebee
Category: 10 Years and Under
Photographer: Amelie Davis, UK
Location: Surrey, England
You do not need a camera or a plane ticket to take an award-winning photo. Davis captured this shot in the garden using her dad's smartphone.
The image freezes in time a single wingbeat from a common carder bumblebee as it prepares to land on a flower.
The Meeting Place
Category: Animals in their Environment
Photographer: James Lewin, UK
Location: Chyulu Hills National Park, Kenya
Lewin captured this dreamy, black-and-white photo of a young bull elephant spraying zebras at a waterhole.
He softened the usually harsh light by using a camera converted to infrared.
A Watchful Eye
Category: Animal Portraits
Photographer: Aaron Sanders, UK
Location: Porthkerris Beach, Cornwall
Common octopuses are usually found in the warmer Mediterranean Sea. But with global warming pushing up springtime sea temperatures, sightings across south-west England have massively increased.
Sanders described the moment he spotted a single eye peeking from behind the kelp: "We remained perfectly still, watching one another with a seemingly shared curiosity."
Scenes from the Swamp
Category: Birds
Photographer: Isak Pretorius, South Africa
Location: Mabamba Swamp, Uganda
Fewer than 5,300 mature shoebill storks are estimated to remain in the wild. Yet Pretorius, while canoeing with a guide, was able to capture these two â likely a breeding pair collecting material for their nest.
Despite their name, shoebill storks are actually more closely related to pelicans, herons and ibises.
Birdsong Painted in Light
Category: 15-17 Years
Photographer: Konrad GrÃ¤eter, Germany
Location: Baden-WÃ¼rttemberg, Germany
Spring sees male blackbirds search for high vantage points to sing and try to attract a mate.
This photo was taken in a vineyard at dawn, when the birds sing their most complex compositions.
Urban Jungle
Category: Urban Wildlife
Photographer: Seth Forestson, UK
Location: Lumphini Park, Bangkok, Thailand
Forestson lowered himself onto the mud to capture this common water lizard against the city skyline.
These adaptable lizards live in cities across South and South East Asia and will take whatever food is available, such as catfish and koi.
Making Morays
Category: Under Water
Photographer: Tony Wu, USA/Japan
Location: Kagoshima Prefecture, KyÅ«shÅ«, Japan
This is probably the first time the courtship ritual of Abbott's moray eels has been photographed, the NHM said.
Wu worked with biologists and used dim red light and a customised fisheye lens to minimise disturbance.
Wily Coyotes of San Francisco
Category: Photojournalist Story Award
Photographer: Loren Elliott, USA
Location: USA
San Francisco is estimated to be home to around 100 coyotes, living alongside a large human population. While they can prey on domestic animals, they also help control disease-carrying rodents, and residents' attitudes towards them are mixed.
Protective Pose
Category: Behaviour: Amphibians and Reptiles
Photographer: Anton Sorokin, US

Sorokin dipped his camera and lights in a murky pond to catch this glimpse of a California newt laying her eggs.
Shifting Sand

A scorpion is photographed burrowing into the shifting dunes of India's Thar Desert.
Exploring the dunes at night, Raul saw many scorpions searching for prey but as temperatures rose after sunrise, the scorpion dug into the sand to escape the intense heat.

ce0f8ccc0869.text: House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) needs Latino voters to stick with Republicans as they did in 2024. But new polling shows they're drifting back toward Democrats at levels not seen in years. Why it matters: Latino voters souring on President Trump has been part of the mood music of the president's second term. Democrats hope this helps them replicate the landslide from Trump's first midterm in 2018. The big picture: Democrats have their widest lead of the year against Republicans, 57% to 31%, on the generic congressional ballot, according to new polling from Equis Research. In battleground districts, Democrats lead 62%–38% among likely Latino voters in two-way races, ahead of the party's 2022 level of 57%. That's well above the 49% of Latinos who voted Democratic in 2024, but below the 67% who backed Democrats in 2018, according to Equis , a leading authority on Latino voting behavior. Zoom in: Republicans were convinced that Trump's undeniable gains in 2024 represented the beginnings of a real realignment, but poll after poll this year has indicated that Latino voters haven't found a permanent home in the GOP. In Florida, GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar has addressed Trump directly in a campaign ad about his immigration crackdown. The Equis survey, conducted Sept. 23–Oct. 2, provides fresh evidence of Trump's declining support among Latino voters. Trump's approval rating stands at just 30%, compared with 65% disapproval. That's a 35-point deficit — and a new low in Equis surveys. Between the lines: Economic concerns — and rising gas prices — are driving much of the dissatisfaction, particularly the cost of living. 76% of Latino voters disapprove of Trump's handling of the cost of living, which 52% identify as their top issue. 54% trust Democrats more on the economy, compared with 33% who trust Republicans. That gives Democrats a 21-point advantage on the economy, up from just 7 points in February. The bottom line: Latino voters helped put Trump back in the White House. The Equis survey is the latest indication they could help Democrats take back Congress. Note: The Equis survey was conducted Sept. 23–Oct. 2 via phone and text-to-web with 1,800 registered voters who identify as Hispanic or Latino nationally. The sample was weighted to match the composition of registered voters modeled as Latino by state, gender, age, education, vote history, voter registration date, VCH score and 2024 vote recall.

a009dec71825.text: Congressional Democrats' private text chains lit up with fear and anger on Monday after Department of Homeland Security agents searched Rep. Ilhan Omar's (D-Minn.) home in Washington, D.C. Why it matters: The search came less than a month before the midterms , immediately setting off alarm bells among Democrats that "more October surprises" could be coming, as one senior Democrat told Axios. Rep. Becca Balint (D-Vt.) told Axios: "We expect more of this kind of thing." Driving the news: Homeland Security Investigations "executed a judicially authorized search warrant" on Omar's home as part of an ongoing immigration probe, the Justice Department said in a statement. DOJ has not detailed the scope or subject of the search warrant. Fox News reported the investigation concerns Omar's immigration paperwork. She came to the United States in 1995 as a 12-year-old refugee from Somalia. Omar's office and Democratic House leadership quickly denounced the action as an "abuse of power," with a spokesperson for Omar saying she "has done nothing wrong." What we're hearing: "People are outraged. ... [This is] what authoritarian tyrants and dictators do," said the senior House Democrat, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to relay colleagues' private conversations. Another House Democrat told Axios "the chatter on texts" is that "folks are irate." Zoom out: Democrats allege the raid fits into a broader pattern of Trump using federal resources to boost Republicans and target his political opponents. DHS became embroiled in controversy just last week after a statement targeting Pennsylvania Democrat Janelle Stelson, which critics said violates federal laws restricting partisan activities by federal officials. Trump has also come under fire for using taxpayer funds to run campaign-style television ads touting him and his administration in the run-up to the midterms. What they're saying: "President Trump will keep trying to intimidate and bully Americans ahead of the midterms," said Balint, adding, "We suspect he will try anything to stay in power and in control." Rep. Mark Pocan (D-Wis.) said that "of course there will" be more like the Omar raid, saying Trump is "the pettiest, worst human being" and "can't help himself." Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.) told Axios: "This is some serious hate-baiting bullshit. This administration is just despicable." Asked whether he expects more, Huffman said, "Of course." The other side: One congressional Republican cheered the raid on Omar, who has long been the target of right-wing attacks on her immigration status. "If the fraud is proven, she should be denaturalized and deported," Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.) wrote in a post on X , also comparing Monday's raid to the 2022 FBI search of Mar-a-Lago . The White House, DOJ and DHS did not respond to a request for comment. What to watch: House Democratic leaders are already signaling plans to wrap this into their oversight agenda if they retake the majority. "We will deliver full accountability for the rogue abuse of power from the Department of Homeland Security and Department of Justice," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) and his deputies said in a statement. House Judiciary Committee ranking member Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) said in a statement: "We will be demanding transparency and accountability as to who authorized this abusive search and who carried it out."

e8a21de2d7d3.text:
- Published
US actress Selma Blair has been charged with two additional assault counts over allegedly kicking an officer and a nurse after being removed from a flight.
Blair was arrested late Sunday in New York after she allegedly attacked flight attendants on a Delta plane travelling from Los Angeles to New York. The FBI issued her a federal summons accusing her of assault on board.
While appearing in court over the additional charges, the Legally Blonde star's attorney asked the judge to consider the actress's "body of work", and called Blair the "gold standard." The judge said she should not "get special treatment".
Blair has pleaded not guilty. She has since been released on bail.
She was taken to hospital after the incident on the flight. Her representatives have told the BBC that she had "experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct".
As the flight landed in New York on Sunday evening, airport officials responded to a call about "a physically abusive passenger" on the flight. Two flight attendants were hurt and one was taken to hospital, the New York Port Authority said.
Audio recorded on air traffic control details a pilot asking for medical help, describing "a bloody nose" and "some bite marks", according to CBS News, BBC's US News partner.
Blair, 54, who also starred in Cruel Intentions and Hellboy, was arrested and taken to hospital. She was issued a federal summons for a charge of assault within the special maritime and territorial jurisdiction of the US.
The two additional charges of assault, filed in state court, came after she was taken off the plane.
One of the alleged assaults happened when she was being transported in an ambulance, where she allegedly kicked a police officer. Once at hospital, prosecutors allege that she also assaulted a nurse.
At her arraignment in Queens, Blair's attorney Shawn Barnes asked the judge for leniency. He said that "violence" is "not who she is" and asked for the judge to consider her body of work.
The actress is somebody that people she look up to, he said, referring to her as "the gold standard".
The judge denied his request and said she "should not get special treatment...because she is a celebrity".
The judge set her bail at $20,000 cash or $60,000 bond with the next hearing scheduled for 19 January. It is unclear when a date will be set for the federal case against her, which concerns the allegations of assault aboard the aircraft.

e5013e59a1d6.text: On her first day at the podium, new White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia made news. She announced that President Trump has asked his son's former fiancée and ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, to resign amid allegations that she sought $100,000 from a donor. White House correspondent Liz Landers reports. Amna Nawaz: On her first day at the podium, the new White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia, made news. Geoff Bennett: That was by announcing that President Trump had asked Kimberly Guilfoyle, his ambassador to Greece, to resign. The move follows allegations that Guilfoyle asked the political donor to pay a $100,000 credit card bill in exchange for access to senior administration officials. Our White House correspondent, Liz Landers, was at the briefing today and joins us now. So, Liz, the news of the Guilfoyle resignation operates on two levels. There's what led to the resignation and the fact that President Trump was willing to part ways with this official, when he has so often stood by others accused of using their public office for personal gain. What more should we know? Liz Landers: This was a surprising announcement today from this new White House press secretary, who made this announcement from the podium, and then two hours later, on social media, Ambassador Guilfoyle confirmed that she was resigning. She wrote that she called the allegations against her false and said that "I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity." She went on to say: "I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service." She also said that she will continue to support President Trump. But all of this comes in light of that bombshell Wall Street Journal reporting that came out last week that said that Guilfoyle had engaged in possible improper conduct. Most notably of that was a political donor who said and accused her of trying to bribe him to pay off a $100,000 credit card statement. And she promised him access to administration officials if he did. The president was asked about this on his way out of the White House today. And he said "I didn't like what I was reading" about what Kim Guilfoyle had been doing. But this may not be over for Guilfoyle, though. PBS News obtained last week this letter from the Democrats -- the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, who had already sent her a letter saying, please preserve your records related to this, and saying that they wanted to investigate this. Geoff Bennett: And, of course, we learned about her parting ways with the administration, her resignation, by way of a very brief White House briefing today, the debut of the new press secretary. You were there. Tell us about it and the new press secretary. Liz Landers: Yes, so Katie Zacharia is most recently an adviser to the Trump Media and Technology Group, which runs the president's social media company, TRUTH Social. She's also worked briefly at the Department of Homeland Security. She's also been a frequent conservative commentator on FOX News and sometimes on CNN. And she's been an ardent defender of President Trump, and she is a MAGA loyalist. She has promoted the falsehood that the 2020 election was stolen. And CNN also found some now deleted social media posts of hers making baseless accusations about Democrats being engaged in pedophilia. Geoff Bennett: And what else stood out from her briefing? Liz Landers: It was only 14 minutes long, and she only took a handful of questions towards the end. Zacharia says that she sees her job as highlighting the administration's policy wins for the American people and promoting the president's message. Katie Zacharia, White House Press Secretary: My goal is to be able to communicate that in complete tandem with the president, as he is his own best spokesperson and will absolutely be leading the way as with that. Liz Landers: President Trump, as they left the White House, was asked what he thought about her performance at the podium. He said he thought she did a great job. And in that exchange, he was also asked about her credentials. She says that she has been an attorney, and she had to kind of clarify and explain that she has been a practicing lawyer in China before, but she does have her law degree from Pepperdine's law school. Geoff Bennett: OK. I want to ask you as we wrap up our conversation here about this moment last night. It was at a Trump rally in Ohio. There was a protester. You see her there physically assaulted, physically assaulted by a man, by the way. And rather than condemn the violence, the president mocked the protester. That's hard to watch. I mean, what more do we know about what happened? Liz Landers: We're increasingly seeing these protesters interrupting the president's midterm rallies, and this happened yesterday in Youngstown, Ohio. That woman was wearing a shirt that said 'Release the Epstein Files." And right beside her, this man starts punching her, hitting her directly in the face before law enforcement steps in. Something like this also occurred in San Antonio, Texas, last week at another Trump rally, where protesters were getting beat up. And actually the sheriff there put out an announcement and said if anybody has any information about these people that were potentially assaulting protesters, please come forward. Geoff Bennett: All right, Liz Landers, our thanks to you, as always. Liz Landers: Of course.

2e95d2483d65.text: The threat of a widening war on the Arabian Peninsula is accelerating. Houthi rebels in Yemen are again targeting Saudi infrastructure and military sites, escalating a conflict which may yet draw in other regional powers. The Saudi-led coalition launched new airstrikes on oil facilities across Houthi-controlled Yemen in response to deadly airport attacks in Riyadh. Ali Rogin reports. Geoff Bennett: The threat of a wider war in the Arabian Peninsula is growing tonight. Houthi rebels in Yemen are once again targeting Saudi military installations and critical infrastructure, raising fears of a broader regional conflict that could draw in other powers. Amna Nawaz: The Saudi-led coalition launched new airstrikes on oil facilities across Houthi-controlled Yemen in response to a deadly attack on an international airport in the Saudi capital of Riyadh. That attack over the weekend killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300. Ali Rogin has this report. Ali Rogin: Today in Yemen's principal port city on the Red Sea coast, plumes of smoke engulfed blue skies, all part of a Saudi-led bombing campaign targeting Houthi-controlled territory and oil facilities. And, in Eastern Saudi Arabia, loud booms echoed in the night skies. Saudi officials said fragments of an intercepted missile launched by the Houthis fell in a residential area. This follows weekend attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis that turned a crowded airport in Riyadh into chaos. Saturday's attack at King Khalid International Airport killed at least 13 people and injured more than 300, among the dead, an Egyptian flight attendant who was 28 years old and a Jordanian father of two who worked at a coffee shop inside the airport. His father called the death an indescribable loss. Hassan Al-Barqawi, Father of Airport Attack Victim (through interpretor): I hope that no other human being ever experiences what I have gone through, because no one can understand this loss except the one who has suffered it. Ali Rogin: For Saudi Arabia, the failure of its air defenses to intercept the incoming missiles and drones has further raised fears and questions on how far the kingdom is prepared to go in response, a sentiment the Saudi energy minister echoed yesterday. Prince Abdulaziz Bin Salman, Saudi Arabian Energy Minister: The events of recent weeks are serious. Our response must be equally serious. For Saudi Arabia, these circumstances have tested our infrastructure, our institution, our people, and our resilience. Ali Rogin: Earlier today, the Houthis renewed their warning against using Saudi airspace, calling the country the -- quote -- "kingdom of the horn of Satan" and released footage allegedly showing attacks on Saudi-backed government forces northeast of Yemen's capital, Sanaa. Saudi allies, including Turkey, called for the Houthis to immediately halt such strikes. Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Turkish President (through interpretor): Turkey stands with Saudi Arabia and its Saudi brothers in the face of unlawful and inhumane attacks. Ali Rogin: Turkey's President Recep Erdogan also said he would submit a defense pact struck among Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan to the Parliament for ratification in the coming days. This comes as Saudi Arabia is pushing Washington for more direct military support. President Donald Trump: The Houthis have acted very badly. Ali Rogin: Today, President Trump weighed in, saying he talked with the Saudi crown prince. Question: Did you speak to the Saudi crown prince? President Donald Trump: I did, yes. I spoke to him. Question: And what did you offer him? President Donald Trump: Well, I can't tell you that. Do you really think I could tell you that? I'd love to tell you, but I'm not going to tell you that. Ali Rogin: But the U.S. has stopped short of sending military assets to attack Yemen, which could further threaten shipping through the Bab al-Mandab, a vital shipping route and southern gateway to the Red Sea that is especially key for oil exports from Saudi Arabia, which the Houthis have targeted. In the meantime, as threats grow, the consequences are already visible, a Yemeni town engulfed in smoke, an airport turned to rubble, and mounting funerals for civilians caught in the crossfire. For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Ali Rogin.

bf3c13a45294.text:
Wyoming has shelved a state-funded project to measure water use in the Green River and Little Snake River basins after it could not get enough data to create a basin-wide estimate of water lost during irrigation.
At a meeting in the Cowboy State capitol of Cheyenne last month, members of the Wyoming Water Development Commission (WWDC) reported that difficulty gaining access to landowners’ ditches coupled with unexpected costs prevented the contractor from securing access to all 20 irrigation ditches the company planned to survey.
With only 12 ditches measured, the company’s data did not produce “statistical significance for larger basin characterization,” said Chace Tavelli, the project’s manager with the Wyoming Water Development Office.
“All data is good data to have,” he added. “We learned about challenges, and there are some ditches that appear to have information that could be very valuable.”
Wyoming water managers said the measuring efforts could one day resume as part of a coordinated effort with Colorado, New Mexico and Utah to gauge water consumption in each state’s portion of the Upper Colorado River Basin, which includes the Green and Little Snake rivers in Wyoming.
The project was part of Wyoming’s ongoing efforts to account for the water it uses in its portion of the basin, where every drop used, lost or saved must be meticulously accounted for amid a punishing drought and difficult negotiations over how to split the river’s dwindling flows.
“Wyoming’s got studies galore going on on irrigation efficiencies,” said Michael Henn, district manager of the Sublette County Conservation District in the Green River Basin. “This was just one piece of trying to make sure that we have an understanding of how the water in Wyoming’s portion of the basin is getting used, and any potential impacts to that.”
In 2023, the Wyoming legislature appropriated $500,000 to study water lost to irrigation in the Green and Snake River basins. The next year, the Wyoming Water Development Commission awarded just over $400,000 to Stantec Consulting Services to measure water in 20 irrigation ditches in the region. The company held two public meetings that April, one in Baggs and another in Pinedale, and “that’s when the project started experiencing some challenges,” Tavelli said.
“It was difficult to get ditches that were good examples of the basin and obtain access and get landowner participation there—to no fault of landowners or the consultant,” Tavelli said.
Henn, who attended the meeting in Pinedale, remembered some landowners being split on the idea of measuring water lost in their ditches. “Some people don’t necessarily care to have government of any level on their property working, and some do,” he said. “Especially with water.”
Tavelli echoed that sentiment in his presentation at the WWDC meeting. “You’re accessing and you’re potentially interrupting their irrigation system,” he said, adding that landowners aren’t to blame for the project falling through.

The geography of the basins may have also complicated the state’s efforts. Farmers and ranchers so close to the basin’s headwaters do not always have mile-long ditches with no diversions in them, a condition required by the study, said Mike Vickery, a rancher in the Upper Green River basin.
“We just [have more diversions] ‘cause we’re so close to the river system,” he said, and as a result, ditches can be smaller with several diversion points branching off.
Tavelli said some ditches did not have water measurement devices, called flumes, installed at the head of the system. This meant Stantec Consulting Services had to install a flume at each end of the ditch, increasing the project’s costs.
Despite the lack of a basin-wide estimate of water loss, gathering data on water losses in the basin is valuable for Wyoming.
“It’s good to understand when you divert water where it’s going. That helps landowners with conservation practices,” Henn said, adding that it better prepares his organization to apply for grant funding for water conservation projects.
The data is also important for Wyoming as it navigates the broader upheaval in the Colorado River Basin, home to roughly 40 million people across seven states, 30 tribes and Mexico.
The agriculture industry is by far the largest water user in the Colorado River Basin.
As a member of the Upper Basin, along with Colorado, New Mexico and Utah, Wyoming has been developing a conservation program within its borders in response to declining flows in the Colorado River, which scientists attribute in part to climate change. Such a program would also help the Upper Basin show Arizona, California and Nevada, the Lower Colorado River Basin states, that it can conserve a meaningful amount of water voluntarily—a major negotiating point across the basin. For such conservation efforts to generate credit for the water they save, Wyoming and other Upper Basin states would need to show they know how much water is lost during transportation.
In Wyoming, “the data is important so we can prove how much water we’re really using, and where it’s going,” said Vickery, who is a member of Wyoming’s Colorado River advisory committee.
“Whatever comes out of my ditch, there’s a strong likelihood it ends back up in the river,” he said. “Those are also things we want to be able to prove.”
At the Cheyenne meeting, WWDC Director Jason Mead said the Upper Colorado River Commission has started an Upper Basin-wide study to measure the difference between water entering ditches and the amount that returns to the river—also known as “incidental use.”
“We’re hoping that will be more successful,” he said.

ce6e104b1d65.text: To discuss the escalating war between the Houthis in Yemen and Saudi Arabia, Amna Nawaz spoke with Michael Ratney. He served as U.S. ambassador to Saudi Arabia during the Biden administration and is now a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. Amna Nawaz: For perspective on the escalating war between Houthis in Yemen and Saudi Arabia, we turn now to Michael Ratney. He served as U.S. ambassador to Saudi Arabia during the Biden administration. He's now a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. Ambassador, welcome back to the show. It's worth reminding people there was actually an informal cease-fire in place between the Saudis and the Houthis in Yemen until just July of this year. What do you make of how dramatically and how quickly this conflict has escalated? Michael Ratney, Center for Strategic and International Studies: So what began as a six-month truce a few years ago was extended into a de facto cease-fire really until just a few months ago, as you point out. And it seems as though, at that point, the Houthis, who had more or less been in abeyance since the start of the Iran war at the end of February, got into the fight. The Iranians were helping them, seemingly transporting advisers and weapons. The Saudis felt they needed to respond. The Houthis, in a sort of lightning campaign, took coastal positions on the Bab al-Mandab that threatened shipping of oil. It threatened Saudi energy infrastructure. And from there, things have just deteriorated badly. Amna Nawaz: It's also worth pointing out Saudi Arabia is the largest customer for U.S. arms exports. They spend tens of billions of dollars for U.S. warplanes and air defense systems. Why have they not been able to intercept or repel these Houthi attacks? Michael Ratney: So the Saudis have considerable air defenses, a lot of it U.S.-origin Patriots, for example, but it's stretched thin. You can imagine they're prioritizing their energy infrastructure, which is still the lifeblood of their economy, and they need more. And the Houthis are able to attack in a very asymmetric way, sometimes in ways that defy conventional air defense systems. So they do have air defenses. They need more. And that attack, that brutal attack on the airport just a few days ago, is really evidence. Amna Nawaz: You were just in Saudi Arabia recently. What was the mood on the ground there? Michael Ratney: So I was there last week, and there was a first attack on the airport the day after I got there, and it created some anxiety. And then this really horrific attack in which multiple people died and many, many casualties was the day after I left. And you had the sense that the Saudi people were, on the one hand, in solidarity. They were angry at what the Houthis were doing, but I think they were somewhat anxious about the direction of this conflict. It's one thing for the Saudis to strike Houthis targets in Yemen, which they're doing in force today, but it's pretty clear that the Houthis have this ability to respond asymmetrically in really, really horrible ways, not just attacking infrastructure, but really targeting civilians, trying to murder civilians in Riyadh and elsewhere. Amna Nawaz: You heard President Trump there say he's been in contact with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. He said he's weighing joining in on this fight. There's also reporting that he rejected a request from Mohammed bin Salman last month to do so. What do you see happening here? Do you see the U.S. joining in this fight? Michael Ratney: So I sense the Saudis are pretty frustrated. We and they have invested decades in this military partnership, and one of the expectations is, when the chips are down, when the country is under attack, that the U.S. would support them. Now, there's credible reports that the U.S. is offering some assistance in the form of intelligence sharing or targeting and planning. But what the Saudis really want and need are U.S. airstrikes that can seriously degrade the Houthis' ability to launch these strikes. Trump has been ambivalent about that. The president at times has said that he's supportive of the Saudis, but it seems like, either because of limitations on U.S. military capacity or because, as a political matter, he doesn't want to open another front in the war, he's been really reluctant to get involved further. Amna Nawaz: What are the Saudi options for dealing with the Houthis at this point and what has to happen in order for this conflict not to escalate further? Michael Ratney: There's no real good options at this point. This was the inevitable, predictable escalation of the Iran war that started months ago. And I think the Saudis and others in the Gulf knew that this would happen eventually. The Houthis, although in some sense are a proxy of the Iranians, are also quite independent-minded or are not necessarily controlled by them. So I think for the moment the Saudi options are take the gloves off, and they're doing that with some concerted airstrikes against the Houthis. But I think ultimately they have to get back to some kind of uncomfortable, imperfect diplomacy to de-escalate this, because the implications not just for global energy markets, for the Saudi economy, for the Saudi public, are pretty dire. Amna Nawaz: That is the former U.S. Ambassador to Saudi Arabia Michael Ratney joining us tonight. Ambassador, thank you so much for your time. Michael Ratney: Any time.

47edb0c44dcb.text: In our news wrap Tuesday, Cornell University is banning parties and other social events at fraternities for the rest of the academic year, a man fell to his death while riding a roller coaster at a Six Flags amusement park outside Atlanta, the Supreme Court will hear a case over access to DOGE records and a bipartisan group of senators is condemning President Trump's diesel deal with Russia. Amna Nawaz: We start the day's other headlines in New York. Cornell University is banning parties and other social events at fraternities for the rest of the academic year. The Ivy League school is also giving state police a role in investigating sex crimes on campus, among other measures. Cornell's president says the steps are aimed at providing time to evaluate whether Greek life there can continue and to find out what he called safe social alternatives. The school has faced an uproar both on campus and around the country over its handling of allegations that a female student known as Jane Doe was gang-raped at a fraternity house in 2024. All seven men she's accused have denied any wrongdoing. In Georgia, police have identified the man who fell to his death while riding a roller coaster at a Six Flags amusement park outside of Atlanta; 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem was an employee at an Atlanta charter school, according to local school officials. He was found unresponsive when investigators arrived on the scene yesterday afternoon at the Goliath. That's the tallest roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia. Authorities say his body struck and injured other riders despite efforts by fellow passengers to save him. Woman: He turns, sideways and he's flipping in the air. He comes down. He slams down on our cart. People reached out trying to grab him. Like, everybody tried to save this man. And we couldn't. Like, we couldn't. Man: We literally could not. There was no -- there was too much force to grab him. Amna Nawaz: Aerial footage shows people on the next train evacuating mid-ride. Six Flags says it is temporarily closing a number of similar roller coasters across the U.S. and Canada as a precaution. The U.S. Supreme Court says it will hear a case over access to DOGE records. A watchdog group argues that the agency, once run by Elon Musk and officially known as the Department of Government Efficiency, should be subject to Freedom of Information Act requests. The Trump administration says it is exempt from that access as a presidential advisory body. Oral arguments are expected early next year. Also today, the court said it would consider whether a Nigerian man who cooked for terrorists can be denied asylum in the U.S. The case could expand how officials view what counts as terrorist activity under U.S. immigration law. In Las Vegas, a former gang leader was sentenced to 40 years to life in prison today for orchestrating the murder of rap icon Tupac Shakur in 1996. Woman: The world never forgot about him and his death, and neither did Las Vegas. It took us 30 years, but, at this time, you are going to face justice for what you did on September 7, 1996. Amna Nawaz: Duane "Keffe D" Davis showed little emotion in court as the judge delivered his sentence. The 63-year-old was convicted of first-degree murder in August. Shakur was the victim of a drive-by shooting off the Vegas Strip and later died in a hospital. Until Davis was arrested in 2023, the murder was one of the nation's most notorious cold cases. And legal questions remain over who actually pulled the trigger. A bipartisan group of senators is condemning President Trump's diesel deal with Russia. In a letter to the president, six Republicans and six Democrats write that -- quote -- "This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our allies. It should be rescinded." Last week, President Trump said Russia would -- quote -- "immediately supply diesel fuel to global markets," including the possibility of the U.S. In their letter, the senators argued that this would have a negligible impact on energy prices and would instead help to fuel Russia's war machine. In France, police and protesters clashed today as demonstrators once again took to the streets to call for improvements to the country's education system. In Paris, authorities used water cannons and tear gas to try to clear the crowds. The country's Interior Ministry estimates that more than 160,000 people took part in demonstrations nationwide today. The protests started last month over a lack of staff and poor school conditions. Since then, hundreds have been injured and the police have made thousands of arrests. The U.S. Treasury Department is fining Bank of America $1.2 billion over alleged money laundering and sanctions violations. The penalty is the third largest in the department's history. Officials say the bank failed to report billions of dollars in suspicious transactions. A company spokesperson said in a statement that -- quote -- "Financial crime compliance is serious" and that the bank is working on getting it right. In the meantime, it was a lackluster day for stocks on Wall Street as the first batch of quarterly earnings rolled in. The Dow Jones industrial average slipped nearly 200 points. The Nasdaq fell about 40 points. The S&P 500 ended virtually unchanged. And NASA's Perseverance rover is now the robotic record holder for driving farther on Mars than any other vehicle. As of this week, the six-wheeled scientist has traveled more than 28 miles, as seen in this animated NASA map. It took Perseverance less than six years to beat the prior record, which was set by the Opportunity rover, which took nearly 15 years to travel about the same distance. Scientists credit the latest rover's self-driving capabilities for its success, and it's not done yet.

24b7789fb16d.text: The Treasury Department has created Trump Accounts for every eligible child, automatically enrolling more than 60 million. The expansion also comes with changes to how the program works. Donors can now donate individual stocks that families can’t choose or reject and must keep for five years. Amna Nawaz discussed more with Wall Street Journal reporter Richard Rubin. Amna Nawaz: The Treasury Department has now created Trump Accounts for every eligible child, automatically enrolling more than 60 million children. That adds to the roughly seven million children whose parents already opted in since the program launched this July. But the expansion also comes with changes to how the program works. Donors can now donate individual stocks to the accounts, stocks that families can't choose or reject and must keep for five years. Direct donations can also be made to specific groups of children based on location or age. For more on all of this, I'm joined now by Wall Street Journal reporter Richard Rubin. Good to see you. Thanks for being here. Richard Rubin, The Wall Street Journal: Hi. Thanks for having me. Amna Nawaz: So how different are these new rules, these changes that came with the enrollment expansion from what was originally in place with Trump Accounts? Richard Rubin: Oh, they're totally different. So, auto-enrollment really expands this program and makes it a universal savings account for kids. So parents who didn't sign up originally who may not have wanted one or didn't know about it, everyone is now in it, so it's universal for kids with Social Security numbers. And then the stock donations are also a big change. The original idea and what Congress had written was that this money was going into low-cost index funds, and that's what parent contributions and employer contributions still go into. But now you have these donors who are able to put in individual stocks and keep them in there for five years. Amna Nawaz: And just to clarify, when we say donors here, who are we talking about? Richard Rubin: So money has to go through a nonprofit and the Treasury Department has to approve any money that can come in. But what everyone is expecting is for wealthy individuals to do this. So we have seen this happen with cash donations. Michael Dell and his wife, Susan, have donated more than $6 billion dollars in $250 chunks. Those are cash donations, not stock donations. But Treasury officials have said that they expect more of those to come and that the change to stock donations will encourage some of those donors who might not have otherwise given. Amna Nawaz: Well, so this is part of the argument from the Treasury Department, right, that it will incentivize private donors and companies to contribute more. They also say that these kind of automatic enrollment benefits children in lower income groups. Is there evidence of that? Is there data to back it up? Richard Rubin: Yes, there's definitely been data over time in that lower-income households may be more confused by this financial product, may not know about it, and may not -- may be busy with other things and not necessarily enrolling their kids. And so the automatic enrollment is something that I think has been sought on the left and the right. I think, for progressives, they really see auto-enrollment as a way to expand access for lower-income households to make sure every kid has starting with something in an investment account that turns into an IRA. For conservatives, I think it ends up being much more of a wealth-building, financial literacy kind of teaching moment. And that's, I think, what's drawn donors and support from lawmakers on that side. Amna Nawaz: I want to ask you more about these individual stock donations. Now, as we mentioned, the families have to keep these stocks. They can't choose them. They can't reject them. They have to hold them four or five years. The Treasury Department says this is going to help families to feel more invested in the companies. What do the experts you talk to say about this and what could be problematic here? Richard Rubin: Yes, so there are definitely some concerns that have come up. The Treasury Department has signaled that they're open to rules that might allow opt-outs and they have asked for comments on those. But for now, there are no opt-outs. And so you have some odd situations that could emerge. The Treasury Department really did say the goal of this was to encourage more donations because they wanted kids and their families to have a stake, not just in America broadly, investing in America, but really in these particular companies. Amna Nawaz: Yes. Richard Rubin: So you could imagine a whole bunch of scenarios. We can go through some. Amna Nawaz: Well, what are some of those scenarios? (CROSSTALK) Richard Rubin: So, you could imagine something where it becomes part of a political or policy debate. If a company is able to ensure that every 9-year-old in a particular state owns a share of their company, then when the state says we want to increase regulations, we want to raise your taxes, you could see companies or CEOs dangle this as an incentive or a reward. So, say a company is trying to get approval for a data center. They could say, oh, well, if you approve this, we will put two shares of stock in every kid's account in the town, and which auto-enrollment allows them to reach more broadly. And I think you also will have issues with conflicts of interest for -- again, because it's so broad and automatic, for federal regulators, state regulators, people who have policies and rules at their employers that prevent their minor children from owning stocks in entities that they're responsible for now may have those. And so there's a number of things that will come up and that may come up and that the Treasury Department is going to have to think about as these roll out and as they approve each of these donations. Amna Nawaz: Since the Trump Accounts launched through to the automatic enr

025581847801.text: More than five million people have lost their Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, benefits since President Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill passed last year. The bill cut SNAP funding, expanded work requirements and recently pushed more program costs to states. As Stephanie Sy reports, that's meant many more people are turning to food banks for support. Geoff Bennett: More than five million people have lost their Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, benefits since President Trump's so-called One Big Beautiful Bill passed last year. The bill cut SNAP funding, expanded work requirements, and recently pushed more program costs to states. And, as Stephanie Sy reports, that's meant many more people are turning to food banks for support. Stephanie Sy: Seventy-year-old Joan Steenburgh rarely misses her weekly trips to the food pantry. In rural Hanover, Virginia, she visits Moments of Hope to supplement SNAP benefits for herself and the two children she cares for. Joan Steenburgh, SNAP Recipient: Now my food stamps have been cut from $500 a month to $300. I would expect the most people that are politicians, $300 meal would be nothing to them. But you expect for us to raise two healthy children for $300 a month. It's no way possible that you can do that unless you have help. Stephanie Sy: More than 100,000 Virginians have lost their SNAP benefits in the last year. And in Central Virginia, SNAP participation is down more than 15 percent. Dennis Hatchett, CEO, Feed More: When SNAP changes, people are forced to either not eat or access food banks. Stephanie Sy: Dennis Hatchett is the head of hunger relief organization Feed More supporting food pantries across the region. He says, in the last year, he's seen a 20 percent increase in visits to local food pantries. Dennis Hatchett: Can food banks be a substitution for SNAP? I'd have to tell you, absolutely not. They're meant to work in conjunction. SNAP is the single most effective means of fighting food insecurity, and food banks are here to provide a supplement at the end of the month. Stephanie Sy: President Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill is projected to cut $186 billion in federal spending on SNAP over the next decade. DONALD TRUMP, President of the United States: In one year, we have lifted 2.4 million Americans, a record off, of food stamps. (CHEERING) Stephanie Sy: The law raised the age limit to be exempt from SNAP work requirements from 55 to 65 and increased the amount of paperwork required to stay enrolled. And starting next year, states with higher SNAP error rates will lose federal funding and have to pick up part of the benefit costs. In the last year, almost every state has seen a decline in people enrolled in SNAP. And many still eligible are receiving much lower benefits. Betty Hayes, Moments of Hope Food Pantry: We have people that are getting as low as $17 a month in food stamps or SNAP benefits. Stephanie Sy: Betty Hayes runs Moments of Hope Food Pantry. She says client visits have doubled in the last two years, but her neighbors' support will help them get by. Betty Hayes: At the beginning of the year in my back warehouse, I had enough surplus, a two-month window. So if I could not get any more food, I had two months' worth of nonperishable items that I could make it through with the clients that we had. I have two weeks' worth of food in the back warehouse. I think the community will step in because the community has stepped in before. And I have never run out of food. We just keep on going. Stephanie Sy: The Trump administration says the changes will cut waste and fraud and decrease dependency on government assistance, a stance echoed by Republican lawmakers. Rep. Mike Johnson (R-LA): I make this very clear. We are not cutting Medicaid. We are not cutting SNAP. We're working on the elements of fraud, waste and abuse. Rep. Tim Burchett (R-TN): Every dollar from this program is intended to help feed eligible individuals in need. That's not where every dollar goes, not by a long shot. Rep. Randy Fine (R-FL): These programs have massive waste, fraud, and abuse in them. Democrats don't want to tackle them. Republicans do. Stephanie Sy: But Dennis Hatchett says the people Feed More serves rely on SNAP to put food on the table. Dennis Hatchett: There's this misconception that people who are on SNAP don't need SNAP. What we're finding is that the vast majority of people who are accessing SNAP are working. They're asset-limited, income-constrained, employed people. We have got stats that show as many as you know 50, 60 percent of the people who are accessing our food banks are people who are working one, two, even three jobs. Stephanie Sy: And Joan Steenburgh, a former nurse, says with less money for food, she now may have to go back to work. Joan Steenburgh: Well, I have worked for all, what are you talking about, 30 years in nursing or taking care of people. France is the most prominent nation facing potential disaster. But while the Mediterranean is in crisis, Scandinavia is starting to boom. Malcolm Brabant: Meanwhile, 130 miles up the Swedish coast, it's what the winemakers call game day, the pressing, the next stage in production, where juice is extracted and separated from skins, seeds, and stems. This year, we are getting grapes for 70,000 bottles. So we're building a new winery for 300,000 bottles starting this winter. Malcolm Brabant: This wine is not intended to compete against Champagne because it comes from a different grape. But just minutes into the pressing, Bartoldsson is upbeat about producing a palatable alternative. Claes Bartoldsson: So this is like the freshest, precious juice, and I think it looks great today, really pure. So the acidity is like up here, but the sugar is perfect, so, yes, it's going to be a great vintage. And we can't wait to taste this in a couple of years. b33e44ad20eb.text: Eleven years ago, Brad Ryan took his grandmother, Joy, camping in the Smoky Mountains after hearing that she had never seen a mountain. That one trip to a national park turned into dozens, and “Grandma Joy’s Road Trip” took them to every one. Brad and Joy joined Geoff Bennett to discuss their book and their travels with Road Scholar, a nonprofit that organizes educational trips around the world. Geoff Bennett: Eleven years ago, Brad Ryan took his then 85-year-old grandmother, Joy, camping in the Smoky Mountains after hearing that she had never seen a mountain herself. One trip to a national park turned into dozens. And eventually, what they called Grandma Joy's road trip took them to every single one, making Joy Ryan the oldest person to begin and finish visiting every U.S. national park. We spoke with Brad and Grandma Joy back in 2022 for "PBS News Weekend." Joy Ryan, Grandmother of Brad Ryan: Well, I have lived in the same district, in the same house for 67 years, and you just hardly imagine all the beautiful, wonderful things that you find outside. And it just made -- it's just been miraculous. And I have enjoyed every minute of it. And it'll give me something, when I get old, that I can sit and talk about. (LAUGHTER) Geoff Bennett: Joy Ryan has plenty more to talk about now. She and Brad have since completed trips to all seven continents. I spoke with them after they got back from Thailand and Australia, where they traveled with Road Scholar. That's a nonprofit that organizes educational trips around the world. Brad and Joy Ryan, welcome to the "News Hour." Joy Ryan: Thank you for bringing us. Brad Ryan, Author, "Grandma Joy and Me: A Journey of Healing, One National Park at a Time": It's good to see you. Geoff Bennett: Yes, you as well. So, what made you decide that, after visiting all of the national parks, all 63 of them, that the next adventure had to be all seven continents? Brad Ryan: Well, American Samoa is 7,000 miles from her front porch. It's a U.S. territory, but they have their own immigration system. So we had to get passports to go to our last national park in American Samoa. And while we were there, we flew across the International Dateline to Western Samoa. So we had one stamp. And then we just realized that we still had a lot of adventure left ahead of us, I think, more chapters to write. And the truth is that our followers on social media kind of ganged up on me. And they were like, we want to see more of these adventures. Where are you taking Grandma Joy next? (LAUGHTER) Brad Ryan: Three national parks was not enough. And I thought, seven continents, that's a grand adventure that a lot of people strive to accomplish, and maybe we might pull that off. Geoff Bennett: And you just got back from Australia. Is that right? Joy Ryan: Yes. Uh-huh. Geoff Bennett: Of all that you have seen now and experienced, what amazes you the most? Joy Ryan: It's amazing how many people are different, but yet underneath they're all just the same, whatever. You can't beat that. When you're in the national park, everybody is just one big group. Brad Ryan: Yes. Joy Ryan: And it's amazing. Geoff Bennett: And you were saying earlier that when you were in Africa... Joy Ryan: Yes. Geoff Bennett: ... in the Maasai village, that in many ways reminded you of the way that you grew up. Joy Ryan: Oh, yes. They all live in this little hut, and I lived in a chicken house that made into a house. And we didn't have any electric. We didn't have -- we had outside bathroom. All of our neighbors was just the same, so we didn't feel like we was poor. And over there, they didn't feel like they were poor either. They dressed in real bright red and orange and yellow outfits, and all the little kids just laughed and played and jumped and just had the best time. So, money isn't everything. Geoff Bennett: Since we last spoke, Brad, you wrote the book "Grandma Joy and Me: A Journey of Healing, One National Park at a Time." And you write very openly about how the two of you for a time had lost touch and that there were things left unsaid. Brad Ryan: Yes. Geoff Bennett: How has the traveling together, how has that for you been a healing process? Brad Ryan: You know, when you're on your normal life path, I think in America, at least, we know our grandparents casually, but then we go to college and we go off and we have our careers and our families, and I don't think most people take the time to really learn the origin story of their family and look for those threads that go through the generations. And when you're in a vehicle driving for -- we have driven over 100,000 miles at this point, but to all the U.S. national parks, we drove about 70,000. And there's really not much you can do sometimes when you're on these long stretches of highway, and you get hypnotized by that yellow line coming at you, and all these questions sort of come to the surface, and there's nowhere to go. And that's what we did. We looked at those things that I think a lot of families choose to keep hidden because it's uncomfortable, it's traumatic. And, ultimately, what we found is that, although those conversations were painful at times, it was necessary to move us forward as a family and to find that ultimate place of healing.
