Coral-fringed tropical atolls are among the landforms most threatened by global warming, but many have a potential superpower: Healthy ecosystems may help them keep pace with rising seas.
Atoll islands with native vegetation and thriving seabird populations are “naturally active systems that can change and adapt to their environmental conditions if they are allowed to do so,” said Nick Graham, a marine ecologist at Lancaster University in the United Kingdom, who led an international team of scientists that studied island resilience across 28 atoll islands in the Pacific and Indian oceans.
Their paper, published Wednesday in Science Advances, shows that restoring atoll ecosystems reinforces their growth. Seabirds ferry nutrients from the open ocean and deposit them on the atolls as guano that nurtures land plants, marine life and coral growth. This provides more material for reef building, as parrotfish and other reef feeders turn dead coral into sand to maintain beaches, while native plants with extensive root networks stabilize sediments.
Eradicating rats and replacing coconut plantations with native forests and brush could give some atolls a “fighting chance” to persist at the rate of sea-level rise expected toward the end of the century with about 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) of warming, Graham said.
The findings provide more evidence that nature restoration can buffer the impacts of global warming. For example, restoring wetlands and forests dampens swings between wet and dry spells, reducing flood and fire hazards. Restoration efforts can also slow global warming by supporting natural carbon storage.
On the 28 atoll islands Graham’s team studied, strengthening the dynamic system of seabirds, native vegetation and reef systems starts a virtuous cycle, as ecosystems become better able to sustain themselves and build resilience to growing impacts. 
The research included data from islands in the Seychelles and Chagos archipelagos in the Indian Ocean, and Tetiaroa, an atoll in French Polynesia in the Pacific Ocean. Graham said terrestrial ecologists, marine ecologists and geomorphologists combined measurements of seabird populations, native vegetation and coral and reef organisms to trace how energy moves through the ecosystems.
The scientific approach, called ecosystem energetics, uses energy flow as a common currency to connect organisms typically studied in isolation.
Seabirds link the open ocean, where they feed, to the land, where they nest. Thousands of birds swarm out across vast seas and the food they digest is concentrated into a nutrient-rich guano. Islands with greater seabird nutrient input tended to have more productive coral communities and a higher energy flow.
Parrotfish and other reef nibblers also contribute to energy flow by scraping the coral to feed on dead organisms and excreting sand-sized particles. Calcifying algae, other reef organisms and shellfish help build the reef framework upward, helping reefs continue to buffer islands from waves.
In the terrestrial part of the cycle, restoring native vegetation that coconut plantations replace is crucial. Coconut palms have small, unstable rootballs that leave the surrounding soil vulnerable to erosion. Native plants, by contrast, have huge networks of finely meshed roots that bind and stabilize the shallow, porous soil, and also provide better habitat for seabirds.
Restoring the nutrient cycle also means eliminating invasive rats brought by colonizers and have devastated seabird colonies for centuries. This cycle has been sustaining atoll ecosystems at least since the end of the last ice age. A 2026 study of 288 reef core growth records found that most kept pace with rising seas, although that capacity varied by location and is not guaranteed at the current rate of warming.
The new study measures the “‘reef accretion potential” for the islands, showing it to be twice as high on lagoonal and ocean-facing reefs around rat-free islands with abundant seabirds as around rat-infested islands. That would be “sufficient to closely keep up with predicted sea-level rises to the end of the century under a 2 degree Celsius warming scenario,” said co-author Casey Benkwitt, a California-based restoration scientist with The Nature Conservancy.
Reef growth rates without seabird populations are less likely to keep pace with projected sea-level rise, she added.
Graham cautioned that the study doesn’t imply a miracle solution for global warming impacts to low-lying islands. It didn’t make direct before-and-after restoration comparisons, and the data came from islands with different levels of seabird abundance and rat infestations, differences the research team tried to smooth out with an ecosystem energetics framework.
And reef accretion doesn’t always mean an atoll is growing vertically, because global warming is also changing waves, winds and currents that affect where the material ends up. The study also focused on mostly uninhabited or sparsely populated islands with room for native ecosystems. On developed atolls, he said, restoration efforts can help but won’t replace the need for engineering solutions.
The study helps show a nearly complete loop, “from ocean-foraging seabirds, through native forests and coral reefs, back to the construction and stabilization of the islands on which the birds breed,” ecologist Hillary Young wrote in a Science Advances Focus commentary. Quantifying the loop provides “much-needed evidence that the fate of an atoll cannot be understood or managed by treating its land and sea separately,” she wrote.
Local conservation can influence physical resilience to rising seas, but, she wrote, “rapid reductions in greenhouse-gas emissions remain essential to long-term viability of these systems.”

Trump admin's retreat from foreign-influence fight is weakening US defenses, sources say
States and industry report getting less help from the federal government ahead of the midterms—even as AI gives foreign operatives a boost.
The Trump administration’s retreat from programs that track foreign influence operations has weakened various cross-sector relationships used to identify and confront those campaigns as midterm elections fast approach — even as artificial intelligence makes those operations easier to deploy — multiple sources told Nextgov/FCW.
State officials say they are receiving fewer election-specific federal briefings than in previous cycles, while others who track foreign influence have observed routine exchanges with government and technology companies fall away. Some also note that federal workforce departures have weakened cooperation with outside partners, including social media platforms, to track false information online.
While the federal government continues to gather intelligence on foreign threats to U.S. elections, some of those who lean on those findings say federal agencies are less reliably sharing information with non-federal researchers and state officials responsible for countering those campaigns. That cooperation began to weaken before President Donald Trump returned to office, and his administration has since dismantled several programs dedicated to countering the problem.
This story is based on interviews with current and former federal officials, state election officials and specialists in cybersecurity and influence operations. Several people spoke on the condition of anonymity to be candid about their views and for fear of retribution. Their concerns come as fast-evolving AI tools now allow foreign influence operators to do more than just generate fake images or audio, instead helping them produce plausible-sounding messages, find audiences to target and autonomously adjust campaigns at a scale not seen before.
The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency referred questions about foreign malign influence to the Justice Department, saying that influence operations fall outside CISA’s mission. DOJ did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
“Election security is national security, and protecting our critical infrastructure remains a top priority for the Trump Administration, DHS, and CISA,” a CISA spokesperson said. “CISA works closely with intelligence and law enforcement partners to monitor threats to U.S. critical infrastructure, including election infrastructure.”
The spokesperson added that the agency is committed to supporting state and local election officials “to protect election infrastructure and safeguard our democracy.”
The Office of the Director of National Intelligence did not respond to a request for comment.
Foreign influence operations aim to shape what people believe and how they act, often without revealing who is behind the message. Around elections, that can mean spreading false voting information, stoking political divisions or casting doubt on results. Such messages can be harder to question when they appear to come from or be amplified by fellow Americans and reinforce views people already hold.
One election nonprofit official told Nextgov/FCW that, during the November 2024 election, they received an early-morning text from a colleague in Georgia asking about bomb threats at voting sites, which U.S. officials later deemed may have been tied to Russia. The official was sitting in CISA’s election operations room. Finding out whether other jurisdictions were facing similar threats meant simply walking across the room and asking federal personnel.
“Any time you have federal support to help connect the dots, it’s a game-changer,” the official said, noting that they have not been alerted to or invited to a CISA elections operations room for the coming midterms.
The CISA spokesperson said that, before and during Election Day, the agency will “activate an Incident Coordination Group to establish a unified operational picture, rapidly share critical information, coordinate essential services for stakeholders in the field and strengthen incident response within its mission and authorities.”
Bret Schafer, senior director of policy and research for information operations at the Institute for Strategic Dialogue, said efforts to bring government, technology companies and researchers together grew during Trump’s first term, after Russia’s interference attempts in the 2016 election exposed gaps in their understanding of foreign campaigns.
Each could see activity the others could not. Sharing those findings helped them recognize operations that might otherwise go unnoticed, Schafer said last week on a panel at a national-security law conference hosted by the American Bar Association.
Those routine exchanges with the government have become harder to sustain. Now, “civil society is out on both sides,” he said, adding that he had gone at least two years without an information-sharing conversation with a relevant technology company, and a couple of years without one involving the government.
Much of that cooling began in the Biden administration, when GOP litigation over federal interactions with social media companies made participants more cautious. The Trump administration has gone further. It shuttered CISA work focused on election disinformation, disbanded the FBI’s Foreign Influence Task Force and closed the State Department’s office for countering foreign information threats, all largely on censorship grounds. The ODNI Foreign Malign Influence Center also faced a similar fate last August under then-director Tulsi Gabbard.
An office can retain its responsibilities while losing the relationships that helped it do the work, according to a person familiar with U.S. efforts to address influence operations. More than 1 billion people per year were exposed to heat waves and fire pollution at the same time from 2010-2019, a sharp jump from the decade before it, according to a new study that highlights the growing public health crisis caused by global warming.
The research, published in Science Advances on Wednesday, is the largest global assessment to date of how many people have been exposed to heat waves and fires—particularly wildfires—at the same time.
“There are two reasons why the total number of days people spend exposed to both hazards can increase: more people are exposed, or people experience these conditions more often,” said lead author Yao Wu, a postdoctoral research fellow at Monash University in Australia, in a written statement to Inside Climate News.
“Our findings show that the second reason plays a much bigger role,” Wu added, noting that “the problem is growing mainly because people are experiencing these two hazards together more often, not simply because there are more people.”
Researchers used detailed environmental data on hourly temperature, fire emissions and air quality, along with population information to map where and when people faced both hazards.
They found that the number of people exposed to at least one day of heat and fire pollution rose from 761 million per year in 2000–2009 to more than 1 billion per year in 2010–2019, with some of the highest exposures in countries that have fewer resources to cope with the problems.
The researchers, from universities in China in addition to Australia, described the trend as “alarming.” Public health plans to address one climate-related hazard at a time aren’t sufficient as disasters increasingly overlap, they said in their study.
Tarik Benmarhnia, a professor of climate epidemiology who was not involved in the study, said the research highlights a growing challenge for public health.
“This study captures how climate change is actually showing up in people’s lives today, and how it will increasingly affect communities in the future: not one hazard at a time, but several at once,” Benmarhnia, at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography at the University of California San Diego, said in a written statement to Inside Climate News.
Climate hazards, which also include events like floods, dust storms and drought, can additionally follow one another in rapid succession, he added.
The hazards covered in the study—fire pollution and heat—can both be deadly. Extreme heat overwhelms the body’s natural systems. The heart strains to move blood, sweating depletes fluids and heatstroke can damage internal organs, including the brain. Wildfire smoke, meanwhile, carries toxic fine particles linked to a wide range of health woes.
The cumulative impacts of simultaneous exposure to heat and fire are not well known and need to be better studied, the researchers said. Benmarhnia also stressed that big research gaps remain, but noted that a handful of studies have found overlapping heat and smoke events send people to emergency rooms with worse heart and lung problems than either hazard would cause in isolation.
The new analysis found the annual average number of days with both heat and fire exposure rose sharply per person, from one day during 2000–2009 to 1.7 days during 2010–2019.
Zambia, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Malawi, Guatemala and Burundi had the highest exposures on a per-person basis, with Zambians having nearly a month of exposure per person every year, according to the study. Measured this way, smaller countries with frequent exposure tend to top the list.
The study also looked at the total exposure days across each country’s population. By this measure, more populous countries tend to rank higher because many residents are affected, even if each person is only exposed for relatively few days. The Democratic Republic of Congo, Indonesia, Mexico, Brazil and Russia collectively accounted for more than half of all global exposure days to both hazards between 2010 and 2019, the study found.
Countries with lower living standards, including poorer health and less education, had the highest exposure per person and the largest increases, the researchers said.
They added that lower-income countries often have less capacity to prepare for and adapt to climate risks, and that fire-related air pollution in low-income countries is four times worse than in wealthy countries.

The study highlighted how climate change, heat waves and fires affect one another.
Human-caused climate change is shifting global fire patterns. In the past, fires were more strongly influenced by how much rain an area received. But today, rising temperatures play a larger role, the researchers said.
Hotter temperatures, drier air and parched soil make fires more likely to start and spread quickly. In turn, fires can worsen heat waves by releasing heat and pollution into the air, making conditions even hotter and drier.
“These processes create a positive feedback loop in which heatwaves and fires amplify one another,” the researchers said.
Global warming also makes heat waves and large fires more likely to happen at the same time. The researchers pointed to the 2021 record-breaking fires in Western Canada and the United States that burned 3.2 million hectares. A heat dome contributed to between 21 percent and 34 percent of the area burned.
The study also cited the 2022 heat-fueled fires that blazed across Portugal, Spain and France, along with the 2020 fire season in Brazil’s Pantanal, which, worsened by heat and drought, destroyed about a third of the world’s largest tropical freshwater wetland.

Reedâs view
One of the most profound takeaways from my interview with Reflection AI co-founder and CTO Ioannis Antonoglou this week on Semaforâs Future Proof is his declaration that the AI era will force us to redefine what each business actually does and rebuild it from the ground up, using AI as scaffolding. And that is going to take decades, a lot longer than most people in Silicon Valley project.
Right now, we are thinking about data all wrong. Today, businesses mostly capture data thatâs measurable or the result of some kind of work product. Whatâs usually not captured is the work itself â the difficult-to-define causal link that connects all of the actions that a company takes. âA lot of the context is like, âwe jump on a call, or someone shared something or said somethingââ Antonoglou told me.
Iâve been thinking about that challenge with my own work. How can a journalist capture gut feelings about what might make a good story? (Itâs a bit like that famous 1960s US Supreme Court case on pornography, âyou know it when you see it.â) What about capturing how reporters decide who to call first, or what questions to ask to get the most revealing answers?
In the AI era, Antonoglou told me, companies have to throw out what theyâve done for decades and come up with new ways to measure and carry out their work. Thatâs part of what Antonoglou is trying to help customers do with his companyâs open-weight models. âIt will take maybe a decade or two decades before people really rethink how things are done and how they can just do them with AI in mind,â he said.
It wonât happen in every industry at the same time â probably a good thing for the economyâs stability â but it does provide another new entry for startups that move faster than incumbents to spring ahead.

177d2da12729.text: By — Hannah Fingerhut, Associated Press Hannah Fingerhut, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/iowas-water-quality-and-cancer-rates-forced-into-forefront-of-state-politics Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Iowa's water quality and cancer rates forced into forefront of state politics Politics Oct 14, 2026 1:48 PM EDT DES MOINES, Iowa (AP) — Iowa is facing a budget deficit, high costs and economic strain from trade disputes that have squeezed farmers. But problems that have simmered for decades — water quality and cancer rates — have been forced to the forefront of state politics this year. They are the focus of debate questions, roundtable events and campaign advertisements for candidates from both parties, up and down the ballot. The issue has historically been politically taboo to avoid pointing fingers at the powerful agricultural industry in Iowa, one of the country's top producers of corn, soybeans and hogs. Chemical fertilizers and animal waste contain nitrates and phosphorus that can get washed with rain or snowmelt into the state's web of rivers. The problem has long caused tension between Iowa's more liberal urban centers, which rely on rivers and lakes for drinking water, and mostly conservative stewards of its rich farmland. Farmers are increasingly participating in practices to prevent runoff, although critics say the lack of regulation forces downstream Iowans to pay for the pollution. The spotlight has grown — and the political calculus has shifted — after back-to-back years of restrictions on water use in the Des Moines area coupled with a burgeoning "Make America Healthy Again" movement in Iowa's small towns and rural communities. Cancer rates are a growing problem in Iowa Iowa has the second highest rate of newly diagnosed cancers in the country. Specific diagnoses, like prostate, breast and lung cancer, are increasing in Iowa faster than in the U.S. overall. It's affecting urban and rural parts of the state. New state-funded research at the University of Iowa shows most — but not all — of Iowa's above-normal rates for five cancers can be explained by demographic and behavioral factors, such as smoking and binge drinking. Researchers next assess environmental factors, including nitrate levels. "The real issue is the water and the nitrates," said Democrat Josh Turek, who is running for U.S. Senate, as he talked with cancer patients last week. "Every Iowan deserves when they turn on the tap to ensure that their water is clean and not giving them cancer." WATCH: As cancer rates fall nationally, Iowa sees a troubling rise in diagnoses Some studies have found a link between nitrates in drinking water and certain diseases, but it remains an area of debate. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency does not currently classify nitrates as a cancer risk. The agency initiated a plan to review that assessment in 2017, but it's been stalled, revived and stalled again under different White House administrations. The Republican congresswoman running against Turek, Ashley Hinson, recently gathered farmers, researchers and local officials to discuss Iowa's water problems. She said there is an ongoing need for investments in infrastructure, water quality monitoring and conservation programs to ensure Iowans have safe drinking water. She also said people can feel safe because treated tap water meets federal regulations. "We all know that we have some challenges here in Iowa," she said. "I don't think water quality is a partisan issue." Farm runoff is a key contributor to river pollution — and political tensions It's been more than a decade since the Des Moines area's water utility, fed up with paying roughly $16,000 per day to remove nitrates from water, sued counties further upstream to get them to help cover the cost. The complaint was ultimately dismissed, and Iowa's Republican leaders celebrated the ruling. Last year, Central Iowa Water Works issued its first-ever ban on lawn watering to reduce demand on its nitrate removal facilities, and state politicians rejected any suggestion of a "blame game" that would implicate farmers. Iowa had been investing nearly $100 million annually in its nutrient reduction strategy in recent years. WATCH: U.S. House candidates James, Mitchell debate in Iowa in race to replace Hinson In May, though, Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds and lawmakers committed an additional $320 million for water infrastructure, conservation initiative incentives and other projects, including millions to Central Iowa Water Works to update equipment. "Water quality isn't a farm issue. It isn't a city issue, and it isn't a political issue," Reynolds said. "But it absolutely is non-negotiable." Still, criticism of slow progress has continued, including from candidates running to replace Reynolds. Governor candidates make the issue central Republican Zach Lahn and Democrat Rob Sand both emphasize that the state needs to better prioritize the water problem, though neither have called for mandating farming conservation practices that reduce runoff. Lahn, who was endorsed early in his primary by political committee MAHA Action, has diverged from many of his Republican peers in directly linking polluted water and agrochemicals to Iowa's cancer crisis. At Lahn's agriculture-focused town hall in northeast Iowa in August, one attendee raised the issue. In the span of weeks, AI altered the video game industry with mashups, which allow people to combine multiple popular games into one â and Xbox is leaning in.
AI-coding models have crossed new capability thresholds that allow users to reverse-engineer and recreate complex game code that would have taken humans years to do. People have created mashups that allow Minecraft characters to play in Elden Ring, or skateboard through Call of Duty.
âThese experiments challenge long-held assumptions about our industry,â an Xbox executive said in a memo sent to employees and posted Tuesday on the companyâs website, adding that the viral mashups mean gamers have become creators. âThese are unmistakably good outcomes for players, even when (and sometimes because) they challenge our existing business models.â
The video game giant announced Xbox Labs, which will aim to work with users as well as its own developers and engineers to make games and experiences stemming from the new AI-fueled creations.

365db38b7d7e.text: ICE is rejecting a Government Accountability Office recommendation for technology that automatically activates body cameras when weapons are drawn and safeguards to ensure agents record arrests, searches and detentions when required. Why it matters: The GAO warns that ICE risks losing crucial evidence on what happened during incidents involving force amid growing distrust over agent accountability in the wake of multiple fatal ICE shootings . The big picture: The GAO report found both CBP and ICE are struggling to manage their body-camera programs amid shifting deployment plans. CBP and ICE haven't updated their camera plans since 2022 and 2024, respectively. The plans fail to account for funding changes, expanded deployment needs and pauses in camera rollouts following one of Trump's executive orders that rescinded a Biden-era federal body-camera mandate. ICE's camera activation dispute is the central flashpoint in the GAO review, as DHS accepted all six other recommendations. CBP uses technology that automatically activates body cameras when officers draw firearms or turn on emergency lights, but ICE doesn't. Zoom in: At six of the 10 locations GAO reviewed, CBP and ICE personnel said they were unsure when they had to turn on their cameras. Some said camera use is "not mandated," "up to interpretation," and "has gray areas." Agents specifically reported uncertainty about whether they should record during "subpoena issuance, in-custody interviews, vehicle searches, undercover operations, and detainee transports." At five sites, people said they weren't sure how to use a newer camera model. The other side: DHS rejected the recommendation, arguing that automatic activation "presents significant operational risks, including inadvertent or false activations during routine movement." DHS warned that accidental activation could expose sensitive interactions with informants and victims or record people engaged in protected First Amendment activities. GAO pushed back, noting that DHS offered no alternative safeguards despite the risks of critical encounters going unrecorded. DHS didn't respond to Axios' request for comment. Worth noting: ICE issued no written reprimands for failing to comply with camera policies from the program's launch through September 2025. CBP issued just one. The bottom line: Both CBP and ICE say their body-camera programs are meant to improve public trust, officer safety and accountability. But without clear standards, the agencies can't determine whether their programs are meeting those goals, GAO found. Go deeper: ICE says all its offices will have body cams in 60 days

Grenell denied the accusations as "absurd" and a "lie." Habba and her husband, Turhan Mildon, declined to comment through a spokesperson. Why it matters: The extraordinary row between the two top-tier presidential advisers and former allies provides a rare and acrimonious behind-the-scenes glimpse into the intersection of power, influence and money in Trump's Washington. We don't know if they're true. This could be a misunderstanding." Said another: "POTUS doesn't want to deal with this. Of course, he's concerned. But if there is missing money, this is a big, big problem." Just a few months ago , Grenell was friends with Mildon and Habba. But he was notably absent from their $10 million wedding that was attended by Trump world officials, power brokers and luminaries last month. "This is the ultimate MAGA blood feud," said one Trump world insider with knowledge of the conflict. Zoom in: The dispute grew out of a friendship between Grenell and Mildon, sources familiar with the conflict say. The men had mutual interests in Venezuela in early 2025, immediately after Trump returned to the White House. Grenell, as a Trump special envoy, was advocating for normalizing U.S. relations with Venezuela's leader at the time, Nicolas Maduro. Mildon, a Turkish national, had extensive Venezuelan business interests that were threatened by Secretary of State Marco Rubio's hardline pressure campaign targeting Maduro. The intrigue: In the spring of 2025, Grenell persuaded Mildon to include a multimillion-dollar Kennedy Center donation in a lump-sum $17.6 million payment for a business deal involving a U.S. company, Habba told the president and White House staffers, two sources said. Habba's attorneys plan to give the White House documentation — reviewed by Axios — to support her allegations about Grenell soliciting a Kennedy Center donation from Mildon to go to a private company in the spring of 2025. "The White House counsel has asked for documents and proof. None has come so far," a White House official said. Grenell called the statements from Habba to Trump "Absurd. I've never asked for one cent to be sent somewhere else pretending it was for the Kennedy Center, and I've never received any payment from him at all. Make him give proof to what he is saying, not make these absurd allegations." When Habba initially leveled her accusations against Grenell, she said the total amount of the Kennedy Center contribution was $17 million, the sources said. He believed it had been credited because he was treated like a VIP donor at the Kennedy Center, where he met Habba in late 2025 before their whirlwind romance and marriage, those sources said. Friction point: Mildon and Habba, the sources said, discovered the issue after their business relationship frayed with Grenell, who lost an internal administration power struggle with Rubio that culminated in the U.S. seizing Maduro on Jan. 3 and taking him to New York City to face narcotics charges. In June, Maduro's successor, Delcy Rodriguez, issued an order revoking one of Mildon's company contracts to operate state-owned cement plants in Venezuela, the New York Times reported Monday. A source familiar with the situation told Axios this summer that her action was partly due to the U.S. government's prodding. Rodriguez then reversed herself, the Times reported, after learning of Mildon's new relationship with Habba because the Venezuelan leader believed Mildon therefore had Trump's backing. Amid the Times' reporting into Mildon's contract, Habba discovered that Mildon's supposed donation never made it to the Kennedy Center, the sources said. Inside the room: Habba then headed to the White House last Friday to tell the president about the situation. "Alina hit the roof" when her husband told her that he hadn't donated the money directly to the Kennedy Center, whose records indicate that Mildon actually owed a $270,000 pledged donation. There was no record of Mildon giving anything close to $5.6 million, officials said. Mildon on Tuesday paid the $270,000, records show, to the Kennedy Center. In partial confirmation of Habba's story , Kennedy Center staff reported that late last year there was a search for Mildon's contribution — then thought to be $6 million — but that it couldn't be found, an official said. But Lisa Dale, who handled finances for the Kennedy Center then, said the only record in her books connected to Mildon showed he owed $270,000. "There was nothing about $6 million," she told Axios. "I would have heard about that." Context: Habba and Grenell trace their roots to Trump's first administration. Grenell was Trump's ambassador to Germany and then his acting director of national intelligence. Habba was Trump's private attorney and briefly was U.S. attorney in New Jersey during this term. Between the lines: The Kennedy Center has been an ongoing sore spot for Trump, beset by controversy over his efforts to put his name on the building and fundraising woes. e81812d62949.text: By — Thomas Beaumont, Associated Press Thomas Beaumont, Associated Press By — Joey Cappelletti, Associated Press Joey Cappelletti, Associated Press By — Mike Catalini, Associated Press Mike Catalini, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/republicans-retreat-from-battleground-districts-as-lines-shift-in-house-races Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Republicans retreat from battleground districts as lines shift in House races Politics Oct 14, 2026 1:30 PM EDT DES MOINES, Iowa (AP) — Republicans were retreating Tuesday from a handful of battleground U.S. House races while Democrats were racing to raise money to boost candidates who seemed like long shots earlier this year. The Congressional Leadership Fund, the leading House Republican super PAC, canceled spending in four races from the Midwest to the East Coast and increased its investment in 16 other races from Texas to Pennsylvania. Another super PAC allied with President Donald Trump is cutting back in a battleground district in the Las Vegas area. The decisions were disclosed by three Republican campaign officials familiar with the plans who spoke on condition of anonymity to share private strategy conversations. Meanwhile, Democrats' House campaign committee is eyeing openings in Republican-held districts and hoping to raise millions of dollars in the next week to fuel a late round of advertising that they say could net at least a half dozen more seats. The shifting money in the final three weeks of midterm campaigns points to an increasingly defensive posture by Republicans, who have already trimmed their expectations in U.S. Senate races, and new aggression from Democrats, who are trying to capitalize on President Donald Trump's weak approval ratings. "You can tell now where people are competing based on where they're putting the money," said Stu Sandler, a Republican strategist working on House and statewide races this year. David McIntosh, president of the conservative Club For Growth, said there are only a few places where Republicans could pick up seats this year. "The economic environment has not been good," he said. "Voters are dissatisfied with their Republican majority and the base is also dissatisfied with that they weren't able to get the SAVE America Act passed," referring to Trump's plan for a strict proof-of-citizenship voting bill. "It looked like Republicans were weak," McIntosh said, "and so you've seen a lot of drop-off in enthusiasm." Republicans cut back in front-line districts The Congressional Leadership Fund is no longer spending on advertising in Iowa's 1st District, where three-term Republican Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks is defending her seat against Democrat Christina Bohannan. Bohannan is running for her third time against Miller-Meeks. Last time, the race was decided by only 799 votes, making it the second-closest in the country. It's an eastern Iowa district where congressional cuts to Medicaid have been linked to hospital service closures and high diesel prices have been a challenge for farmers. Likewise, the officials said the group won't keep spending in New Jersey's 7th District, where second-term Republican Rep. Tom Kean is facing off against Democrat Rebecca Bennett. Kean has been under scrutiny for his four-month absence from Congress, which he left unexplained until disclosing a mental health crisis upon his return. Kean, who won by 5.4 percentage points two years ago, has also faced questions over his support for Trump's tariffs and the Iran war. These races, as well as one in the Cincinnati, Ohio, area and one in east-central Michigan, have accounted for $13.3 million in Congressional Leadership Fund spending, more than 12% of its total through Oct. 13. The group will instead reinforce districts where Trump beat Democrat Kamala Harris by narrow margins in 2024. Safety and Affordability, an offshoot of MAGA Inc., pulled nearly $1 million in ad spending aimed at helping Republican Marty O'Donnell's campaign in Nevada's 3rd District. Republicans had hoped that Trump's tax-cut legislation — specifically no taxes on tips — would resonate in Las Vegas and help defeat Democratic Rep. Susie Lee, who voted against the bill. Sandler said his party needs to turn out voters who usually participate in presidential elections but often stay home in the midterms. READ MORE: Can Democrats win the Senate? Here are some pathways "One thing you can't say is that they've been under-resourced," he said. "Republican resources are at a high. They've never been this well-funded in the midterm." Democrats try to scrounge up more money As House Republicans have retrenched, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee believes at least a dozen more races could be within striking distance. However, they need more money to take advantage. The committee launched a $17 million fundraising drive, with a deadline of Oct. 22, to pump advertising onto the air in districts that were once seen as out of reach. "It's not that we need the money to win in the districts where we have been running to get to 218 seats," said Courtney Rice, the committee's communication director. "We're talking about the next level." One is Ohio's 10th, a Dayton-area district represented by 12-term Republican Rep. Mike Turner. Democrats see Turner as beatable despite the former Dayton mayor's durability and 18 percentage-point victory two years ago. Trump carried the district by six percentage points in 2024. Turner didn't begin advertising until late September, according to AdImpact, later than most competitive House incumbents, and the National Republican Congressional Committee started spending there this week. Kenya has confirmed a second case of Ebola, 10 days after a businessman died of the virus after he had travelled to the East African nation from the Democratic Republic of Congo.
The new patient, a 39-year-old man, is a close relative of the first case and was already in quarantine when he fell ill on Tuesday, Kenya's health ministry says.
The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks.
Detecting his illness early had improved his chances of recovery and limited the chance of him passing the virus on to others, the ministry said, as it urged the public to "stay calm but vigilant".
"Both cases are linked, and there is no evidence of spread in the wider community," the ministry said.
"Kenya remains open, with no restrictions on travel, trade or public gatherings", it added.
The 40-year-old Kenyan man who died on 5 October was diagnosed with Ebola shortly after being admitted to hospital in the capital, Nairobi.
A relative had taken him there shortly after picking him up at the airport. He had travelled from DR Congo, through Uganda to Kenya without his illness being detected.
Since his death, officials had determined that he had been in contact with 128 people - and since Tuesday 113 of them had been found, the health ministry said.
Of these, 108 were in quarantine in Kenya and tracing of the remaining 15 continued, it said.
More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date.
The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
"Anyone with fever, unusual tiredness, muscle or joint pains, vomiting, diarrhoea or unexplained bleeding should seek care promptly at the nearest health facility," Kenya's health ministry said.
The current outbreak in DR Congo, which began in May, has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.
Shortly after DR Congo declared an outbreak of Ebola in May, it was also reported in Uganda, where two people died.
However, the World Health Organization (WHO) declared that county free of the disease in August.
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, the continent's leading public health agency, has reconstructed the Kenyan patient's movements for the six weeks leading up to his death.
It revealed that he first started feeling unwell in DR Congo on 15 September - and showed how several opportunities to detect the infection were missed, including during several visits to Congolese medical facilities.
He then managed to travel through Uganda to Kenya - and was again not detected at airports screenings.
Health experts say it highlights the limitations of relying on temperature checks and self-declarations.

Bernie Sanders of Vermont and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani as part of his campaign. “Exponentially exploding,” mathematician Thomas Bloom told me by phone, describing the flood of new results in his field. Little did he know that hours later, OpenAI was going to post 722 mathematical manuscripts an unreleased AI model had produced.
The firehose of new work lends new urgency to the question: How is AI changing mathematical discovery? In their race for headline-grabbing breakthroughs, AI companies typically do not disclose their methods and data. That competition among AI companies threatens to overwhelm human collaboration and understanding.
This tension had been playing out in miniature on a website Bloom runs that tracks progress on more than 1,000 problems originally posed and collected by Paul Erdős, one of the 20th century’s most prolific mathematicians. Here, people used to collaborate to discuss open problems, or ones for which the best solution either hasn’t been found or isn’t known to the greater math community. But increasingly, visitors were competing to close open problems with AI proofs that they often didn’t understand. Bloom, a mathematician at the University of Manchester in England, doesn’t want to spend his days refereeing AI-generated work. So, soon after we spoke, and before he knew that OpenAI would be announcing its latest results, Bloom posted that he’d no longer tag problems as open or solved, and he also closed comments.
It’s definitely exciting that AI can tackle so many open problems so quickly. But can it help mathematicians understand the answers and build on them?
Just two days after OpenAI’s deluge of results, the peer-reviewed edition of a Google DeepMind study became public. First reported in a preprint earlier this year, it offers an inside look at how one AI system tackles open math problems. The system called AlphaProof Nexus solved 9 Erdős problems and made a number of other interesting mathematical advances, researchers report October 8 in Science.
The report includes a detailed description of how the results were obtained. Plus, human mathematicians vetted many of the proofs. That’s “quite different” from how OpenAI and Anthropic are handling their math results, Bloom says.
“The ultimate objective of any AI for math research,” says research scientist and study co-author Swarat Chaudhuri of Google DeepMind in London, should be “to advance mathematics as done by human mathematicians.”
A look inside an AI math machine
In the recently published study Chaudhuri and his colleagues tested different configurations of their system. To tackle a collection of 353 open Erdős problems, they used multiple agents powered by the Gemini language model. These could call on AlphaProof, an AI model specially trained to do math, and the inspiration for the name of the overall system, for difficult steps. The agents also relied on Lean, math software that identifies steps that remain unproven, to check their logic. The agents shared their work, circulating promising proof attempts and discarding ones that weren’t going well.
The team also tested a simpler setup on the nine problems the full system solved. Independent Gemini agents worked through proofs using Lean’s feedback, without sharing attempts or consulting AlphaProof. That setup solved all nine, too. It was cheaper—using fewer computing resources—than the full system on easy problems and more expensive on the two toughest ones. The team did not establish whether the simpler setup would solve any of the problems the full system had missed.
The fact that the simpler setup could solve the same nine problems as the full system surprised Chaudhuri. It suggests that increasingly capable language models can tackle research mathematics with relatively simple checking tools.
But computer-checking comes with a caveat. Lean checks only the statement it’s given, as it is written in its code. And a mathematical statement may be incorrectly translated to or from Lean code. An October 6 preprint shows why this translation matters. In the paper, the researchers pinpoint mismatches between parts of OpenAI’s written Navier–Stokes proof and its Lean counterpart. The mismatches do not mean the written proof is wrong, the team writes, but they note that a valid Lean proof does not automatically validate an AI-generated math paper.
That’s why the vetting human mathematicians did for the DeepMind publication is so important. “The human mathematician has to really think through the problem and set goals for the system,” Chaudhuri says. And even if the system failed to finish a proof, its checked steps helped mathematicians focus on the remaining gaps. “Math is ultimately a human art,” Chaudhuri says. “The system enhances the human user’s insights, and the human user is able to guide the system with new ideas.”
With math ability comes responsibility
The mathematical results that the AlphaProof Nexus system achieved are “not really at the top level of importance,” says Bloom, who wasn’t involved with the work. But that underscores the team’s more measured approach. Google DeepMind, he says, is “trying to be more responsible with the science,” while companies like OpenAI are using math to showcase their software. OpenAI’s papers and accompanying Lean proofs were entirely AI-generated, leaving it up to the math community to work out what’s useful or useless.
OpenAI says they worked with an independent advisory group to develop best practices on how to share their AI math results. But that group has said their advice was to not test unreleased AI models on advanced math, guidance the company clearly ignored.
The company’s fast-moving, competitive approach continues to alienate mathematicians such as Bryna Kra of Northwestern University in Evanston, Ill. She says the company made some improvements in their efforts to cite past literature. And she’s excited about AI’s potential to solve important problems in math. Netflix has said it will cut 1,000 jobs globally as the streaming giant faces competition from rivals.
The cuts - the steepest since 2022 - will mainly affect its human resources, legal, product and technology teams and equates to around 6% of its total workforce.
Last month, Netflix 's co-chief executive, Ted Sarandos, told the Bloomberg Screentime summit that the company was "not growing as fast as I want us to".
The streaming industry is going through a period of consolidation following Paramount's $110bn (Â£83.6bn) merger with Warner Bros, the owner of HBO, while free platforms such as YouTube and TikTok continue to attract viewers.
In an email to staff, Sarandos and co-chief executive Greg Peters said Netflix would "continue to invest aggressively in high-impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation".
Netflix had come close to its own deal with Warner Bros but was outbid in the end by Paramount.
Commenting on the "organisational changes", Sarandos and Peters said: "Our mission - to entertain the world - is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritise our people and resources."
Managers will tell employees whether their job has been cut "soon".
The email added that the firm was on track to meet its financial forecasts. The streaming service is due to report its latest results on 20 October.
Investors have been weighing up user engagement - the amount of time customers spend on Netflix - as it competes with platforms such as YouTube and TikTok.
The firm has continued to commission shows - its most popular at the moment is "Below", an underwater mystery series.
It has also been attempting to expand its business, including gaming and allowing adverts to play before and during shows and films.
However, "they haven't been able to find another line of major revenue," said Ross Benes, senior analyst at eMarketer.
He added that the company remains reliant on a subscription business that could be approaching a plateau.
"Eventually, because they're nearing a ceiling with that, they'll need another revenue stream to diversify, and that's where it's been more of a struggle," he said.
The last major redundancy round at Netflix was in 2022, when it cut about 450 jobs after losing subscribers for the first time in more than a decade.

The wife of Pope Leo XIV's brother says her husband is also receiving treatment for cancer after the Vatican announced the Pope has the disease.
Deborah Prevost, the wife of the Pope's eldest brother, Louis Prevost, told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, on Tuesday that her husband has a form of blood cancer. It is unclear how advanced it is.
Her comments came on the same day that Pope Leo, 71 - the first US-born head of the Catholic Church - underwent what the Vatican described as "successful" surgery for lung cancer. He is expected to remain in hospital for a week.
Deborah Prevost said the family was "going through a lot" and that they are "keeping spirits up for both of them".
She said her husband was being treated for multiple myeloma as part of a clinical trial at a hospital in Florida where they live. He was first diagnosed with cancer in 2017 and had undergone treatment in 2019, but "fell out of remission" three months ago.
Multiple myeloma affects the blood, bone marrow, and can impact kidneys, according to a factsheet by the UK's National Health Service (NHS).
It is not currently considered curable but the Multiple Myeloma Research Foundation says on its website that survival rates have significantly improved in the past decade.
Louis Prevost confirmed his cancer diagnosis in a separate interview with US news outlet Newsmax, saying he was undergoing CAR-T cell therapy.
This involves reprogramming a patient's immune cells to recognise and destroy blood cancers, the NHS states.
Louis Prevost told Newsmax's Finnerty programme that it had been a shock to learn his brother also had cancer.
"I got a message from his right hand that he was out of surgery, awake, feeling good, and was in no pain," he said of the Pope's condition.
"So, we were all in high hopes and high spirits hoping for the best."
Deborah Prevost said the brothers spoke last week as her husband prepared to go to hospital.
"He called to let us know what would be happening," she said. The Pope announced on Sunday he would be operated on "in the coming days" after a nodule was found on his lung during a medical check-up.
"We keep praying, keeping spirits up for both of them," said Deborah Prevost.
The Pope, whose birth name is Robert Francis Prevost, underwent a 90-minute surgery on Tuesday at Rome's Gemelli Hospital and was subsequently diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma - a type of cancer usually found in the outer part of the organ. During the surgery, a lower lobe of his right lung was removed, the church said in a medical bulletin.
"The operation was successful and there were no complications," the Vatican said. "After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room."
The pontiff had a "peaceful night" in the hospital, the Vatican said on Wednesday morning.
Adenocarcinomas develop in cells that produce mucus and are one of the most common types of lung cancer.
The long-term prognosis depends on a number of things, including the stage of the cancer when identified and the person's overall health. The earlier it is spotted, the better, and treatments have improved over the last few decades.
Some adenocarcinomas are picked up early - before symptoms develop - during routine tests. At later stages, lung cancer can cause a persistent cough, breathlessness, fatigue and weight loss.

374fe2efed6e.text: By — Lisa Desjardins Lisa Desjardins Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/can-democrats-win-the-senate-here-are-some-pathways Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Can Democrats win the Senate? Here are some pathways Politics Oct 14, 2026 12:40 PM EDT Unforeseen a year ago, Democrats' now have a real chance at taking the majority in the U.S. Senate. (Gamblers in some betting markets now see it as likely, even.) What are the potential paths for Democrats to take over the Senate — or for Republicans to block them and hold on? The math The current Senate has 53 Republican members. The Democratic caucus is made up of 47 Senators, or 45 Democrats and two independents (Sens. Angus King of Maine and Bernie Sanders of Vermont). Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Democrats need to pick up a net of four Senate seats in order to gain a majority of 51 seats. Republican Vice President JD Vance would break a 50/50 tie, so Democrats need 51 seats minimum. The 13 seats in play President Donald Trump said Tuesday that the Republican Party faces an equally hard battle to retain control of the Senate and the House in November's vote. Watch the clip in the player above. Our friends at the Cook Political Report have listed 13 Senate seats that are competitive, some more so than others. But all are on the board here. What to know about these 13 seats: Republicans are on defense in nine of these seats. Of those Republican seats, six are considered toss-ups, aka competitive enough for either party to have a good chance of winning. That gives Democrats a range of options to get the four flips they need. However, Democrats are on defense in four seats themselves, including one "toss-up" in Michigan. The nine Republican seats the Cook Political Report has in play right now: Six toss-ups: Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Ohio, and Texas Two "likely Republican." Nebraska and South Carolina One "likely Democratic." North Carolina The four competitive Democratic seats are: One toss-up: Michigan One "lean Democratic." New Hampshire Two "likely Democratic." Georgia and Minnesota The three paths A key factor when thinking about these Senate races is to assume — as both parties do — that Democrats start with one likely flip, in North Carolina. Given that, here are three paths for the math and the map. 1. The Democrats-do-it path: Democrats get a 51-seat majority. Democrats win where? North Carolina, plus any four of the following six states: Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Ohio, or Texas. That is a wide range of options at a time when Republicans in those states face tough polling. In other words, there are many possible paths here for Democrats and this is why betting markets are leaning their way. Democrats lose where? This scenario assumes Democrats lose in their toss-up race: Michigan. (Their candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan is holding his own against Republican Mike Rogers, but this is their most vulnerable race.) Or potentially, Democrats get a surprise loss in New Hampshire. Result: Democrats pick up a net of at least four seats. 2. The Democrats' tsunami path: Democrats get a 54-seat majority. Democrats win where? North Carolina, plus all of the six toss-up states. Or perhaps, Democrats notch a surprise win in a place like South Carolina and one toss-up state, maybe Maine, stays Republican. (I'm heading to the Pine Tree State soon and will update you.) In this scenario, expect oddball deep-red places like Arkansas or Alabama to be closer than ever before as results come in. Democrats lose where? Nowhere. Which would be a tall order. But Democrats have done it before. Result: Democrats pick up seven net seats. 3. Republicans' survival path: Republicans keep a 50- or 51-seat majority or more. Democrats win where? In this scenario, Democrats would win North Carolina and then have just one or two toss-up wins, perhaps in Alaska and Ohio. Or perhaps Ohio and Texas. (Yes, we are in a different universe when discussing Texas this year.) Democrats lose where? Michigan, a toss-up seat. Thus, even if Democrats keep their seats in New Hampshire and Minnesota, and if they lose Michigan, they must win current Republican seats (as above). Result: Democrats pick up two or three net seats. But Republicans retain control of the Senate with a bare majority. Watch the segment in the player above. So, what will happen? This is a close election. But Democrats are entering voting season with some big advantages. One is the history of a president's first midterm, in which voters generally vote with the opposing party. Another are President Donald Trump's sagging approval numbers and voter discontent with the biggest issue in any recent election: the economy. It is a fascinating election. Get your popcorn. Or your aspirin. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Donate now By — Lisa Desjardins Lisa Desjardins Lisa Desjardins is a correspondent for PBS News Hour, where she covers news from the U.S. Capitol while also traveling across the country to report on how decisions in Washington affect people where they live and work. @LisaDNews

b7d2a188ed70.text: Data: Gallup ; Chart: Axios Americans' trust in their fellow citizens' democratic judgment has fallen to its lowest recorded level in more than five decades, according to a new Gallup survey. The big picture: Americans' growing distrust of political leaders and institutions now extends to one another, with Democrats and Republicans showing similar levels of skepticism. By the numbers: 51% of U.S. adults have a great deal or fair amount of trust in Americans as a whole to make democratic judgments, per Gallup. That's the lowest reading since Gallup began tracking the measure in 1974. The distrust cuts across party lines: 53% of Democrats, 51% of Republicans and 49% of independents trust Americans' ability to make democratic decisions. Flashback: Trust stood at 86% in 1976 and 78% in both 2002 and 2005. Trust has stayed below 60% since 2018, according to Gallup. State of play: Americans have more trust in their local government (67%) and state government (55%) than in their fellow citizens' democratic judgment (51%). The survey also found that 42% of Americans trust politicians who hold or seek public office, while 33% trust the news media. Zoom out: Americans' confidence in major U.S. institutions, including Congress, the presidency and the banking system, has also fallen to historically low levels. Methodology: Gallup surveyed 1,000 U.S. adults by landline and cellphone Sept. 1–17, 2026; the weighting-adjusted margin of error was plus or minus 4 percentage points.

Davidâs view
YOUNGSTOWN, Ohio â Toward the end of Monday nightâs MAGA rally, after Jon Husted heard Donald Trump compliment his jawline and his âass,â he thanked the president for making Ohio so much easier for Republicans to win.
âThe Youngstown area, for decades, used to vote Democrat,â the Republican senator said. âAnd then you ran for office in 2016, and flipped it red forever.â
For a decade after that, Youngstown has become the first stop on what media critics derided as âTrump voter safaris,â journeys into the working-class counties that never voted Republican until he showed up. Hustedâs claim of a permanently red state, however, isnât adding up for Democrats: As soon as I arrived this week, they insisted that MAGAâs advance was over.
This isnât because Democrats have snapped back to the image and values they ran on in the 1970s, when they had a lock on this state. No, the party insists that Republicans are in charge, making voters angry with their handling of the economy and the Middle East, so the culture-war politicking that worked for a decade wonât be as potent in November.
âPeople arenât buying that again because theyâve realized you canât deposit culture war into your bank account,â said Chris Anderson, the chairman of the Mahoning County Democrats, whoâd spent years trying to limit their losses and defections. âYou canât fill your gas tank with it.â
Campaigns have a queasy rhythm to them â hype followed by panic followed by hype. Weâve reached the time in the cycle where the party that built a post-Labor Day polling lead begins to question its own confidence.
âTheyâre undersampling Republicans,â Speaker Mike Johnson told the faithful in South Texas on Tuesday, a part of that state that seemed to be following the same rightward march as northeast Ohio â and before that, Appalachia.
Republicans around Youngstown expected the trend of underestimating their vote to hold this year, but not accelerate. They agreed that Democrats would at least be competitive. Rep. Michael Rulli, who represents the Mahoning Valley in Congress, said that the GOP got an opening when âClinton came in and lied about NAFTA,â which made local Democrats thrash around in search of a populist alternative.
âWhen Trump came around, the people just took to it, and so theyâre giving us a shot,â Rulli added. âThis area will not always stay Republican or Democrat.â
This yearâs Democrats are making hard plays for northeast Ohio, at least to trim the GOP margins. Former Sen. Sherrod Brown, who lost the five most Democratic counties east of Cleveland for the first time in 2024, has painted Husted as a âBig Techâ shill, captured by the next industry thatâll threaten working-class jobs. Amy Acton, the partyâs gubernatorial nominee, takes every chance to talk about her Youngstown roots; her ads often portray Vivek Ramaswamy, the billionaire GOP nominee, playing tennis as he daydreams about cutting Medicare and Social Security.
âI know what itâs like to not have the heat on, or live in a tent in the winter and experience a lot of neglect and abuse,â Acton told me on Tuesday, when I asked her to respond to the president rallying in Youngstown â specifically, about him telling voters theyâd get rebate checks and energy bill relief only if Republicans won. âAnd I can also tell you that I wouldnât be here today if it wasnât for the institutions that gave me a chance.â
A Democratic comeback in Ohio is unlikely to look like the winning maps of Barack Obamaâs campaigns, much less Bill Clintonâs. While losing to Bernie Moreno two years ago, Brown ran stronger in the suburbs of Cleveland and Cincinnati than he had in elections he actually won.
On Monday, the standard Trump rally scene of MAGA-hatted voters in line and liberals yelling at them from free speech zones showed how the coalitions had changed. The protesters skewed older; the younger they were, the more profanity they were comfortable putting on cardboard. A âprogress prideâ flag was hoisted on a pole, right under an American flag. Any Trump fan who objected got an earful about the âpedophile presidentâ they were lined up for.
Trump, at this point, was not the rebel candidate who first showed up in Youngstown 10 years ago, with rally speeches about the threat of mass Muslim immigration. He was the party leader every Republican wanted to borrow some aura from, by communing with his superfans.
Ramaswamy posed for selfies a few steps away from MAGA activist Vince Fusca. Blake Marnell, who wears a brick-patterned suit to every Trump rally, got a seat near the main stage. Both men were at the 2024 Trump rally in Butler, Pa., where a failed assassinâs bullet clipped his ear; neither needed convincing that he was saving eastern Ohio, where they didnât live, from neoliberalism.
The Covelli Centre, where Trump had rallied before, was a bit more than half-full when the president got onstage. Like Democrats used to, he described all the investments he was bringing to the region. Submarine construction was coming to Cleveland; nearby Warren was getting a new ââKimberly-Clark plant; he would figure out how to save the local heating utility company.
The applause thinned out when he talked about how heâd rebranded artificial intelligence as âSuper Intelligence.â

c30752f1cb06.text: By — Hanna Arhirova, Associated Press Hanna Arhirova, Associated Press By — Samya Kullab, Associated Press Samya Kullab, Associated Press By — Barry Hatton, Associated Press Barry Hatton, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/sudden-starlink-limits-sap-ukraine-drone-power-as-kyiv-fears-u-s-intelligence-squeeze Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Sudden Starlink limits sap Ukraine drone power as Kyiv fears U.S. intelligence squeeze World Oct 14, 2026 12:09 PM EDT KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Ukrainian drones lost some of their fighting capacity after restrictions were suddenly imposed on the battlefield use of the country's U.S.-made Starlink communication terminals, officials said Wednesday as the capital endured another night of missile attacks. At the same time, Ukraine did not receive the usual advance warning from its Western partners of the devastating Russian ballistic missiles that have struck Kyiv for two consecutive nights, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, triggering fears that Ukraine is being starved of vital intelligence, especially from the U.S. READ MORE: Trump's diesel deal with Putin draws bipartisan criticism from a frustrated Congress Zelenskyy did not specify which partners he was talking about when referring to the lack of warning. U.S. President Donald Trump has said the U.S. has not stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine. The developments frustrated the Ukrainian military and deepened fears that Kyiv's relationship with Washington is unraveling. Ukrainian officials fear U.S. support for the war effort is falling away after Trump struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel despite international efforts to sanction Russia for its invasion and isolate Putin. READ MORE: Ukraine had no intelligence from partners about missiles headed to Kyiv, Zelenskyy says Trump said Saturday that it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Zelenskyy has not done enough to end his country's war with Russia and blaming him for high diesel prices in the U.S. Trump's efforts to stop the fighting have resulted in no progress. Starlink is an essential tool for Ukraine Ukrainian officials are concerned that U.S. support, especially related to the sharing of military intelligence and the use of American tech titan Elon Musk's Starlink satellite communications system, may be in jeopardy. Musk's SpaceX overnight imposed a speed limit on Ukraine's Starlink terminals mounted on drones, Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Zelenskyy, said on social media. The restriction disrupted operations, including making the slower-flying attack drones easier targets for Russian defenses. READ MORE: Zelenskyy gives Ukraine's Order of Freedom award to Musk for Starlink's role in war effort Starlink is a vital tool for the Ukrainian military, both in offensive and defensive operations. The network is used for long-range drone missions, interceptor air defense systems and front-line logistics, Beskrestnov said. "Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation," Beskrestnov said, without elaborating. Neither SpaceX nor the White House offered any immediate comment. Kyiv got no warning about initial ballistic missile attack, official says Yurii Ihnat, Ukraine's air force spokesman, said there was no warning of an initial Russian ballistic missile attack on Tuesday night, although Kyiv was warned about three later waves of missiles. A lawmaker on Ukraine's parliamentary Defense Committee told The Associated Press that intelligence sharing with international partners has not stopped. The lawmaker spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to give statements to the press. READ MORE: Kremlin relishes in U.S.-Russia diesel deal and Trump's criticism of Zelenskyy Five people were killed and 36 injured in a Russian attack on the Ukrainian capital that lasted from Tuesday evening into Wednesday morning, Kyiv police said. Russia keeps bombing Ukraine's power grid despite Trump's truce demand Zelenskyy voiced outrage Wednesday over Russia's continuing aerial bombardment of Ukraine's energy infrastructure in apparent defiance of Trump's demand for a ceasefire. "We ask America and EVERYONE in the world who does not turn a blind eye to reality to respond — and to respond forcefully" to Russia's ongoing aerial barrages, Zelenskyy said in a social media post Wednesday. "Russia has squandered the opportunity for de-escalation and has clearly chosen to continue its insane war of annihilation," he said. Moscow's forces pounded Ukraine's power grid, as well as oil and gas facilities, for the third straight night, Zelenskyy said, after Trump claimed that Russia and Ukraine had agreed not to strike energy infrastructure 4 ½ years after Moscow's forces invaded. Zelenskyy, meanwhile, has agreed to halt Ukraine's monthslong campaign targeting Russian oil refineries that caused fuel shortages for Russians. Ukraine's last reported hit on an oil refinery was Friday. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Wednesday that details of the energy ceasefire are still being decided. "The work in that direction is continuing," he told reporters. Russia hits three Kyiv power plants in attack, causing outages The Russian Defense Ministry said in a statement Wednesday that its forces attacked Ukraine's energy infrastructure in Kyiv, the wider Kyiv region and the northeastern Kharkiv region overnight, striking a total of six power plants. Russian forces hit all three of Kyiv's combined heat and power plants overnight into Wednesday, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said. At least 600,000 people were left without power, Zelenskyy said. Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 drones at energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, the Kyiv region and Kharkiv overnight, Zelenskyy said. Ukraine claims it is pushing Russia back on the battlefield Ukrainia

A new study in the journal Seismica presents the first comprehensive seismic analysis of what happened during the disastrous flood in Nepal on Aug. 26. But exactly what triggered the mountainside to give way remains unclear.
A massive section of a Himalayan mountainside collapsed near the Nepal-China border, sending millions of cubic meters of rock and ice crashing downhill. The collapse unleashed a devastating flash flood that tore through valleys and communities along Nepal’s Trishuli River. At least 1,455 people were reported dead, and 5,285 remained missing as of Oct.7, according to the Associated Press.
Since this main event, at least two major flooding episodes have happened in the same broader river system, including one on Monday.
To reconstruct the August disaster, the researchers precisely timed the initial mountain collapse. Using data from seismic stations in Nepal and China, they placed the start of the main mass movement at 8:37 a.m., Nepal time.
USGS initially reported a magnitude 4.4 earthquake before realizing it was coming from the landslide itself. Then, Nepalese researchers looked at their records and also reanalyzed the signal, which did not resemble an ordinary earthquake.
“We tried to see the signals, and we didn’t find any earthquake signals,” said Lok Bijaya, chief of the National Earthquake Monitoring and Research Centre in Nepal, and one of the authors of the study.
They found a small magnitude-2.5 seismic event that occurred only about 17 minutes before the catastrophic collapse, less than 10 kilometers away. Although it could have contributed to the slide, “we are not sure the magnitude of 2.5 is enough for this kind of mass failure. It is not clear yet,” said Shiba Subedi, a geophysicist at the Nepal Academy of Science and Technology in Kathmandu, Nepal, and another author of the study.
The researchers detected more than 60 smaller seismic events in the area during the preceding two weeks, including several others in the hours immediately before the collapse.
But “seismic activity doesn’t mean it’s earthquakes,” Bijaya explained. They suggest that at least some of these seismic events may instead have been near-surface “slide-quakes” associated with gravitational movement of the mountainside. In other words, some of those signals could potentially have been the mountain destabilizing before it failed.
But it’s hard to tell how much they contributed to the main event. “Other people are now analyzing and having a closer look,” said György Hetényi, professor of geophysics at the University of Lausanne in Switzerland and another one of the authors. “Given that they’re all clustered in this area, it’s hard to believe it’s not a precursor,” he said.
The collapse itself was so enormous that seismometers around the world detected it. The authors say the seismic amplitudes were actually larger than those from the 2025 Tracy Arm landslide in Alaska.
“The size [of what collapsed] was almost 1.5 kilometers long,” said Bijaya. “It was situated at 5,200 meters, and that mass just dropped down, maybe just slid for 30 seconds, and then dropped down more than a kilometer.” The glacier and rocks sliding created a crater, which now resembles a lake.
Climate change could be part of the story, but it’s likely not the only factor. Changes in ice and glacier movement can alter stresses in the underlying rock and may have contributed to the slope’s instability, Hetényi said.

“Given the amount of rock that has fallen, I think this phenomenon would have happened anyway. Maybe next year if there’s no climate change, or maybe last year, if climate change was more important. But the fall of rock at this volume cannot be only climate change,” he said.
Reconstructing the disaster also exposed another vulnerability in the Himalaya: scientists across the region do not routinely share seismic data.
The lack of available data is a serious issue, the authors said. “It’s creating a very big uncertainty—issues for early warning systems and for locating these kinds of events,” said Bijaya.
For this paper, the team negotiated with Chinese teams and got data they needed the next day. “It was very surprising to me that the Nepalese organized some exchange with the Chinese. That’s great. Usually, it’s not so easy,” said Hetényi.
“That was the first motivation for us, for this paper,” said Bijaya.
India, China and Nepal do not have any protocols to share their data. Because much of the Himalaya is remote and difficult to access, any monitoring is valuable. According to Hetényi, this needs to change.
“I hope this major event will change the view of the politicians, and that they will commit to regional data exchange for monitoring,” he said. “It doesn’t have to be open to the whole wide world.”
Researchers say sharing data would help improve early-warning systems, but the monitoring systems themselves also need to be upgraded.
“If I had plenty of power and money, I would put in water-level measurements, water gauges,” said Hetényi. “I would also use remote sensing, so a satellite-based monitoring system, and I would also use infrasound, which is basically vibration through the air at a lower frequency than we can hear, but that propagates fast enough to give alerts,” said Hetényi.
Subedi said the scientific community must be prepared. “We can have this kind of event many, many times in the future,” he said. “So we have to invest in different kinds of warning mechanisms.”
