The News
President Donald Trump is pushing ahead with his deal to import Russian diesel, blowing past his partyâs growing complaints about taking help from Vladimir Putin.
âThe presidentâs main priority and commitment is to the American people and to help lower costs for the American people, and heâs doing that,â a White House official said after days of withering complaints by Republicans. âThe president has not shifted his stance on it.â
The Trump administration caused an intraparty furor earlier this month by announcing that the US will import roughly 2.2 million tons of Russian diesel in an effort to ease fuel price spikes that have hurt Republican candidates on the midterm campaign trail.
Itâs unclear exactly when the imports will officially arrive, but the economic boost from Moscow is sparking discontent as Republicans in tight races scramble to message around the surprise announcement.
Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, who is running for the Senate, said on Tuesday in a debate that she vastly preferred other options to bring down fuel prices â among them, suspending the gas tax, creating a diesel rebate program, and using more biofuels.
âWe need to lower diesel prices, but I donât think we need to be making a deal with Russia to do it,â Hinson said.
The Russia deal completes a trio of Trump economic moves that are politically toxic to swing-state Republicans, joining his bid to encourage beef imports and his Canadian trade war. All three are unpopular enough among members of Trumpâs own party to create significant discord about the GOP plan to tackle rising prices.
Republicans are signing onto letters bashing the Russia diesel agreement and distancing themselves on the campaign trail: Former New Hampshire Sen. John Sununu, seeking the Senate again, said this week that the move would do little to lower prices in the US and âprovides an advantage to Russiaâ In Michigan, former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers similarly broke with Trump.
But other Republicans defended Trumpâs policy change.
âThe presidentâs got energy security and economic security front of mind right now. Heâs focused on Americans first,â Sen. Bill Hagerty, R-Tenn., a top Trump ally, said this week.
Hagerty dismissed the prospect that US diesel purchases would unfairly aid Russia in its war against Ukraine: âWeâve got a number of sanctions in place and a number of efforts to bring Putin into alignment.â
For the White House, the argument is simple: Diesel prices are too high, and even a smaller-scale import plan helps ease the burden.
Others in the administration privately acknowledge, however, that thereâs a clear reason for the recent rise in prices: Trumpâs ongoing war with Iran. His administration also has long entertained ways to unwind certain sanctions on Russia in a bid to secure a peace deal with Ukraine â one that would also help ease inflation.
âHaving to do this is yet another inevitable consequence of the Iran war,â said a second Trump administration official, who added a hope that the diesel deal becomes part of âa broader diplomatic strategy.â
Know More
Already, two bipartisan groups of senators have pushed back on the decision, including seven Republicans. One House Republican has said heâll introduce legislation to block it.
âTrump and his team have misread the room on the Republican caucuses in the House and the Senate on this issue,â Bloomberg economist Chris Kennedy told Semafor. âTheyâre trying to respond to concerns from congressional Republicans in farm states about diesel prices â¦ and it doesnât seem to be landing very well.â
Fueling that discontent is Republicansâ dimming faith that Trump will choose to impose recently enacted Russian sanctions that were passed in honor of his longtime ally, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said earlier this month that the administration planned to âname namesâ â but whether to use that sanctions power would be âfor the president to decide.â
Asked this week about GOP skeptics of his diesel purchases from Russia, Trump dismissed them as âRepublicans that canât really be serious,â adding that itâs âa deal for the rest of the world.â White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers praised Trumpâs âgreat deal to supply the global market with massive amounts of diesel.â
âLowering prices for Americaâs great farmers, truckers, and families remains a top priority as the President simultaneously urges both sides of the Russia-Ukraine conflict to stop strikes against refineries, which are driving up costs and hurting American consumers,â Rogers said in a statement.
âWe didnât think [the bill] would change anything on the sanctions front â¦ and I think that this decision just reinforces that view,â said Kennedy, who served on the National Security Council during the Trump and Biden administrations.
Room for Disagreement
A handful of GOP lawmakers, including Senate Armed Services Chair Roger Wicker of Mississippi, are taking a different tack by predicting the diesel imports never materialize.Some Republicans posit that Trumpâs new import deal violates a 2022 law that bans the US from purchasing Russian energy products. Others point to hurdles like European sanctions and Russian shortages.
Even if it does become real, it wonât do much to lower prices. Investors are already pricing in âlittle near-term impact,â Kennedy said, since the world uses far more diesel than Russia will export.
Wicker said heâs pitched the administration on alternative ideas. Itâs unclear what those could be.
Shelby, Eleanor, and Burgessâ View
Whether itâs red-dye diesel or Russian diesel, the Trump administration is pulling out all the stops to convince voters that itâs bringing prices down â¦ even as it maintains an Iran war that is driving costs up.
So far, the presidentâs advisers have little to show for it beyond making life harder for the rest of their party.

7e46d4fbd232.text: By — Christopher Rugaber, Associated Press Christopher Rugaber, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/lawyers-for-federal-reserves-lisa-cook-say-white-house-hearing-set-up-by-trump-is-biased Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Lawyers for Federal Reserve's Lisa Cook say White House hearing set up by Trump is 'biased' Politics Oct 14, 2026 5:46 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook's lawyers say that a committee set up by the White House last week to investigate an accusation against her is "demonstrably biased," though they did not close the door on the possibility that she would appear before the panel. Lawyer Abbe Lowell also said in a letter Tuesday that Cook would not be able to participate in a hearing Nov. 5 because she "will be executing her official duties as Governor at financial and monetary policy meetings in Europe." Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The earliest that Cook could appear before a "committee of inquiry" that the White House set up last Friday would be after the Fed's policy meeting Dec. 8-9, the letter said. The letter was sent to William Scharf, a counsel to President Donald Trump. Lowell's comments are the latest turn in the Trump administration's extended efforts to fire Cook from her position as one of seven members of the Fed's board of governors. Trump has accused Cook of committing mortgage fraud in 2021, before she joined the board, a claim she has denied. No criminal charges have been filed. READ MORE: Trump establishes committee to investigate Federal Reserve's Lisa Cook in latest effort to fire her No president has fired a Fed governor before, a reflection of the Fed's traditional independence from politics. Yet Trump, who has repeatedly demanded that the central bank lower its key interest rate, has taken numerous steps that economists say have threatened that independence. The Justice Department earlier this year sought to investigate then-Chair Jerome Powell over brief testimony he had given about an extensive building renovation, though a judge threw out subpoenas in the case and it was later dropped. Cook was appointed by former President Joe Biden and is the first Black woman on the Fed's board. Trump first tried to fire Cook in August 2025, but the Supreme Court ruled earlier this year she could remain in her position while litigation continued. The court also suggested, in a footnote to the ruling, that Trump could try again to fire her if the administration provided her adequate notice and an opportunity to respond. The committee of inquiry announced by the White House last Friday is an effort to meet those conditions. WATCH: Supreme Court ruling proves Federal Reserve is unique agency, Lisa Cook's lawyer says Under the law governing the Fed, the president can only fire a Fed governor "for cause," but the Supreme Court didn't address whether Cook's actions met that standard. The committee of inquiry will ultimately recommend whether there is cause to fire Cook, a White House memo last week said. Lowell also said in the Tuesday letter that "we have significant concerns regarding the objectivity and fitness of the committee for its assigned purpose." One of its three members, Kevin Hassett, a top economic adviser to Trump, has already said the president has "cause" to fire Cook, the letter noted. The other two members — Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling and chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Andrea Rich — are also Trump appointees. "A hearing with demonstrably biased members, unspecified additional allegations, and an unclear schedule for the disclosure of any additional evidence – with no explanation for why it was not previously produced – is not a process that respects the appearance or history of independence," Lowell's letter said. The strike, in the eastern Saudi Arabian city of Dhahran, was the latest demonstration of the Houthis' ability to attack high-profile targets. Elon Musk has suggested that the US government may be behind restrictions on the speed at which some of Ukraine's weapons can travel and stay connected to SpaceX's Starlink internet network.
Starlink is a vital tool allowing Kyiv to guide drones to Russian targets and also protect its own skies, but on Tuesday night Ukraine said unexpected new speed limits were disrupting its battlefield missions.
An adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky said he believed the restrictions were not a coincidence and were related to the latest strains between Kyiv and Washington.
Musk said that Starshield, the military-grade sister service to Starlink, is controlled by the US government, and "any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately [the US president]".
Musk - writing on X - had been responding to pleas from Ukrainian officials to restore connectivity, including from Zelensky who told UK media: "I hope that it's a mistake, maybe [a] huge technical problem. I don't know, but we are asking to... switch [it] on."
Starlink, which is owned by Musk's SpaceX, restricted speed limits on Tuesday night to 100mph (160km/h), meaning any weapons that travelled faster than that lost connectivity to the network.
It had been partially restored by Wednesday evening, Ukraine's former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov said.
"Removing Starshield's speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine's defense," he wrote on X, thanking Elon Musk and asking for his "continued support".
About an hour later, Musk replied to that post, defending his company's involvement.
"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," he wrote.
Musk added that Starlink is for "civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company".
The US government has not commented.
While both companies are owned by Musk's SpaceX, Starlink is a civilian service that uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide internet access, particularly in remote areas, while Starshield is designed for government and military use.
The restrictions on Tuesday night came as Russia launched deadly attacks against Ukraine that killed several people in Kyiv, officials said, and hit communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military.
President Zelensky said it was "one of the largest attacks" from Russia, and while "a significant part of the drones were shot down" there were "also hits".
At least 600,000 people across Ukraine were left without electricity, and residents said they received no warning of incoming drones before they hit.
"It is clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation," Zelensky's adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram on Wednesday morning.
US President Donald Trump has grown increasingly frustrated towards Ukraine as it continues to strike Russian energy facilities.
Zelensky has said that the US threatened to restrict intelligence sharing if he did not sign up to Trump's energy ceasefire, but on Tuesday, Trump denied this.
Speaking during a visit to London on Wednesday, President Zelensky agreed that he had felt betrayed after the US made a deal with Russia to import 300,000 tonnes of its diesel.
"Really yes... but it's a little bit more complicated than just my emotions or my feelings," Zelensky said, when asked by UK journalist Piers Morgan if he felt betrayed.
During his one-day visit, Zelensky was greeted with a hug by UK PM Andy Burnham at Downing Street and held an audience with King Charles.
Ahead of the president's arrival, No 10 announced it would speed up delivery of lightweight multirole missiles to Ukraine, which have been used to bring down Russian drones.
"We are behind you and that will not change," Burnham told Zelensky.

470ff0eac0b9.text: By — Heather Hollingsworth, Associated Press Heather Hollingsworth, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/a-gang-rape-allegation-at-cornell-highlights-how-title-ix-guides-campus-sex-assault-cases Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter A gang rape allegation at Cornell highlights how Title IX guides campus sex assault cases Nation Oct 14, 2026 4:52 PM EDT Cornell University's handling of an alleged fraternity house gang rape is raising questions about how a decades-old federal civil rights law shapes colleges' treatment of campus sexual assault. The focus on Title IX, which prohibits sexual discrimination in education, comes after a woman identified only as Jane Doe filed a lawsuit last month against Cornell and seven fraternity members. She said she was assaulted at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024 after being pressured into snorting the fast-acting sedative ketamine, smoking marijuana and drinking alcohol. The accused men have all denied her allegations, either saying the sexual activity was consensual or they weren't involved. WHAT: What the Cornell case reveals about how sexual assault allegations are handled Title IX was best known for most of its 54 years for opening doors for female athletes. But guidance issued in 2011 under President Barack Obama's administration made clear it also protects people who say they were sexually assaulted or harassed. The rules have changed with new presidential administrations, but Title IX proceedings are intended to help colleges decide how to discipline the people involved, regardless of whether they face criminal or other legal repercussions. Dual systems sow confusion A sexual assault case can be handled in criminal court and through the campus-run Title IX disciplinary process at the same time. In theory, the criminal proceeding could lead to prison time and the Title IX case to expulsion. In reality, serious consequences are rare in either system, said Megan Greeson, a professor of community psychology at DePaul University. She was among the authors of a review of studies involving 288,066 cases that found around 20% of those reported to police are prosecuted and 8% lead to convictions. WATCH: New details intensify scrutiny of Cornell's handling of gang rape allegations Jane Doe was no exception. Days after she gave her first substantial interviews to campus police, the county district attorney in upstate New York decided not to prosecute. Long after that, Jane Doe believed the criminal investigation was ongoing. Her attorney, Thomas Giuffra, said she was "misled." Her case illustrates a common complaint with the dual-track system. Greeson said she often hears: "What do you mean there's two different investigations?" How does the Title IX process work? On the surface, Title IX investigations look a lot like police investigations. Witnesses are interviewed, and the accused often hire attorneys. The process is so demanding that many victims drop their case or choose to go an informal route, in which the accused might be asked not to take classes with the accuser, or to switch universities — often with no mark on their record. WATCH: News Wrap: Cornell students protest handling of alleged rape When cases proceed to a hearing, schools have a lower bar for determining culpability than the justice system's standard of beyond a reasonable doubt. Title IX requires schools to find an accused student responsible if the evidence shows the allegations are more likely true than not. Beyond expulsions, consequences can include suspensions, loss of scholarships or withholding of a degree. A culpability finding can be noted on transcripts, which can make it difficult to get into graduate school or to obtain a state license in certain fields. The process ping-pongs between presidential administrations At some universities, including Cornell, Title IX offices handled fewer complaints after regulations narrowed the definition of sexual harassment during President Donald Trump's first term. Critics argued the rules discouraged students from coming forward with abuse allegations. Those who did faced a live hearing and cross-examination by a person of their alleged attacker's choosing. Former President Joe Biden's administration overhauled the rules to expand the type of behavior that's considered sexual harassment. Rules finalized in 2024 also provided recognition that Title IX protects LGBTQ+ students and made live hearings optional. WATCH: Appointing Cornell sex assault special prosector, Hochul says she won't let anyone 'sweep this case under the rug' A federal judge in Kentucky overturned Biden's changes in early January 2025. Trump's current administration subsequently reverted to the 2020 rules in a change that became official last month. Cornell's Title IX complaints fluctuated as the regulations changed, falling from 205 in 2019 to 98 in 2020, when COVID-19 also shut down campuses, before rising to 166 in 2024. Additionally, the Education Department 's Office for Civil Rights used to serve as a powerful enforcer in cases of campus sexual violence. Under Obama and Biden, it brought the weight of the government against schools that mishandled sexual assault complaints involving students. But investigations have dwindled since Trump returned to office. "There's become fewer and fewer avenues for accountability and support that students are able to access with the way the current administration is enforcing or really choosing not to enforce Title IX," said Emma Grasso Levine, the manager of Know Your IX, which works to address campus sexual violence. What do we know about how the Cornell Title IX case was handled? It started about three weeks after the alleged assault, when Jane Doe went to campus police. That same day, the head of Cornell's fraternities contacted the school's Title IX office. The Chi Phi fraternity house was immediately suspended and later closed for good.

Why Zelensky's meeting with Burnham matters
Prime Minister Andy Burnham welcomed President Volodymyr Zelensky to Downing Street on Wednesday, as the Ukrainian leader looks to shore up his European allies five years into Russia's war on Ukraine.
Burnham told Zelensky that Britain "would forever stand by you" and that he was accelerating the delivery of air defences to Ukraine.
Burnham previously told MPs that he would try to "repair bridges" between Ukraine and the United States and that Ukraine won't leave "empty-handed".
The two leaders met at No 10 Downing Street where Zelensky was welcomed with a military ceremonial guard - thought to be a first for a foreign leader.
BBC World News correspondent Joe Inwood explains what we know about the meeting.

Thousands of students have taken to the streets in the Albanian capital of Tirana, attacking several government buildings on the second day of violent anti-government protests.
The demonstration began outside the ministry of education on Tuesday, as students called for better university conditions and job prospects.
Wednesday saw part of the education ministry's building set on fire, while the prime minister's office, finance and interior ministry, and several surrounding businesses were also attacked.
Albania's Deputy Prime Minister âAlbana KoÃ§iu has called for "calmness, self-restraint and maturity" and said "Albania does not need to burn to change".
Riot police have clashed with the protesters, using tear gas and water cannons to disperse them.
One demonstrator, Enida Bimi, told Reuters news agency that the protest is not just for the students, but "for all the people of Albania".
"The people are very angry at the system. They need to change everything. With this corruption all around, the crime and everything else is happening. And the people now are angry. They need to change the system," Bimi said.
Another protester, Arber Leshi, said people are angry at "the most corrupt government our country has ever seen".
Education Mirela Kumbaro said that while she respects the right to protest, "civic student protest and violence against public buildings and property are two different things".
Officials have criticised the behaviour of some protesters.
"Setting fire to an institution is not a peaceful protest. It is an act that endanger's peoples lives", said economy minister Delina Ibrahimaj, responding to a video appearing to show protesters throwing rocks at the finance ministry building.
Sixteen people were arrested "in connection with violent acts" during Tuesday's protest, Albania's state-run news agency said.
Sali Berisha, the leader of the opposition - the Democratic Party of Albania - has praised the protesters.
"The streets and squares of Tirana have never seen lions like these students," he said during an evening meeting on Wednesday, Albania's state-run news agency Ata reported.
This student-led protest comes after months of anti-government protests, known as the Flamingo Revolution, which is calling for Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign.
The protests were sparked by a luxury tourism project linked to Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, which fuelled anger over alleged corruption and a lack of transparency from Rama's government.

f964ec80d2f1.text: By — Leah Willingham, Associated Press Leah Willingham, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/cornell-president-admits-he-never-followed-up-on-gang-rape-allegation-ahead-of-no-confidence-debate Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Cornell president admits he never followed up on gang rape allegation ahead of no-confidence debate Nation Oct 14, 2026 4:23 PM EDT Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff knew in 2024 that a student had reported being gang raped at a fraternity house, but never followed up to learn what had happened to her or whether any of the accused students had been punished. In an interview with The New York Times published Tuesday, a day before Cornell's Faculty Senate was set to begin debating a no-confidence resolution in his administration, Kotlikoff acknowledged that he did not know until recently that the woman had dropped out of Cornell or that students had been expelled or suspended over the incident. READ MORE: Cornell president calls alleged gang rape 'deeply disturbing,' pledges greater transparency Kotlikoff publicly addressed what he called "deeply disturbing" allegations involving drug use and sexual violence at the Chi Phi fraternity house in a November 2024 message to the Cornell community, saying criminal and university investigations were underway. He subsequently convened a presidential task force to examine how Cornell handles sexual assault, but said this week that he never followed up to learn the outcomes of the criminal or Title IX investigations into the woman's allegations. Case has drawn national attention, roiled campus The case has drawn national attention since the woman, identified in court documents as Jane Doe, filed a lawsuit alleging that seven Chi Phi fraternity members sexually assaulted or exploited her in October 2024 and that Cornell mishandled her complaints. On Tuesday, Kotlikoff announced a ban on fraternity parties through the end of the academic year and plans to give state police a role in investigating sexual assault reports. WATCH: New details intensify scrutiny of Cornell's handling of gang rape allegations Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten initially declined to pursue charges after reviewing a summary prepared by Cornell University Police, but later said it omitted key details. He reopened the investigation after the lawsuit was filed. Gov. Kathy Hochul subsequently removed him from the case, appointed Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor and ordered an independent review of Cornell's handling of the allegations. The Cornell Faculty Senate's proposed resolution, declaring no confidence in the administration's ability to handle reports of sexual assault on campus, reflects growing concerns among some faculty members that people who report sexual misconduct face institutional barriers and fear retaliation. Some have called for Kotlikoff's resignation, while others have urged patience as independent investigations proceed. Kotlikoff was scheduled to address the Faculty Senate on Wednesday before members begin debating the resolution. Debate was expected to continue Oct. 28, followed by electronic voting by the Faculty Senate, which has approximately 130 voting members. A simple majority is required for passage. Professor who reported harassment says it nearly cost her career For Ariana Kim, an associate music professor at Cornell and co-sponsor of the resolution, Kotlikoff's acknowledgment that he had not followed up on the woman's case was deeply troubling. "I mean, that's appalling in and of itself, right?" Kim said. "That you don't know about a student who faced an alleged horrific crime, that you don't think to check in." Kim, a Grammy-nominated violinist, said she was motivated to take action after being struck by Jane Doe's story, as well as her own personal experiences on campus since she started at Cornell a decade ago as a young academic in her 20s. She said when she experienced bullying and sexual harassment by senior colleagues, Cornell failed to properly document her complaints and that she was never clearly informed what disciplinary action, if any, had been taken. "I was asked what I had done to provoke the situation," she said. WATCH: What the Cornell case reveals about how sexual assault allegations are handled Kim said she continued to be expected to work alongside colleagues involved in the dispute. She believes reporting the misconduct later affected her tenure review. She spent 18 months appealing an adverse tenure decision, a process during which she lost 20 pounds (9 kilograms) and struggled to eat or sleep. A university appeals board ultimately overturned the original decision, and she secured tenure. Now seeking promotion to full professor, Kim said she recognizes that publicly criticizing university leaders could again jeopardize her career. "I'm speaking out publicly against this administration that may very well deny my promotion," she said. Kim said she has considered leaving Cornell many times over the years but is determined to stay and make the university safer for those who come after her. "If by me fighting, it helps move the needle a little bit so that my female students aren't going through this in 10 years or my female colleagues aren't going through this in five years, then maybe it's worth it." Faculty members question whether Cornell can investigate itself Anne Marie Brady, a senior extension associate at Cornell's School of Industrial and Labor Relations and another co-sponsor of the resolution, questioned whether Cornell University Police can independently investigate serious allegations of sexual misconduct. "There doesn't seem to be independence between the administration and the Cornell Police Department," Brady said. She pointed to its handling of campus protests as one reason for her concerns and said serious criminal allegations should be investigated by outside

d49c0f37a64c.text: The rupture between President Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky over last week's diesel deal deepened Wednesday after an Elon Musk -owned satellite system used by Ukraine unexpectedly restricted service — undercutting Ukraine's fight against Russia. Why it matters: The Ukrainian military uses SpaceX's Starlink satellite communications system to control and operate its reconnaissance and intercept drones. When it doesn't operate at full capacity, Ukraine's ability to gather intelligence, use interceptor drones and conduct long-range strikes against Russia is impeded. Service was partially restored on Wednesday, but Ukrainian officials were still searching for answers about why the service was throttled and who was responsible. The limitations came days after a new crisis erupted between the U.S. and Ukraine over Trump's agreement to lift sanctions on Russian oil sales. Zelensky criticized the move, then Trump called for Ukraine to elect a new president. A senior U.S. official said the Trump administration had nothing to do with the alleged Starlink service constraints. But Ukrainian officials remain suspicious. Driving the news: Ukrainian officials said SpaceX imposed the restrictions Tuesday night. The system turned off, they said, when a drone exceeded 160 kph. In some cases, it disconnected when the speed went over 80 kph. The Starlink restrictions came several hours after the Ukrainian military did not receive an early warning about a Russian ballistic missile attack. Ukrainian officials said the U.S. has provided such alerts over the last several years as part of intelligence sharing between the countries. U.S. officials pointed to a technical malfunction in the system, but Ukrainian officials suspect that it was a warning shot from the Trump administration. "We had massive [Russian] attacks today and it's a pity that we also had difficulties ... about Starlink and about intelligence and a lot of different surprises," Zelensky said at the top of a meeting in London with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. "We count on the partnership with the U.S. but we just want to be very honest and very clear and be a strong partner." The latest: The Ukrainian Ministry of Defense said SpaceX continues to restrict Starlink to 160 kph — significantly higher than earlier but still well below its normal speeds. The ministry said it remains in communication "with partners and SpaceX regarding stable service conditions and the prevention of sudden restrictions." "The situation is better than it was this morning, but 160 kph is not enough for intercepting" some Russian jet drones, a Ukrainian official added. The intrigue: Ukrainian officials think the restrictions were imposed intentionally by SpaceX to press Ukraine to accept Trump's demand not to attack Russian oil refineries. Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski wrote to Musk on X on Wednesday: "Hey, big man, are you playing politics with your products again? As your European customers, we are watching you." Between the lines: Ukraine relies on two satellite systems. One is SpaceX's Starlink, which is used for communications, ground forces, logistics and defensive drones — ones that shoot down incoming drones. The other is Starshield, which is controlled by the U.S. government and used for offensive military purposes. Both systems were restricted, according to Ukraine. What they're saying: In a post on X , Musk did not directly address the throttling of Starlink, but he did indirectly comment on which entity would have been responsible for the limitations imposed on Ukraine. "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," he wrote. "Starlink," he added, "is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company." Behind the scenes: Zelensky's top advisers spoke with their White House counterparts Wednesday and asked whether there'd been a decision to shut down Starlink services and what could be done to fix the situation, two sources said. Ukrainian officials made similar calls to the CIA and the Pentagon. White House officials told the Ukrainians they don't have control over SpaceX, the sources said. One of the sources said the Trump administration is going to reach out to SpaceX to figure out what happened. The White House didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

Incumbent New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and Republican challenger Bruce Blakeman clashed over high energy costs in the state’s only gubernatorial debate, offering sharply different visions for how to keep electricity affordable as demand rises.
Average residential electricity bills in New York rose 10 percent from 2024 to 2025, outpacing the national average. The state has the eighth-highest residential electricity prices in the country, which has made affordability a central issue in the governor’s race.
With less than three weeks until Election Day, recent polling data suggests Hochul leads Blakeman by around 12 percentage points. Blakeman has served as Nassau County executive since 2022.
During the debate, Hochul touted her “all of the above” energy strategy, which includes developing renewable energy and expanding nuclear power. Blakeman blamed the state’s high utility bills in part on clean energy programs, calling them a “slush fund” for “science projects,” such as offshore wind farms and solar panels that he claimed were “ruining agriculture.”
But state data shows that decarbonization programs account for only a portion of residential electricity costs. A 2025 Public Service Commission report found that measures mandated by New York’s Climate Act made up between 5 and 9.5 percent of a typical monthly residential electric bill in 2024.
Most of the bill reflects the cost of buying and delivering electricity. Rate increases in the state are often linked to surging electricity demand, which raises prices, as well as an over-reliance on gas-fired power generation, which in turn is tied to the natural gas market.
Utilities are also investing more in expanding electrical infrastructure to accommodate new power generators—and new customers.
The candidates also shared different visions of how to generate more power. Wind and solar projects, paired with battery storage, can typically be built at cheaper costs than fossil fuel infrastructure, potentially helping to meet rising electricity demand while supporting the state’s climate goals.
Hochul emphasized her push to build more nuclear power in the state, though she did not say whether she would reopen Indian Point, a nuclear plant north of New York City that closed in 2021.
Nuclear power remains a controversial topic in New York, with activists and critics raising concerns about costs, public health and possible environmental impacts linked to the long-term storage of “spent fuel,” which is extremely radioactive.
Blakeman has offered few details about his energy policy beyond attacking renewable energy initiatives. To lower energy bills, he has pledged to bring fracking back to New York, though the practice was banned statewide more than a decade ago over public health concerns.
The statewide debate over energy costs comes as New York faces growing electricity demand, driven partly by data centers, building electrification and manufacturing. The state’s grid operator faces a growing backlog of applications from proposed data centers, which could put even more pressure on the power supply.
Hochul touted her executive order for a yearlong statewide moratorium on data centers and pledged to require new facilities to “bring their own power.” In other states, meeting data centers’ rising electricity demands has led to plans for a buildout of polluting natural gas plants. Environmental advocates have called for greater public input on the state’s proposed data center policy.
Hochul also described herself as “laser-focused on affordability” and pointed to her administration’s energy rebate policy, which will send checks of up to $200 to 8.2 million households to offset rising costs. She did not answer a question about whether the rebates would become an annual benefit.
Blakeman has aligned himself with President Donald Trump, recently praising him at a rally in Syracuse. During the debate, Hochul challenged Blakeman over Trump administration policies, including tariffs and the Iran war, which have contributed to higher prices. In response, Blakeman said he and Trump have “significant policy differences.”
Hochul became governor in 2021 after Andrew Cuomo resigned amid a sexual harassment scandal. In 2022, she defeated current Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin, a former congressman from Long Island.

The Scoop
The White House played a central role in the Justice Departmentâs antitrust investigation into major TV networksâ temporary suspension of pooled coverage of the president, three people familiar with the matter told Semafor.
While the probe is progressing, some inside the DOJ are concerned about its legal merits. Two former DOJ officials said that the networks suspending their pool participation after three news outlets got barred from the White House are likely protected by the First Amendment â one cited a 1982 Supreme Court ruling that afforded those constitutional protections to group boycotts for political purposes.
Two of the people familiar with the matter suggested that the idea of an antitrust inquiry was first discussed inside the White House, which ultimately pushed for it from the DOJ. A third described the White House-DOJ interplay as a âdistinction [without] a difference,â given how closely the two are intertwined under President Donald Trumpâs administration.
A DOJ official disputed that the White House first raised the idea of a probe, saying that âseasoned attorneys within the Justice Department, including the antitrust division, first discussed this.â The official added that any requests for information from networks which may have been sent were written âbecause there is sound legal footing to investigate.â
In addition to the longstanding Trump-era blur between the DOJ and White House, the departmentâs antitrust division has close ties to presidential priorities. Sara Matar, formerly the divisionâs chief of staff, joined the White House counselâs office in August as an associate.
Notably, Laura Loomer â a staunch MAGA ally whose outside influence has occasionally resulted in changes within the White House â tweeted last month wondering why the DOJ hadnât âfiled an antitrust lawsuitâ against outlets that âcolluded to refuse to coverâ Trump.
Loomer attacked Woodward in her post; the following week, she traveled with Trump to Alabama, though itâs unclear whether she raised the issue with the president personally during that trip.
The White House referred Semafor to the DOJ in response to a request for comment.
Know More
The Trump administration has long argued that the Justice Department is not wholly separate from the White House, counter to the norms that took root after the Nixon era. At Semaforâs World Economy Summit in April, Attorney General Todd Blanche indicated that it is Trumpâs ârightâ to suggest targets for investigation â a stance he has echoed repeatedly since settling into his role at the top of the department.
âCertainly if the leader of the Free World learns about something or hears about something or wants us to focus on something, a certain area, that is, of course, what every Department of Justice has done,â Blanche told Semafor at the time.
âThis idea that President Trump has some sort of outsized control because of things that he says, that thatâs absolutely his right and his duty to do that,â Blanche added.

0c7fba5f803a.text: By — Mike Stobbe, Associated Press Mike Stobbe, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/how-proposed-cuts-to-this-major-national-health-survey-could-disadvantage-americans-with-disabilities Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter How proposed cuts to this major national health survey could disadvantage Americans with disabilities Health Oct 14, 2026 3:55 PM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — The federal government is planning to dramatically shrink its most influential health survey, and some researchers worry that the changes will underestimate how many Americans are disabled. At least half the survey questions could be axed. The cost-saving change is part of an ongoing effort to slim down the 69-year-old National Health Interview Survey, which for years has been suffering from declining response rates. READ MORE: Civil rights enforcement cuts mean fewer staff, closed offices, longer waits for students with disabilities As many as a quarter of wheelchair users and more than a third of people who are blind or deaf could be miscategorized as not disabled because of the shorter survey, according to some advocates and researchers. That could leave the government unable to recognize the health needs of many disabled Americans, or the damage caused by changes to Medicaid or other health insurance programs, they say. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The cuts are being ironed out and officials predict the whittling won't be as severe as what's been suggested in earlier proposals. Questions that have been proposed for removal deal with memory, fatigue, arthritis, difficulty walking and climbing stairs, as well as others about the use of hearing aids, canes, wheelchairs and scooters. READ MORE: Trump's actions signal a move toward institutionalizing people with disabilities, advocates warn "We just won't know any of that anymore," said Scott Landes, a Syracuse University sociology professor who researches people with disabilities. Officials are still determining exactly how much cutting will take place. Currently, the survey has 490 health questions for adults. U.S. officials expect that the 2028 questionnaire will have about 200 to 225 questions, said the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's Stephen Blumberg, who oversees the survey. U.S. Census Bureau workers conduct the survey every year on behalf of the CDC. It's a $40 million annual project, and around 30,000 households answer the questions each year. Their answers have shaped the public's understanding of topics including how common chronic fatigue syndrome is, how many people get X-rays, what proportion of U.S. children suffer seizures, and how many Americans have health insurance. The survey's responses also are the foundation of how we measure the nation's progress — or backsliding — on problems such as obesity and smoking. Fewer people are interested in participating in such surveys. And the National Health Interview Survey is particularly daunting, as it can take an hour or more and has traditionally involved an in-person interviewer asking the questions. The planned redesign should cut it to about a half hour, Blumberg said. "People are busy. They're more protective of their privacy, and some don't trust the government to protect their data and use it only for statistical purposes," he said. "Fewer people see sharing information with the government as their civic duty." The survey was first conducted in 1957, and has been updated every 15 to 20 years. The latest update was put into the field seven years ago, prompting some advocates to ask why it was being changed so quickly. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and the White House Office of Management and Budget were behind dramatic staff reductions, research funding overhauls and other federal health agency changes under the current Trump administration. But neither ordered this redesign, Blumberg said. Rather, the factors driving the current redesign include tightening budgets and difficulties fielding enough workers to do so many in-person interviews — which was affected last year by a federal hiring freeze. Another factor: The Census Bureau is reconfiguring its data collection platforms for the 2030 census in a way that affected the health survey, he said. Related to all that is a proposed change in how the health survey is conducted. Instead of starting with in-person or telephone interviews, people will receive an invitation to fill out the survey online or to fill out a paper questionnaire. That's because in-person interviews have proven difficult with the proliferation of gated communities, locked buildings without door attendants and doorbell cameras, according to officials. However, Census Bureau staff will visit homes for a smaller second round of surveying, Blumberg said. A notice about the survey redesign appeared in the Federal Register in August, opening a public comment period that runs through Oct. 20. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Starlink satellites operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX provide high-speed internet - something modern war relies heavily on.
Kyiv has adopted it as a vital battlefield communications tool and also uses it in drone warfare.
Using Starlink, Ukrainian drones are able to maintain stronger connections with operators over longer distances than conventional radio networks and are less vulnerable to jamming.
But a sudden speed restriction for drones connected to Starlink means some battlefield "missions" have been disrupted, according to a top Ukrainian official.
Serhiy Beskrestnov also said officials had not been told about the 100mph (160km/h) speed limits set overnight on Tuesday by Elon Musk's SpaceX company.
Throttling drones connected to the network at this relatively low speed makes Ukrainian efforts to intercept jet-powered Russian drones all but useless, according to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW).
Starlink is "the backbone of military communications in Ukraine", the institute's George Barros says, and is used across Kyiv's naval, land, and air forces.
Barros, who is the ISW's Director of Innovation and Open Source Tradecraft told the BBC that the restrictions could have major implications as the technology allows "drones, artillery and command posts to function as a single real-time network where the time between sensor-to-shooter is minimized."
Starlink does not work inside Russia, but Ukrainian drones can use the satellites to communicate back to their operators during strikes. There is no ready replacement for the network.
Starlink-enabled interceptors are also among Ukraine's most effective solution against jet-powered Russian Shahed drones, he said.
Shaheds fly at speeds in excess of 198mph, meaning SpaceX's restriction makes Ukrainian efforts to chase them down all but impossible.
Tom Whittington, electronic warfare expert and associate fellow at RUSI, told BBC Radio 4's PM programme that the satellite system allows Ukraine to move large amounts of data - like video, text and voice calls - in a similar way that smartphones do but without the infrastructure that phones need.
The speed restrictions "effectively preclude" anything connected to the network going above 100mph, Whittington said, making drone navigation difficult within Ukraine and Russian-occupied territory inside Ukraine.
Serhiy Beskrestnov - Zelensky's adviser - says he believes the restrictions are not a coincidence and are related to the latest strains between Kyiv and Washington.
President Trump has criticised Ukraine's long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries and called for a new leader - criticisms which have been echoed by Elon Musk.
Ukraine's complaint about the restrictions has drawn attention to both Starlink, and Starshield - a military-grade version of the network developed for the Pentagon by SpaceX.
Musk says the two systems are separate, but in many cases they share the same underlying satellite technology.
And in a post on X, external, Musk suggested the US government could be responsible for the slowdown afflicting Ukrainian usage of the technology.
"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," he wrote. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.
"Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company."
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.
SpaceX's satellite communications have proved vital to both armies during the four-year war, including a Russian attack on a moving passenger train, but earlier this year Musk cut the use of Starlink terminals for Russian forces in a move that blunted Moscow's advance in Ukraine and caused confusion among Russian commanders.

0c925ea05951.text: AI tools are now exacerbating a largely hidden problem that frontier AI companies have been contending with for years: the risk that employees will exploit their access to spy on their employers. Why it matters: The same AI tools that companies are racing to release can also help people plan crimes and develop the technology to carry them out, creating another security headache for the companies building them. Driving the news: Federal prosecutors charged Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national who has been an OpenAI engineer since July 2025, with allegedly attempting to intercept private conversations at OpenAI. Around Sept. 30, the company found a "surreptitious audio recording device" that was plugged into a USB port in the back of a television in an executive conference room. OpenAI said in a post on X that it used its own AI models to help "understand the device and where it had come from." Zoom in: Investigators allege Alfozan used AI tools to research company meeting rooms and develop recording equipment, according to an FBI affidavit . Alfozan used a "productivity agent" to ask basic information about OpenAI's offices, the documents say. Those queries included: "What meeting was this presented at and when was it record?," "List meeting rooms in (company) that are 6+", and "can you list today's meeting in this room." Investigators also said that an AI chatbot account tied to his spouse asked the model to build a "continuous audio recorder" and to add "browser access an controls," as well as encrypt the memory card where the recordings were saved. The complaint didn't say whether any sensitive conversations were successfully recorded. The big picture: This is just the latest case where AI tools have helped people carry out alleged crimes. Prosecutors say they discovered a Nebraska man's use of ChatGPT before a bank robbery, including asking the model for assistance with stripping and repairing a handgun. He was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison in August. Last year, authorities said a man used ChatGPT to help plot the explosion of a Tesla Cybertruck outside of the Trump International Hotel in Las Vegas. Flashback: Alfozan's case has caught viral attention across news sites and social media, but it isn't the first time a tech employee has been arrested for allegedly stealing AI trade secrets. In 2024, the Justice Department indicted ex-Google software engineer Linwei Ding for stealing AI technology secrets and sharing them with two Chinese companies. Earlier this year, a federal jury found Ding guilty on several counts of economic espionage and theft of trade secrets. Threat level: Now, AI tools are adding a new dimension to corporate espionage, potentially making it easier for less-sophisticated actors to build spying devices while giving investigators new ways to retrace their steps. The bottom line: AI models are creating security headaches for companies not only when they break out of containment , but also when people use them to plan and carry out crimes — including espionage against their own internal workings.

f9caa0f06f94.text: By — Safiyah Riddle, Associated Press Safiyah Riddle, Associated Press By — Eric Tucker, Associated Press Eric Tucker, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/justice-department-threatens-california-with-legal-action-over-claim-of-noncitizens-on-voter-rolls Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Justice Department threatens California with legal action over claim of noncitizens on voter rolls Politics Oct 14, 2026 3:19 PM EDT LOS ANGELES (AP) — The U.S. Department of Justice has threatened California with possible legal action over what it says are noncitizens believed to have received mail ballots for next month's midterm elections. WATCH: Examining the DOJ's effort to prosecute non-citizens accused of voting A letter sent Tuesday to Secretary of State Shirley Weber from Trent McCotter, the acting deputy U.S. attorney general, says the department has provided officials in Los Angeles County with a password-protected thumb drive with a list of names the federal government believes are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots to participate in the Nov. 3 election. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. California mails ballots to all registered voters. The letter obtained by The Associated Press gives the state 48 hours to determine whether any citizens are included on the list. For individuals whose citizenship cannot be independently verified, the state is to instruct local election officials to segregate their mail-in ballots until their status can be determined, and to not provide a ballot to anyone who has not yet received it. The letters warns that legal action may follow if the state does not meet the 48-hour deadline to review the list. "If you cannot implement this process by then, given the ongoing federal election, the United States will have no choice but to seek emergency relief," the letter states. WATCH: DOJ threatens to arrest state election officials if noncitizens vote A separate, similar letter was sent to the registrar's office in Los Angeles County, which the U.S. attorney's office had investigated during the state's June primary. Neither the California secretary of state nor the Los Angeles County registrar immediately responded to requests seeking comment. The Trump administration has made the hunt for noncitizen voters a priority this year, even though the problem is exceptionally rare. The Justice Department has charged about 90 people for various types of election misconduct so far this year, including 50 who are alleged to have voted as noncitizens. There were more than 227 million registered voters in the United States during the 2024 presidential election. READ MORE: Trump's focus on noncitizen voting has led to 160 arrests. That shows it's rare, experts say In July, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin sent letters to California, Nevada, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, alleging that as many as 250,000 noncitizens were registered in those states. Election officials there were skeptical of the claim, including Weber, the California secretary of state. "I have serious doubts about the reliability of your data and accuracy of your claims, since my office has not shared our statewide voter registration list with DHS or any other federal agency or official," Weber said in response. That same month, the Republican administration claimed Nevada had 1,500 noncitizen voters on its voter rolls. But after the federal government identified them to the state, the number of actual registered noncitizens turned out to be zero. WATCH: How local officials are testing voting machines to ensure election integrity As part of its project to find noncitizens on the voter rolls, the Justice Department has been seeking detailed voter information — including dates of birth, addresses, driver's license numbers and partial Social Security numbers — from the states. Some Republican-led states have turned over the information, which has been run through a U.S. Department of Homeland Security database that has been criticized as inaccurately flagging U.S. citizens. The Justice Department has sued 30 states and the District of Columbia for that information, but so far has lost those cases in court. California is among the states that successfully sued, in part by arguing that turning over the data would violate state privacy laws. Santa Cruz County Clerk Tricia Webber, who is president of the California Association of Clerks and Election Officials, said she had not seen the letters but said the 48-hour deadline to vet voters flagged by the federal government was "completely unreasonable." READ MORE: How Trump's mail voting claims are affecting voters She said when there is a report of an ineligible voter incorrectly on the rolls, her office does due diligence to investigate. That involves looking at the voter's registration history, identifying whether that person had voted before and, most importantly, reaching out to the voter, she said. "It would take more than 48 hours to even begin to get the full picture," Webber said. She also questioned how the federal government came up with a list of alleged noncitizen voters since it doesn't have access to the state's detailed voter information. Webber added that throughout the course of her decades-long career working for local election agencies, she has "never seen anything that would make me believe that our voter records are filled with fraudulent voters." acf4adc1aa51.text: By — Lekan Oyekanmi, Associated Press Lekan Oyekanmi, Associated Press By — Anna Wilder, Associated Press/Report For America Anna Wilder, Associated Press/Report For America Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/ice-officer-appeared-to-intentionally-hit-a-man-with-a-vehicle-in-houston-texas-prosecutor-says Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter ICE officer appeared to intentionally hit a man with a vehicle in Houston, Texas prosecutor says Nation Oct 14, 2026 3:04 PM EDT HOUSTON (AP) — A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer appeared to intentionally drive a vehicle into a man in Houston, breaking his leg, a Texas prosecutor said, warning an investigation by his office could result in criminal charges. Miguel Parra Hernandez, 48, underwent surgery for a broken leg after he was hit by a car Saturday, said Cesar Espinosa, executive director of FIEL Houston, an immigrant rights organization that is helping the man's family. WATCH: Mullin says he won't pause immigration enforcement after NYC ICE shooting Parra Hernandez remains in ICE custody at a hospital and still needs ankle surgery, his lawyer, Kim Bruno, said during a news conference Wednesday. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The encounter has set off new criticism over immigration enforcement in Houston, where local prosecutors are also investigating a July fatal shooting by a federal immigration officer. Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare, a Democrat, expressed concern Tuesday over surveillance footage that shows Parra Hernandez and another person jumping out of a white truck and running as a dark SUV pursues them. A vehicle strikes Parra Hernandez, who is seen on the ground seconds later. READ MORE: New ICE guidance bans high-speed car chases and sets tighter rules for traffic stops, memo shows "The most obvious criminal charge is aggravated assault with a deadly weapon," Teare told FOX 26 Houston. "Meaning the car was used as a deadly weapon. And it certainly is what appears to have happened, based on the surveillance footage." ICE denies intentionally striking Parra Hernandez Allegations that officers intentionally struck Parra Hernandez are "reckless" and "false," ICE said in a statement. Parra Hernandez had been in a vehicle with the target of an enforcement operation, and when officers tried to stop the car, the two men fled on foot, the agency said. He "ran in front of an ICE vehicle and was struck," ICE said. Espinosa flatly denied this claim during the news conference Wednesday, citing surveillance video. The footage shows a man running from the white truck as a black SUV approaches him from behind. The video does not show the car hitting the man — that view is blocked by another vehicle — but it shows the SUV inches from the man before stopping. After, the man is on the ground behind the car. Attorneys and relatives of others who were arrested by ICE during the operation Saturday denied during the news conference that the man ICE named as the target of its operation — Jose Mendoza-Cervantes — was even in the white van, saying they didn't know anyone of that name. Espinosa said Parra Hernandez comes from Mexico and has been in the U.S. for 34 years. He declined to share Parra Hernandez's status, but said he is living in the U.S. without authorization. He said two ICE officers were in the room when he visited Parra Hernandez at the hospital. "He already had a surgery for the injury under his knee and now we're waiting for swelling to go down in his ankle to be able to have a reconstructive surgery on his ankle," Espinosa said. He remained in ICE custody Wednesday, Espinosa said. Prosecutors are still investigating a fatal ICE shooting in July Teare said ICE and the Department of Homeland Security have not cooperated with his office during its investigation. In July, Teare said DHS also ignored his request for information after an ICE officer fatally shot 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo. The shooting was one of at least 10 deaths involving encounters with immigration officers since the start of President Donald Trump's mass deportation campaign. Wilder reported from Austin, Texas. c0d1f3dde882.text: By — Elaine Kurtenbach, Associated Press Elaine Kurtenbach, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/imf-chief-urges-wealthy-nations-to-rein-in-debt-to-ease-global-economic-pressure Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter IMF chief urges wealthy nations to rein in debt to ease global economic pressure World Oct 14, 2026 2:59 PM EDT BANGKOK (AP) — The U.S. and other wealthy nations need to urgently tackle mounting global debt levels that are weighing most heavily on low-income countries and straining the global financial system, the head of the International Monetary Fund said Wednesday. IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other U.S. leaders recognize that the federal deficit and national debt are too high. But economic growth alone would not be enough to address the country's more than $40 trillion in national debt, she said. READ MORE: 7 questions about the national debt hitting $40 trillion Meanwhile, rising bond yields, reflecting higher premiums demanded by investors for taking on greater risk, have been disrupting financial markets. "We believe that growth, of course, helps, but it cannot deliver fast enough the necessary adjustments," Georgieva said at the autumn meeting of the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok. "There is no magic," she said, adding that other measures would be needed. "You have to go in a direction of tightening, bringing it down, bringing the deficit down." 'Fiscal consolidation' faces challenges Rising debt levels and global inflation, partly resulting from high energy costs due to the Iran war, have pushed interest rates to multidecade highs, adding to the burdens of the world's poorest nations. Efforts to bring debt under control with what Georgieva and other experts call "fiscal consolidation" have suffered setbacks from heavy spending during the COVID-19 pandemic and since. "Fiscal risks are rising, and a proper reaction is largely absent in many countries," said Rodrigo Valdes, director of the IMF's Fiscal Affairs Department. "And in major advanced economies, the effect of fiscal indiscipline does not stop at the border. It travels to the rest of the world." "Among the world's poorest countries, interest payments have reached historic highs relative to revenue, and declining amounts of aid are creating gaps that some countries have been unable to finance," the IMF's latest Fiscal Monitor said. That is forcing countries to make hard choices between supporting their most vulnerable people and meeting their debt repayment obligations. "The Global South is paying the price for rising interest rates in wealthier countries," U.K. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said at an event on the sidelines of the IMF meetings. "We need a new deal on debt, a deal that supports countries to repay over longer time horizons and, crucially, refinancing with better rates to give developing countries precious fiscal space," he said. Nations need help with job creation and investment The median developing country pays three times as much in interest as developed countries, said Alexander De Croo, former Belgian prime minister and administrator of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP). On average, nearly 10% of government spending goes toward debt repayments. High fuel and fertilizer prices, the effects of the El Niño weather phenomenon and rising borrowing costs have left many low-income countries with little room to recover. "I mean, we don't see really a light at the end of the tunnel," De Croo told The Associated Press. Creating jobs is another top priority, particularly as the growing use of artificial intelligence threatens to make many traditional occupations obsolete. More than 1.2 billion young people are expected to enter the global workforce over the next decade or so, while forecasts suggest only 400 million net new jobs will be created. The UNDP this week announced its "Jobs for Prosperity" initiative to bring together governments, development banks — such as the World Bank — and private businesses to encourage investment in sectors such as tourism, healthcare and food processing. The initiative and related efforts will help countries attract investment by strengthening governance and policies and developing pipelines of "investible projects," De Croo said. "These are things that are feasible. It's been proven that you can do it in many places of the world," he added. Separately, the IMF, Bank of Thailand and World Bank Group announced a "Bangkok Blueprint" on Wednesday to combat cybercrime, financial fraud and online scams. The announcement came a day after cyberattacks caused refrigeration systems to overheat at hundreds of stores in France. Associated Press journalists Haruka Nuga and Tian Macleod Ji contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 89ddc03eec32.text: The Trump administration is threatening emergency court action unless California officials investigate potential ineligible voters within 48 hours and set aside ballots from anyone whose citizenship they cannot verify, according to two letters sent to state officials from the Justice Department. Why it matters: With voting already underway, President Trump 's DOJ could delay ballots from eligible Californians mistakenly flagged as noncitizens and set up a court fight just three weeks before Election Day. Driving the news: Acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter sent a letter Tuesday to Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk Dean Logan along with a thumb drive of "likely noncitizens who were sent a vote-by-mail ballot," according to a copy of the letter shared with Axios. McCotter asks local officials to investigate their citizenship status by noon October 15. The letter did not say how many people are on the list. For anyone whose status can't be confirmed, DOJ asks the officials to "segregate—not cancel" those ballots and suspend signature verification or counting of any ballots already returned. DOJ also asks officials to withhold ballots from people on the list unless their citizenship has been confirmed. California Secretary of State Shirley Weber received a similar letter . Friction point: McCotter closed his letter with a threat: "If you cannot implement this process by then, given the ongoing federal election, the United States will have no choice but to seek emergency relief." What they're saying: "This should not be controversial, as the criminal statute is clear: only American citizens may vote in federal elections. It is a federal crime for noncitizens to vote in U.S. elections, and the DOJ is asking California to ensure that is not occurring," a DOJ spokesperson said in a statement. The California secretary of state's office and the Los Angeles County office did not respond to request for comment. The other side: "One must question why the Justice Department would violate its own rules about investigating elections so close to Election Day, particularly when their past claims have been full of errors," said David Becker, executive director of the nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation & Research, in a statement. Becker added that the administration could have investigated California's voter rolls long before mail-in ballots began going out Oct. 5. The big picture: The demand escalates the administration's push to uncover suspected noncitizen voters. In July, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin alleged more than 190,000 voters were erroneously registered in California, a claim state officials disputed. ICE investigators, FBI agents and DOJ prosecutors have dedicated significant resources to ramp up the number of cases and charges against illegal voting, with about 1,600 on-going cases as of mid-September. Yes, but: The administration's sweeping claims of mass illegal registrations and noncitizen voting have quickly deflated after inspection. After alleging 16,000 illegal registrations in Nevada, a review from state election officials saw that number dwindle to potentially 185, according to the New York Times . In Pennsylvania, DHS officials conceded it had varying degrees of confidence in the flags it made on about 14,000 voters, according to Votebeat . DHS also claimed that New Jersey had 35,000 noncitizen voters. Gov. Mike Sherril (D-NJ) did admit to mistake registrations from a software error, but the number was a fraction of DHS' claim: about 6,600 . Flashback: There have been software errors leading to registrations problems before , particularly for people using DMV services like getting a driver's license. But election experts note actual voting by noncitizens remains rare.

Artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic saw its revenue surge by 45% to $16.8bn (Â£12.7bn) in the three months to the end of September, the BBC understands.
The figures were reportedly revealed by the Claude-developer as it briefed prospective investors on Wednesday at its headquarters in San Francisco as it lays the groundwork for what is expected to be a blockbuster share sale by the end of the year.
It comes as some tech stocks, including firms that make the chips and other hardware that power data centres, have come under pressure over concerns about the large amounts of money being spent on AI infrastructure.
An Anthropic spokesperson declined to comment.
Anthropic's revenue has risen in successive quarters this year, from $4.7bn in the first three months to $11.6bn the following period.
Its revenue figures, along with those of rival OpenAI, offer an important gauge of the AI industry's growth and ability to finance the infrastructure needed to develop the technology.
The ChatGPT-developer is also eyeing a bumper stock market listing, which is expected to value the firm at more than $1tn.
But OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said in September that his company will not go public this year as it addresses concerns about the technology's safety.

A working dog from the Scottish Highlands has been named animal of the year by a charity for hunting down an invasive marine creature called the carpet sea squirt.
This organism, also nicknamed "sea vomit", is particularly harmful to coastal wildlife and economies.
Working at low tide with her owner, Dr Texa Sim, black Labrador Sgiath has found hundreds of colonies of the sea squirt, which - if left uncontrolled - can smother and kill native species.
Sgiath (pronounced Skee-ah) is thought to be the UK's first sea squirt-hunting dog.
"She's a natural," says Sim proudly.
The International Fund for Animal Welfare (IFAW) , external is awarding Sgiath animal of the years at its 26th annual animal Action Awards ceremony on Thursday 15 October.
Sim, a marine ecologist based near Glencoe, has had Sgiath since she was a puppy and the bond between the two is strong.
"Sgiath is incredibly clever. Her problem solving and her ability to take on new challenges and learn so quickly are just phenomenal, and it's so amazing to watch."
As a pup, Sgiath was trained as a mountain rescue dog. The Labrador proved to be so good that Sim wondered if she could use her skills to help with marine conservation work.
Sgiath has been trained to recognise the scent of the carpet sea squirt. And now, the six year old joins her owner on the beaches to sniff it out.
Sim says the dog is always right when pointing out a sea squirt, which can be difficult to spot, looking like slime among seaweed and on structures like pontoons and oyster cages.
"When I first started this project, I genuinely didn't know whether it would work," said Sim.
"No one had really explored whether dogs could help tackle this problem in the marine environment. It began as a proof-of-concept project and has exceeded every expectation I had."
Dogs' scent detection skills are often used in conservation work on land, including tracking endangered species and helping investigate environmental crime. At low tide, Sgiath can, as Sim puts it "dive down under the seaweed".
"She just does a survey with her nose, essentially, she can pinpoint exactly where it is, so it's much easier," she said.
Marine experts believe that carpet sea squirt, formally named Didemnum vexillum, came from Japan. It arrived on the shores of the south of England and Wales in 2008.
It can appear in various shades - from orange to cream - and has now spread to several seaside locations across the UK.
It reproduces quickly during the warmer summer months and, with warming seas, there are fears it could spread further.
Dr Martyn Kurr, a marine biologist from Bangor University told BBC News that non-native or "biofouling" species, like the carpet sea squirt, can outcompete native wildlife for valuable nutrients.
"These species also clog up aquaculture pens, marine infrastructure, and machinery such as boat propellors," he explained.
Efforts to control and clean up these problematic marine invaders costs millions of pounds every year across Europe.
Multiskilled dog
To get Sgiarth proficient in both mountain rescue and marine conservatuion has needed hard work and long hours from both dog and owner.
To locate and draw attention to a lost hiker on mountainous terrain, Sgiath is trained to bark and bounce around.
Conservation work requires a quieter approach.
Sim explained that she trains Sgiath to give what's known as a "passive indication" when she finds the sea squirt.
"It's a kind of a stillness, or a stare."
When we speak to Sim over Zoom from her home, her two dogs are curled up in their beds at her feet. Apparently, when Sgiath is not out finding lost people or marine creatures, she likes to be wrapped up in her dog blanket.
Sgiath, and Sim's younger Labrador Uisage, are both working dogs that are driven to do their jobs with treats and play.
Kurr, from Bangor University, said that scientists were just starting to realise that "these wonderful animals can smell changes in water that signal a marine invasion which otherwise might have gone unnoticed".
He added: "It's fantastic to see Sgiath get this much deserved award, and I'm very excited to see what other wonderful work we can do with sniffer dogs."
