Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah used much of his speech at the recent UN General Assembly to warn of the growing threat of climate-related disasters in the Himalayas, recalling the devastating debris floods that struck his country in August.
But it was his ambitious proposal to bring together regional rivals India and China, alongside Nepal, to tackle these shared threats that drew particular attention.
Shah called for the creation of a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism to strengthen cross-border disaster response and the sharing of scientific data and expertise in one of the world's most environmentally fragile and geopolitically sensitive regions.
"Let the Himalayas become a laboratory of international co-operation rather than a frontier of fragmented information," he said.
A senior official at Nepal's foreign ministry, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the proposal was still at an early stage.
"The PM's proposal has given a political direction. Our ministry is working with other relevant agencies to put forward a preliminary framework which can be the basis for building common understanding," the official said.
Neither India nor China has formally responded to the proposal. The BBC has contacted their foreign ministries for comment.
But can Nepal really bring the two regional giants together to confront a shared climate threat in a region where they have long been locked in bitter territorial disputes?
India and China share a disputed frontier stretching roughly 3,500km (2,175 miles), much of it across the Himalayas. Their competing territorial claims have led to a war, deadly clashes and repeated military stand-offs along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the de facto boundary separating areas under their control.
But the mountains that have long been a source of friction between the two countries are also facing an urgent climate threat.
Temperatures in the Himalayan region are rising faster than the global average, accelerating glacier retreat and permafrost thaw and contributing to growing risks of landslides, rockfalls, avalanches and glacial lake outburst floods.
Such disasters can sweep across national boundaries, threatening lives, infrastructure and livelihoods far downstream - making co-operation between the countries sharing the Himalayas increasingly important.
A report by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, external released in March found that glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) region are melting at an accelerating pace, with the rate of ice loss having doubled since 2000 compared with the 1974-1999 period.
Further east, on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, glaciers have shrunk by 24% in area over the past six decades, Kang Shichang, director of the Chinese Academy of Sciences' Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment, told China's People's Daily Online.
Experts say the retreat of glaciers can cause glacial lakes to expand, increasing the risk of sudden, potentially devastating floods that can cross borders into countries such as Nepal, India and Bhutan. Several major rivers flowing through these countries originate on the Tibetan Plateau.
The plateau now has more than 14,000 glacial lakes, covering over 1,100 sq km, according to People's Daily.
And the dangers extend beyond flooding.
A 2024 study published by the American Geophysical Union projected a significant rise in landslide hazards across the Himalayas and Tibet in the coming decades due to increased rainstorms.
While the largest absolute increases are expected in already vulnerable areas, including India's Garhwal and Kumaon regions and Nepal, the greatest relative increase is projected on the Tibetan Plateau.
The growing risks make co-operation more urgent. But past efforts by India and China to work together on Himalayan environmental issues have made little progress.
The two Asian powers have often found common ground at UN climate negotiations, pushing back against Western demands for emissions cuts and arguing that developing countries should not bear the same burden as industrialised nations.
Yet they have no dedicated agreement to jointly address the impacts of climate change in the Himalayas.
In 2009, India and China agreed to undertake joint research into the impact of global warming on glaciers in the Himalayas and Tibet.
Following a visit to Beijing, India's then environment minister Jairam Ramesh announced that the Wadia Institute of Himalayan Geology and China's Cold and Arid Regions Environmental and Engineering Research Institute would collaborate on the project.
But the initiative went nowhere, according to a scientist involved in the effort.
"One meeting was held between us and the Chinese side and that was it, nothing came out of it," said Dr DP Dobhal, a retired glaciologist who headed the glaciology programme at the Wadia Institute.
"What happened after that no one knows," he added.
Since the early 2000s, India and China had agreements under which Beijing provided flood-season hydrological data on the Brahmaputra and Sutlej, two major rivers originating in Tibet.
But in August 2025, India's junior foreign minister Kirti Vardhan Singh told parliament that both agreements had expired. China had stopped sharing data on the Brahmaputra in June 2023, while India had received no data on the Sutlej since 2022.
China has not publicly explained the latest interruption. But when it withheld similar information in 2017, amid a tense military stand-off with India, Beijing blamed technical problems at its hydrological monitoring stations in Tibet, Singh said.
Some analysts see a glimmer of hope in the recent thaw between India and China, marked by high-level political engagement and moves to revive cross-border trade through Himalayan routes.
"These developments suggest there might be more room for the three countries to explore climate-related co-operation," says William Yang, senior analyst for North East Asia at the International Crisis Gr

ba9b1f0db392.text: Republicans who haven't faced serious reelection fights in years are suddenly campaigning like they're running in swing districts. Why it matters: Democrats are eyeing House districts so Republican that they weren't even on the party's radar at the start of the 2026 midterm election cycle. That includes incumbents like Reps. John McGuire (R-Va.) and Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.), neither of whom were seen as remotely vulnerable coming into the second Trump term. Most of these seats haven't elected a Democrat in years or even decades and are only truly in play if the party is winning nationally by double digits. Even then, some are a stretch. But candidates in Trump country say frustration with rising prices, corruption, the war in Iran and political incumbency in general have led to a sea change that could precipitate some shock results on Nov. 3. State of play: Rep. Jack Bergman (R-Mich.) is running scathing attack ads against Democratic opponent Callie Barr, labeling her "Crooked Callie" and tying her to Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Rashida Tlaib and Abdul El-Sayed. That's a stark change from 2024, when Bergman defeated Barr by 21 percentage points. His ads that cycle made at most a passing reference to Barr , according to AdImpact. Rep. John McGuire (R-Va.) won by 15 points in 2024, a sleepy general election with minimal spending or ads. He too is running attack ads amid a challenge from former Democratic Rep. Tom Perriello. What we're hearing: Democrats say they are astounded by the level of anti-establishment frustration in their districts. "We're in a real race. It's unreal," Barr said in an interview, telling Axios voters regularly come to her campaign offices "just to vent their frustration" with the incumbent. "I ran in '24, and I can see, in real time, the shift," she said. "I mean, look at the commercial Jack Bergman ran about me. There's a track behind it that's whispering, 'lies.'" Richard Ojeda, who is running against National Republican Congressional Committee chair Richard Hudson (R-N.C.), told Axios his district is "ripe for the picking" because voters are "absolutely tired, they're done with this, they know they deserve better." "People here are equally disgusted with everybody involved in politics ... There's an enormous appetite for change," said Don Coover, the Democrat challenging Rep. Derek Schmidt (R-Kan.). Zoom in: Perriello, asked to compare the 2026 election cycle with the 2008 Democratic wave in which he was elected to his first stint in Congress, said Republican presidential nominee John McCain "was a very serious, credible Republican." Then-Democratic presidential candidate Barack Obama "was driving a wave that turned Virginia blue, but it wasn't like the bottom was dropping out on the Republican side," he told Axios. "This election has the bottom dropping out on the Republican side," he said. What they're saying: "The bottom is falling out so fast from House Republicans, they are scrambling to shore up deep red districts that the MAGA clowns cosplaying as operatives mocked us for targeting over a year ago," said Viet Shelton, a spokesperson for the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee. Shelton added, "Who's laughing now?" CJ Warnke, a spokesperson for House Majority PAC — House Democrats' main super PAC — told Axios: "Coming into the cycle, our strategy was to recruit stellar candidates in order to contest races deep into Trump territory — and it's paying off." Warnke pointed to Democratic efforts in Texas' newly redrawn 15th District, which Trump carried by 18 points in 2024, and North Carolina's 11th District, which he noted hasn't been won by a Democrat since 2006. Yes, but: Despite the DCCC adding many of these races to its aspirational "Districts in Play" list, neither it nor House Majority PAC has committed any money. In some cases, smaller outside spenders are filling the gap: Progressive group Science Victory Fund plans to spend $200,000 on ads and phone banking in 15 strongly Republican districts, a spokesperson told Axios. That includes going after Reps. French Hill (R-Ark.), Abe Hamadeh (R-Ariz.) and Nick LaLota (R-N.Y.), as well as open GOP seats in Kentucky, Nevada and South Carolina that Trump won by double digits. In other races, the candidates are doing the heavy lifting: Eileen Laubacher, the Democrat running against Boebert, raised over $10 million as of June 30 compared with the Republican incumbent's $1 million. The other side: "Democrats are doing an awful lot of celebrating before a single vote is counted, confusing a laughable target list with an election result. ... We have the stronger candidates and winning messages," NRCC Spokesman Mike Marinella told Axios in a statement.

5cc2215434da.text: Speaker Mike Johnson's sudden frank talk about his political future is upending the quiet maneuvering ahead of a post-election GOP leadership contest. Why it matters: The race could become a three-way fight if Johnson follows former Speaker Nancy Pelosi's example and tries to stay in leadership if Republicans lose the majority. Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) has widely been viewed as a top contender for the job — and Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) did not seek a waiver to remain Judiciary chair, fueling speculation that he's preparing to run for leader. Many Republicans privately worry they're going to lose and expected Johnson to step aside if the majority slips away. But his new blunt and unexpected musings on his own future challenge that assumption. Driving the news: "In the unlikely scenario where we lost the majority, I would expect my colleagues would ask me to continue leading this conference, even if we have divided government," Johnson told CBS News. But some members aren't buying it: "Why would you want to be minority leader after speaker?" one House Republican told us, adding they would support new leadership. One leader not taking the bait is Scalise: "There are no races that any of us need to be talking about until after the election's over," he told Axios during an in-flight interview while campaigning out west. Scalise acknowledged Johnson's comments: "I think early on he said he wasn't going to play in hypotheticals, and you know, and he might have gone down that path for a minute. We're focused on holding the House, and that's where my energy is." Between the lines: A bad enough defeat could spark calls for an entirely new leadership team, three House Republicans told us. But Johnson has his defenders: "Johnson has done everything humanly possible to keep us in the majority," one House Republican told Axios. Zoom in: Some GOP sources believe a three-way contest could split support between Johnson and Scalise, potentially benefiting Jordan. Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) intends to stay in his current role and has no plans to move up the leadership ladder, he told Axios last month . Emmer staying put means three candidates would compete for one job, minority leader, without a clear fallback for the two losers beyond challenging Emmer. Becoming party leader requires only a majority vote by secret ballot, rather than a public vote on the House floor. The bottom line: The jockeying frustrates some Republicans who argue they should focus only on winning in November. "How sad we have members bidding for MINORITY leadership positions," one House Republican told us in a text.

A year ago, a longtime US senator was not thinking much about data centres. ââ
Now, according to one of his advisers, he is having regular meetings with staff to track their impact and working on new legislation aimed at curbing their rapid expansion across the country.
"This happens sometimes, something starts slow and then it goes fast", the senior policy adviser to the Democratic senator told the BBC. The person spoke on condition of anonymity as they are not permitted to speak to the press.
The 180-degree turn in this senator's attention was driven almost entirely by a growing wave of public backlash that has seen politicians across the country scramble to keep up. Public sentiment has turned against the expansion of data centres, the large warehouses that store processing power needed for internet activity.
Packed with rows and rows of computer chips, sometimes seven-feet high, data centres have turned into more than infrastructure for the internet. They are now the physical embodiment of the recent and explosive growth of artificial intelligence (AI) technology, and the varied fears people associate with it.
"I don't want to be the guinea pig for this," Indiana resident Angelita Soriano told the BBC.
A new Amazon data centre is being built directly across the street from her home. When complete, the 26-building structure will take up more than a square mile in her neighbourhood and maintain 782 diesel-powered generators.
Some data centres are even larger. In Ohio, a joint effort between OpenAI, Nvidia, SB Energy and the US Department of Energy is set to build a data centre complex that will stretch for roughly six square miles, the same size as most townships in the US.
There are about 3,000 data centres currently operating in the US, with that number potentially doubling in the next few years, according to a report by, external Pew Research Center.
Data centres are built through very local rules and permits, meaning federal lawmakers like US senators have little say in the process.
Yet, opposition has become so strong so quickly in the US that suddenly, politicians at all levels are now all but required to take a stand.
"This isn't just an issue on the left, there is huge pushback among conservatives to data centres," Chloe Autio, an AI policy adviser, said. "Whoever articulates a clear position and sticks to it, in either party, really stands to benefit."
Her analysis was echoed by the adviser to the US Senator working on data centre legislation.
"There is a clear policy need here that we're looking to fill," he said. "This is a major backlash across the country - constituents are seeing the impacts of data centres and they do not like them."
That has put many on Capitol Hill - even Republicans - in direct conflict with President Donald Trump, who has championed the unrestrained growth of AI technology.
Trump has dubbed the backlash to data centres a "sick conspiracy" and said people and towns working to keep the buildings out are "backwards and poor".
His ire has been used as a boon to Democratic politicians looking to draw midterm votes from unhappy or undecided constituents.
The BBC spoke to residents of Indiana, Arizona, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Oregon, all of whom have been organising locally against the development of data centres. They expressed concerns about many aspects of the buildings, including their size, construction and operational noise, their impact on air, water and energy resources, as well as the speed at which they seem to be approved by local authorities.
During the first few months of this year, community groups organising against data centres more than doubled to 833, cropping up in almost every US state, according to research from Data Center Watch. The firm collects data for AI industry stakeholders and is part of an AI startup 10a Labs.
Stephanie Maldonado, the political director of LUCHA, a community organising group based in Arizona, referred to the push back against data centres as "a David and Goliath story" that began several years ago.
"People have been ready to put a stop to it," Maldonado added. "Now, people are angry."
New national polling, external shows that AI regulation and data centres are among some of the top issues for voters this election cycle, behind the ongoing Iran War and various aspects of the economy.
Proponents of building data centres often argue the projects will create more, and better paying, local jobs.
Yet, recent research, external from Brookings Institution, a non-partisan policy research group, found that a new data centre creates between 100 and 200 local jobs, which is "fewer than industry advocates claim". The projects also have essentially no impact on local wages.
Arizona Governor Katie Hobbs was one such proponent - until public pressure pushed her to the other side of the issue. In July, she enacted a three-year pause on any new tax break given to a company for a data centres project.
Arizona is far from the only state to see politicians react to data centre backlash.
Abdul El Sayed, a Democrat running for Senate in Michigan, made new rules and regulations for data centres a clear part of his successful primary campaign for Senate.
In the race for governor of Georgia, a Democrat who is calling for a pause on data centre development is in a dead heat with a Republican who disagrees.
Republican Senator John Husted of Ohio, who is fighting to keep his seat against Democrat Sherrod Brown, has also had to shift his position. Recent polls, external have found that the majority of Ohio voters oppose data centres. He has softened his support, saying that their arrival should be up to local citizens and elected officials.
Meanwhile, Brown has stumped on his opposition to new data centres. He leads Husted in recent polls.
Husted's trouble in Ohio led the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the major fundraising arm for conservatives in the Senate, to write in a private memo, external that Republican p

d8bda14c741e.text: With the midterm elections just three weeks away, a new inflation report shows prices rising faster than expected, putting more pressure on Americans struggling with the cost of everyday essentials. To discuss what the latest numbers mean for Americans, Amna Nawaz spoke with Heather Long, vice president and chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union. Geoff Bennett: With the midterm elections just three weeks away, a new inflation report shows prices rising faster than expected, putting more pressure on Americans struggling with the cost of everyday essentials. Amna Nawaz: Prices climbed 3.7 percent over the past year and by more than half-a-percent in just the last month. It's the largest monthly increase in five months. The price increase was driven by gasoline, up 9 percent in September. For more on all of this, I'm joined by Heather Long. She's vice president and chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union. Great to see you. Heather Long, Chief Economist, Navy Federal Credit Union: Good to be here. Amna Nawaz: Well, let's start with that headline number, Consumer Price Index rising 3.7 percent from a year ago, rising faster than a month ago. How much of that is due to those rising gas prices? Heather Long: Yes, that's the key question. Half of it is coming from the high gas and diesel prices. But, honestly, the reason most people gasped today when they saw this data is because the other half is coming from everything else. Sure, it's spilling over into higher airfares and higher home heating oil, but the war in Iran is not causing medical care, dental care, toys, apparel. I hope nobody's shopping for a suit. Those really jumped up. Software prices. There were just so many items, repairing a car, that rose, and that's what really caused the alarm bells today that this is way more broad-based than we thought, and that's going to take a long time to ease. Amna Nawaz: We saw core inflation, which excludes those energy and food prices, also edging higher. What does that say to you? Heather Long: Yes, it says that this is more than a gas and oil problem, and that it's going to be harder to get it down than we expected. The Federal Reserve will have to raise those interest rates again. It's already a pain point with the mortgage rates back above 7.5 percent. And so that's the pain that a lot of Americans feel, and probably the most important data point today, and people are feeling it, inflation up 3.7 percent, wage growth only 3 percent. Amna Nawaz: And that combination of the higher inflation, weaker wage growth, we have talked about it before. I want to take a listen to what two people, Andrew Larcher in South Dakota, and Craig Underwood, who's a farmer in California, had to say about the pressure they're feeling. Andrew LarcheR, Sioux Falls, South Dakota, Resident: I'm on VA disability as a 100 percent disabled veteran. And, given, when I get a month, I used to be able to afford things easily. Now it gets to the point to where I have to really watch my budget. How much food can I afford a month, or how much -- or if I buy this much food, can I pay rent? Or can I afford the car? I don't have a car right now because there's no way that I can afford a car. Craig Underwood, Fillmore, California, Resident: It's pretty hard for us to budget for a dramatic increase in the cost of diesel. It grinds on you know. When I wake up in the morning, I'm thinking about it. When I go to bed at night, I'm thinking about it. Trying to put it out of my brain in order to sleep. But you do think about it a lot. Amna Nawaz: Heather, people are clearly feeling this pressure in lots of ways. Are we seeing consumers pull back or start to pull back on their spending in a significant way? Heather Long: The pain is definitely real right now. Since President Trump took office again, there's been no wage growth once you adjust for inflation. And we already see the strain, and you could hear it in some of those clips. People in the bottom 30 percent don't have any extra money and are reliant on credit cards and starting to miss payments. The real question is, how long can the middle class hold on? They have been surprisingly resilient, but we see more and more stories at Navy Federal Credit Union, just like that first clip you played, of people who are pulling back on groceries in order to try to have enough money to pay their other bills. You can see them stretching every dollar. You can see them making those hard choices. We think it's going to be a more tepid holiday season as the hard choices are here. Amna Nawaz: We should also mention Social Security benefits will see a bump in January. The cost of living adjustment is going to go up by about 3.6 percent. It's about $75 a month on average. It's the largest increase in three years, and it is a few months away. But what kind of a difference can that make, and for whom? Heather Long: Well, there's obviously a lot of people living on fixed incomes who are struggling right now. But, as you mentioned, 3.6 percent is the highest in three years. There's a lot of hope that inflation won't go much higher from here. But the question is, how much relief do we get in 2027? As we were talking about, there's a lot of parts of the economy that are really hot inflation right now. You can't just coupon your way out of that. Amna Nawaz: Heather Long, vice president, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, thanks for being here. Heather Long: Thanks.

a5740c34ff7c.text: In our news wrap Wednesday, Iran says a cargo ship sank after hitting a mine in the Strait of Hormuz, the Vatican says Pope Leo is eating and walking again following surgery to remove a cancerous portion of his lung, the Supreme Court heard arguments in a privacy case rooted in the era of VHS tapes and Netflix is cutting about 6% of its global workforce. Geoff Bennett: And we start today's other headlines with the latest from the Middle East. Iran says a cargo ship sank after hitting a mine in the Strait of Hormuz. State TV aired footage today claiming to show the tanker on fire, though this video has not been independently verified. It's the first time Iran has reported such an incident since the war started. Separately, Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen say they struck the headquarters of Aramco, the Saudi state-owned oil company. No injuries were reported. And Saudi Arabia says it intercepted two ballistic missiles in Riyadh just days after the Houthis repeatedly struck the city's international airport. The Houthis vowed to continue targeting such facilities in the coming days. The Vatican says Pope Leo is eating and walking again following surgery to remove a cancerous portion of his lung. Officials say his recovery is proceeding as planned. The 71-year-old pontiff was diagnosed with a common form of lung cancer that is often highly treatable when detected early. Leo is scheduled to visit Latin America next month, including Peru, where he spent two decades as a missionary. The U.S. Supreme Court heard arguments today in a privacy case rooted in the era of VHS tapes, but with major implications for privacy in the digital age. At issue is the Video Privacy Protection Act of 1988, which barred video rental stores like Blockbuster from disclosing their customers' rental histories. Congress passed the law after a reporter obtained the video rental records of Robert Bork during his unsuccessful nomination to the Supreme Court. Today, the justices appeared open to allowing a Tennessee man's privacy lawsuit to move forward. The man argues that the sharing of his online viewing information with Facebook violated the decades-old law. Archaeologists say they have discovered what may be the world's oldest known shipwreck dating back some 4,700 years. The ship itself has long since disappeared, but roughly 30 clay jars remain intact on the seafloor. Their distinctive shape dates them to the Bronze Age, around the time the Pyramids of Giza were built. Researchers believe the jars originated in the Jordan Valley and likely carried olive oil or wine when the vessel sank along an ancient trade route. The expedition's leader calls the discovery -- quote -- "a time capsule at the bottom of the sea." In the business world, Netflix is cutting about 1,000 jobs, or 6 percent of its global work force. The streaming giant says most of the cuts will affect the company's tech, legal, and human resources teams, among others. Netflix has struggled to boost user engagement amid a rise in streaming competition. Its stock ended a touch higher today. Elsewhere on Wall Street, stocks dropped after the latest rise in inflation. The Dow Jones industrial average fell less than 50 points. The Nasdaq dropped almost 2 percent. The S&P 500 posted its fifth loss in the last six sessions. And famed soprano Martina Arroyo has died. With her luminous voice and ease on stage, the Harlem native broke barriers as one of the first major Black opera stars in the 1960s and '70s. She was also familiar to the nation's TV viewers at the time as a frequent guest on Johnny Carson's "Tonight Show." In 2013, she was honored by the Kennedy Center, just one of her many awards. Speaking to PBS in 2015, she reflected on her breakout years at New York's Metropolitan Opera. Martina Arroyo, Opera Singer: The audience will not let you down if you do what you're supposed to do, especially a New York audience. I think the New York audience is one of the best in the world. I have been in many other opera houses for the first time and people -- and well greeted very well, greeted very, very well, but not like when the New York people say, you got it, run with it. Geoff Bennett: Arroyo announced her retirement in 1989 and devoted herself to teaching. She died yesterday in her home in Manhattan. Martina Arroyo was 90 years old.

c7e8b3e3d22f.text: A key component of Ukraine’s communications network was partially disabled on Wednesday. The Starshield satellite network, funded by the Pentagon and operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX, was not operating at full capacity, hampering communications within the Ukrainian military. Liz Landers reports and Amna Nawaz discusses the developments with retired U.S. Navy Rear Adm. Mark Montgomery. Amna Nawaz: A key component of Ukraine's communications network was partially disabled today, perhaps by its ally the United States. The Starshield satellite network, funded by the Pentagon and operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX, was not operating at full capacity today, hampering communications within the Ukrainian military. Liz Landers has that story. Liz Landers: Overnight in Kyiv, homes engulfed in flames, as rescue workers rushed to put out the blaze and save the victims of Russia's latest brutal onslaught, as it continues to target Ukraine's energy infrastructure, plunging the nation's capital into darkness. This comes just three days after President Trump announced on TRUTH Social a -- quote -- "energy cease-fire" in the war between Russia and Ukraine and that -- quote -- "both parties have agreed." Since Trump's announcement Sunday, Russia has struck at least 26 energy facilities across Ukraine. And the war-weary nation feels it is being abandoned by its ally, President Zelenskyy told Piers Morgan today. Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukrainian President: We are a losing strong partner. So this is my opinion. And... Piers Morgan, FOX Nation Host: You think you're losing America? Volodymyr Zelenskyy: Yes, but not because of us. We -- I mean this. We can't be weak. Otherwise, we can't survive. It's painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side. But we are OK that he's in the middle. But if you're in the middle, you have to stay in the middle, not on the wrong side. I think his advisers are wrong. I don't know who is pushing him not to the right side. This is not right side of history. Liz Landers: As the two allies' relationships shows signs of fraying, Ukraine has accused the United States of not providing advanced warning of the Russian strikes, although the Ukrainian president told NPR it was a -- quote -- "technical glitch," and of temporarily limiting their usage of the Starshield satellite system, a military version of the Starlink network, which is integral to Ukraine's targeting of Russian military installations within Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory. Starshield's thousands of satellites provide Ukraine with the broadband connection needed to find and target Russian military equipment and personnel across Ukrainian territory, along with data for interceptor drones that take down Russian attacks, that ability severely curtailed, as President Zelenskyy stressed today. Volodymyr Zelenskyy: It's a big mistake, a lot of losses. This decision will bring a lot of human losses. Piers Morgan: People are dying because of this decision? Volodymyr Zelenskyy: Of course. People will die, of course, if attacks will continue and if Starlink will not work. Of course, I mean, this -- it's not helpful. So my message is, absolutely, I hope that it's mistake, maybe huge technical problem. I don't know. But we are asking to do it, to switch on. Liz Landers: Late today, former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov posted on X that Starshield link connectivity is being -- quote -- "restored," to which SpaceX CEO Elon Musk responded on X that -- quote -- "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately POTUS," as Ukraine grapples with a war and an ally it fears it can no longer depend on. For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Liz Landers. Aman Nawaz: For more on all of this, we turn now to retired rear admiral mark Montgomery, who served on the National Security Council staff, later on the Republican staff of the Senate Armed Services Committee. He's now a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies. Admiral, welcome back to the "News Hour." Let's just start with some context here. How crucial is this Starshield satellite system to Ukraine's war effort? What does it allow them to do offensively and defensively? Rear Adm. Mark Montgomery (RET.), Foundation for Defense of Democracies: So the Starshield system, particularly in this, what we're talking about here, which is operating over Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory, is critical to what you call mid-range strike, the ability to hit, say, the logistics lines that flow Russian equipment and supplies into Crimea and the logistics and command-and-control that support their frontline units. So that mid-range strike is really critical to the military resilience right along the front line where the two forces are engaged. But you can't understate the criticality of maintaining communications with the mid-range strike drones before they hit their targets. Amna Nawaz: So if those communication systems are limited, if they are throttled, if they are slowed down, what is the practical impact of that on the ground? You heard President Zelenskyy there say people could die as a result. Is that true or is that hyperbole? Rear Adm. Mark Montgomery (RET.): Absolutely. In the case of this, the people are Ukrainian military personnel, because this mid-range strike is really about hit hitting assets to support the Russian military in conducting operations against the Ukrainian corps and task force along that fortress belt. So they will lose -- if they don't conduct these strikes, they will eventually lose personnel. Amna Nawaz: So it does seem now as if that service, those communications are mostly back up. You heard President Zelenskyy also say he hopes the limitation there was a mistake or could have been a technical glitch of some kind. Do we know for sure if there was an intentional decision behind that slowdown or if this could have been a technical issue? What's more likely here? Rear Adm. Mark Montgomery (RET.): So we don't know for sure yet,

41b33cfcb66f.text: A federal judge has once again ordered the White House to restore access for three news organizations President Trump banned last month over their coverage of his administration. The judge ordered full access for CNN, MS NOW and Politico while their legal challenge moves forward. Geoff Bennett discussed more with Ted Boutrous, the attorney representing the three outlets. Geoff Bennett: A federal judge has once again ordered the White House to restore access for three news organizations President Trump banned last month over their coverage of his administration. In a ruling issued late last night, the judge ordered the White House to restore full access for CNN, MS NOW, and Politico while their legal challenge moves forward. The order remains in effect until the judge reaches a final decision or a higher court intervenes. Joining us now is Ted Boutrous. He is the attorney representing CNN, MS NOW, and Politico. Thanks for being with us. Theodore Boutrous, Attorney for Media Outlets: Thanks for having me. Geoff Bennett: So, walk us through this ruling. What did the judge find most troubling about the White House's actions and what does all of this mean in practical terms? Theodore Boutrous: The judge ruled on two fundamental questions, first found that we were likely to succeed on our due process claim, which is that President Trump, out of the blue, without any notice, without any notice of the standards that might cause someone's hard pass to be taken away at the White House and to be banned from the White House grounds, took away their hard passes, announced what he called this ban on the free press. And the Due Process Clause requires fair notice and an opportunity to be heard when the liberty interest like the First Amendment is being taken away by the government. And there are D.C. Circuit cases at the Court of Appeals on this very issue. So the court said we were likely to win on that because none of my clients had any notice of anything and they didn't do anything wrong. The second fundamental question the court addressed were the First Amendment issues. And this is really important, because the court ruled that the stripping of the hard passes and banishment from the White House was done first in retaliation for free speech and for First Amendment activity by MS NOW, CNN and Politico and their journalists. President Trump didn't like what they were reporting, and that he took away their credentials to lash out and retaliate. Geoff Bennett: Our team reached out to the White House for a statement. And they responded by saying, in part -- quote -- "The fake news has no place demanding a spot in the president's Oval Office." Now, the White House argues that news organizations have no inherent right to access the president, which is true. So where do you draw the line? Where's the constitutional line, I should say, between a president's discretion to determine who gets access and unlawful retaliation against journalists for their coverage? Theodore Boutrous: It's a really great question, and the judge addressed that, that the test is, has the government opened up a government building to First Amendment activities, what's called a nonpublic forum? And, if it does that, if it says, look, normally, we keep this closed to the press and to others, but we do open it up and we allow people in here, journalists, to ask questions and engage in journalism, once that happens, the Constitution, the Supreme Court cases, the D.C. Circuit cases, talking specifically in the D.C. Circuit's case about the White House press facilities, require that the restrictions be reasonable on those who are allowed in who have press credentials here, and also that they cannot be thrown out because of their viewpoint. It has to be -- those restrictions have to be viewpoint-neutral. So the White House, in their statement, they're just playing right into our hands. They're basically confirming what the judge said, that the reason that the press passes were vacated by President Trump is because he doesn't like these news organizations and what they publish and broadcast. And that is a fundamental First Amendment violation, and the judge found we were likely to win on that as the case moves forward. Geoff Bennett: A question about the precedent this could set, because this White House, this Trump White House has granted access to a number of pro-Trump MAGA-friendly outlets. If a future Democratic administration excludes those same organizations because it objects to their legitimacy and objects to their coverage, would that raise the same First Amendment concerns? Theodore Boutrous: It absolutely would. And that's why you see such solidarity among news organizations and journalists. The Reporters Committee filed an amicus brief, with 77 news organizations joining, including from all across the political spectrum, if we want to call it that. The head of the White House Correspondents' Association, the president this year is Jacqui Heinrich from FOX News. She's been advocating against these restrictions and these banishments because it's a two-way street. If one president can do it, another president can do it. And that's not what the First Amendment is all about. It's really an equal playing field. It doesn't take sides. That's the whole notion of why you can't have viewpoint discrimination. So it's really counterproductive. President Trump can spar with these reporters. He should just go back to normal and spar with reporters, answer their questions, instead of lashing out like this and banishing news organizations and reporters because of what they publish and broadcast. Geoff Bennett: Attorney Ted Boutrous, thanks again for joining us this evening. We appreciate it. Theodore Boutrous: Thanks for having me. And a note that PBS News is among the more than 70 news organizations that signed a legal brief supporting the effort to restore White House access for CNN, MS NOW, and Politico.

1940f1f86d9a.text: The fallout from sexual assault allegations at Cornell University continues. Faculty members plan to introduce a resolution of no confidence in how leadership handled an alleged gang rape at a fraternity. The university has suspended fraternity parties through the academic year and committed to “a thorough review of fraternity life." Amna Nawaz discussed more with Jud Horras and John Hechinger. Amna Nawaz: The fallout from the 2024 sexual assault allegations at Cornell University continues. Tonight, faculty members plan to introduce a resolution of no confidence in how the university's leadership handled an alleged gang rape at the Chi Phi fraternity. The Jane Doe in that case is suing the university and has accused seven men of the assault, all of whom deny any wrongdoing. Cornell has since banned the Chi Phi fraternity. And university President Michael Kotlikoff suspended all fraternity parties through the end of the academic year. He also committed to a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue. For more now, we turn to Jud Horras. He's president and CEO of the North American Interfraternity Conference, and to John Hechinger. He's a deputy managing editor of Bloomberg News and author of the book "True Gentlemen: The Broken Pledge of America's Fraternities." Welcome to you both, and thank you for being here. And, John Hechinger, I will begin with you because the Cornell case is forcing a closer examination of fraternities in America. In your view, based on your work, is this case an outlier or is it indicative of a larger culture or pattern of behavior within fraternities? John Hechinger, Deputy Managing Editor, Bloomberg News: Well, I think it's a particularly horrific example of a pattern of behavior that I have seen throughout my research. If we're talking about sexual assault, fraternity houses are a dangerous place for women. My research shows that women who go to fraternity parties run 1.5 times the risk of sexual assault, and sorority women who are most exposed to fraternity parties run three times the risk of rape. And in my book, I looked at one very one large fraternity. I looked at 230 chapters over five years and found 15 examples of sexual assault. As with the case in Cornell, most of them kind of did not receive any kind of reckoning. I only found one case where anyone was -- faced criminal charges. So this is definitely a broader problem in fraternity life that I think now is -- people are starting to address. Amna Nawaz: Jud Horras, I'd love for you to respond to that. Does this deserve more attention and scrutiny? Jud Horras, President and CEO, North American Interfraternity Conference: Well, let's start with Cornell. Those men, directly and indirectly, they agreed to a higher standard by being a fraternity man, and they completely failed that. The closure of the chapter, the expulsion of members is the right decision. Let's let the courts play out on the rest. But we know that. We also know that there's a quarter-of-a-million young men in a fraternity today in college. And the vast majority of them are having a wonderful experience. But specific to fraternities, we have to take accountability for any problems that we create. But it's important to note, even Cornell in their study, follow-up study, said you were twice as likely to have sexual misconduct happen in a residence hall on campus than you were in a fraternity house. So we have to lead the change. So many of the undergraduates I talked to are angry about what happened at Cornell, that it represents -- in some way is connected to them. And we are redirecting that anger into addressing cultures on their campus and in their chapters. Amna Nawaz: John Hechinger, respond to what you just heard there, especially in terms of the idea that there are similar crimes, similar misconduct being carried out across college campuses, not necessarily just at fraternities, which is an alarming issue we can talk about separately, but why the focus on fraternities in your view? John Hechinger: There's a sort of disproportionate amount of drinking and sort of out-of-control behavior at fraternities. Fraternity men and sorority women are among the heaviest drinkers on campus, and fraternity men are hosting parties where there's an enormous amount of underage drinking that's not well supervised; 75 percent of the people in fraternities are underage. And yet they're kind of the hosts and the unofficial bartenders at -- on most campuses. And what people in public health told me is, that's kind of a recipe for a dangerous environment, where sexual assaults are likely to happen. And, again, I would point out that Cornell found that half of the women and affiliated with sorority life said they were they were subject to sexual assault, which was almost twice the level of those who weren't. So I think there's -- there is a disproportionate risk there. And I think that's why people are so concerned. Amna Nawaz: Jud, go ahead. Jud Horras: Well, again, you're citing what sorority women -- it doesn't say who did it. And this is kind of, I think, confirmation bias sometimes people have. Let's look at the facts. We advocated for a federal law that was enacted two years ago, along with parents who've lost sons to hazing. Part of that is, you have to list all student organization discipline. So if you go to the Cornell Web site, as an example, which is consistent, five of the seven student organizations listed last year for hazing were not all-male fraternities. They were sports clubs and other business fraternities that are co-ed. So we have to take responsibility for our actions, no doubt about it. That's why we're advocating for -- on hazing specifically, we have had a dozen states where we have advocated and got stronger felony criminal laws. Part of our approach is, we are -- we have to hold individuals visibly and publicly accountable for this behavior, because we can do prevention work

d039d580482f.text: By — Hannah Grabenstein Hannah Grabenstein Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/what-is-the-social-security-cola-for-2027-heres-how-it-could-affect-you Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter The Social Security COLA for 2027 is set. Here's what experts say you need to know Economy Updated on Oct 14, 2026 8:56 PM EDT — Published on Oct 14, 2026 6:31 PM EDT Social Security checks will increase by roughly $76 per month for the average retired worker in 2027, the federal government announced Wednesday. The payment jump is due to the Social Security Administration's annual COLA, or cost-of-living adjustment, which has been determined each fall for decades. Next year's increase is 3.6%, based on inflation data, amounting to a little more than $900 next year. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "The COLA is really one of the only things in most people's retirement portfolios that is inflation-adjusted," said Bill Sweeney, senior vice president for government affairs at AARP. "That really means that Social Security becomes an increasingly important part of your retirement portfolio as you get older." People 62 or older and those with a disability or blindness can receive Social Security benefits. Some dependents or surviving spouses of people who have died can also collect payments. Here's what experts say Social Security beneficiaries need to know about the cost-of-living adjustment for 2027. What is the COLA and how is it calculated? Next year's cost-of-living adjustment of 3.6% is the highest since 2023, when payments increased 8.7% from the prior year's already higher 5.9% jump. The COLA is a mathematical formula tied to consumer prices. For more than 50 years, Social Security beneficiaries have gotten annual adjustments to keep up with inflation. If inflation is low, so too are COLAs, but when inflation spikes, as it has on-and-off for the past six years, the COLAs can be big jumps. Next year's adjustment is "not wildly outside of the norm," said Shai Akabas, vice president for economic policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center. Because inflation has remained above the Federal Reserve's target of 2% year over year since 2021, COLAs have generally also been higher than that, he said. The Bureau of Labor Statistics calculates the adjustment by finding the percent change between the average consumer price index for workers for July through September of the current year and the same figure for the previous year. If the percent change is negative, there's no adjustment for the following year. Because inflation has been so volatile sector by sector, it may be hard to predict what a COLA will feel like when it takes effect in January, Akabas said. But the adjustment isn't necessarily meant to be a perfect fix. "It's meant to be as close to an approximation and current a measure as can be done," Akabas said, that then "needs to be incorporated into millions and millions of benefit payments and be communicated throughout the system." What does next year's COLA mean for people who receive Social Security? The 3.6% increase is "a significant amount of money," Sweeney said. But with rising costs, it can still be hard for consumers to keep up, he said. READ MORE: Inflation worsened last month to 3.7% as midterm elections near An AARP poll of some 1,000 adults aged 50 and older found that 76% of respondents said a projected increase of 3.5% would not be enough to keep up with rising prices. That includes 80% of Social Security recipients. Instead, about 7 in 10 of older adults said an increase between 5% and 8% would be "sufficient" to help Social Security recipients afford expenses — a number that has remained relatively consistent over the past three years AARP has conducted its poll. Over time, older Americans lose buying power, said Mary Johnson, an independent Social Security and Medicare policy analyst who receives benefits herself. That's partly because older adults spend more on healthcare than younger adults, while the COLA is based on the costs of urban wage earners, which does not include retired people. People 65 and older spent nearly 2.5 times the amount working-age people spent on healthcare in 2020, according to the government. Next year's COLA may also be undercut by a rise in Medicare Part B premiums, which wasn't the case when Social Security recipients got a huge COLA in 2023. That could take a bite out of people's COLA increases, Akabas said, though recent estimates put premium increases at probably less than $20 per month, he added. The effect of the Social Security payment increase will also vary from household to household, Akabas said. Gas has remained particularly elevated recently, he added, so the COLA may overcompensate for people who use less gas and be insufficient for those who fill up more frequently. Even within the older population, there's spending nuance, Akabas said. When Johnson tracked her own budget in 2025 and 2026, for example, she saw spending spikes that exceeded 3.5% in every category, including medical and dental insurance, electricity, groceries and property taxes. There's debate on how and whether the Social Security Administration should change its formula for calculating COLAs, but a perfect solution may be elusive. "It's difficult to create one cost-of-living index that applies to everybody in a group as diverse and large as Social Security beneficiaries," Akabas said. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Donate now By — Hannah Grabenstein Hannah Grabenstein @hgrabenstein

477c2fa20562.text: The latest polling for the upcoming midterms shows a tilt in Democrats' favor. For an inside view of the final weeks of the campaign, Geoff Bennett spoke with Democratic strategist Mo Elleithee and Republican strategist Doug Heye. Geoff Bennett: Well, the latest polling for the upcoming midterms shows a tilt in Democrats' favor. For an insiders' view of the final weeks of the campaigns, we turn now to the insights of Democratic strategist Mo Elleithee and Republican Doug Heye. It's always great to see you both. Doug Heye, Republican Strategist: Thank you. Mo Elleithee, Democratic Strategist: Hey. Geoff Bennett: So, Doug, Republicans are asking voters to give them two more years of unified government. Beyond defending President Trump, what's the affirmative case they're making for what they would actually do with that power? Doug Heye: I think the tough reality for them is, there's not much more that they're able to do because of that. And in large part, that's because of Donald Trump. He so dominates the call the conversation all day, every day, usually with things that aren't on topic for what candidates want to be talking about. If I'm Michael Whatley in North Carolina or Ashley Hinson in Iowa, I want to be talking about, here's what Republicans have done to lower costs, and here's what they're going to do over the next two years. But the reality is, it's harder for them to have that conversation because of the self-created Trump outrages du jour that may be happening right now while we're shooting this and we're unaware of it. But the reality with Donald Trump is, these happen all the time. Geoff Bennett: And, Mo, there are echoes of 2006 here. You have got an unpopular war, a president with low approval ratings, a midterm election that has become a referendum in many ways on this White House. Democrats picked up 31 House seats that year. What's different this time, if anything? Mo Elleithee: Well, look, I think Donald Trump makes everything different, right? And he has for the past decade. But there are two issues that are dominating the minds of most voters, I think, today. One is the high cost of living, primarily as it plays out at the gas pump, and, number two, corruption in government. That does have echoes of 2006. But Democrats have a very easy way to point to that with Donald Trump. Cost of living is up primarily because of President Trump's tariffs and because of this war in Iran. And every day, he's giving more fodder. He and his administration are giving more fodder for the belief that they're -- that government is corrupt. Democrats can just step up and say, Congress has abdicated its responsibility under Republican control. Give us a chance, and we can finally hold his feet to the fire. Doug Heye: And, Geoff, I worked a Senate campaign, Republican Senate campaign, in 2006. And it's a very hard needle to thread when your president is unpopular to try and be critical, but also appeal to voters. On a rainy Wednesday afternoon, a novelty toy and games store in the quiet Brooklyn neighbourhood of Cobble Hill was seeing much busier foot traffic than usual.
Inside, the shop was packed with cameramen and customers, while passersby looked inside, asking: "Where's the bird?"
Art of Play has found itself at the centre of a social media storm since the weekend when Grammy-winning musician Kelly Clarkson complained online that the boutique store would not let her buy a singing and dancing mechanical bird that was perched on the wall.
The Since U Been Gone singer claimed she was "looked at as if I couldn't afford" the bird - which she said had a price tag of $15,000 (Â£11,000).
"Y'all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts' character in Pretty Woman," she said, referring to a scene from the 1990 romantic comedy film where Roberts' character is treated poorly by staff at a shop, who imply she cannot afford various items.
In a follow-up post on social media, Clarkson said the store had told her the bird cost $15,000 and that they could find her something else "comparable".
Art of Play has defended how it treated the star on social media, saying the wooden bird - which is called Molly - is permanently attached to the wall and is not for sale.
It said that during Clarkson's five-minute visit on Saturday, an employee suggested to her that she could buy an identical bird for $15,000.
They also said they had offered her a different singing bird for $2,000 from a clock-making shop in Germany, which she could have purchased that day.
"Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by eight million people who have never visited our store," Art of Play said.
"It's been a surreal experience to be the focus of such widespread outrage after just one mention by a celebrity."
Clarkson defended her decision to criticise the store on social media, saying: "I never blast people but you my friend were an exception."
When the BBC visited the store on Wednesday, there were more reporters than customers.
A shopkeeper said they would not comment on the story anymore and just wanted to get back to business as usual.
Molly still hung on the wall at the shop, this time next to a price tag of $15m.
The sign jokes that the sculpture is the "world's most famous singing bird automata!"
The store's owner has said he and his staff have faced threats and harassment after Clarkson's complaint, telling the BBC's US partner CBS News that the singer had endangered them.
This week, a man filmed himself yelling expletives outside the store, before accusing its employees of "racially profiling" Clarkson.
The kerfuffle lingered in headlines on Wednesday as a news outlet released surveillance video from Art of Play purporting to show Clarkson's visit.
The grainy footage, which has no audio, is said to show her wearing a yellow shirt, a baseball cap and a backpack while browsing items, including Molly the bird.
She can be seen talking with an employee - apparently about the bird as she points at it - and later moving to leave the store. She comes back in to say something animatedly to the cashier.
But while the argument over the bird has gone viral online, some of Art of Play's customers had not heard about it before being greeted by news cameras on the premises.
One customer who was in town visiting his daughter said he was not familiar with the controversy.
For others, Clarkson's claims that those at the store had treated her rudely came as a surprise.
Kiran Ramineni, who lives next door, described Art of Play as a "very nice small mom and pop store" and said he had seen flocks of journalists there in recent days.
Shopgoer Emily Trantanella, 27, said: "I feel like a pretty woman and I've always been treated very well here.
"I really like it here."

A little tern colony has experienced its toughest breeding season since establishing themselves at a site.
Since 2019 the seabirds have travelled about 3,000 miles (4,828km) from West Africa to Seaton Carew, near Hartlepool.
But this year the colony's 83 nesting pairs produced just 17 fledglings, compared to 67 in 2025.
Tees Valley Wildlife Trust said flooding and damage to the colony's perimeter fence contributed to difficult conditions for the birds.
The protective fencing around the nesting ground was washed away in high tides earlier this year.
Lead warden Derek Wood said a late arrival of their inshore food supply as well as predation also contributed to the birds' tough season.
In June, it was reported numbers were down 50%, which the team attributed to dogs being inside the exclusion zone.
"The season has been a difficult one for the dedicated wardens and volunteers who work tirelessly to protect the colony," Wood said.
But the team is hopeful the colony can bounce back when they return from Africa in spring, with plans to improve the site and further protect the birds under way.
Little Terns are currently classed as amber on the UK list of conservation concern.

The White House is defending its new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, as she faces scrutiny over her legal credentials.
President Donald Trump described Zacharia as an attorney when announcing her appointment last week and she has referred to herself as a lawyer.
But when she was asked on Tuesday by a reporter in which state she had passed the bar exam required to be an attorney in the US, she said standing alongside the president: "When I moved to China."
She does not appear to be registered to the bar in any state where she has lived. White House communications director Steven Cheung said Zacharia is "uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people".
Responding to questions about her credentials, Zacharia said in a statement this week: "I practised international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials."
On Wednesday, a watchdog group, Campaign for Accountability, filed a complaint with the California State Bar Association.
They are seeking an investigation into whether Zacharia "repeatedly held herself out to the public as entitled to practise law without a licence to do so, conduct California law treats as a crime".
The 42-year-old political strategist graduated from law school at Pepperdine University in California in 2011, the university confirmed.
A law degree is not a licence to practise law in the US.
The new White House press secretary told the New York Times on Wednesday that when she first began appearing on cable news, she had asked Pepperdine how she should identify herself.
She said she was advised by the university president that she could call herself a lawyer, but not an attorney.
Zacharia took the bar exam in California after graduating from law school but did not pass, according to the Wall Street Journal. California's bar exam is widely regarded as one of the hardest in the US to pass.
A person with direct knowledge of the matter told the outlet that Zacharia took the exam around the same time that she was planning a wedding and preparing to move to China with her husband-to-be.
She moved to Beijing because of her husband's job at an American private equity firm. Zacharia has said she worked on "international transaction law" there.
Her LinkedIn profile states that she worked as an associate at Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing from 2011-13.
In China, only Chinese citizens are eligible to obtain a licence to practise law. Foreign employees may work at law firms in other roles.
In February last year, Zacharia said on conservative radio programme The Clay Travis and Buck Sexton Show that she had worked as outside counsel for the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and the World Bank during her time in China.
The BBC has contacted the World Bank and IFC for comment.
It is understood the World Bank Group sometimes retains outside law firms, and that those firms decide which of their lawyers are assigned to which parts of any work.
Zacharia has also served as general counsel for Fix California, a conservative non-profit started by Trump ally Ric Grenell, according to her LinkedIn profile.

A group of 72 retired US generals, admirals, and other high-ranking military officers are pressing the US government to cancel plans to livestream an execution by firing squad.
"We ask the President, our Congressional representatives, and our fellow citizens to act to prevent this barbaric abuse of authority," they wrote in a letter where they also argued the livestream would turn the mass killer into a "martyr".
Last week, the Pentagon announced it would publicly show the 3 December execution of Nidal Hasan, an Army psychiatrist who shot dead 13 unarmed US soldiers at the Fort Hood military base.
Lawmakers from both parties, as well as religious leaders, have criticised the plan.
Last week President Donald Trump said he "absolutely" approved of the livestream plan, but some administration officials are now leaning against it, according to CBS News, the BBC's US media partner. CBS reported that Trump had not yet made a final decision on the livestream as of Tuesday.
In the open letter released on Wednesday, the former military leaders - which included 45 generals, 12 admirals and several former judge advocates general - said they did not oppose the death penalty being carried out.
But they argued a public execution would violate the US Constitution's protections against cruel and unusual punishment and turn what should be a "solemn and grave punishment" into "a carnival for the enjoyment of voyeurs and spectators".
"This type of exploitative broadcasting - that debases human dignity- will taint the honor of the military that employs it, and a nation that allows it," they also wrote.
"It will be used by our nation's enemies to stoke hatred, harm American soldiers and citizens in the future, and will ensure that Hasan becomes a martyr for attacking and killing his fellow soldiers."
The letter's signatories came from throughout the military and included a handful of officers who retired during Trump's first term. Some also had served during the Iraq and Afghanistan wars.
Hasan said in court that he carried out the shooting at Fort Hood, the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American base, believing he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan from the US military. Hasan was shot during the attack and now uses a wheelchair.
Retired Maj Gen Tony Taguba, who led the Army's investigation into reported prisoner abuses at Abu Ghraib in Iraq, and retired Air Force Coll Moe Davis, a prosecutor at the Guatanamo Bay detention centre who called waterboarding torture, signed the letter.
So did Charles Bolden, a US Marine Corps Major General who became the head of Nasa, and a retired Lt Gen Claudia Kennedy, the first woman to become a three-star general in the Army.
Trump has said he signed off on the execution, but while he approves of the livestream plan, a final decision is yet to be made.
It would be the first public execution in the US in almost a century.
The plan, which was announced by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth last week, has been heavily criticised by politicians, academics and experts.

On the underside of most children's toys on sale in the US you'll find the same three words â "Made in China".
Nearly eight in 10 toys (78.3%) imported into the country in 2024 came from China, according to US government figures. , external
Last year, toys imported from China were worth $9.8bn (Â£7.4bn), trade figures show. , external
With Christmas on the horizon, the toy industry in the US and elsewhere is about to have its busiest time of the year by far.
As retailers prepare their stocks for the festive rush, be they online giants or "mom-and-pop" physical stores, the BBC World Service's Follow the Money series traces how a toy gets from a factory in China to the US. And where the money goes.
The factory
Guangdong province, which neighbours Hong Kong in southern China, is the heart of the country's toy manufacturing industry.
In the city of Dongguan workers on the floor of the Mihox factory pop plastic toys out of steel moulds, and pile them into crates ready for painting.
The company says it employs more than 800 people and makes around 55 million toys a year for the American market, which represents half of its business.
Every toy starts with a design from a customer, such as an American toy company. The factory then makes a prototype, and builds moulds from which plastic parts and other components are formed.
Going from the first idea to finished toy takes one to two years, says Melanie Wang from the Mihox sales team. Much of that is the customer going back to the drawing board. "They modified the design again, again, and again to improve it."
Once the design is signed off, things move more quickly. A mould takes about a month to make, and the production run lasts about three months.
So, how much of the US retail price does the factory get? "About 20%," says Wang.
On a $30 toy, that's $6, which has to cover the price of the plastic and other materials, production costs including wages, and what profit the factory makes.
Chinese factories typically make a profit of between 3% and 10%, according to Jay Foreman, chief executive of US toy firm Basic Fun. So for a $30 toy that's between 60 and 18 cents of the $6 the factory charges to make it.
Samson Ko is president of the Toys Manufacturers' Association of Hong Kong. Many of his members moved their factories across the border into mainland China in the 1980s, attracted by cheaper land and labour.
He says the way toys are made has barely changed since then. "Automation now takes place mostly in the moulding and the packaging process. But for soft toys, or even some of the electronics nowadays, it's still very labour intensive."
And Chinese labour isn't cheap anymore, he adds, after recent rises.
Average pay in Vietnam is about half of that in China, said one report, external at the start of this year.
Yet fewer than 10% of Ko's members have moved any production outside China, and in those cases mostly only because customers asked them to do so.
The Chinese factories remain busy, he says, because a single toy can undergo more than one manufacturing process, from moulding the parts, to adding electronics, sewing materials, and final assembly. This often requires it travelling to different factories.
Ko adds that in Guangdong these separate facilities are located close to each other, and used to "working in harmony". He says this makes the whole manufacturing process run more smoothly than in other countries.
The ship
From the factory, the toy goes by truck to a port, such as Shenzhen, the biggest in Guangdong.
Ivy Tse is co-founder of FreightAmigo, a Hong Kong logistics company that runs an online platform for both Hong Kong and mainland China exporters. These businesses can book a cargo container, sea passage to an overseas destination, arrange insurance cover, and secure finance.
Tse says it takes about 15 days for a cargo ship to get from Shenzhen to the US west coast, and 25 to 30 days to the east coast. This year's Christmas toys left China in August and September.
Freight, from factory to the US, usually adds about 10% to the manufacturing cost of a toy, adds Tse. So if we stick to a toy that retails for $30 in the US, and therefore costs $6 to make in China, the cost of getting it to the states is 60 cents.
The US border
Once the toy reaches the US there is currently a tariff on Chinese toys that has to be paid to the US Customs and Border Protection (CBP).
Following talks between President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping last month, the two governments have recommended toys for lower tariffs. But no new rate or start date has been set, and the US must first hold a public consultation. For now the basic rate is 12.5%, and some toys pay more.
This is charged on the manufacturing price of the toy, not on how much it retails for. So for a $30 toy, that basic rate is 12.5% of $6, which is 75 cents.
This tariff is paid for by the American company that has imported the toys. One such firm is Learning Resources, a family business based near Chicago that sells educational toys. Half of these it imports from China.
"We pay 100% of the tariffs, let there be no doubt about that," says the company's chief executive Rick Woldenberg.
The US toy company
The cost of making the $30 toy, getting it to the US, and paying the import tariff, comes to $7.35. So that leaves $22.65, or 75.5% of the total.
That money never leaves the US, explains Foreman from Basic Fun. His firm, which is based in Florida, makes Tonka trucks and Care Bears cuddly toys.
"It's kept by my company, the [US] transportation company, the retailer," he says.
If we allow $2.65 for the US delivery firm, the toy company and the retailer will typically share the remaining revenues 50-50. So that would give them $10 each.
While profit margins are commercially sensitive and therefore not generally revealed, industry studies show that the toy firm and retailer would usually make a profit of up to 25% or $2.50.

Lizâs view
The bottleneck in the AI boom was chips, then power, then memory. Itâs about to become money.
That might sound strange as Anthropic prepares for a $1 trillion-plus IPO and data centers keep sprouting like big-box poppies. But the fear and exasperation among the lenders whose money fuels this game sharpened noticeably over the past week.
Itâs not just the days-long chip selloff thatâs messing with global markets. âThereâs shortages in chips. Thereâs shortages in power. And soon, there will be shortages of capital,â the CEO of Singaporeâs biggest bank, DBS, warned Semaforâs Shelly Banjo in Bangkok this week.
âWeâre not an ATM for your dystopian future,â a major financier of data centers told me yesterday. Rest assured, he would happily play the part if the risk-return math made sense, but it doesnât. Good luck enforcing Potemkin guarantees from hyperscalers or arguing that local protests excuse a construction delay that blew a hole in the financing.
Investors get scared the same way moguls go bankrupt, gradually, then quickly. You see it in deals like Voltaâs $5 billion Norwegian data center, which months ago would have been waved through by investors now demanding tougher terms. You see it in CoreWeaveâs tanking bonds. You see it in the cost of a policy to protect against SpaceX defaulting on its debt, which goes for 80% more than it did three months ago. And in the early price talk for the rocket companyâs $40 billion loan being marketed this week, which Iâm told is around 1 percentage point higher than its existing bonds. To quote Elon Musk himself: Yikes.
Yes, OpenAI will have no trouble raising the $30 billion itâs looking for and equity markets will probably recover from this weekâs chip selloff. But itâs worth remembering that telecom bonds began cracking six months before the dot-com crash. In 2007, subprime mortgage bonds peaked eight months before the S&P 500 did. Equity investors get paid to be dreamers. Lenders get paid not to lose money.

Leo's post-operative tests remained within normal levels and his physiotherapy session Thursday involved full mobility exercises, with the pope going about his daily activities independently, said the update from Leo's personal doctor, Dr. Luigi Carbone, and the head of thoracic surgery at Gemelli hospital, Dr. Stefano Margaritora. WATCH: What we know about Pope Leo's lung cancer and prognosis "The chest X-ray revealed good recovery of the operated lung," they reported. Separately, the Vatican said Leo had resumed working from the hospital, looking at documents, and had for a second day celebrated Mass with other priests in a special chapel set up for him near his room on the 10th floor of the hospital. The 71-year-old Leo had the lower right lobe of his right lung removed on Tuesday after doctors identified a suspected cancerous nodule. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. READ MORE: Pope Leo is eating and recovering after cancer surgery, doctors say Doctors are still awaiting the results of tests to understand the precise molecular makeup of the cancer, whether it has spread beyond the lobe and whether any further treatment is necessary. Asked if any changes to Leo's planned trip to South America from Nov. 6-17 were expected, spokesman Matteo Bruni pointed to Leo's words on Sunday when he announced the discovery of the nodule and impending surgery. "Thank you for your prayers for the pastoral visit I will make to Peru," Leo said Sunday in Spanish, in a greeting delivered to a Peruvian group. The trip is also scheduled to include stops in Uruguay and Argentina. Leo is expected to remain hospitalized until at least Oct. 20. Colleen Barry reported from Milan.
