52ad503c4fa6.text: By — Lisa Mascaro, Associated Press Lisa Mascaro, Associated Press By — Joey Cappelletti, Associated Press Joey Cappelletti, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/authorities-investigate-letters-with-suspicious-substances-sent-to-congressional-election-offices Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Authorities investigate letters with 'suspicious substances' sent to congressional, election offices Politics Oct 15, 2026 12:27 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Federal authorities are investigating letters with "suspicious substances" that have been mailed to congressional and election offices nationwide and are urging recipients to treat the mailings as "potentially hazardous." The investigation by the FBI, U.S. Postal Inspection Service and U.S. Capitol Police was first disclosed in a message from the Senate Sergeant at Arms obtained Thursday by The Associated Press. The notice, sent to Senate offices, said that law enforcement officials were working to intercept any additional letters, but "it is possible that some letters may reach their destinations." In Congress, the threat appeared limited to the Senate, though the House was monitoring the situation, according to a person familiar with the matter who was not authorized to discuss the investigation publicly. An FBI statement said the bureau and the Postal Inspection Service were "investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices." "Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident," the statement read. "We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters." Mailed packages containing a powdery substance led to the evacuation this week of election offices in at least two states, Louisiana and Oklahoma. The Ohio secretary of state said the Postal Service intercepted a package containing a white powder intended for its office and noted that similar mailings had been sent to election officials in multiple states. News of the letters comes just three weeks before Election Day and is reminiscent of a similar threat in 2023, when election offices in six states received mailings that contained a white powder. In some cases, the incidents disrupted work around local elections. Some of those letters contained threats and traces of the powerful opioid fentanyl, leading some election offices to stock up on the overdose reversal medication naloxone. The National Association of Secretaries of State and the National Association of State Election Directors issued a joint statement condemning what they said were threats against election staff. "Those who administer our elections should never fear for their safety while carrying out their essential duties," they said in their statement. Deputy Postal Inspector Brendan Donahue told reporters Thursday that "any threat or attack on election officials is unacceptable" and that "we are also working with our partners on identifying the individual or individuals responsible for the letters." Associated Press writer Nicholas Riccardi in Denver contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. b36cec555154.text: Data: Bureau of Labor Statistics; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios Data this week has all told the same story: This is a rip-roaring U.S. economy with all the inflationary pressures that might imply. The big picture: It puts Warsh and the Fed in a difficult jam. Top officials have signaled patience in further interest rate hikes in recent weeks, but the latest data implies broader inflationary pressures than previously thought, testing that conviction. There is scant evidence that price pressures are receding on their own and growing reason to fear that they are becoming more entrenched, which could compel a more aggressive rate-hiking response. Driving the news: On Thursday the government said the Producer Price Index rose 1.3% in September, the highest since 2022 and far above the 0.6% analysts expected. It came on the heels of a too-hot-for-comfort reading on consumer prices Wednesday. Also Thursday, September retail sales notched a 0.8% rise, versus the 0.4% analysts had expected. And the August number was revised higher. There were only 199,000 initial claims for unemployment benefits last week, remaining near historic lows. Between the lines: The U.S. growth juggernaut shows no sign of diminishing — but neither do the price pressures that have bedeviled the economy for nearly five consecutive years. If anything, the PPI and CPI data released this week suggest inflation is broadening, showing up in sectors well beyond energy. State of play: In his appearance at the International Monetary Fund's meetings in Thailand Friday (11:30pm ET Thursday), Warsh has a final opportunity to comment before the Fed enters its customary quiet period in advance of a policy meeting that concludes Oct. 28. Colleagues including New York Fed president John Williams and vice chair Philip Jefferson gave rather clear signaling in the last couple of weeks that they see little urgency to raise rates at a second consecutive meeting this month. Warsh faces a dilemma. If he affirms that stance in spite of the hot price data, it could raise doubts about his determination to bring inflation under control. If he seems inclined to raise rates, he could seem overly reactive to a couple of economic releases, contrary to his stated goal of making the Fed less "data-point dependent." The intrigue: Surprisingly, bond yields are down Thursday despite the hot PPI number — and a surge in yields following the CPI number Wednesday mostly reversed later in the trading session. It seems to reflect a flight to quality among traders as optimism around the AI buildout fades. With semiconductor and related stocks down, money looks to be flowing into safer Treasury securities. The policy-sensitive two-year Treasury yield briefly touched 4.95% after the CPI number Wednesday, implying significant Fed rate hikes ahead. It was down to 4.72% Thursday morning — an astonishing move for any 24-hour period, let alone one that included hotter-than-expected inflation data. What they're saying: "Today's September PPI report reinforces Wednesday's CPI message that inflation is turning higher and moving in the wrong direction for the Fed," Nationwide financial market economist Oren Klachkin wrote in a note. "AI continues to lend upside pressure from categories directly and indirectly tied to the buildout. Businesses seem to be passing higher costs onto customers as the proxy for margins rose heftily in September."

"You are telling me, I can't come to school?" says a teenage girl in a navy blue Islamic headscarf, captured on video challenging a staff member at the entrance to her school.
The footage has been shared widely on social media, and shows a group of girls in hijabs standing behind her applauding as she continues: "Why should I have to give up my religion?"
Last Monday the education ministry in Azerbaijan began enforcing new uniform rules, turning away female pupils wearing hijabs. Protests began outside state schools in the capital, Baku, and in several southern districts including Masally and Jalilabad.
Protests are rare in this oil- and gas-producing country of 10.5 million people.
Azerbaijan is constitutionally secular and the government strongly enforces that.
President Ilham Aliyev has been in power since 2003 and has little tolerance for dissent. Opposition politicians and many independent journalists are in jail.
Azerbaijan is pulled between two neighbours, Turkey and Iran. Azerbaijanis belong to a Turkic group of nations, speaking a language close to Turkish, and Turkey is its closest ally.
But like Iran to the south, Azerbaijan is mainly Shia - over 60% of its people identify as Shia Muslims, while most Turks are Sunni.
The interior ministry said it had detained 37 people on Monday who tried to obstruct the rules and "grossly violate public order".
The rules, approved on 21 September, ban clothing which contradict "the principle of secularism in education" in state schools. They do not mention the hijab. Similar guidelines were extended to teachers on 6 October.
In one video, pupils outside School No. 69 in Balakhany, outside Baku, hold a banner reading: "The hijab does not prevent anyone from getting an education."
Shahiza Huseynova, a mother who was protesting outside a school in the Mashtaga district of the capital, was detained on Tuesday.
In an interview with Meydan TV, an independent Azerbaijani-language channel based in Germany, Huseynova's husband Agha said she had been given a warning: "Either you take off your child's hijab and send them to school, or you go to prison."
Friends have also lost contact with Ilkin Huseynov, an activist who on Tuesday launched an online platform called "Let Leyli Go to School". It offers free lessons from volunteer teachers to pupils barred from class.
According to a friend, Huseynov left his home in Baku with unidentified men at about 16:00 on Wednesday, and his phone has been switched off ever since.
The authorities have not commented, but friends believe he has been detained. On Thursday, the platform's Instagram page could not be accessed.
Since the protests began, users have reported problems accessing Instagram and TikTok without a virtual private network (VPN).
Most of the protests have been in religiously conservative neighbourhoods in Baku's outlying settlements and in southern districts near the 765km (475-mile) border with Iran.
The authorities have long been wary of religious influence from Iran, where more ethnic Azerbaijanis live than in Azerbaijan itself.
On the night of 13 October, Azerbaijan's State Service for Special Communications and Information Security said a "foreign hacker group" had attacked more than 100 state websites.
A pro-Iranian group calling itself the 313 Team (Cyber Islamic Resistance) claimed responsibility.
Azerbaijani officials have defended the rules. One MP, Nigar Arpadarai, told the 1news.az website that children did not choose to wear the hijab themselves but were influenced by their families.
"A child has no freedom to choose a religion. This is a conscious prerogative of adults," she said.
The row has now spilled over into Turkey, Baku's closest ally, which provided vital support during Azerbaijan's 2020 war with Armenia over Nagorno-Karabakh.
The two countries call themselves "one nation, two states".
President Recep Tayyip ErdoÄan, a devout Muslim, has spoken of creating a "pious generation".
His chief adviser, Oktay Saral, has called the Azerbaijani restrictions "unacceptable" and urged Baku to "reverse this mistake".
"A headscarf is not an obstacle; it is a requirement of one's faith!" Saral wrote on X.
Several MPs from Turkey's governing AK Party joined in.
Small demonstrations were held outside Azerbaijan's embassy in Ankara, organised by KÃ¶klÃ¼ DeÄiÅim, an Islamist movement linked to Hizb ut-Tahrir, and outside its consulate in Istanbul, organised by conservative Islamist group ÃzgÃ¼r-Der.
President Aliyev's New Azerbaijan Party accused Turkish officials of an "openly defamatory" information campaign and of "baseless accusations", warning that Oktay Saral's comments risked harming ties, and cautioned against interference in Azerbaijan's internal affairs.
Earlier this month, Ilham Aliyev himself said no one should "stick their noses into our way of life".
Behind the dispute there may lie another source of friction. Turkish protesters have linked the headscarf rules to Azerbaijan's close ties with Israel, which sells weapons to Baku and buys Azerbaijani oil.
Turkey's relations with Israel have collapsed over Gaza, but Azerbaijan has tried to maintain relationships with both countries.
That is a difficult balancing act. On Thursday, when Israel's President Isaac Herzog addressed a regional security summit hosted by Azerbaijan in Baku, delegations from Turkey, Iran and other countries walked out of the hall.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved bemotrizinol — sometimes called BEMT — in June. The first sunscreens containing it are now hitting U.S. store shelves, including formulas from Neutrogena and other manufacturers. WATCH: Dermatologist explains benefits of newly approved sunscreen ingredient Dermatologists say the chemical fills an important market gap by offering broad protection, like the most well-established sunscreen ingredients, but without their cosmetic downsides, including white streaking. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. BEMT has decades of safety data behind it, including studies showing it has minimal absorption into the skin. That's been a concern with some older sun-blocking chemicals. WATCH: Why sunscreen in the United States is behind the rest of the world "It's not a brand-new ingredient that you're going to be the first person to try," said Dr. Jennifer Stein, a dermatologist at NYU Langone Health. Here's what to know. New ingredient offers broad protection without streaks To be effective, sunscreens must protect against both forms of ultraviolet light that can damage the skin — UVB rays, which cause most sunburn, and UVA rays that pose the greatest risk of skin cancer and wrinkles. Sunscreens that block both forms are labeled "broad spectrum protection." Those that don't must carry an FDA warning label. READ MORE: Do you need SPF 30, 50 or 100? Dermatologists answer your burning sunscreen questions BEMT is the first chemical-based sunscreen in the U.S. that offers this dual protection. Previously, manufacturers had to mix multiple ingredients to protect against both UVA and UVB light. "This ingredient provides a solution for what is currently a big gap with respect to providing strong UVA protection," said David Andrews, chief science officer of the Environmental Working Group, a nonprofit that advocates for higher sunscreen standards. A different class of sunscreens, using minerals such as zinc oxide and titanium dioxide, has long been shown to offer strong protection against both forms of ultraviolet light. These mineral-based formulas work by physically blocking harmful rays from the skin. READ MORE: Why it's important everyone wears sunscreen — even if you have a darker skin tone But some people — particularly those with darker complexions — tend to avoid them because they cause white streaking and discoloration. In other cases, people don't like their texture or consistency. "Those are good sunscreens," Stein said. "But for people who aren't so inclined to use them — maybe they don't like how it feels on their skin — this is a nice option." There's less skin penetration with the new formula The fact that chemical-based sunscreens are absorbed into the skin means they have to be carefully studied to make sure they aren't building up in the body at unsafe levels. Last month, the FDA revoked approval of an older chemical ingredient, oxybenzone, after determining it was "absorbed through the skin to a greater extent than previously understood." READ MORE: How these ingredients make your sunscreen work That's not a problem with BEMT. "It's a molecule that's too big to really penetrate through the skin and get absorbed into the bloodstream," Stein said. "The older chemical sunscreens had small molecules." As part of its safety review, the FDA reviewed studies of BEMT in more than 500 patients conducted by Dutch manufacturer DSM Nutritional Products. Levels of the chemical absorbed into the skin were nearly undetectable, the studies found. Agency reviewers said research in people who used the sunscreen daily for up to three weeks showed that BEMT "did not cause irritation" or allergic reactions. As a result, the FDA designated the ingredient as "generally recognized as safe and effective," alongside the older mineral ingredients zinc oxide and titanium dioxide. More than a dozen other ingredients are currently used in U.S. sunscreens, but the FDA has said they will require additional evidence to support their safety and effectiveness. The FDA review is part of an ongoing effort to overhaul U.S. sunscreen ingredients that kicked off in 2019. More evidence is needed about the impact on coral reefs Scientists have shown that some sunscreen ingredients can trigger bleaching and damage coral reefs. That's led to bans on two chemical ingredients — oxybenzone, the ingredient recently targeted by the FDA, and octinoxate — in Hawaii and parts of Florida. It's estimated about 25% of the sunscreen people apply to their skin washes off while swimming or wading in the ocean. The U.S. government doesn't classify the environmental impact of sunscreens, and marketing claims like "reef safe" or "reef friendly" have no standard definition or requirements. The European Union's environmental agency has found "limited evidence of environmental toxicity" with BEMT, but longer-term research is needed. Mineral ingredients like zinc oxide are generally considered safer for the environment, although some experts recommend staying away from so-called nano formulations. Severe drought has been declared in parts of southern England after months of dry weather drove some reservoirs to exceptionally low levels.
Most of England and all of Wales were already under drought conditions after both nations' hottest summers on record, which has taken its toll on rivers, crops and nature.
Roughly 30 million people across parts of England and Wales are covered by hosepipe bans, as part of water companies' efforts to manage supplies.
So how is your area doing and are you in a drought?
First 'severe drought' declared
"Severe drought" - the highest category - has now been declared for parts of Cornwall, Devon, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex and West Sussex.
It means environmental authorities will ramp up monitoring of reservoir levels, river flows and water quality, as well as carry out extra checks on businesses withdrawing water from natural sources.
The "severe drought" classification was introduced following the 2012 drought and this is the first time it has been implemented.
The UK government says two previous events would have met the "severe drought" classification, had it been in place. They are:
- August 1976, for Devon and Yorkshire in England, and Gwent, Monmouthshire and Glamorgan in Wales
- November 1995, for Yorkshire only
Most of England and all of Wales were already in drought, following earlier announcements by the Environment Agency (EA) and Natural Resources Wales.
Parts of north-east and north-west England are in the category below drought, called "prolonged dry weather".
There are no official droughts currently in Northern Ireland.
There is no single definition of drought, but it is characterised by a period of low rainfall. As the ground dries out, crops and vegetation can begin to struggle.
If dry conditions persist, rivers, reservoirs and groundwater levels can also fall, putting pressure on water supplies.
The EA says that south-east and south-west England have experienced their driest April to September in more than a century.
Scotland does not declare droughts but monitors "water scarcity" - when there is not enough water of sufficient quality to meet demands of people and the environment.
While conditions have improved in parts of Scotland following recent rainfall, some south-eastern areas remain in the most extreme categories of "moderate" or "significant" scarcity, according to the Scottish Environment Protection Agency.
Hosepipe bans for millions
Both drought and water scarcity can lead to hosepipe bans - officially called "temporary use bans" - if they are not already in place.
So far, 11 UK water companies have announced hosepipe bans in 2026. This means hosepipes cannot be used for watering gardens, washing vehicles and windows, and filling pools.
Ten companies are spread across central, southern and eastern parts of England, and one is in Wales.
Rivers, reservoirs and groundwater - how are supplies?
Our three main sources of water are reservoirs, rivers and from deep underground.
A key reason why parts of southern England have entered "severe drought" is low reservoir levels.
At this time of year, the Environment Agency says it would expect England's reservoirs to be about three-quarters full, but they are just over half full on average.
Ardingly Reservoir in West Sussex and Wimbleball Reservoir in Somerset are among those at "exceptionally low" levels.
DÅµr Cymru Welsh Water says most reservoir levels in Wales are normal for the time of year.
And reservoir levels in Northern Ireland and Scotland are close to average, according to the latest available data.
Many of the UK's rivers have also been affected by the low rainfall.
Most monitored river flows in England were classed as "below normal", "notably low" or "exceptionally low" in July, according to the UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology (UKCEH).
South-east England relies more heavily on groundwater than reservoirs. Groundwater originates as rainfall and is naturally stored beneath the surface in the pore spaces and fractures in rocks.
Groundwater levels are generally declining following the prolonged dry weather. In September, about half of monitored sites across the UK recorded levels considered "below normal" or lower, with southern England and Wales typically faring worst.
Water can flow more slowly through some rock types than others, sometimes taking years to fully respond to current conditions.
These groundwater stores "respond more slowly to changes in the climate than rivers, which is why they provide a useful buffer during periods of drought", said Prof Alan MacDonald of the British Geological Survey.
It is why groundwater droughts in the south of England generally take a longer time to develop but can be longer-lasting if they do occur.
Is climate change to blame?
Droughts are complex phenomena, driven by a mix of natural and human causes.
The Met Office expects the UK to experience drier summers on average in future as the world warms, though there has been no clear trend so far.
But rising temperatures can play a more direct role by drawing extra moisture from the soil via evaporation.
"A warmer atmosphere is thirstier for moisture and this can mean water in the soil, rivers and reservoirs are depleted more effectively, leading to more rapidly onsetting droughts, heatwaves and wildfires," said Richard Allan, professor of climate science at the University of Reading.
But there are other factors that determine whether dry conditions lead to water shortages, including how we use water.
In a landmark review into the water sector of England and Wales, water companies were criticised for historic underinvestment in water infrastructure.
And while spring and summer were relatively dry for much of the UK, winter was much wetter than usual, raising questions about how effectively water is being managed.

7bb70cba00f9.text: By — Lauren Neergaard, Associated Press Lauren Neergaard, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/what-is-adenocarcinoma-heres-what-to-know-about-pope-leo-xivs-form-of-lung-cancer Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter What is adenocarcinoma? Here's what to know about Pope Leo XIV's form of lung cancer Health Oct 15, 2026 11:18 AM EDT Pope Leo XIV had the lower section of his right lung removed after doctors diagnosed him with the most common form of lung cancer. While lung cancer is a leading killer, survival rates can be high if it's caught early, as the pope's tumor appears to have been. Here are some things to know. What is lung adenocarcinoma? The Vatican announced the pope's diagnosis as lung adenocarcinoma, which is one of many forms of lung cancer. WATCH: What we know about Pope Leo's lung cancer and prognosis There are two main groups, small cell and non-small cell lung cancers. The non-small cell kind make up the vast majority of the world's cases and adenocarcinoma is its most common subtype. Even it comes in varieties that can grow faster or slower. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "While it's still very dangerous, it has slightly higher cure rates than other types of lung cancer," said Dr. John Heymach of the MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston. Smoking is the leading cause of lung cancer. But as many as 1 in 5 lung cancers occur in people who have never smoked and it's not clear why, maybe in some cases just random chance, Heymach said. READ MORE: Doctors say Pope Leo's lung has recovered well from surgery and say his post-operative tests normal Other risks include exposure to radon gas, asbestos, radiation, secondhand smoke and air pollution, according to the American Cancer Society. How is lung cancer detected? Lung cancer symptoms don't usually appear until the cancer is advanced, according to the cancer society. They can include a persistent cough, chest pain, a hoarse voice, shortness of breath, and recurrent pneumonia or bronchitis — symptoms important to get checked. Sometimes, lung cancer can be found early when someone has an X-ray or other scan that shows a spot in a lung that needs further investigation. That's called an incidental finding, leading doctors to investigate well before symptoms and possibly early enough that the cancer remains small and hasn't spread. In the pope's case, a nodule in his lung was spotted during another exam. READ MORE: South Americans pray for Pope Leo's recovery as uncertainty hangs over his visit In the U.S., yearly screening with a low-dose CT scan, a type of X-ray, is recommended for certain people at high risk because of heavy smoking. How is it treated? Surgery is a mainstay when lung cancer is detected early, and increasingly is used even in more advanced stages. The pope had the lower section, or lobe, of his right lung removed to try to ensure that all of the cancer was removed. The right lung has three sections or lobes while the left has two. Each lobe has its own airway branch and dedicated blood vessels and when one is removed, "the other lobes actually pick up some of the work," said Dr. Ben Zhang, a thoracic surgeon at Allina Health in Minneapolis. The lungs gradually compensate over several months until most people, especially those who already were physically active, notice little to no difference with exertion, he said. The pope is known to engage in weekly tennis games and swimming. In the U.S., the average hospital stay after lung cancer surgery is two nights, Zhang said. It depends in part on how quickly the patient can get up and walk around, as well as pain and how long a tube that can drain air and fluid from the chest is needed. The pope was walking the next day, which Heymach called "typically a harbinger of a quicker recovery." Whether additional treatment is needed depends on the tumor's stage, based on factors such as its size and whether it shows signs of spreading via the lymph nodes, and if markers on its cells suggest it may be aggressive. Additional treatment can be chemotherapy, used before surgery to shrink a tumor or afterward to attack any lingering cells. Other options include radiation, immunotherapy or what are called targeted drugs aimed at specific molecular drivers of a tumor. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 70907431e33d.text: Data: AP-NORC; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios A quartet of polls out this week carry a stark message: Americans feel disgruntled, dizzy and down on the man in the White House. Why it matters: The vibes going into the midterms are bleak, with a large majority of voters wanting significant change. But the question remains whether those sentiments will drive them to the polls. Driving the news: Nearly two-thirds of Americans rate the economy negatively, per a Fox News poll out Wednesday. Seven in ten voters say they feel like things in the country are out of control, per a The Economist/YouGov survey conducted October 10-12. And eight in ten, new AP/NORC polling found, want to see either "substantial change" or "complete and total upheaval" in how the country is run. Among Republicans, 58% share those sentiments. Zoom out: That national angst appears to be dragging down the president's approval. Fox News found that Trump's approval rating on inflation, which picked up last month, is at a new low: 22%. His overall job approval rating has also fallen to a new floor in Fox News surveys for either term: 36%. Fox says that drop is largely driven by voters under 45, those with household incomes below $50,000, non-white voters and those without a college degree. The White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Yes, but: Polling suggests that disgruntlement doesn't necessarily translate into a wellspring of positive energy toward Democrats. Far more voters say they're somewhat or very pessimistic about the Democratic Party's future (47%) than those who say they're optimistic (21%), per AP/NORC. About half say they're pessimistic about Republicans' future, while around 23% say they're optimistic. Still, Fox found that if the election were held today, 54% of voters would back the Democrat in their House district, while 45% would support the Republican — a wider lead for Dems than the prior month. Plus, Fox found that Republicans have lost ground to Democrats in earning voters' trust on key issues like inflation and foreign policy. Between the lines: Republicans know that they're playing defense in an uphill midterm battle . They have flooded the airwaves in once-safe states and are pulling ads in those that look like a lost cause, Axios' Hans Nichols reports. But it's not smooth sailing for Democratic leadership — they are still navigating tough races and risk welcoming a new, rebellious caucus to Washington that says it's willing to buck the party. The bottom line: Pollsters don't have crystal balls — and whether Americans' discontent translates into a midterm upheaval will only be clear after votes are cast. Go deeper: Americans are losing faith in their fellow voters Methodology: The AP/NORC poll was conducted October 8-12, 2026. Online and telephone interviews using landlines and cell phones were conducted with 1,119 adults. The overall margin of sampling error is +/-3.9 percentage points. The Econmist/YouGov poll was conducted October 10-12, 2026, with 1,403 U.S. registered voters surveyed via web-based interviews. The overall margin of sampling error is +/-3.5 percentage points. The Fox News poll was conducted October 9-12, 2026 under the joint direction of Beacon Research (D) and Shaw & Company Research (R), with 1,202 registered voters nationwide. Respondents spoke with live interviewers on landlines (114) and cellphones (786) or completed the survey online by following a link received via text message (302). The overall margin of sampling error is +/-2.5 percentage points.

A Neanderthal who died 75,000 years ago may have been struck through the chest by a sharpened wooden spear, archaeologists say.
They say a 15mm hole found in a shoulder blade in a cave in Iraqi Kurdistan could be the earliest evidence of lethal violence involving such a weapon.
From the angle of the wound and other evidence, the researchers believe the spear entered the individual's chest and passed through the body - probably damaging a lung and major blood vessels - and exited through the left shoulder blade to leave a near-perfect hole.
The research is the latest in emerging evidence that suggests Neanderthal societies experienced more violence than previously thought.
Neanderthals were a separate species of humans that went extinct around 40,000 years ago. They lived across a large expanse of Europe and western and central Asia, and sometimes overlapped with our species, Homo sapiens.
The wounded Neanderthal's remains were found in a cave in Iraqi Kurdistan. As well as the left shoulder blade, the individual's right hand, three ribs and some teeth were also found.
A hole in the shoulder blade may be the earliest evidence of "lethal interpersonal violence" from a wooden spear, according to Dr Emma Pomeroy, study lead author from Cambridge's Department of Archaeology.
"The fatal strike may have been an intended heart shot," she told BBC News.
Archaeologists call the remains Shanidar A, named after the cave in which they were found. Remains of at least 10 Neanderthals were discovered in excavations in the cave in the 1950s.
The wound is thought to be the first evidence for use of sharpened wooden spears in the prehistoric Middle East, according to Pomeroy.
"It is not the kind of break that you would get naturally, because it is so circular," she said. "Experiments with reconstructed wooden spears produce very similar round holes in bone."
But the interpersonal violence is by no means certain, she says. It may be a case of friendly fire, a wound caused as a result of a hunting accident.
But Prof Chris Stringer of the Natural History Museum in London, who was not involved in the research, told BBC News that an attack by a rival was the more plausible explanation.
"The researchers leave it open whether this resulted from a hunting accident or interpersonal violence, but in my view the latter seems more likely, given the positioning and extent of the wound," he said.
This discovery has echoes of an earlier find in the same cave, in 1957. Those remains involved another Neanderthal who lived more recently, around 50, 000 years ago. Their ribs had evidence of a partly healed wound, which archaeologists believe was probably caused by a stone-tipped spear.
We can't tell for sure whether these Neanderthals were hurt by a companion during a hunt or murdered by a rival. But they join a small but growing body of evidence which point to the possibility that human-on-human violence was more common and goes back further than the current scientific consensus would suggest.
"I unfortunately see the growing body of evidence as an indication that interpersonal violence goes deep into human prehistory," Stringer told BBC News.
A key piece of that evidence is a study published in 2022 of very early Neanderthal skulls from northern Spain at an archaeological site called "the Pit of Bones". It suggests that deadly violence was taking place about 430,000 years ago.
Researchers found 57 healed head injuries among 20 individuals. Nine individuals had potentially fatal skull fractures. Six had similar puncture wounds at the back-left of the head. Because the wounds repeatedly occurred in almost the same place, the researchers concluded that deliberate blows were more likely than accidental damage. One skull had two wounds that had probably been inflicted with the same object.
The Pit of Bones findings do not show that everyone in this population was habitually violent, but they provide strong evidence that repeated killing occurred among these people hundreds of thousands of years ago.
For decades, many archaeologists linked the beginnings of organised warfare to farming, when people began living in permanent settlements and competing over land, livestock and food stores.
But evidence from earlier hunter-gatherers and still older human relatives has since shown that individual killings pre-date farming by a very long way.
The live scientific debate is over how common such violence was, and when sporadic attacks became organised conflict and wars between groups.
The research has been published in the journal Scientific Reports.

A new set of remains found in modern-day Iraq suggests that one Neandertal probably suffered a devastating blow to the face before dying at the point of a spear many years later.
The size and structure of a puncture wound in a shoulder blade suggest that it was made by a wooden spear shortly before or after death, researchers write October 15 in Scientific Reports. But violence isn’t all this Neandertal may have known. A shattered tooth found with the remains hints that the deceased suffered a facial injury at some point in their life. Surviving this injury indicates that Neandertals may have helped each other in times of need, the study authors speculate.
These remains with visible trauma are “super cool,” because “there’s a lot of ways to die that leave absolutely no mark on your skeleton,” says Libby Cowgill, a biological anthropologist at the University of Missouri in Columbia who wasn’t involved with the study.
Neandertals were often injured throughout their lives, probably from hunting. But archaeologists have also uncovered occasional signs that Neandertals and other hominids — modern humans and their extinct cousins — were stabbing and pummeling each other, maybe even intentionally, as far back as 430,000 years ago. Signs of injuries caused by other hominids have included another Neandertal at the same Iraq site whose rib was probably stabbed.
During an excavation that began in 2019 at Shanidar, the famous Neandertal burial site in Iraqi Kurdistan, researchers uncovered remains from at least three previously unknown individuals. The set included ribs, hand bones, teeth and a perforated shoulder bone that probably belonged to a single individual who lived around 75,000 years ago.
At first, the team had no idea what caused the hole, says Emma Pomeroy, a biological anthropologist at the University of Cambridge. “It’s so round, it’s like, what is it?” she recalls thinking at the time.
The team removed the shoulder blade with the surrounding sediment and tested for evidence that roots or insects had damaged the fossil. But that didn’t fit the nature of the damage.
Instead, they found fragments of bone from the shoulder blade in the dirt that suggested it had been pierced when the individual, which the team named Shanidar A, was alive. The team also didn’t see any signs of healing around the puncture wound when they analyzed the bone under the microscope and using X-rays — suggesting that the injury had occurred around the time of death.
The next task was to find out what instrument might have caused the injury. The team compared the puncture with the fossilized remains of butchered animals found alongside human tools, as well as wounds created by archaeologists stabbing animal corpses with re-created Paleolithic weapons. Stone-tipped spears usually create a diamond-shaped hole. Wooden spears, on the other hand, tend to leave round puncture wounds.
The wound was “absolutely, without any question,” made by a wooden spear, says Bruno Maureille, an anthropologist at the University of Bordeaux in France who wasn’t on the study team.
The team also found a broken incisor alongside the rest of the remains. The tooth was so shattered that Shanidar A probably experienced a serious injury to their face. Tartar buildup suggests that the tooth splintered in half years before Shanidar A died, meaning they lived with their disability for a long time.
“Given it would have affected their ability to eat, to drink — they’d have been in massive amount of pain at first — it’s likely [to] have needed some care,” Pomeroy says. That one set of remains suggest both violence and care show that Neandertal “behavior is complex,” Pomeroy says. “Like us.”

Belfast Harbour is to become a live environment for testing zero-emission transport and energy systems.
It comes after a Â£15m investment from UK Research and Innovation's Local Innovation Partnerships Fund.
The cluster led by Artemis Technologies, will connect electric vessels, high-power marine charging, autonomous transport and energy systems through secure digital twin technology.
Testing these technologies in an operational port will show how they work as an integrated system and help reduce barriers to commercial adoption.
Artemis Technologies CEO Dr Iain Percy said they are creating a digital network that will allow them to "optimise" both transport and energy use.
"What does that mean for most people? It means your bus turns up at the right time in terms of transport.
"But in terms of energy it means, more significantly that when the wind is blowing too hard, the network tells our boat 'take the power' and ultimately as we build up, it tells Belfast Harbour which uses a huge amount of energy 'take that energy'.
"Equally when the wind doesn't blow, it says 'don't use that energy' and what does that mean?
"It means we don't have to shut down windfarms and ultimately lower energy prices," he added.
This is the second project announced from the Â£30m allocation to the Belfast-Derry Innovation Corridor.
Economy Minister Dr Caoimhe Archibald said: "It will be developing to try and match up the energy supply with the demands of the harbour, which is a really big user.
"We are really world leading in terms of this so it is a really good investment," she added.
It's hoped what is learned in this project could have wider applications across Northern Ireland.
Dr Percy said: "Where the real accelerator value add comes in here, what can be done on that network can be rinse and repeat anywhere else."
"We already have real buy in from Foyle Port and other regions within Northern Ireland," he added.

For four generations, Neil Heseltine's family have worked on Hill Top Farm, perched on the hillside of Malhamdale amid the dramatic landscape of the Yorkshire Dales. And for most of that time, sheep were the mainstay of the business.
But, Neil says, over the past 20 years there has been "a complete turnaround" and he has shifted away from sheep farming to stay afloat. In that time the 1,500-acre farm has gone from a peak of over 800 lambing sheep to just 45 this spring.
"I dread to think where the farm would have been financially had we not started to make those changes," he tells me. "I either continued along the sheep-farming route because of sentimentality or made bold decisions."
While most upland farmers still keep sheep on their land, the changes here have been mirrored across not just the Dales but the entire British farming industry. The shepherd's life has never been an easy one, but for many it's getting tougher and more difficult than ever to make a profit.
The average British farmer is 60 years old, according to the National Farmers' Union (NFU), and prices for everything from fuel to fodder have risen hugely for them in recent years. Meanwhile, many farmers are facing significantly reduced income from subsidies and there are worries that recent trade deals will mean increased competition from overseas.
The UK's recent trade deals with New Zealand and Australia, struck since Brexit, eliminate tariffs and give producers in both countries large quotas on the amount of lamb they can export into the UK.
There are now 14.7 million breeding ewes in the UK - the lowest figure in living memory according to Phil Stocker, chief executive of the National Sheep Association.
Overall the national flock is also falling, down to 30.4 million sheep in 2025 - numbers last seen in the mid-20th Century, when the UK population was smaller and thus the potential market for lamb and mutton reared here was much lower.
And over the last 50 years there has been a significant fall in lamb and mutton consumption according to Becky Smith, a senior analyst at the Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (AHDB), which represents farmers.
In 1980 the average UK household purchased 128g of sheep meat (lamb and mutton) per person, per week. In 2024 that same measure was down to 23g per person, per week.
Sheep farming has shaped the image many of us have when we picture somewhere like the Dales with drystone walls to keep livestock enclosed and green, rolling hills kept short by seasonal grazing.
But any desire to protect the heritage of one of the UK's oldest agricultural industries is rubbing up against not just a diminishing appetite for sheep meat but also the question of whether some of our uplands might be better used to promote nature recovery and biodiversity.
All this raises the question of whether we have passed "peak sheep" in the UK - and, in turn, what that might mean for consumers. Will my children still be eating our lamb for their Sunday roast or in their baltis and bhunas in 25 years time?
And, what will happen to some of our most revered and beloved landscapes like the Lake District, Yorkshire Dales, Scottish Highlands and Welsh mountains, and the people who live and work there?
Why sheep farming has become so tough
At Craven Cattle Mart on the outskirts of Skipton, North Yorkshire, the auction ring is buzzing as farmers from across the Yorkshire Dales and Pennine Moors come to buy and sell livestock.
To an outsider, business might look brisk - but general manager Jeremy Eaton says it's nowhere near as busy as when he started in the industry 47 years ago.
"We'd have some sales at this market where we'd regularly be selling 19,000 store lambs," he says. "Now we're fortunate if we get to 8,000 or 9,000."
People who work sheep know that it's some of the hardest farming there is. A former shepherd once told me that sheep are only ever trying to do one of three things: "Escape, or die, or escape and then immediately die."
Globally, lamb consumption is expected to grow by 15% between now and 2032, according to a report from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development and the Food and Agriculture Organization.
But changing tastes in the UK mean mutton, made from mature sheep, is no longer eaten in the same volume it was by previous generations and lamb has seemingly gone from a weekly staple to a meat more often eaten on special occasions, with "white meat" like chicken being increasingly chosen over lamb and beef.
The drop in the national flock has actually led to robust growth in the price paid for lamb according to Becky Smith from the AHDB, with the sheep price hitting record highs in 2024.
But despite the higher price for their sheep, upland farmers with tight margins feel the pinch more than many when diesel and oil costs go up. And on top of that, the cost of feeding sheep has also rocketed - the average cost of a bale of hay is Â£155 a tonne this spring compared to Â£75 a tonne this time last year.
Farmers and groups such as Compassion in World Farming have also raised concerns that new trade deals could undermine UK agriculture because farms here must meet high welfare standards that may not be not required in several partner countries.
Extremely tight margins mean growing numbers of younger people can't see a future in farming.
This is immediately apparent as you wander around Craven Cattle Marts. "You can see here today, most of the generation of farmers are over 60," says Hayley Baines, a 39-year-old sheep farmer from Gisburn in the Ribble Valley. "There [aren't] many young ones because there's better options."
And some welcome the decline in sheep farming.
"Fewer sheep means less suffering [â¦] a sheep's life in the wool and mutton industries belies our reputation as a nation of animal lovers," says Mimi Bekhechi, senior vice president at the UK's People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (Peta).

5589a2d198d9.text: Secretary of State Marco Rubio pressed Lebanon President Joseph Aoun not to return to Hezbollah a truck full of explosives it attempted to smuggle into Beirut several days ago, according to a State Department official and another source with knowledge of the call. Why it matters: The issue is a test case for the Lebanese government's resolve to stand up to Hezbollah and implement its policy of keeping weapons outside the control of state security forces. Driving the news: Lebanese security forces intercepted the truck last week at a checkpoint on the highway connecting the Bekaa Valley to Beirut. The truck was carrying approximately 780 kilograms of explosives, including TNT and C-4, Lebanese officials said. Two suspects were arrested for transporting the shipment. After the arrest , Hezbollah acknowledged that the explosives belonged to them but claimed they were intended for use against the Israeli military in southern Lebanon. Hezbollah's opponents in Lebanon seized on the incident as further proof of the danger of the Shia militia's weapons and its independent military activity. Hezbollah and its allies in Lebanon have since pressed the government to release its two members and return the explosives to the militia. Behind the scenes: The State Department official said Rubio urged Aoun to "hold accountable all those who ordered, financed, and directed the shipment, and underscored that returning explosives to Hezbollah should be out of the question." Aoun assured Rubio that the Lebanese army and security forces are fully implementing decisions to prevent armed displays, confiscate weapons and ammunition, and combat smuggling, the president's office said. Aoun also stressed that the judicial authorities will show no leniency toward those responsible and will enforce the laws without favoritism. "No one will be released unless he is innocent," Aoun told Rubio according to a Lebanese official. The big picture: Rubio also raised Lebanon's 1955 Boycott Law, which bans any contact with Israelis, during the call, the State Department official said. The topic stems from a complaint filed in a Lebanese court against Nada Hamadeh Moawad, Lebanon's ambassador to the United States, when she called her Israeli counterpart Yechiel Leiter after his son was wounded in a West Bank terror attack. Rubio told Aoun this Lebanese law "is routinely used for politicized prosecutions that deter steps towards peace with Israel." State of play: Israel has continued its strikes in southern Lebanon and claims it is targeting Hezbollah targets. Aoun asked Rubio to press Israel to stop these attacks and allow farmers to access their fields without being targeted, his office said. After his call with Aoun, Rubio spoke with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, though the State Department would not comment on the conversation. What to watch: Negotiations between Israel and Lebanon have slowed down ahead of the Israeli elections. The implementation of the U.S.-brokered agreement over the IDF withdrawal from pilot zones in southern Lebanon is also moving slowly. U.S., Lebanese and Israeli military officers are expected to meet at CENTCOM headquarters next week to discuss the implementation.

775bc76cff4e.text: By — Anne D'Innocenzio, Associated Press Anne D'Innocenzio, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/retail-sales-saw-0-8-bump-in-september-but-big-chunk-of-spending-went-to-paying-for-gas Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Retail sales saw 0.8% bump in September, but big chunk of spending went to paying for gas Economy Oct 15, 2026 5:49 PM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — Shoppers showed their willingness to spend in September even after a better-than-expected splurge in August. But a big chunk of their purchases last month went toward paying the bills at the gas pump, according to the Commerce Department's latest snapshot on retail sales released Thursday. Retail sales increased 0.8% last month, after a revised 1.3% gain in August, the Commerce Department said. Economists were anticipating a 0.3% increase for the month, according to FactSet. Excluding business at gas stations, retail sales rose 0.2% in September. The government figures aren't adjusted for inflation, which accelerated last month as gasoline and many other goods and services became more expensive. WATCH: Economist breaks down new inflation report and what's driving prices higher In fact, business at gas stations rose 6.4%, according to the Commerce Department's report. Elsewhere, business at furniture and home furnishings stores rose 1.3%, while electronics and appliance stores saw a 0.6% increase. Business at online retailers rose 0.3%, according to the report. Clothing and accessories stores saw business unchanged from the previous month. The data offers only a snapshot of consumer spending and doesn't include activities like travel and hotel stays. But the lone services category – restaurants – registered a solid 1.1% increase. "The large jump in headline retail sales in September was almost entirely due to rising gasoline prices," Michael Pearce, chief U.S. economist at Oxford Economics, wrote in a note. Pearce noted that consumer spending is still on track for a 3.3% annualized gain during the third quarter, but he expects spending to lose momentum heading into the key holiday shopping season as the drag from higher prices weighs more heavily on consumers. Many Americans have continued to spend despite skyrocketing gas prices that have accompanied renewed fighting in the Middle East. The average price for regular gasoline rose overnight to $4.33 per gallon Thursday, according to motor club AAA. Before the war began, the cost of gas per gallon was less than $3. The retail sales report comes as U.S. employers added a disappointing 29,000 jobs and the unemployment rate ticked up last month, the government reported earlier this month. Still, the U.S. job market has proven solid in the face of a series of shocks, from tariffs to the Iran War. But rising prices are still a big challenge for shoppers. The Labor Department reported on Wednesday that the consumer price index rose 3.7% in September compared with a year ago, up from 3.4% in August. On a monthly basis, costs jumped 0.6% from August to September, the biggest gain in five months, up from a 0.4% increase the previous month. The cost of toys, new and used cars, sporting goods, and shoes all rose at a rapid clip last month, the government said. Natalie Kotlyar, national leader of BDO's retail and consumer products practice, noted that she wouldn't read the retail sales report as a reflection of broad consumer strength. "With inflation running above 3% and gas prices high, part of this gain is simply higher prices, and many shoppers are leaning on savings and promotions to stretch their budgets," she said. Kotlyar noted that strong sales alongside paychecks that aren't keeping pace with prices can't last forever, so retailers need to protect their profit margins and keep inventory flexible as they head into November and December. Federal authorities say they are investigating "potentially hazardous" letters containing "suspicious substances" that have been sent to congressional and state election offices around the US.
The FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service (USPIS) said they were trying to trace the "suspicious mailings", some of which were intercepted before they were received.
Authorities declined to say how many offices had been targeted, but several secretaries of state and congressional offices reported receiving the letters.
Coming just weeks before the US midterm elections, it echoes previous security scares involving suspicious mail.
The suspicious letters were sent to at least five Democratic senators' offices, most of which were intercepted before delivery, the BBC's US partner CBS News reported.
They were Delaware's Lisa Blunt Rochester, California's Alex Padilla, and the two senators for New York, Chuck Schumer and Kirsten Gillibrand, CBS reported.
Connecticut Democrat Chris Murphy was also sent a letter containing a suspicious substance, which was intercepted before reaching the office, his spokesman told the BBC.
Several state offices have also received the suspicious mailings.
Delaware's Department of Elections said its office received and opened a letter containing a white powdery substance on Thursday, adding that staff followed security protocols on handling suspicious mail.
The Oklahoma State Election Board and the Louisiana secretary of state both said this week that their offices had received letters containing a white powder.
The Louisiana office was evacuated after a staff member opened the package on Tuesday, but it has since reopened after law enforcement found no evidence of harmful substances.
Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose said his office was the intended recipient of a letter containing white powder, but the USPIS had intercepted it.
The New York State Capitol in Albany and the Wyoming State Capitol in Cheyenne also received suspicious packages, according to emergency responder scanner feed reviewed by the BBC.
"This FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service will continue to safeguard the public and secure elections for American citizens," the agencies said in a statement on Thursday.
The suspicious mailings come just weeks before election day, which will determine the balance of power in Congress.
Ahead of the 2024 election, vote officials in 17 states received suspicious packages.
A year earlier, suspicious envelopes, some laced with fentanyl, were sent to election offices in at least five states.

The News
More investors are looking to hedge against a potential downturn in the AI boom, driving up the cost of credit default swaps tied to hyperscalers.
Investors are piling into the insurance contracts as anxiety grows over the huge amount of capital it will take to scale up artificial intelligence and how quickly the revenue will materialize to support it.
The cost of protection on hyperscalers that have taken on the most massive levels of debt is going up the most, including cloud provider CoreWeave, whose debt load has tripled over the past year, and Oracle, whose $160 billion debt load is teetering just above junk-rated status.
The cost to insure $1 million of CoreWeaveâs bonds against the risk of a default has risen from under $40,000 a year ago for five years to $100,000 today. This week, CoreWeave bondsâ prices fell sharply, causing yields on the debt to top 15%. Its CEO sent a memo to employees saying the market was acting âirrationally.â
The cost of hedging against an Oracle default has risen 12% in a week, with a $1 million policy now costing $28,000. Part of investorsâ concern about the company is tied to a data-center project in New Mexico that Oracle is building thatâs run into setbacks.
The company last month informed one of the lenders, including Blue Owl, that it would defer lease payments and other financial obligations tied to the deal if the datacenter fails to come online as planned in 2028. It has already faced regulatory snags and opposition on the ground. Oracle still has to pay some interim costs, as well as the rent for the space.
âThereâs a derivative market. If you want to make a bet that Microsoft could default and not pay their lease, you can go in the derivative market and do that,â Blue Owl CEO Doug Ostrover said on a recent episode of Compound Interest. âWe donât. But itâs available to us.â
New debt deals are struggling, too. This week a deal for Volta Infrastructure faltered as investors feeling full-up on data center debt demanded higher yields.
Know More
Credit default swaps are a financial engineering tool that allows investors to protect themselves against potential defaults, similar to paying a premium on an insurance policy. Should something go awry, the swap would compensate the buyer.
Record amounts of debt have been issued over the last year as companies look to rapidly build the infrastructure and compute capacity needed to power the AI boom. That issuance has slowed in recent months, as interest rates are rising and as investors get more selective about who theyâre willing to lend to.

(AP) — Elections officials in battleground Wisconsin on Thursday approved guidance for local clerks to help them know what to do if federal law enforcement officials show up at the polls on Election Day, as some activists fear might happen. WATCH: Patel grilled on whether he'll send FBI agents to the polls in November A Republican on the bipartisan Wisconsin Elections Commission cast the lone vote against sending the guidance, saying it "is only going to scare away some people from the polls." A hotly contested race for governor tops the ballot in Wisconsin. "I personally think this guidance is unnecessary because we have not seemed to need it the past 201 years," Republican Commissioner Bob Spindell said. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Clerks have been deluged with questions from voters about what they would do if agents showed up at the polls, Wisconsin elections administrator Meagan Wolfe said. The guidance is intended to explain how to handle it, she said. "I see this as just like any other contingency planning we do to assist our clerks," she said. The memo tells Wisconsin's roughly 1,800 clerks who administer elections what to do if U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers, Department of Homeland Security officials, FBI agents or local law enforcement shows up at the polls. If officers arrive, the guidance says the head of the polling site should inform the municipal clerk, who should then tell the county clerk and the state elections commission. If the agents are there to observe, they must check in like any other observer and be subject to rules governing them, the guidance says. Democratic commissioner Ann Jacobs said she was concerned about uniformed officers intimidating voters. The commission agreed to her recommendation that the guidance tell clerks to encourage law enforcement agents planning to come to the polls to be in plain clothes and not uniforms. "I don't think we want full flak jacket, whatever, law enforcement three feet from our voters," Jacobs said. "I think that is much different from an ordinary, quiet observation by somebody in plain clothes." Department of Homeland Security officials have said they don't plan to send immigration enforcement officers en masse to patrol the polls and have dismissed concerns that they plan to do so as "fearmongering." Election legal experts say federal law clearly prevents the government from deploying any armed troops, agents or officers to election sites except to "repel armed enemies of the United States" — a high bar to clear. But organizations who represent Latino, Black and Asian American voters say the rhetoric and ICE's own activity make them worried at a time the number of immigration arrests is soaring as President Donald Trump carries out his mass deportation agenda. Wisconsin elections officials have been traveling the state in recent days holding news conferences to discuss the process for casting and counting ballots. They have been saying they don't anticipate anything unusual at the polls this year. "I expect this election will go like all other elections," Republican Don Millis, chair of the elections commission, said Thursday. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. A bus has hit a stationary freight train near the French entrance to the Channel Tunnel, injuring the driver and 18 passengers, the French authorities say.
The bus, which was carrying lorry drivers due to take a shuttle rail service, struck the train at the loading platform of the tunnel in Coquelles, near Calais.
Two people were severely injured and evacuated by helicopter though no one's life appeared to be in danger, a local official said.
Local sub-prefect Agathe Cury said that freight traffic and Eurostar passenger traffic through the tunnel had not been disrupted by the incident, which occurred at 19:27 (17:27 GMT), apart from a brief stoppage to allow the injured to be evacuated.
Those involved in the crash are all men and of different nationalities, she added.
Photos published by local French newspaper La Voix du Nord, external show a small bus with damage to its front and side standing alongside a train, among a crowd of emergency workers.
Eurostar released an update saying: "An incident occurred several kilometers away from the Channel Tunnel.
"This incident does not involved or impact Eurostar trains running from and to London. All of Eurostar trains will run as expected."

Economy Oct 15, 2026 4:21 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — High gas prices are intensifying inflation and vacuuming up more of Americans' dollars, yet consumers are still digging deep to spend, powering the economy, at least for now. A slew of economic data Thursday showed that inflation accelerated last month as more expensive oil and gas began to lift prices in other parts of the economy, including shipping and warehousing, before the increases reach most Americans. READ MORE: Wholesale inflation hits levels not seen since 2022 Wholesale food prices jumped, which could make groceries more expensive in the months ahead. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. At the same time, consumers also ramped up their spending, according to data released Thursday. Though much of the increase reflected higher prices, consumer resilience is powering solid U.S. economic growth. Workers are enjoying an unusual degree of job security despite scattered layoffs, which likely encourages spending despite surveys showing that many Americans have a gloomy economic outlook. It all adds up to an economy in which people are spending money but don't feel good about it. READ MORE: Inflation worsened last month to 3.7% as midterm elections near "Consumers may have gritted their teeth and looked through higher gas prices," said Jim Baird, chief investment officer at Plante Moran Financial Advisers. "They're not happy, but they're still spending." Higher costs strain producers, the last stop before they reach consumers A report Thursday on wholesale prices helps explain the gloom: The government's producer price index, which measures costs before they reach the consumer, jumped 6.3% in September from a year earlier, the biggest increase in nearly four years. On a monthly basis, prices soared 1.3% from August to September, powered by a 20% rise in gas prices. READ MORE: 3 things to know about rising diesel prices and how they affect you Higher diesel prices have made shipping more expensive because long-haul trucks and freight trains rely on the fuel. Higher transportation costs may have helped push up food costs, which rose 1.2% from August to September, the biggest monthly gain since February. The wholesale price report followed the latest consumer price figures, released Wednesday, which showed inflation rising to 3.7% in September, far above the Federal Reserve's 2% target. "The jolt to transportation prices affects every good in the economy, since inputs to manufacturing move to factories and goods at all stages of production move from producer to wholesaler to retailer by truck, train or rail," wrote Carl Weinberg, chief economist at High Frequency Economics. "This is how increases in energy prices 'bleed through' to prices of core goods." Farmers also rely on diesel to power most of their equipment, which could further push up food prices. Diesel prices averaged $6.32 a gallon nationwide Thursday, according to AAA, up from just $3.66 a year ago. WATCH: How the diesel price spike is rippling through nearly every part of the economy Despite those cost pressures, retail sales rose a solid 0.8% from August, more than economists had forecast. The increase was driven by a 6.4% jump in spending at gas stations, but consumers also spent elsewhere, including a healthy 1.1% rise at restaurants and bars. Excluding gas, retail sales rose just 0.2% last month, with much of that also reflecting higher prices. Economists say that as long as unemployment stays low and Americans continue working, spending will likely stay resilient. Hiring has been sluggish, but layoffs are also unusually low. The U.S. job market remains relatively strong Another report Thursday showed that the number of people seeking unemployment benefits stayed below 200,000 last week, a historically low figure. Applications for unemployment aid are a proxy for layoffs. "If the unemployment rate remains low, meaning consumers have a job, they will continue to spend, even if more cautiously and leaning increasingly on savings and credit," Kathy Bostjancic, chief economist at Nationwide, said in an email. Many economists worry, however, that as inflation stays high, it will steadily erode Americans' spending power and start to weigh on the economy. Weekly paychecks, adjusted for inflation, actually declined in September compared with a year ago for the first time since May. READ MORE: What the Fed rate hike likely means for you And September hiring slowed to a disappointing 29,000 jobs from a revised 133,000 in August, according to the Labor Department early this month. The unemployment rate ticked higher to 4.2% from the previous month, which is still low. Yet economists had expected September payrolls to come in around 90,000. Inflation may soon boost the cost of credit cards, mortgages and more Stubbornly elevated inflation also means the Federal Reserve will likely raise its key interest rate in the coming months in an effort to slow spending and bring down inflation. When the Fed raises its rate, that can raise borrowing costs for mortgages, car loans, and credit cards over time. According to minutes released from the most recent meeting, most Fed officials expect that another interest rate increase will likely be needed this year to combat inflation. (AP) — The Trump administration sued California election officials Thursday, asking a judge to bar the state from counting mail-in ballots for next month's midterm elections from people the federal government has identified as "likely" noncitizens until their status can be confirmed. READ MORE: Justice Department threatens California with legal action over claim of noncitizens on voter rolls The lawsuit comes after the Justice Department said California officials failed to meet a 48-hour deadline to review a password-protected thumb drive that contains a list of 20,000 names the federal government believes are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots to participate in the Nov. 3 election. The state mails ballots to all registered voters. A top Justice Department official had sent a letter earlier this week threatening potential legal action if California didn't comply. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said in a letter to the Justice Department that the federal government hasn't provided evidence to support its allegation that 20,000 names on the state's voter rolls are of noncitizens. She referenced an instance in which the federal government alleged nearly 16,000 possible noncitizens were listed on Nevada's voter rolls, but the state determined that all were, in fact, U.S. citizens. She also noted that voting is already underway in the state. Weber, a Democrat, said the Justice Department was "demanding unprecedented measures that threaten thousands of Californians' right to vote, based on unverifiable information or methodology that you still fail to explain or provide." California's elections are in "full compliance" with federal law, she added. Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan said in a statement that his office received the letter and thumb drive this week, along with a "hand written note providing a password" to access the list of alleged noncitizens on the voter rolls. He said he did not consider the thumb drive a secure device. The secretary of state's office said the password was written "on a sticky note." The Justice Department's lawsuit says the federal government sought to "work collaboratively" with California to identify noncitizens registered to vote in the state, and "California made no serious effort to do so." "The United States thus seeks commonplace election relief when a ballot is called into question," the lawsuit says. "This Court should enjoin California from presently tabulating vote by-mail ballots from likely noncitizens in the upcoming federal election until the voter's citizenship status can be determined," the lawsuit says. Weber, who is named in the lawsuit, suggested the federal government's outreach had not been collaborative. She said that over the summer, the Department of Homeland Security claimed that California had 190,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls but refused to provide the methodology or data sources when the office asked for them. In her letter Thursday, she called the recent demands "an emergency of the DOJ's creation." The letter sent by acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter gave the state 48 hours to research the list of the 20,000 people it claims might not be citizens. For those whose citizenship cannot be independently verified, the state is to instruct local election officials to segregate their mail-in ballots until their status can be determined, and to not provide a ballot to anyone who has not yet received one. READ MORE: Trump's focus on noncitizen voting has led to 160 arrests. That shows it's rare, experts say California Attorney General Rob Bonta said at an unrelated press conference Thursday morning that state officials would not carry out the federal government's requests to withhold ballots for the alleged noncitizen voters. He noted that the administration's alleged number of noncitizens on the state's voter rolls had dropped from the 190,000 flagged over the summer by the Department of Homeland Security to the 20,000 noted by the Justice Department. "What happened to those 170,000? They just got those wrong," Bonta said. Bonta also said the Trump administration was violating a federal law that prohibits states from changing voter rolls within 90 days of an election. "They are in unprecedented, baseless, lawless territory," he said. The Trump administration has made the hunt for noncitizen voters a priority this year, even though the problem is exceptionally rare. The Justice Department has charged about 90 people for various types of election misconduct so far this year, including 50 who are alleged to have voted as noncitizens. There were more than 227 million registered voters in the United States during the 2024 presidential election. Austin reported from Sacramento, California, and Riddle from Los Angeles.
