WASHINGTON—Six anti-war protestors disrupted an autonomous warfare discussion featuring Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth and the military service secretaries Wednesday at the Army’s annual conference. By the time the third protester shouted denouncements of the U.S.-Iran war, some members of the audience had begun chanting “USA, USA.”
The politically charged atmosphere isn’t typical at the show. But this year, it served as a contrast for what appeared to be a more prominent international presence than previous years—from the number of international companies represented to the size of the displays.
Ukrainian companies made their debut with a massive tent just two blocks from the convention center. Overall, there were 165 international companies and nine international pavilions on the showroom floor, representing Australia, Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, Greece, Israel, Korea, and Norway, the Association of the U.S. Army, or AUSA, told Defense One.
The roughly 2,000-member international delegation was about average, representing 92 countries—including 27 army chiefs, 14 sergeants major of the Army, 17 ambassadors, and two ministers of defense, according to AUSA.
But the ambassador count this year was also higher, AUSA said. That could be an indication that while political tensions rise, there’s still an appetite for diplomacy—and foreign military sales.
Welcome
You’ve reached the Defense Business Brief, where we dig into what the Pentagon buys, who they’re buying from, and why. Send along your tips, feedback, and song recommendations to lwilliams@defenseone.com. Check out the Defense Business Brief archive here, and tell your friends to subscribe!
1:1 with Mike Wior, CEO + co-founder of Allen Control Systems. ACS was one of 10 companies to land a counterdrone IDIQ contract with the Pentagon’s Joint Interagency Task Force-401 last month, and things haven’t slowed down since. The company makes a robotic turret, called Bullfrog, that can turn machine guns into a counterdrone weapon using AI and autonomy.
- “We just got our $500 million IDIQ. We are, obviously, working on getting funds into that as quickly as we can…getting to that point where we can prove on the battlefield, yes this works, and we should be replicating this across all the different services that need this type of capability,” Wior told Defense One during a break from the bustling AUSA conference showfloor.
- But the lack of a budget could stymie progress the Pentagon is trying to make in cultivating a tech-forward industrial base, he said.
- “Is the military going to be able to sustain this new ecosystem of defense tech companies? Can companies survive in this environment? What do they need to survive in this environment…when the military ultimately doesn't have full control over their own budgets?” he said. “It's a challenging environment as a startup.”
- But ACS is still pushing forward with a new facility.
- “We just opened a 200,000 square foot facility in North Austin” with the goal of increasing production capacity beyond 50 turrets a month once the orders come in, Wior said.
- “Whenever the orders come in, we start to fill out that IDIQ, and we can expand pretty quickly…by leveraging commercial off-the-shelf components, we have a lot of flexibility there, and then it's just a matter of expanding the workforce.”
- And they’re eyeing international deals.
- “We want to see more of an international economy for defense products…and we want to make our technologies available to other countries. Because that's needed, I think, in this environment where if it's just the United States government and they have a two-year appropriations problem, you might lose some really, really great technologies to attrition—just the ability to stay around long enough and participate.”
Up, up, and away. The Army Space and Missile Defense Agency wants “a family of stratospheric systems,” such as high-altitude balloons, in a range of platform sizes that can provide “space-like capabilities” closer to Earth, Col. Joseph Mroszczyk, who leads the agency’s transformation integration directorate for space superiority, told reporters Wednesday.
- “From about 60,000 feet to 100,000 feet is what we focus on in the stratosphere. That operational space allows some persistence and broad coverage in an area where you can deliver space-like capabilities in terms of payloads” while also being able to “take advantage of winds that are pushing you where you want to go already…to get either launched effects or other types of payloads for sensing and communications.”
- The agency hopes to start multiple experiments in the coming year.
Bonus: The agency is also “working on a virtual space training environment,” Mroszczyk said. “We're building the virtual space layer to be able to visualize and understand how space effects can play in modern operations.”
Biodefense prep. The Army wants biothreats to be a routine feature in major military exercises, as outlined in its updated biodefense strategy released last month.
- Turning that doctrine into actual readiness requires incorporating biothreats into “big” military exercises where it's “an operational constraint, and the whole of staff has to come to bear against it,” Alison Tamasi, the Army Nuclear and CWMD Agency’s chief of survivability and effects analysis division, told reporters Monday.
- “Our next target on the wall is looking toward some of those routine things like [Army warfighter exercises] where we can start to put bio defense in as one of the injects.”
- Context: These can be tabletop exercises, typically at the corps level or lower, where commanders and subject-matter experts map out responses to proposed scenarios, such as a viral outbreak at a port.
Making moves + other news
- Anduril will let employees sell shares through a tender offer, bringing the company’s value to about $90 billion.
- BAE Systems now has two new counterdrone systems: a multi-domain artillery cannon system and high-power microwave

The complaint adds to the growing list of legal challenges to the mass terminations under FBI Director Kash Patel of agents who participated in investigations of the Republican president or are seen as opposed to Trump administration interests. Their firings, the lawsuit says, create an "immeasurable loss" to "America's national security." To this administration, this is an offense. To the rest of us, it is heroic," said a statement from their attorneys, Margaret Donovan, Abbe Lowell and Rebecca Tinio. READ MORE: Fired FBI officials sue Patel, claiming he bowed to Trump's 'campaign of retribution' The investigation resulted in a dramatic 2022 FBI search of Mar-a-Lago that recovered classified records and later produced an indictment in federal court in Florida charging Trump with dozens of felony counts. Trump denied wrongdoing, and the case was dismissed in 2024 by a Trump-appointed judge, Aileen Cannon, who ruled that the special counsel who filed the charges, Jack Smith, had been illegally appointed by the Biden administration Justice Department. The nine fired FBI employees did not volunteer for the investigation but were rather assigned to it as part of their work on specialized counterintelligence and counterespionage squads, according to the lawsuit, which says they were nonetheless terminated because of baseless perceptions that the performance of their law enforcement duties had run "afoul of the political and personal loyalty to Trump that Defendants demanded." "By casting Plaintiffs' work on the Plasmic Echo investigation as 'politically weaponized,' Defendants incorrectly presumed to know the personal political convictions of Plaintiffs and took unlawful action based on that presumption," the lawsuit says, using the FBI code name for the classified documents investigation. "Worse still, Defendants incorrectly concluded that those personal political convictions affected or drove their work." The lawsuit notes how Patel, in his capacity as a conservative podcaster before becoming Trump's FBI director, had derided the FBI's Mar-a-Lago search as "unlawful" and had accused the agents who had participated in it as being "corrupt government gangsters." The most important alliances will lead to critical minerals
In the 21st century, geopolitical and economic advantage will depend on forging new links in strong supply chains.
The raison d’être of the “Concert of Europe,” the preeminent compact between the great powers of the 19th century, was to maintain the balance of power and suppress revolutionary movements. The post-World War II alliance systems sought collective security and deterrence. And the most relevant alliances of the 21st century will be the ones that secure the materials needed for key armaments and new technologies.
In the first decades after the Cold War, the global economy seemed to settle on a dispensation that was heavily digital, light on assets, and tilted toward “just-in-time” manufacturing. It also leaned on heavily financialized business models that privileged services, software, and ever smaller and faster microprocessors.
Then came what American mining entrepreneur Robert Friedland dubbed the “revenge of the miners.” Emerging technologies—starting with electric vehicles and running through data centers and artificial intelligence—required prodigious quantities of material inputs from bulk metals to rare earth elements. And so did modern conflicts, from Russia’s war on Ukraine to the American-Israeli conflict with Iran.
The physical economy is back, and with a vengeance. Years of underinvestment and long lead-up times mean that surging global demand will exceed supplies of most critical minerals for the foreseeable future.
Further exacerbating the challenge for many countries, especially the United States and its traditional allies, is the dominant position that a single country, China, has painstakingly consolidated in the global production and processing of many critical minerals. It produces up to 98 percent of the world’s processed gallium and germanium, 95 percent of its refined magnesium, more than 90 percent of its rare earths and battery-grade graphite, 80 percent of its cobalt and tungsten, and 70 percent of its titanium. China is even the top producer of several metals that are mostly mined elsewhere.
The military effects of this commercial advantage are highlighted by this year’s conflict in the Middle East. One study by researchers at the Payne Institute for Public Policy at the Colorado School of Mines looked at the first 96 hours of combat after the war was launched on Feb. 28. In that period, the scholars estimated, U.S. and Israeli forces deployed 5,197 offensive and defensive munitions, consuming some 2,197 kg of cobalt and 11,444 kg of tungsten—materials of which China controls roughly 80 percent of the supply. (Remember that, unlike metals used in buildings or other manufactured good, metals used in armaments get only one use and cannot be readily recovered or recycled.) The much-discussed challenge of replacing the Pentagon’s depleted arsenal is not only about production facilities but about the materials they need.
The need to reduce this dependence on a geopolitical competitor was the impetus behind President Trump’s Executive Order 14415. It restricts defense contractors’ use of waivers to source critical minerals and other material inputs from foreign adversaries, expanding oversight over supply chains of subcontractors. It also instructs the Secretary of War to fast-track efforts to identify alternatives and other remedies to supply-chain gaps.
Nor is defense materiel the only driver of demand for critical minerals. The AI revolution has turbocharged competition for some two dozen minerals for everything from power infrastructure (prices for copper, for example, hit near-record highs in early September) to transformer cores where grain-oriented electrical steel has been identified as an especially constrained enabling material, while shortages of gallium, germanium, graphite, lithium, cobalt, and rare earths threaten both chip manufacturing and the buildout of data centers.
The U.S. administration’s concerns about supply-chain vulnerabilities are shared with some of America’s closest allies, with the leaders of the G7 striking an urgent tone in the joint declaration on securing supply chains for critical minerals coming out of their June summit in Évian-les-Bains: “In light of the high degree of market concentration, the need to reduce vulnerabilities regarding those resources and the growing use of arbitrary trade restrictions, we recall the urgency of diversifying our supply chains and building our collective resilience.” Moreover, in a marked departure from the past G7 communiqués on the subject which tended to be long on platitudes and short on substance, the group committed to specific quantifiable targets for reducing its members’ dependence on the unnamed “single supplier outside the G7 and partner countries” whose “use of non-market policies and practices and economic coercion, including arbitrary export restrictions and retaliatory measures on critical minerals and their related dual-use items” threaten the security of G7 to less than 60 percent by 2030 for REEs and permanent magnets and thereafter to half “as soon as possible.”
This undertaking will not be easy and is only possible as a collective effort to develop resources where they can be found among friends (or, at least, non-adversaries), supporting processing value chains, and incentivizing production through the judicious use of guaranteed offtake agreements. Success for any alliance will be predicated on its expanding the political geography. While Australia, Brazil, and South Korea were included in the G7 discussions this year, noticeably absent was anyone from Africa, the continent being home to one-third of the earth’s mineral resources, including a majority of some key minerals like cobalt, manganese, and the platinum group metals. Meet the agency using AI to screen grant applicants for links to potential adversaries
The Transportation Department is deepening its background checks on people and organizations that apply for research grants.
The Department of Transportation has been using artificial intelligence to determine whether grant recipients have ties to adversarial nations, an agency official said on Wednesday.
The federal government has taken a variety of steps in recent years to limit hostile foreign governments’ access to American research, including restricting access to individuals or entities connected with countries like Iran or Russia. As the U.S. seeks to maintain its dominance over China in the global tech race, the Trump administration and Congress in particular have also been tightening the rules on collaborating with organizations or scientists who could conceivably share sensitive technologies or information with Beijing.
It’s not easy, however, for officials or research institutions to unravel these threads, particularly when bad actors are surreptitiously working on behalf of nation states. But new capabilities could help to better chart these connections.
Neil Chaudhry, senior advisor for AI at Transportation, said his agency has worked with partners to create “some really robust AI tools” to analyze the recipients of its research grants.
“When we get to a down-select from grants that are some really promising research projects, we sort of do a deep dive on the [principal investigators] in the grant that says … do they have direct links to the [Chinese Communist Party] leadership, or do they have links to Russian oligarchs?” Chaudhry said during a panel at the SAP Public Sector Summit in Washington, D.C.
“What we don't want to do is go on a fishing expedition,” he said, adding that identifying these kinds of relationships is “not based on the color of their skin and their nationality or something,” but on factors such as whether an individual or entity may be receiving funding from questionable sources.
“If it's a company that's funded by a [venture capital firm] in Silicon Valley, that VC is probably funded by another VC in the Middle East or in Malaysia, and that VC is then wholly funded by the Chinese industrial bank,” Chaudhry said. “And then when that startup goes out of business, we don't know what just happened to that IP that the U.S. government spent money developing.”
Transportation did not respond to a request for comment by the time of publication.
Transportation’s latest AI use-case inventory, which was published earlier this year, does not include the research grant-focused capability. Although other agencies have been using automation or more in-depth analysis tools to identify potential connections to foreign adversaries, Transportation’s use of AI seems to be relatively unique.
A November 2024 report from the Government Accountability Office found that reviewed agencies had taken a variety of steps to comply with federal requirements mandating that they better identify foreign risks in the Small Business Innovation Research and Small Business Technology Transfer programs. GAO noted that the programs, which were created to allow U.S. small businesses to engage in federally funded R&D, “face risks of foreign actors seeking to illicitly acquire federally funded research and technologies.”
The watchdog noted at the time that some agencies — like the Air Force, National Science Foundation and NASA — were taking some steps “either to automate the processing of due diligence disclosure forms or support the vetting of applicants and identify associated risks.”

- Published
Two security personnel have been killed in a Houthi missile attack targeting the presidential palace in the port city of Aden in southern Yemen, which is the seat of the internationally-recognised government, officials say.
Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani told the BBC that the prime minister and other ministers were unhurt when five ballistic missiles hit al-Maashiq Palace, but that many others were injured.
The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said they struck "the Saudi enemy's military operations headquarters in Aden".
A coalition led by Saudi Arabia backs the government and is providing air support for an offensive by pro-government forces against the Iran-backed Houthis.
Yemeni Prime Minister Shaya Zindani condemned the Houthis' attack on Aden, calling it "cowardly" and a "continuation of their criminal behaviour".
He said the government continued to carry out its duties and vowed that it would not weaken the resolve of its forces to continue operations against the Houthis on Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and other front lines.
Earlier, the Houthis denied that they had attacked Saudi Arabia on Thursday, after the coalition said its forces had intercepted a cruise missile in the Medina region, home to one of Islam's holiest shrines.
The Houthis have been launching missiles and drones at airports, oil and gas facilities, and military bases in Saudi Arabia in retaliation for the strikes on the territory that they control in western Yemen, including the capital Sanaa.
On Saturday, a Houthi missile strike killed 13 people at Riyadh's international airport, which was the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.
Saudi Arabia's deputy foreign minister accused Iran of encouraging the Houthis to escalate their conflict with the kingdom.
"Iran continues to arm, train and support the Houthi militia in violation of UN Security Council resolutions," Rayed Krimly told reporters, according to AFP news agency.
"We think that the escalation by the Houthis at this latest stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran," he added.
There was no immediate response from Iran's government. However, it has previously denied supplying weapons to the Houthis and said it only supports them politically.
Iran's foreign minister has also said it is ready to provide "any assistance necessary to facilitate the start of talks" between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.
The conflict escalated in September after the Houthis seized part of Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for global shipping. Their advance contributed to a rise in oil prices following six months of war between the US, Israel and Iran.
Last week, pro-government forces said they had regained control of territory overlooking Bab al-Mandab after launching a major counter-offensive with the support of Saudi air strikes.
At least 1,282 people have been killed and 5,890 injured in the fighting in Yemen since 6 August, according to the government's health ministry.
The UN says another 201,000 people have been displaced and that there has been an alarming surge in suspected cholera cases.

The White Houseâs AI task force has formally adopted its charter, kicking off the short 120-day window itâs been given to answer some extremely thorny questions about how the government should handle the rapid development of AI technology.
According to an announcement shared first with Semafor, the task force agreed after its first official meeting Thursday to commission a report from the Presidentâs Council of Advisers on Science and Technology to evaluate AI risk in three areas: cybersecurity and critical infrastructure protection, biosecurity and dual-use applications, and model control and accountability.
âThroughout its work, the [task force] will engage with frontier model developers and other SI companies, consumer protection groups, and civil liberties advocates, industry stakeholders, and federal and state law enforcement agencies to inform and implement its efforts,â a White House official said in a statement. âThe [Super Intelligence Force] stands ready to ensure implementation of the Accord and continued U.S. leadership on SI for the benefit of the American people.â
It also agreed to make a working group tasked with implementing the White House Accord on Super Intelligence that major AI CEOs signed this month, a process led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, the task forceâs chair, along with National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross.
Defense Undersecret Emil Michael, a task force vice chair, will lead an effort to develop protocols for labs to tell the government about breaches, hacks and other cyber issues. Michael is also in charge of interfacing with frontier AI labs and figuring out long-term coordination on AI across the government.
The task force also agreed to create a âlaw enforcement and consumer protection coordination committeeâ including the Justice Department and Federal Trade Commission, led by FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson, also a vice chair. And the last vice chair, Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor, will work with the public and private sector on critical infrastructure protection, and will work with the Department of Labor on studying the impact of AI on the American workforce and economy.
Members of the task force beyond the chairs include: Vice President JD Vance, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios, plus Cairncross, Chris Klomp, the nominee to be the No. 2 at the Department of Health and Human Services, Social Security Administration Commissioner Frank Bisignano, and National Security Agency Director Joshua Rudd, along with White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and her deputy, Richard Walters.
Itâs not yet entirely clear how compliance with the task force will be enforced or how current law may apply to companies who donât adhere to the new protocols. A White House official told Semafor one stick could be export controls, which the Pentagon at one point temporarily imposed on Anthropic after the company refused to grant the government unfettered access to its models.

fe59e7311ded.text: Maine Republican Sen. Susan Collins and her Democratic challenger Troy Jackson were sparring in a testy debate Thursday night when a protester loudly interrupted them. "So this is obviously one of Troy's supporters," Collins said. "Oh, shut up," Jackson shot back. "I don't even know that kid." Why it matters: Collins and Jackson are competing in one of a handful of races that will determine the Senate majority. The two have traded barbs in a series of tense debates, but this was the first time they sounded like children arguing on a playground. Zoom in : At another point in the debate, Collins, who's been accused of not standing up to President Trump enough, was asked by a moderator to name a time when she opposed him and it changed the outcome. "At one point, I had organized people to vote against Secretary Hegseth," she responded, referring to the Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's confirmation. "As you undoubtedly have read, at the very last minute one of our Republicans changed his mind. Otherwise he would've been defeated for that job." Collins was talking about Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who went on to call his eventual decision to vote for Hegseth the "biggest regret of my career." "So that didn't change the outcome," the moderator said.

68702258f951.text: President Trump is preemptively blaming Sen. John Cornyn and Karl Rove for "doing everything possible to make it hard for Ken Paxton" to win the Texas Senate race. Why it matters: The president is publicly spinning what would be a disaster for Republicans on election night. Texas hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988. "If Ken Paxton loses , it will be because of WEAK and INEFFECTIVE Political Hacks like John Cornyn and Karl Rove," Trump posted on Truth Social. Trump won Texas by 14 points just two years ago. What to watch: Trump's post comes the same day FEC campaign finance reports confirmed Elon Musk's efforts to help Paxton across the finish line. Musk gave $158 million to the Senate GOP's main super PAC in September over two transactions, as Axios reported Thursday morning . The day after each Musk donation , SLF made an equal-sized transfer to a Texas PAC— a pop-up super PAC dedicated to electing Paxton. The big picture: A new poll this week in Texas showed Democrat James Talarico with a narrow lead over Paxton, 50% to 47%. Republican leaders warned Trump for months that if Paxton won the primary against Cornyn it would be cost the party far more to keep the seat. Those predictions are proving true, with more than $500 million in ad spending already flowing into the Texas Senate race, according to AdImpact. "Got to be more careful when you run with the big dogs," Cornyn told Semafor earlier in October after audio leaked from a Paxton event in D.C. The other side: Talarico is getting pummeled with some of that money, but he's far from defenseless. He was already on the air in August, when Paxton and Republicans were still figuring out their game plan — and who would foot the bill. Talarico raised $64 million in the third quarter off an army of small donors. His campaign said 97% of contributions were under $100. Talarico's fundraising prowess allowed him to raise hard dollars, which command lower ad rates. "Oh my god, holy crap, I saw Talarico," Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) said on Thursday. "I don't even know how you raised $64 million in a quarter. I mean, that's a number that's mind-blowing." Paxton brought in $18 million.

c5a2353e8b35.text: By — Graham Dunbar, Associated Press Graham Dunbar, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/infantino-apologizes-to-fifa-council-for-world-cup-furor-but-leaves-critics-unhappy Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Infantino apologizes to FIFA Council for World Cup furor but leaves critics unhappy World Oct 15, 2026 8:20 PM EDT ZURICH (AP) — Gianni Infantino apologized to FIFA's ruling council on Thursday for "mistakes" in his secretive investment plan for the World Cup but didn't give details sought by his toughest critics who want to oust him as the president of soccer's governing body. Soccer officials came to the meeting in Zurich hoping to receive more information about two of the biggest controversies that have surrounded Infantino this year: his now-aborted $4.2 billion World Cup sell-off plan and the Folarin Balogun red-card case at the World Cup where President Donald Trump intervened. READ MORE: Infantino abandoned his World Cup equity plan after seismic FIFA backlash. Here's what to know Despite Infantino's apology, European delegates said they left the meeting disappointed about what they saw as a lack of clarity about the two disputes. "No satisfactory answers were provided," said German soccer leader Bernd Neuendorf, one of eight delegates from European soccer confederation UEFA in the 37-member FIFA Council that Infantino chairs. Infantino provided no documents about the $4.2 billion World Cup sell-off plan he launched and quickly dropped in July amid a fierce backlash led from Europe. Nor did he give details to explain the Folarin Balogun red-card case at the World Cup or how U.S. President Donald Trump intervened to help the national team forward, European delegates at the meeting later told reporters. FIFA will, however, review whether to continue awarding the peace prize that was created to give to Trump last December. Infantino frustrated European delegates by asking for questions in writing at their only meeting before the Nov. 18 deadline to propose a candidate to oppose him at FIFA's presidential election in March. "The man has to answer those questions. If he doesn't answer those questions, no, he is not fit to be the FIFA president," said Debbie Hewitt, who leads the English Football Association and is a FIFA vice president. She said Infantino offered his apology "with some contrition." FIFA says details of investment proposal are confidential Infantino was pressed by European soccer officials for written evidence about his secretive private equity plan for a World Cup commercial rights subsidiary with investor Joshua Kushner, Trump's son-in-law. Known as FIFA Forward Enterprise, the proposal provoked a global rift and the biggest crisis of Infantino's near 11-year presidency. The FIFA president didn't speak to media after the 3 1/2-hour meeting in Zurich but issued a video statement. "I apologized for the mistakes that we made in relation to the communication and consultation process related to the FIFA Forward Enterprise project, which then led to many consequences," Infantino said. He noted that it was "just a proposal, so in no way a done deal." FIFA said in a separate statement details of the investor project "remain confidential due to ongoing legal proceedings in the United States." The council is the main decision-making body at FIFA with a global spread of officials — most are presidents of their national federation, like Cindy Parlow Cone of the U.S. — who are elected by their continental soccer bodies for four-year terms. FIFA pays each an annual stipend of $250,000, with $300,000 for the continental presidents. UEFA pursues legal action against FIFA, Infantino and Kushner in the U.S. European soccer's ruling body UEFA is leading attempts to remove Infantino before or at the FIFA presidential election in March. Infantino infuriated soccer leaders in Europe, North America and Asia by working for months in secret on the Kushner plan. It deepened a long-standing perception in UEFA that the FIFA boss plans his biggest projects without consulting them. "We need a person of integrity, someone who can be expected to restore the reputation of the association, which has undoubtedly been lost," Neuendorf told reporters. UEFA also has asked courts in the United States for the right to get evidence for a criminal complaint against Infantino in Switzerland. The court filings allege possible mismanagement of FIFA finances in the value he put on the intended subsidiary running tournament commercial rights. It was to be at least 20% owned by investors led by Kushner, the brother of Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner. FIFA lawyers' filings in response to stall or stop the evidence requests said they were a "smear campaign" by UEFA. Support for Infantino comes from Africa For most of the last 50 years, FIFA voters from Africa — which now counts 54 of the 211 member federations — have been key to gaining and staying in power. "The key point for us," said FIFA Council member Ahmed Yahya, the head of Mauritania's soccer federation, "is that we see Gianni as the right person to continue leading football." Infantino's offer to add $15 million in FIFA funding to each of the 211 members over the next four years made progress Thursday. They already were sure to get $10 million each from FIFA through 2030. "I've said that President Gianni Infantino is taking football forward worldwide," Yahya said. "I come from the African continent and know what I'm talking about." The FIFA presidential election meeting is on March 18 in Rabat, the capital of Morocco, which is a political ally of Infantino. Its soccer leader Fouzi Lekjaa is an influential council member. Morocco will co-host the 2030 World Cup with Spain and Portugal. Morocco also is competing with Spain, an influential member of UEFA, to host the final in 2030. That FIFA decision is a potential factor in election alliances until March. Next FIFA Council in Q

755f6fdb3322.text: By — Danica Kirka, Associated Press Danica Kirka, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/prince-harry-and-meghan-make-first-joint-appearances-since-returning-to-uk Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Prince Harry and Meghan make first joint appearances since returning to UK World Oct 15, 2026 7:57 PM EDT NOTTINGHAM, England (AP) — Prince Harry and his wife Meghan appeared together in a trio of charity visits Thursday, their first joint public appearance since moving back to England, as they seek to rebuild their brand in Britain after walking away from royal duties six years ago. READ MORE: King Charles clarifies status of Prince Harry and Meghan in a letter after their return to the UK The couple started their day at the Community Recording Studio, in the city of Nottingham in central England, that uses music, performance and athletic programs to help young people build confidence and develop practical skills. The couple, who have the royal titles of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, received a warm welcome and cheers, especially from the schoolchildren present. "We love you, Duchess Meghan, we love you," one woman shouted. The couple then went to Himmah Hub, central England's biggest food bank, and Epic Partners, which offers sports, education and mentoring programs for disadvantaged young people. Across their three stops, Harry and Meghan, who wore a long burgundy coat, stopped to take selfies, give hugs and shake hands with fans. The Sussexes remain non-working royals The visit to Nottingham was particularly significant as it was there they made their first joint appearance after announcing their engagement in 2017. The day's events were presented with touches of royal style, including an announcement that features the couple's Sussex titles and a prearranged media pool chronicling their movements. Archewell, the philanthropic venture that often took center stage when they were living in the U.S., is hardly mentioned. But King Charles III, Harry's father, has made clear that the couple remain non-working members of the royal family, a status they accepted when they abandoned royal duties and moved to California. In a letter sent on behalf of the king to senior government officials shortly after Harry and Meghan returned to the U.K. in September, the palace stressed that the couple would continue to refrain from using their royal forms of address — His Royal Highness or Her Royal Highness — and any charity work would be carried out as private citizens. The decision to send the letter and, more importantly, to release it to the media demonstrated the concern among some palace officials that Harry and Meghan's celebrity could allow them to become a sort of parallel royal court, competing with the Prince and Princess of Wales and other working royals for press coverage and public support. The couple are back to working with familiar partners Harry has been involved with the Community Recording Studio and Epic Partners for more than a decade, and Meghan worked with Himmah on "Together: Our Community Cookbook," published in 2018. While the couple continued to support charities in the U.K. after they left Britain, their focus was elsewhere. When Harry and Meghan gave up their royal duties and moved to California in July 2020, they said they wanted to earn their own living, later signing lucrative contracts with Netflix and Spotify. Relations with the rest of the royal family quickly deteriorated as the couple said palace staff had been insensitive to Meghan's mental health and leveled charges of racism and media manipulation at other members of the family. Harry wants his children to get to know their grandfather But tensions began to ease in recent months as Harry expressed a desire for reconciliation with the king, saying he wanted his children to have a chance to get to know their 77-year-old grandfather. Charles is undergoing treatment for an undisclosed form of cancer that was discovered in 2024. The couple and their children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, are reportedly living at a private, nonroyal residence in the Cotswolds, a rural area of rolling hills, villages and farms to the west of Oxford. While the couple have expressed their happiness about returning to the U.K., the move hasn't been without controversy. Harry continues to lobby for publicly funded police protection, which was canceled when he and Meghan gave up royal duties. The prince says he and his family remain under threat simply because of his royal status. Just days into the new school year, the children have changed schools because of security issues. Kirka reported from London. Pan Pylas in London contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Bernie Moreno wants his fellow Republicans to cancel their holiday plans and jam through "everything that we could possibly get" if they lose the majorities in November's midterms. Why it matters: Republicans couldn't muster the votes for a megabill this summer, and leadership is not confident they can now. But Moreno (R-Ohio) is calling for the GOP to make a bigger push in the event of losing power. "We will do a reconciliation bill, one way or the other," Moreno — who said it is "more likely" the GOP holds the Senate — told reporters outside the Capitol on Thursday. But if Republicans lose: "It'll be the 'Last Supper.' So it'll be a giant reconciliation bill where we take all the Republican priorities that we can get done." "If we lose the House and the Senate, we should be here from Nov. 9 until Dec. 31 with no break at all," he said. "Like, we'll have turkeys here for Thanksgiving." Zoom in: Conversations have been ongoing in congressional offices about what a reconciliation package might look like in the lame-duck session between the election and the new Congress next year, a source familiar with the matter tells Axios. "We are working with the House and White House to develop what all is included to be able to sell to the public and our Republican colleagues when we return," Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.), chair of the Budget Committee, told Axios. Election outcomes won't substantively change much for frequent holdouts like Sens. John Cornyn (R-Texas), Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), Bill Cassidy (R-La.) and Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) who are on their way out. That's not to mention Sens. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) and Susan Collins (R-Maine), who are appropriators and known to break from the party. What to watch: Republicans face a long to-do list in the lame-duck, including funding the government past Dec. 11, passing emergency defense spending and raising the debt ceiling. Those could all be considered part of a massive reconciliation package that requires just a majority vote to pass. But not everything qualifies for the reconciliation process — and big bills can cause big headaches. Other to-do items include: Passing the National Defense Authorization Act Reauthorizing FISA Section 702, the warrantless wiretap authority Passing the farm bill Passing permitting reform Confirming nominations Between the lines : Some of the administration's top priorities are banking on the partisan-led funding maneuver of reconciliation, including Trump's sprawling Golden Dome missile defense system, autonomous weapon advancement efforts and upgrades to the F-35 fighter jet. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told attendees at an Army conference on Wednesday the Pentagon needs "a minimum" of $350 billion to "rebuild the military." The intrigue: If Republicans lose their Senate majority, it will almost certainly be Moreno's job to try to win it back. He is running for National Republican Senatorial Committee chair — so far, unopposed. Axios Defense reporter Thomas Novelly contributed to this story.

754d32574023.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/drone-strike-on-ship-in-romanian-waters-raises-fear-that-war-in-ukraine-is-spreading Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Drone strike on ship in Romanian waters raises fear that war in Ukraine is spreading World Oct 15, 2026 7:38 PM EDT BUCHAREST, Romania (AP) — Romanian authorities launched search and rescue operations off the Black Sea coast Thursday after a drone struck a ship which then caught fire, the latest in a spate of strikes that has raised fears that Russia's war in Ukraine is spreading. WATCH: Ukraine resumes strikes on energy targets, saying Russia never stopped its attacks Five people were rescued after the San Marino-flagged Wine Trader, a chemical tanker traveling from Tunisia to Romania, caught fire in the attack about 13 nautical miles (15 miles) southeast of the port town of Sulina, according to the Romanian Naval Authority. Seven others are still missing. Romanian President Nicusor Dan said in Brussels that the cargo vessel had been struck by a drone, as was another ship in a separate incident the night before. Dan did not state the drones' origin. "There will be a reaction from the Romanian state," he said. Similar drone incursions have occurred this month in the exclusive economic zones of Romania and Bulgaria, both NATO and European Union members. According to initial medical assessments, one person rescued from the Wine Trader sustained scalp burns and another suffered from mild smoke inhalation, while the three others appeared unharmed, the Department for Emergency Situations said. On Wednesday evening, a fire was also reported on the Comoros-flagged Yara J, a chemical and oil tanker traveling from Turkey to Sulina, Romania, in Romanian territorial waters. The crew was safe. Romania's Ministry of National Defense said earlier that a "group of air targets" was monitored overnight near Ukraine's Snake Island, and that a drone briefly entered Romania's airspace at 1:34 a.m. southeast of Sulina, before disappearing from radar. Romania's acting defense minister, Radu Miruta, said that an investigation was underway, but that no drone was seen on military radars heading toward the Yara J. On Tuesday, drone strikes on two ships off the coast of Bulgaria prompted emergency rescue operations for 11 crew members from the HS Dignity, a Guinea-Bissau-flagged cargo ship, who remain missing. The other ship, a Ukrainian-operated coastal freighter named the Chelsea 3, was sailing under a Maltese flag. Rescuers evacuated all 15 crew members, with five receiving treatment for minor injuries. The crew reported that the ship's deck and hull were hit by three aerial drones. The incidents on Tuesday, for which Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said Russia was likely responsible, came a week after sea and aerial drones struck two other commercial vessels in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea. A Togo-flagged ship sank, while a Bulgarian ferry evacuated the 18-member crew of a damaged Palau-flagged vessel. A day earlier, on Oct. 5, a Turkish-owned cargo ship carrying corn caught fire following a drone attack and later sank in the Black Sea off Romania's coast. Two people died and 11 crew members were rescued. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said on X on Thursday that he met with Radev and Dan to discuss security in the Black Sea and "the latest attacks on commercial shipping." "NATO has strengthened our posture along the eastern flank including with increasing counter-drone capabilities," he said. "NATO will continue to work closely with our Allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defense posture as needed." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. The French passion for protest is legendary in Europe.
Over the last few years, we have regularly witnessed farmers angry about costly regulations lobbing manure at local mayoral offices, while masked youths periodically hurl homemade grenades at riot police in disadvantaged city suburbs.
For over three weeks now, thousands of students have barricaded entry to high schools and taken their grievances to the streets.
This Saturday, hundreds of new demonstrations have been announced across France.
Students are expected to be joined by workers' unions and key figures from the so-called "yellow vest" movement.
France's prime minister, SÃ©bastien Lecornu, suggested this week that student anger was being manipulated as politics heats up ahead of next year's presidential election.
The gilets jaunes (yellow vests) demonstrated against cost-of-living hikes for over a year from 2018 - becoming one of the longest-lived protest movements in French history.
JÃ©rÃ´me Rodrigues, a prominent gilets jaunes activist, has used Instagram to encourage people to join Saturday's demonstrations.
The protests should give a voice to those who "want to be able to live decently, no longer have to count every cent, and no longer have to choose between eating and driving", he said in a video.
"Anger has no political party. An empty fridge has no political party," he added.
So what is going on in the EU's second largest economy?
Social unrest, government borrowing costs at eye-watering highs, a deeply divided French parliament and an apparent revolving door of exasperated French prime ministers - six prime ministers over the last five years - all claiming to want to reduce their country's public debt.
Is France at breaking-point - and what does this all mean for the eurozone currency the French are such a huge part of?
"You can't compare France to the Greece debt crisis of 2012 or Argentina in 2001. And the financial markets know it," economist Anne-Laure Delatte told me.
She is a CNRS Tenured Researcher at the Economics Department of Paris Dauphine University; a well-known face in debates on French media on the parlous state of the country's public debt.
"The markets recognised already in 2024 that we would have a budgetary problem after [snap] elections left parliament deeply divided between three [opposing political] blocs but they also realise France is a big country with the ability to raise taxes if necessary."
"Our situation is more like the UK in 2023 with Liz Truss," suggests Delatte, referring to the then UK prime minister's so-called mini budget, which triggered a sharp drop in the pound, a spike in government bond yields and soaring mortgage rates.
"The crisis was relatively short-lived because the markets recognised the UK had the financial tools to right itself."
"Here in France it would be painful, but a 4% increase in VAT would raise the 120bn euros needed to plug government debt. Investors know that," she concludes.
Maybe, in theory. And, as Delatte also points out, the European Central Bank would likely intervene if France's finances nosedived to the point where other European economies would be affected.
But with so many French citizens already visibly unhappy with the status quo, imagine the reaction if taxes were to increase, or welfare and education budgets decrease, further.
France's national motto is libertÃ©, Ã©galitÃ©, fraternitÃ© (freedom, equality and fraternity), but that is certainly not the sense you get on seething streets and in viral social media posts.
I met 17-year-olds Maxime, Madeleine and Elodie this week, perched on big green dustbins that have been used to block the entrance to their high school as part of the weeks' long protest.
They told me things were bad enough here, in the 3rd district of Paris, with holes in classroom walls, swelling class sizes and a dearth of teaching staff, but the teenagers were more than aware, they said, that the situation was far worse in their capital city's disadvantaged suburbs.
"France likes to speak of Ã©galitÃ©," they told me "but the reality is the poor here are prejudiced against, while the rich benefit."
None of them will be old enough to vote in the presidential election in France next spring but they questioned whether the changing face of politicians in power made all that much difference anyway.
The three young women told me large-scale protests seemed the only way to get heard by French authorities.
They are part of a defiant French tradition.
Cultural icon Victor Hugo, the 19th-Century author of French Revolution classic Les MisÃ©rables, also an activist for the French Republic, proclaimed: "Si vous n'Ãªtes pas contents, manifestez, criez, hurlez, mais ne subissez pas."
("If you are not happy, protest, shout, scream but do not give up and give in.")
Amongst crowds of protesting students walking through Paris on Thursday, I came across a number of mums, with placards around their necks, reading: "Mums in solidarity."
Were they there to protest or to protect their kids, I asked? "Both!" was the emphatic response.
Gwen, 37, said she and other mothers were taking it in turns every morning to co-ordinate between students and police at their local school lock-in.
This came after mounting accusations of police brutality, denied by France's interior ministry, during protests earlier this month in which hundreds were injured and a 15-year-old boy in the town of Lens lost a hand.
France's interior minister has since suspended the use of stun grenades by police at high school demonstrations.

Milpitas, an affluent city in California's Silicon Valley tech hub, has an odour problem.
For decades, residents have had to endure rank smells wafting from industrial sites, among them a 342-acre landfill.
"When I first moved here, I could not open my window for over 10 years," says Chia-Ling Kong, an engineer for a tech firm who lives around half a mile from the dump.
While things have got better in recent years, Kong says she and her neighbours must still contend with around "two or three hours of bad smells a day".
Perhaps befitting Silicon Valley, the community is putting its hopes in technology.
The operators of Newby Island landfill have been ordered by local authorities to use drones and install monitors to systematically track and measure the chemicals responsible for bad odours. They have also been told to automate the collection of landfill gases responsible for smells.
Kong is optimistic a data-driven approach will make a difference. "Hopefully with this continuous monitoring, it makes it easier to pinpoint problems at the moment it starts."
The operators of the landfill say they are committed to operating it safely and protecting air quality.
Just like in Milpitas, where Kong is part of a citizen's campaign against the odours, communities around the world are raising a stink about bad smells making day-to-day life miserable. Sometimes a rubbish dump is to blame, or it might be a sewage treatment works, or a reeking factory.
When the complaints start stacking up, resolving them is not always simple. Many countries have no regulations in place dictating how to manage smells.
In the US, for example, the Environmental Protection Agency does not regulate environmental odours as a pollutant. This leaves states and local governments to take charge of the issue.
Urban sprawl is often part of the problem, bringing communities closer to stinky facilities that may historically have been kept at a distance.
This is creating more demand for technologies to monitor and prevent smells. Odour consultant Micheal Bull says people are increasingly concerned about neighbourhood stinks.
"You're getting developments being built nearer to odorous processesâ¦ as land has become more valuable, there is also infilling," Bull says. He is speaking about his experiences in the UK, but it's a similar story in many parts of the world.
The technologies used to tackle industrial pongs generally fall into three categories: they absorb odours; convert them into something less smelly through a chemical reaction; or burn them away.
Experts on fixing industrial odours say that the best technologies, when used correctly, can remove 90% or more of the target compounds responsible for smells.
But this can be expensive and some operators opt for simpler and cheaper solutions. These include masking odours from landfill or sewage processing by spraying giant quantities of deodorisers.
Odour experts contacted for this article were dubious about the effectiveness of such industrial scale air fresheners. "In my view they're not likely to change the odours," says Bull, who likens them to fabric conditioner.
Bad smells from waste sites â a common cause of complaints â are among the stinkiest and most difficult to resolve, according to Carlos Diaz, an environmental consultant based in Spain. "Landfill is difficult to treat because you have a very large surface," he says.
In some places at least, technology is making a real difference. Residents in Des Moines, Iowa, have long complained of the so-called Eastside Funk, a putrid scent that residents report drifts over parts of the city.
A study commissioned by city authorities showed that a trio of industrial meat companies were among culprits.
"Within 10 miles, there's about half a million people," says Dalton Jacobus, who works in the Department of Neighborhood Services. "If the winds are out of the wrong direction, 100,000 people can be in the middle of that odour plume."
The authorities are now paying around $240,000 (Â£182,000) a year on technology to track the stink, so they can take action. "What we wanted to do was build a ring of odour monitors around the facilities that we suspected of emitting odours," says Jacobus.
The monitors, which measure levels of chemical compounds in the air, work in combination with a weather station to provide real-time data on the concentrations that are coming from each facility based off the wind patterns.
This has put an end to finger pointing about who's to blame each time a smell sparks complaints, says Jacobus. "Now we can say with reasonable certainty that 'this odour event did originate from your facility, what was going on'?"
Meanwhile, some of the sites that have been blamed for causing unpleasant smells in Des Moines have spent millions of dollars to upgrade their own odour control systems.
Smithfield Foods, which operates a meat processing in Des Moines, says it has invested $2m to install a regenerative thermal oxidiser that destroys the chemicals associated with bad smells. Even so, the company says it does not believe it is the source of odour complaints.
Before installing the monitors â which some local companies help pay for â officials in Des Moines would drive out to the source of a complaint to sniff the air.
Relying on the human nose to sniff out industrial smells is still commonplace. Claudia Barrios ObregÃ³n from Kunak, the company behind the monitors in Des Moines, says: "Right now, the way that cities control or measure odours is olfactometry: a human panel measures and gives an opinion of what the odour is like. But that's not that realistic."
The Spanish company's monitors are an example of so-called electronic noses that make it easier to detect smells.

26055e1c283b.text: By — Victoria Eastwood, Associated Press Victoria Eastwood, Associated Press By — Samy Magdy, Associated Press Samy Magdy, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/saudi-diplomat-says-iran-is-encouraging-houthi-escalation-of-attacks-on-the-kingdom Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Saudi diplomat says Iran is encouraging Houthi escalation of attacks on the kingdom World Oct 15, 2026 7:16 PM EDT CAIRO (AP) — Iran's government is encouraging the latest escalation in attacks by the Tehran-backed Houthi rebels and doesn't seem ready to make the needed concessions in the wider war with the United States, one of Saudi Arabia's top diplomats said Thursday. Rayed Krimly, deputy minister for public diplomacy at the foreign ministry, spoke to journalists in a rare briefing following more than a week of Houthi attacks targeting the Riyadh international airport, the headquarters of Saudi oil giant Aramco and other aviation, oil and military facilities across the kingdom. READ MORE: Iran-backed Houthis strike Saudi oil company Aramco's headquarters, officials say At least 19 people, including foreigners, have been killed in what Krimly called war crimes. King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital alone has been targeted 20 times by the Houthis this month, a spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting the rebels said Thursday. The escalation between the Saudis and the rebels in neighboring Yemen has exposed the kingdom's challenges in intercepting the attacks in the latest front in the Iran war, while further rattling global markets. It also has reinforced Saudi appeals to allies including the United States for more military help. Saudi Arabia says the Houthis had turned down a meeting Krimly said the Saudis had reached out and called for a meeting in Oman with the Houthis in July "to resolve outstanding differences and bring an end to this escalation," but he said the rebels refused to participate. Days later, the Houthis made one of their most significant territorial grabs yet, racing down Yemen's Red Sea coast to seize land on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a crucial shipping alternative to the Strait of Hormuz. Earlier this month, the Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive in Yemen to retake those areas. That caused new friction between Mideast rivals Saudi Arabia and Iran. "We think the escalation by the Houthis at this later stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran," Krimly said, adding that Iran "continues to arm, train and support the Houthi militia in violation of relevant U.N. Security Council resolutions and in violation of its commitments in the Beijing agreement." That deal saw Saudi Arabia and Iran restore diplomatic ties after a seven-year rift. While Iran's government has said it is open to dialogue on helping to find an end to the fighting, Krimly said Saudi Arabia has not requested any Iranian mediation. "We maintain direct channels of communication with the Houthis, and Oman serves as a facilitator of these talks and not as a mediator," he said. Saudi Arabia still has direct communications with Iran, he added. In the middle of the series of attacks on the Riyadh airport, the Saudi and Iranian foreign ministers spoke at least once by phone. At the same time, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi as recently as Thursday called the Saudi blockade on the Houthis unjust and illegal. Iran takes a 'long, long time' to respond to mediators On the wider Iran war, Krimly said the kingdom continues to support the mediation efforts of Qatar and Pakistan in trying to maintain talks between Washington and Tehran. Mediators are trying to work out two issues, he said. One is a solution that would ensure safe passage for ships through the Strait of Hormuz in return for ending the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports, which is aimed at bottling up Iran's oil exports and applying economic pain. The other issue is a "clearer commitment" on how negotiations over Iran's nuclear program will take place and what they will include. "In both fronts, the Iranians take a long, long time to come back to the mediators with any new proposal, and what they come with is insufficient," Krimly said. "And then they begin to talk about a temporary arrangement in (the Strait of) Hormuz, and a temporary arrangement to this and that, and then we spend sometimes weeks and months discussing this, back and forth. "They don't seem to be able to reach consensus on the needed solutions that will pave the way for a peaceful solution of the conflict," he said. Iranian officials did not immediately respond to requests for comment. China and Russia are thought to be helping Iran and the rebels Krimly also said the kingdom believes that China and Russia are involved in supporting both Iran and the Houthis, but he gave few details. "Of course, some of the capabilities of Iran, and of the Houthis, do come -- or the intelligence -- do come from at least elements in Russia or China, even commercial elements sometimes, but we do discuss these matters regularly with China and Russia, and we will continue to do so," he said. A new report this week said the Houthis are attempting to build a new advanced medium-range ballistic missile system with the help of Chinese parts. Krimly said Saudi Arabia continues to have direct communications with members of the Gulf Coordination Council including the United Arab Emirates, which had been a key member of the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis until friction led the UAE to withdraw its support months ago. As for the mutual defense agreement the kingdom recently signed with Pakistan and Turkey, Krimly offered no new details on what assistance the two partners might offer as the Houthis keep attacking. It’s not unusual for Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin to be on the road touting the Trump administration’s agenda, but his travel itinerary in the weeks before the midterm election looks like a trail of political hot spots.
On Thursday, Zeldin traveled to an auto repair shop and a construction firm in central Pennsylvania with Rep. Scott Perry, one of the most endangered Republicans in Congress. Earlier in the week, Zeldin was in Iowa with Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson, who is in a neck-and-neck race for the state’s open Senate seat. Zeldin later headed to a family farm in Wisconsin with Republican Rep. Derrick Van Orden, who is fighting to keep his seat representing the state’s 3rd Congressional District.
Zeldin’s slew of stops with candidates—all promoted with press releases from EPA headquarters—generates concern, in the view of the political watchdog group that is taking on a $20 million taxpayer-funded advertising campaign praising Trump and his administration.
“It does raise questions on whether the EPA administrator is engaged in political activity in a way that violates the Hatch Act,” said Kedric Payne, senior director of ethics for the Campaign Legal Center, referring to the 87-year-old law that limits the political activities of federal employees. Although cabinet officials like Zeldin get more leeway under that law than most civil servants to attend campaign events and the like, they are not permitted to use taxpayer resources to do so.
“With the use of the EPA and its press and communications shop to put a spotlight on this travel, an investigator truly needs to know what is being said at these gatherings,” Payne said.
Federal employees whose travel is supported by taxpayers can violate the Hatch Act even if they don’t explicitly urge people to vote for a candidate, he said. The series of taxpayer-funded ads the Campaign Legal Center and others sued over did not call for support of any political candidate, but a federal judge blocked the TV spots until after the election.
Payne said there is often “a fine line” between permissible and impermissible activities under the Hatch Act. The determination hinges on whether there could be any other explanation for the cabinet official’s activity, other than promoting a candidate.
An EPA spokesperson said Zeldin’s visits are fact-finding ventures and part of his job as the nation’s top environmental regulator.
“Administrator Zeldin’s travels are driven by one thing: his commitment to getting regulators out of Washington to meet with the regulated,” the spokesperson said. “Every day of each of these trips, Administrator Zeldin has asked for feedback from Americans on what the Trump EPA can do better, and he’s taking that feedback back to D.C. to make decisions.
“His main message to people wherever he goes is that EPA is back to its core mission, protecting human health and the environment, and we want to know how we can do that better,” the spokesperson said.
One environmental aide in a past administration who spoke on background said it was not unusual for cabinet members to fan out across the country to sell their accomplishments.
For example, during President Joe Biden’s administration, EPA Administrator Michael Regan made one visit with a member of Congress in the month prior to the 2022 midterm elections. Regan traveled with Rep. Pat Ryan of New York, a Democrat, who was then in a fight to keep his seat, to see an EPA-managed asbestos removal site in Ulster County. In 2024, none of the visits Regan made with members of Congress were in contested districts. In one case he traveled with Republicans, Sen. Thom Tillis and Rep. Chuck Edwards of North Carolina, to see the impacts of Hurricane Helene.
But under Trump, who held the 2020 Republican National Convention on the grounds of the White House, the lines between federal activity and political activity often have blurred.
The Atlantic reported last month that the Trump White House had launched an unofficial competition encouraging cabinet secretaries to travel the country to promote the administration agenda in advance of the midterm elections, with officials getting points for visits to politically competitive districts or states and getting docked for visits to solidly blue areas. By The Atlantic’s count, seven other cabinet members had eclipsed Zeldin’s visits to political hot spots during the summer.
But in recent weeks, in addition to his trips to Iowa, Wisconsin and Pennsylvania, Zeldin made what an EPA press release called a “three-day swing” across Michigan with two Republicans whose races will be crucial to deciding congressional control: Rep. Bill Huizenga and Rep. Tom Barrett. Zeldin also traveled to Maricopa County, Arizona, which has a close congressional race and two states with key Senate races—Maine and New Hampshire—although he did not travel with any candidates on those trips.
According to EPA press releases, Zeldin’s October visits to battleground districts resembled other stops he has made in a tenure that took him to all 50 states within his first nine months in office, touting the Trump agenda. In Iowa with Hinson, Zeldin unveiled an “American Farmer First” policy including support for corn ethanol demand. In Pennsylvania, four days later, Zeldin appeared with Perry, who in a debate with his challenger the previous night said that he wanted federal support for ethanol ended. Zeldin and Perry focused on Trump’s deregulatory agenda and how they say it has helped small business. And in Wisconsin, Zeldin talked about how the Trump administration had lifted a requirement for anti-pollution sensors on diesel engines that were blamed for engine failures and shutdowns.
The message that the Trump administration is putting American farmers first and lowering costs comes when Republicans are facing headwinds from the pain Trump’s tariffs and the Iran War run-up in energy prices, especially diesel fuel, has inflicted on consumers.
