f9305a7d2275.text: The tense alliance between Ukrainian President Zelenskyy and President Trump is nearing a new low point. After days of bitter back-and-forth between the two leaders, Ukraine has resumed strikes on Russian energy targets. Trump had demanded an "energy ceasefire" this past Sunday between the two. Russia never stopped its attacks. Lisa Desjardins reports. Amna Nawaz: The tense alliance between Ukrainian President Zelenskyy and President Trump is nearing a new low point tonight. After days of bitter back-and-forth between the two leaders, Ukraine has resumed strikes on Russian energy targets following three days of Ukrainian cease-fire. The president had demanded an energy cease-fire this past Sunday between the two. Russia never stopped its attacks. Lisa Desjardins begins our coverage. Lisa Desjardins: In Ukraine's capital city today, Russian strikes reverberate in broad daylight, that after Ukrainian officials say Russia launched a large-scale overnight attack, more than 850 drones. But Russia too is burning. The Associated Press reports Ukraine hit this oil refinery. Volodymyr Zelenkskyy, Ukrainian President: Three days, we didn't attack any energy, diesel and et cetera systems of Russia, and three days they attack us. Lisa Desjardins: Late yesterday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenkskyy told The Financial Times that Russia never abided by the cease-fire announced by Trump. Zelenskyy criticized the U.S. for limiting intelligence resources like Starlink. He was blunt. His patience is gone. Question: If they keep doing this, how much longer will you maintain the stoppage of attacks on Russian refineries? Volodymyr Zelenkskyy: That's it. Block is out. Lisa Desjardins: His candor continued when asked about Trump's relationship with Russian President Vladimir Putin and their deal on diesel. Volodymyr Zelenkskyy: He speaks about it, I mean, openly and loudly that he loves such people and he respects such people, because, for him, I don't know, people who can be leaders 20 years, 30 years, 40 years, it's means they're very strong because they -- you can, I mean, hold the power. How it can be when some people are surviving, fighting, dying, you make some business with the guys with such aggression? Lisa Desjardins: For his part, Putin accused Ukraine of violating the truce. Vladimir Putin, Russian President (through interpreter): They made a first step. We started to respond by striking at energy facilities, which they are now squealing about. It was them who started it. They should have thought properly about consequences. Lisa Desjardins: And Russia's foreign minister said Zelenskyy's comments point to a deepening rift between Kyiv and Washington. Sergey Lavrov, Russian Foreign Minister (through interpreter): The fact that this is such a direct and indeed crude challenge to President Trump is, in my view, something everyone already understands. Lisa Desjardins: Zelenskyy spent his day at an E.U. summit in Brussels focused on support from his European allies. Kaja Kallas, High Representative, European Union: We definitely have different approach to this war. We see that we have to pressure the aggressor to stop the war, not the victim to surrender. Squeezing Ukraine is not the right approach. Lisa Desjardins: The talks come as the entire region grows more war-weary. Two cargo ships were set ablaze today in Romanian waters in the Black Sea. Seven crew members are missing. Nicusor Dan, President of Romania (through interpreter): There are attempts by Russia to destabilize societies and to reduce support for Ukraine. And our response is, we continue to support Ukraine. Lisa Desjardins: European leaders also rejected Trump's push to control and release frozen Russian assets, he said, as a bargaining ship. Friedrich Merz, German Chancellor (through interpreter): These are assets that are frozen in Europe. And they should remain frozen in Europe. This is our business. And we decide on it. Lisa Desjardins: And, as world leaders talk, the war grinds on, on the ground. For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Lisa Desjardins.

1c81e86f4ab7.text: For perspective on the tensions between President Trump and Ukrainian President Zelenskyy, Amna Nawaz spoke with former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine William Taylor. He’s now a distinguished fellow at the Atlantic Council. Amna Nawaz: For perspective now on the tensions between President Trump and President Zelenskyy, we turn to former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine William Taylor. He's now a distinguished fellow at the Atlantic Council. Ambassador Taylor, let's begin with Ukrainian President Zelenskyy's decision to resume strikes on Russian energy targets after complying with President Trump's demand to stop those for a few days. Is that the right call for Ukraine right now? William Taylor, Former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine: Amna, it's absolutely the right call. As you say, the president held off for three days. He had agreed to this cease-fire, energy cease-fire, that President Trump suggested or demanded without consultation. But, nonetheless, President Zelenskyy said, yes, good idea. He suggested this before. He made this proposal before. And the Russians have always said no before, but maybe President Trump had had a conversation with President Putin and was going to get President Putin to agree this time. So President Zelenskyy stopped firing at the refineries for three days while the Russians continued to batter the Ukrainians, energy, civilian targets, killing civilians. He couldn't -- he couldn't stop. President Zelenskyy had to resume the attacks when the Russians had never stopped. Amna Nawaz: Ambassador Taylor, you heard there the remarkable public expression of frustration, of anger from President Zelenskyy. Is that a risky move for a nation that is still so dependent on support from the U.S.? William Taylor: Amna, less support from -- less dependent on support from the U.S. at this point than it was, say, a year-and-a-half ago, because the United States doesn't provide any weapons. We don't provide any financial support. We don't provide any political leadership. We don't lead the Ramstein process, by which we coordinate the assistance going, the military assistance going. We don't do any of that. So we're -- the Ukrainians are not so dependent on us as they were. Now, it is true that military intelligence is important to the Ukrainians coming from the United States, but they also get that from other places as well. But in answer to your question, I guess I would not have gone the ad hominem with that. I wouldn't have made comments about President Trump and why he wants to stay in power. You know, you don't need any of that. You just stick to the results that he's after, which is pressure on Putin to stop the war. And the pressure point on Putin to stop the war is attacks on refineries. Amna Nawaz: You heard Russia's Sergey Lavrov there point to the rift between the U.S. and Ukraine. At this moment, does this deterioration in relations between the U.S. and Ukraine, does that further embolden Putin? Could we see a ramping up of Russian attacks? William Taylor: They're already at the top of the ramping up of Russian attacks. And, Amna, what Lavrov says, what Putin says, they would love to have this dispute, this rift, as you say. This is what their goal has been, is to cut off support for Ukraine. The United States has indicated, the Senate, the House has indicated strong support. When you ask Americans if they support Ukraine, they do, and they oppose Russia. The United States will continue to have a strong relationship with Ukraine, and I believe this administration will as well. Amna Nawaz: You have heard President Trump recently strongly criticize President Zelenskyy very directly, saying Ukraine needs a new president. We should point out Zelenskyy's term did expire back in 2024. He's operating under a constitutional wartime extension in Ukraine. What about people on the ground in Ukraine? Do they want elections? Do they want a new president? William Taylor: They don't, Amna. They don't. I have been there many times. I have been there 15 times since the big war started in 2022. And I have talked to the people about -- I have talked to opposition parties, who you would think would want to have elections so they can get -- no. The opposition parties, the people, civil society, the election experts, democracy experts are all united at this point in Ukraine. They don't think elections are appropriate now. They can't have elections now. They don't want it. They support their president for now. They're eager to have elections, Amna. They're really eager to have elections when the cease-fire comes, when the war is over. They are eager. They're going to be -- there's going to be real competition, but not now. Right now, they support their president. Amna Nawaz: In the 30 seconds or so I have left, I have to ask, do you see this as a new all-time low in relations between the U.S. and Ukraine? William Taylor: An all-time low. Again, the Ukrainians are in better shape now than they have been before because they're less dependent on us. They have seen that they can't really depend on one thing to the next day, one commitment to the day, a withdrawal of that commitment the next. So, they're in better shape now. They have got strong support from the Europeans. That's going to keep them going, and maybe the Americans will come back as well. Amna Nawaz: That is former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine William Taylor joining us tonight. Ambassador Taylor, always good to speak with you. Thank you. William Taylor: Thank you, Amna.

b023eb3ef735.text: In our news wrap Thursday, President Trump canceled plans to livestream the December execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan, federal law enforcement agencies are investigating a series of letters containing what they're calling "suspicious substances" that were sent to congressional and state election officials and police report multiple victims in a shooting at a school in Bend, Oregon. Amna Nawaz: We start the day's other headlines with a late-breaking story out of Bend, Oregon, where police say there are multiple victims following a shooting this afternoon at an elementary school. Officials say children are among the victims. Their status is unclear, but at least two people were hospitalized. Officials also say the shooter was shot and killed at Silver Rail Elementary School possibly by a bystander, though that is not yet confirmed. Federal law enforcement agencies are investigating a series of letters containing what they're calling suspicious substances that were sent to congressional and state election officials. In a statement provided to the "News Hour," the FBI says it's investigating each incident and -- quote -- "working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters." Elections officials in at least six states have reported receiving such mail, including Ohio, South Dakota, and Maryland. It comes less than three weeks before the midterm elections. President Trump has canceled plans to livestream the December execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan amid growing bipartisan backlash. The president posted online that he still believes -- quote -- "Streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent," but he added -- quote -- "Many very good and well-meaning people would rather not watch him die." Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the livestream plan last week. But a growing number of Republicans, including Vice President J.D. Vance, said they would not watch. In Texas, voting rights groups are suing the state's Department of Public Safety and the secretary of state over the delay of nearly 600,000 online voter registrations. Officials say a software glitch in their online portal caused the backlog. The lawsuit claims that Texas failed to provide a reliable online registration system. Local election staff are working overtime to process the registrations before early voting starts on Monday. In Northwest Pakistan, the roof of a private school collapsed during morning classes today, killing at least 34 children and a teacher. Authorities in the city of Peshawar said rescue workers arrived within minutes, and that rapid response saved dozens of lives. Crews cleared debris, with officials saying everyone trapped beneath the rubble was eventually pulled out. Hospital officials say more than 50 other people were injured, some in critical condition. The local police chief says the school's owner has been arrested. Mian Saeed, Peshawar Police Chief (through translator): This is a truly tragic incident, and we will certainly investigate and file a report against the owners. Holding classes for children in such a fragile building located within such narrow streets, this clearly represents a grave instance of negligence. Amna Nawaz: Thousands of mourners attended a mass funeral later in the day. The children killed or injured were all between the ages of 6 and 14 and all lived in the same neighborhood as the school. In Albania, violent clashes erupted in the capital of Tirana today as anti-government protests stretched into a third day. Alarms sounded as protesters attacked this bank. Riot police retaliated with water cannons and tear gas. The nation's Health Ministry says more than 80 people were injured, most of them police officers. The student-led demonstration started amid anger over a major development project backed by President Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner. They're also demanding better school conditions and for Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign. He has refused to do so. In New York City today, ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, pleaded not guilty to new charges of torture. He's accused of overseeing a violent campaign against opponents and others, including three Americans. The allegations were added to an earlier drug trafficking indictment against the couple. Maduro told the court today the indictment contains what he called false accusations and false testimony. The couple were seized from their Caracas home by the U.S. military in January, and their trial is set for next June. President Trump's new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, is facing questions about her legal credentials. Multiple news outlets report she has not passed the bar exam in any state. Zacharia holds a law degree from Pepperdine's Caruso School of Law. She's referred to herself online as general counsel in past roles, and Mr. Trump has called her an attorney. But legal experts say neither of those titles should be used unless someone has passed the bar. Zacharia held her first briefing as press secretary this week, taking questions from three outlets in a 15-minute appearance. On Wall Street today, stocks managed to end higher despite ongoing worries about AI. The Dow Jones industrial average jumped more than 550 points. The Nasdaq added just 20 points, so a small gain there. The S&P 500 rose a third of 1 percent. And we cover news big and small here at the "News Hour," and in this case, very small. The London Zoo announced the birth of 15 Afia Birago puddle frogs, one of the world's smallest and rarest amphibians. The frog is about a fifth of an inch in size, no larger than the tip of a pencil. These are the first to be born in captivity. Researchers are racing to save the species, which was only identified in its native Ghana eight years ago. Now there are a few more.

4bda74177fc1.text: The CDC has confirmed more than 4,000 cases of measles this year as the country grapples with the largest outbreak of the highly infectious virus in 35 years. Nearly a fifth of cases comprise children under the age of five, and 95% are among unvaccinated people. Amna Nawaz spoke with Dr. Evan Shirey, a pediatric infectious disease doctor based in Pennsylvania. Amna Nawaz: The CDC has now confirmed more than 4,000 cases of measles this year as the country grapples with the largest outbreak of the highly infectious virus in 35 years. Nearly a fifth of cases comprise children under the age of 5, and more than 90 percent are among people who are unvaccinated. Pennsylvania is the epicenter of the outbreak with more than 1, 100 cases. That includes five measles-related deaths and potentially a sixth still being investigated. For more on what we're seeing and its impact, we're joined now by Dr. Evan Shirey. He's a pediatric infectious disease doctor based in Hershey, Pennsylvania. Dr. Shirey, welcome and thanks for joining us. Dr. Evan Shirey, Penn State Health: Thank you for having me. Amna Nawaz: So you're in Hershey in Central Pennsylvania, the middle of your state's measles epicenter. Just tell us what you're seeing at your hospital right now. Dr. Evan Shirey: Yes, unfortunately, I have been seeing a lot of children and a lot of babies who have been admitted to our hospital and have been very sick. I am seeing the severe consequences that can come from this virus. Amna Nawaz: Tell us about those consequences. What are the measles like in those young children you're seeing? How does it present? Dr. Evan Shirey: So there are a number of complications that can come about from measles. One that we really worry about is encephalitis, and that's when the virus causes infection of the brain. Children with encephalitis from measles in some cases may be unresponsive. In other cases, they may be awake and aware, but confused. They don't know where they are. They're scared, in some cases, not even able to recognize their own parents. These cases are really, really tragic to see. We see infections where the virus infects the lungs or the airways, and we call that a bronchopneumonia. These children might come in breathing really fast, breathing really heavily, gasping for air, in some cases needing different forms of respiratory support and oxygen, and in some of the extreme cases we have seen have even need to be put on a ventilator. We have seen babies who have come in who are unable to nurse or unable to take bottles, and just all forms of various different kinds of suffering from the manifestations of these infections. Amna Nawaz: And, Dr. Shirey, do we know what's driving this outbreak, how it's gotten so severe in Pennsylvania? Dr. Evan Shirey: So we know that, historically, the measles virus caused a lot of infections. We had three or four million infections every single year in this country, and that also resulted in 50,000 hospitalizations, around 500 deaths every year. So we know this is really bad virus. We know the measles virus can spread like wildfire. It is famous for how infectious it is. One person with measles can infect up to 18 others. The reason that we have not been seeing measles cases up until now is because we had a very safe and a very effective vaccine that we had been using for decades that actually resulted in elimination of the virus from this country. The virus is back because of a failure to vaccinate. Amna Nawaz: Given that we thought measles was eliminated about 25 years ago, is this something you ever thought you would be seeing during your time practicing as a doctor? Dr. Evan Shirey: Absolutely not. I spent a lot of time learning about measles as a medical student and as a resident and as an infectious diseases fellow going through all of my training. I always expected that measles was going to stay in the textbooks, and I did not expect that I would live in a world where I was in an ICU taking care of patients in real life. Amna Nawaz: Can I ask you about the rhetoric we're hearing from some of the nation's leaders? I mean, famously, the HHS secretary, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., has had some anti-vaccine views and vaccine skepticism he's expressed. How does that complicate your job on the ground? Dr. Evan Shirey: I think it's a real shame. I think that this outbreak just really highlights how important it is that, when we communicate about these important health issues, that we lead with honesty and the truth. I think it's -- overall has been a shame that the anti-vaccine movement has gained the power that they have and that they have gained the influence in reaching ordinary Pennsylvanians. I see in my clinic when I talk to people about vaccines that the types of fears that people have over these last five, 10 years are really just a different dynamic from the way things used to be. And I think that is largely -- unfortunately, it's related to the success of the anti-vaccine movement as a whole. Amna Nawaz: Whenever we cover these kinds of stories, I should mention to you we hear from people who say, look, if you or your children are vaccinated, you will be fine, so there's not much to worry about. What do you make of that argument? Dr. Evan Shirey: So, first and foremost, I want to be very clear that the vaccine is extremely safe and extremely effective. We have been using the MMR vaccine really in the same form since the late 1960s. So we have decades of experience with this. Billions of people have received this vaccine. So I lead with reiterating the truth that the vaccine is very safe and very effective. For people who are vaccinated, I do want to give reassurance, if you are vaccinated, the vaccine is protective. The unfortunate thing that I think people need to understand is that not everyone can receive the vaccine. And so the vulnerable among our communities have been relying for decades on the rest of us to be vaccinated at a high enough rate to achieve herd

The UK said Thursday it was prepared to align its tariffs on Chinese EVs with those of the EU, delivering a boost to Brussels as it negotiates with Beijing to narrow the trade gap.
European leaders have adopted a more aggressive stance to shield native businesses from a tidal wave of Chinese imports, which policymakers have blamed for deep job losses among European automakers and other sectors.
So far, counter-efforts have involved both protectionist and industrial policies, including âMade in Europeâ rules that have stoked discord among some of Europeâs largest economies.

de9e899f5801.text: President Trump is cutting checks to Americans and promising more with less than three weeks left in a midterm cycle largely focused on affordability. Trump argues they’re refunds for excessive healthcare costs and promised economic dividends that only his party can deliver. Democrats contend he’s trying to bribe citizens to vote for Republicans. Liz Landers has an accounting of the payouts. Amna Nawaz: President Trump is cutting checks to Americans and promising more with less than three weeks left in a midterm cycle largely focused on affordability. Trump argues they're refunds for high health care costs and economic dividends that only his party can deliver. Democrats contend he's trying to bribe citizens to vote for Republicans. Our White House correspondent, Liz Landers, is here with an accounting of those payouts. Good to see you, Liz. Liz Landers: Yes. Nice to see you. Amna Nawaz: So let's start with those checks some Americans have already started to receive in the last week or so for Affordable Care Act fees. How much are people getting and what's the president's rationale for those? Liz Landers: People are starting to get these $500 checks really in the last week or so. It's gone out to about a million Americans so far across 30 different states. And this is for people that don't get premium assistance. With these checks was a personal letter that the president wrote. And it says in part: "I'm proud to return your money to you, and I will never stop fighting to put the American people first, restore affordability, protect your hard-earned money, and lower the cost of health care." Now I spoke with Cynthia Cox about this. She's the director of the Affordable Care Act Program at KFF. And she said that this move from the administration is unprecedented. But she also explained how this can help Americans and how these checks will factor into overall rising health care costs. Cynthia Cox, Program on the ACA Director, KFF: For people who get ACA coverage, in particular, the people who lost subsidy this year, they're probably paying a couple thousand dollars more in their premiums this year than they were last year. So the $500 checks are probably going to help. I mean, $500 is nothing to sneeze at, but they're still having a much higher cost beyond that $500 this year than they were last year. Liz Landers: Cox says that the timing of this is political. She said she first heard about this idea floated out there last year, but, of course, now it's being implemented just a few weeks before a midterm election. The White House fact sheet that they put out claimed that the Biden administration -- quote -- "accumulated a significant surplus of funds that were not used to benefit the Americans who paid these higher premiums." But I asked Cox about this, and she says that the different administrations between the Biden and Trump administration have collected different user fees, and that the Trump administration inherited this surplus from the Biden administration, and now they're sending it out as checks. Amna Nawaz: Meanwhile, that's not the only check the administration is sending out. There's more than 20 million Medicare enrollees who could receive a payment as well. What's the reasoning behind those payouts? Liz Landers: These are $90 checks, so much less money, only one-time payments. And this is going to Medicare Part B participants. But Medicare Advantage enrollees and other people with disabilities and some low-income Medicare recipients are not eligible for this. Of course, Medicare Part B covers things like ambulance services, doctor visits, lab tests. So this is helpful, of course; $90 is not nothing. And this will go out to about 21 million Americans. This payment is coming through the Medicare Improvement Fund created by Congress in 2008. And it's not the first time that the fund has been used. The Obama administration and Congress redirected money to expand coverage, but it's the first time that it's been used for direct payments like this. Amna Nawaz: Liz, meanwhile, there's this other promise the president made you reported on that he first made from the midterm convention stage in Dallas that he would send $5,000 to all American adults. Let's just start with what that would cost. Liz Landers: It would cost about a trillion dollars and add that much money to the national debt, which is why you have seen people raise immediate questions about this. This, of course, made big news when the president announced this from the stage during the midterm convention about a month ago. And he has been repeating this and promising this over and over to Americans throughout just about every midterm rally that I have watched and covered. And, yesterday, he talked about this yet again. President Donald Trump: If Republicans can win the House of Representatives and the U.S. Senate, I am going to give all adult citizens in the United States of America $5,000. (CHEERING) President Donald Trump: Think of it. Liz Landers: President Trump was asked in September, sort of right after this announcement, why are you doing this if your economic policies are working? And he said that this is not to turn out voters. He said instead it is a -- quote -- "reward" for voters having to put up with Biden's economic policies. There are, of course, lingering questions about congressional approval of this. Just a reminder, Amna, we're hearing the president make all these promises. He also promised in November of last year, almost a year ago now, that a $2,000 dividend check would be going out to every American for a tariff revenue refund. That has yet to materialize.

cee9de1b6aa0.text: President Trump will travel to Georgia on Friday to stump for Republican Senate candidate Mike Collins. Collins is in an uphill battle against incumbent Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff. Liz Landers visited Georgia for a closer look at that race. Amna Nawaz: So we just heard some of the president speaking in Montana this week. We know he's been out on the road. Where is he heading next? Liz Landers: Yes, Amna, he is traveling to Dalton, Georgia, tomorrow to stump for the Senate candidate there, Mike Collins. I was in Georgia recently for a closer look at that race, where Collins is in an uphill battle against the incumbent Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff. On his vineyard in Southern Georgia, Gary Paulk feels the impacts of many of President Trump's policies firsthand. Gary Paulk, Paulk Vineyards: The fuel today is twice as high as it would have been this time last year. Liz Landers: Polk is a fifth-generation muscadine grape farmer in rural Ray, Georgia. Gary Paulk: Pick them up and eat them, yes. Liz Landers: Mmm. Gary Paulk: Sweet. Liz Landers: Really sweet. He says fuel prices, tariffs that have raised his costs, and an immigration crackdown that has made it harder to find workers have all taken a toll. The president says all the time that he is doing these mass deportations because noncitizens, people who are here illegally in some cases are taking jobs from Americans. Is that the case? Gary Paulk: That's just -- that's not true. They're not taking -- they're not taking jobs from Americans, and, actually, a lot of times that they are filling jobs that Americans don't want, more ag jobs and more remedial -- you know, labor-intensive jobs, construction jobs. Liz Landers: Paulk also worries about access to health care in rural areas after his 36-year-old daughter, Amy, suffered serious strokes that nearly took her life. Gary Paulk: Amy has come a long way. She still can't speak very well. She's just now starting to eat some soft foods, but she's a fighter. Liz Landers: After weighing all these factors, Paulk has decided for the first time in his life to cast a ballot for a Democrat, incumbent Senator Jon Ossoff. He doesn't agree with the Democrat on all issues, notably abortion, but it is Ossoff's help in getting federal aid after Hurricane Helene wreaked havoc on Paulk's grape crop that won his vote. Gary Paulk: He's done a lot of things and proposed a lot of things. And he's crossed party lines to do it, especially with the hurricane disaster. They got $531 million appropriated for the hurricane disaster for farmers in this area. Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-GA): The country needs us to work. Liz Landers: At 39, Ossoff is the youngest sitting U.S. senator and the only Democrat running for reelection in a state Trump won in 2024. A hotly contested swing state in recent elections, Georgia was expected to be a tight contest again. But Ossoff has built a comfortable lead, in part by relentlessly focusing on affordability. Sen. Jon Ossoff: Millions are just one medical bill, short paycheck, or bad alternator from disaster. You work harder and harder, but the treadmill gets faster and steeper and the bills get higher and higher. Liz Landers: Ossoff's opponent is Congressman Mike Collins, whose campaign has been plagued with troubles from the beginning, from a campaign kickoff ad that misspelled Georgia to lackluster fund-raising and a series of scandalous headlines that two former aides and even Collins' son-in-law have promoted antisemitism and white nationalist views. Sen. Jon Ossoff: If John Lewis were marching today from Selma to Montgomery, Mike Collins would be grabbing a billy club. His office has been in cahoots with some of the most notorious white supremacists around the country. Liz Landers: Collins strongly denies the allegations. Rep. Mike Collins (R-GA), Senatorial Candidate: I have condemned racism, antisemitism, hate. I don't care where the source is. And I tell him that too. It's wrong. We have no place in this world for that. Liz Landers: A lifelong Georgian whose father was a congressman for 12 years, Collins attacks Ossoff as left-leaning and out of touch with Georgia values. Rep. Mike Collins: I am unapologetically pro-God, pro-Trump, pro-Second Amendment. I believe in a strong military. Peace through strength works. If it's not good for Georgia and it's not good for this country, I will never support it. 680993da8d47.text: By — Steve Peoples, Associated Press Steve Peoples, Associated Press By — Linley Sanders, Associated Press Linley Sanders, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/frustrated-with-trump-voters-overwhelmingly-want-change-ap-norc-poll-finds Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Frustrated with Trump, voters overwhelmingly want change, AP-NORC poll finds Politics Oct 15, 2026 6:27 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — A strong majority of voters believe that President Donald Trump is falling short at home and abroad, and they want major change in the upcoming midterm elections, according to a new AP-NORC poll that raises serious warning signs for the Republican Party at a critical moment. The survey from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research, conducted less than four weeks before Election Day, finds that registered voters who identify as Democrats are more enthusiastic than Republican voters about casting a ballot. More voters want Democrats to win control of Congress and have a more negative view of Republicans. Please check your inbox to confirm. The Democratic advantage is small in some cases, but, taken together, the findings paint a challenging picture for Republicans, who are clinging to control of Congress under the weight of an unpopular war with Iran and surging prices at home. READ MORE: Retail sales saw 0.8% bump in September, but big chunk of spending went to paying for gas About 8 in 10 voters overall say the economy or the cost of living is among their top issues for the upcoming election, while about two-thirds say this about healthcare and the war in Iran. Other issues that are stronger for Trump — like immigration or crime — are lower priorities. "The world is going backwards. We can barely afford anything," said Diana Walker, a 65-year-old Democrat from Decatur, Georgia. "Everybody's down. I don't care if you're a Democrat or Republican, we're all catching hell." Democrats are more enthusiastic about voting than Republicans Less than a month before the final midterm votes are cast, the poll finds that Democratic voters are more motivated to vote. Overall, about two-thirds of registered voters say it's "extremely" important to vote in the upcoming election, while about 2 in 10 say it's "very" important. But about three-quarters of Democratic voters say that voting in this November's midterm elections is "extremely" important, compared with roughly 6 in 10 Republicans. READ MORE: Democrats see voter enthusiasm in fundraising haul from small-dollar donors before the midterms Ryan Longbrake, a 52-year-old Democrat from Columbus, Ohio who works in technology marketing, said he's especially excited about casting his ballot, and he's already taken steps to ensure that his wife and two college-age daughters will vote as well. "I believe that there is change on the horizon and there is an excitement within our party," he said, pointing to Democrats' momentum in Ohio's elections for governor and U.S. Senate. The party is also investing resources in Republican-leaning states, like Iowa and Kansas, where the political environment has put Democratic candidates on friendlier footing. Republicans have controlled Congress for the past two years, but about half of registered voters now say they'd prefer to see the Democratic Party control the House or the Senate. A smaller percentage, roughly 4 in 10, say they want the Republican Party to control each chamber, while 15% are undecided. The vast majority of voters want change One thing is crystal clear on the eve of the 2026 midterms: Voters want change. About half of voters say they want "substantial change," and roughly 3 in 10 want "complete and total upheaval" in the way the country is run. Democrats and independents are much likelier than Republicans to want a full overhaul of the country's direction. But even Republican voters are still looking for something different. Slightly fewer than half, 45%, want substantial change, while 13% want upheaval. "I'm kind of tired of sending people there and nothing gets done," said Krista Kohles, a 70-year-old Republican from near Davey, Nebraska. "Nothing's changing." Trump's numbers on key issues are weak Voters are deeply frustrated with Trump and his leadership on the issues they say matter most. Only about one-third of registered voters overall have a "very" or "somewhat" favorable view of the Republican president, and a similar share approve of his performance as president. Voters continue to be frustrated by the high cost of living, an issue that Trump vowed to address before winning a second term in the White House. Nearly two years after his successful election, about 8 in 10 registered voters disapprove of how Trump is handling the cost of living, in line with a September AP-NORC poll. About three-quarters disapprove of his performance on the economy. READ MORE: Most Americans blame Trump for high prices as his economic approval hits new low, AP-NORC poll shows Even among Republican voters, only 44% approve of Trump's performance on the cost of living, while 54% approve of his leadership on the economy. That's a sharp contrast with other issues, like crime, on which Republican approval is much higher. There are cracks in Trump's Republican base on other issues, too. Just 69% of Republican voters support Trump on foreign policy as the war in Iran stretches into its eighth month, despite his promises that it would only last four or five weeks. DonnaJean Weber, a 72-year-old Republican from Manistee, Michigan, says she will continue to support Republican candidates this fall, but she's not happy with the state of the economy under Trump's leadership. It's part of our higher education series, Rethinking College, and produced in collaboration with the Hechinger Report. Amna Nawaz: Across the nation, scores of small private colleges and universities are either closing or under threat. With each shuttering, students, faculty, and the surrounding community struggle to find a way forward. Tonight, Paul Solman reports on one such school. This story was reported in collaboration with The Hechinger Report and is part of our higher education series Rethinking College. Ken Burns, Documentary Filmmaker: I don't recognize the person who entered Hampshire College in the fall of 1971 and the person who graduated in the spring of 1975. Paul Solman: Filmmaker Ken Burns. Paul Solman: History professor Jim Wald taught at Hampshire for nearly 40 years. Jim Wald: When it opened, it was the hot place, I'm told, more selective than Harvard or equally selective as Harvard. Hampshire was always way up there in really making students do a lot of work, because the idea was to show people how to be scholars. This is what it means to be a historian or a biologist. Paul Solman: Or become a filmmaker like Barry Sonnenfeld or writer like Jon Krakauer. Jim Wald: Our students were challenged much more than others in a lot of other schools. The college has a Latin motto, non satis scire, to know is not enough, embodying this idea of wisdom and critical thinking. Paul Solman: An ethos that persisted for actors like Lupita Nyong'o of the "Black Panther" and "The Odyssey" and Liev Schreiber. Liev Schreiber, Actor: Hampshire was interested in radical questions. The faculty and the other kids were interested in things that were different. Challenging the world in which you live in, in a positive and constructive way was certainly the ethos. Paul Solman: What would be an example? Chloe De Lisle: "Apocalypse Now" and how the signature helicopter sound that really permeates the film is part of the protagonist's experience and trauma, and then a collective cultural trauma. Paul Solman: Ken Burns' final thesis 51 years ago? Ken Burns: My half-an-hour film called "Working in Rural New England" for Old Sturbridge Village, which is a living history museum. Paul Solman: So you mean you literally began your career doing what you have been doing ever since at Hampshire? Ken Burns: It's even worse than that, Paul, which is the last shot of the film for Old Sturbridge Village was a pan across a painting from an agrarian to a kind of industrial or preindustrial sequence. Paul Solman: Just like so many pans in his PBS films, and thus Hampshire's hallmark from then to now, focused exploration. Chloe De Lisle: Here has allowed me to really do whatever I want and really create my own major, and that's meant everything. And I have just gotten to pull all my interests together and create something really cool. Paul Solman: A result of deep connection with the school. Mars Richman, Former Hampshire College Student: With the class structure, without those prerequisites, able to do what you want, chart your own course, I feel that I was able to be focused faster than most people would at a traditional college. Paul Solman: First year student Jupiter Brady-McCullough feels the same. Jupiter Brady-McCullough, Former Hampshire College Student: I made some great friends. I had some really amazing classes with some really amazing professors, and I learned a lot about myself. So I think I'm not alone in feeling kind of hopeless, in that we see a lot of these small schools closing right now. One analysis finds that, in the next decade, of the nation's 1700 nonprofit private colleges and universities, more than 400 are on the brink, meaning the nearly 700,000 students projected to go to them are at risk. In fact, when Hampshire announced last April that it would be closing at the end of this year... Mars Richman: I cried all day. Everyone cried all day. We were... Paul Solman: Really? Everybody? Mars Richman: Everybody cried all day long. Paul Solman: But you knew that school had been in trouble? Mars Richman: We all -- I mean, we all knew, but it kept not dying. Logically, we all knew someday it would, but it kept kind of escaping death. Madeline Keating, Hampshire College Student: Hampshire means everything to me. These are among the questions explored by musician, writer and visual artist David Byrne in his new book, "Sleeping Beauties." Senior arts correspondent Jeffrey Brown recently joined him in Brooklyn for our arts and culture series, CANVAS. Amna Nawaz: Why are some great ideas and works of art forgotten, and why are others revived? These are among the questions explored by musician, writer, and visual artist David Byrne. Senior arts correspondent Jeffrey Brown joined him recently in Brooklyn for our arts and culture series, Canvas. (MUSIC) Jeffrey Brown: Questions and more questions. David Byrne is a man with a curious and quirky mind, including when it comes to writing songs. David Byrne, Musician and Author, "Sleeping Beauties: Why Good Ideas Go Dormant and How They Wake Up": Sometimes, I will start with the title of a song. I did a song called "I Met the Buddha at a Downtown." And I go, all right, what happens? What's he like? What's he doing? Jeffrey Brown: What's this Buddha guy doing at the party? David Byrne: What does he say to you? What do you say to him? What does he say to you? Jeffrey Brown: He's a man of many turns, front man for the rock band Talking Heads, musical experimenter and collaborator with artists around the globe, Oscar winner for co-writing the score for "The Last Emperor," Broadway star in "American Utopia," and a lot more, including cycling man about town, a regular sight on New York streets, and the subject of his 2009 book, "Bicycle Diaries." Now he's asking new questions stemming from the fairy tale of Sleeping Beauty, the princess cursed to sleep 100 years, who can be awakened only by the kiss of a prince. Byrne came across an article in a science journal that applied the term to studies that for various reasons have been ignored or forgotten, only to be later recognized and given renewed prominence. David Byrne: I immediately thought, I know this phenomena. I know it from musicians that I might like, but I feel like didn't get their deserved appreciation. I know of we're always reading about this or that or the other, and they're suddenly rediscovered, and it's like now we understand it. Now what they did makes perfect sense. Jeffrey Brown: Something's lost and then found. David Byrne: Found again, yes. And it's -- I just love these stories, the stories of kind of a resurrection or that kind of thing, of somebody -- somebody or some work kind of coming back to life and being re-appreciated. Jeffrey Brown: The result is the book "Sleeping Beauties: Why Good Ideas Go Dormant and How They Wake Up." David Byrne: This kind of clocklike device will kind of keep the telescope always pointed at the object you're observing. Jeffrey Brown: It's a mix of art, science, and technology that reflects his own interests. He asked to meet us at Pioneer Works, an artist- and scientist-led cultural center in Brooklyn that he loves for its focus on creativity in its many forms. His book offers many examples of world-famous artists lost to history for a time, sometimes centuries, thankfully rescued. Perhaps you know this image by Italian early renaissance painter Sandro Botticelli. David Byrne: Botticelli is really well-known. Jeffrey Brown: Very well-known today. David Byrne: Very well-known. He's on tea towels. You can get a watch with Venus on it. You can get you name it, and those images that are on there, Birth of Venus and all that stuff. Jeffrey Brown: Yes. David Byrne: So when you tell people, no, this guy went way out of favor for hundreds of years... Jeffrey Brown: Byrne tells the story of Botticelli's artistic death at the hands of the crusading religious zealot Savonarola and his much later rebirth in the late 19th century. David Byrne: Gradually, he gets re-appreciated, until, by the beginning of the 20th century, there were more books written about Botticelli than any other artist. Jeffrey Brown: There are as many or more examples in the fields of science and technology, such as Gregor Mendel, today known as the father of genetics, whose initial paper in 1866 went largely unrecognized. David Byrne: For various reasons, it didn't click until, later on, two scientists were doing a very similar kind of research, and they thought, before we publish this, let's take a look and see if maybe someone else has done something similar before we take all the credit. Yes, they found Mendel's paper. And they go, oh, my God, he kind of did it all. Jeffrey Brown: And then there's something you might not expect in a book like this, concrete. David Byrne: This is one of my favorite ones. When people ask me, what's your book about, and I go, concrete. Jeffrey Brown: Concrete. David Byrne: Yes, concrete. And they go, what? What? Concrete's everywhere, yes, highways, buildings, everything. Jeffrey Brown: Yes. David Byrne: And I go, yes. The Roman concrete, the Pantheon, for example, the dome of that is unreinforced, and it's lasted 2,000 years and doesn't have a crack in it. The companies that make concrete now rate their concrete as guaranteed to last 50 years. Jeffrey Brown: Fifty years. David Byrne: Five-zero. Jeffrey Brown: Yes. David Byrne: That's a little bit of a difference. So you go, what happened? Who lost the recipe? Jeffrey Brown: Not so much lost, Byrne shows, as not understanding or ignoring Roman materials and building practices, a bias thinking we know better than people of the past. The key for Byrne, the rediscovery to benefit us today. David Byrne: Let's focus on how these things got rediscovered, because that's really what we want to know. We want to know if there's other ones out there and how can we find them? The question is, what are we suppressing, or what have we forgotten that's out there? Because we do the same things. Jeffrey Brown: Byrne himself is still very much producing his own art. He just finished a long tour for his most recent album titled "Who Is the Sky?" A

The number of ships that have reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz has hit a record high, BBC Verify analysis of data from a UK maritime agency shows.
Twelve vessels were attacked between 5 and 11 October - the largest number of weekly strikes reported to the UK's Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency since the US-Israeli war with Iran began. The previous week saw 10 ships reporting attacks.
Six of the vessels were struck last Sunday, according to the UKMTO - a one-day high. So far this week, there have been four reported attacks.
As the number of strikes has risen, the recovery in oil shipments through the strait seen last month has slowed, industry data suggests.
BBC Verify collated incident reports published by the UKMTO on its website and created a timeline based on the first date cited in each report. This is approximate because some incidents use the date of the attack and some the date on which it was reported.
Experts say Tehran has been attacking ships in an effort to assert greater control over the waterway as the US military has increased the number of tankers it is shepherding through the south of the strait to evade Iranian strikes.
Iran is also carrying out more attacks on vessels further away from the Strait of Hormuz, according to experts.
The US military's Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, posted on social media that despite the attacks "commercial traffic continues to flow through the Strait of Hormuz with co-ordinated protection from US forces and regional partners".
Two crew missing after one of Sunday's attacks
The aftermath of one of Sunday's six reported attacks was captured in verified footage showing the Nicaragua-flagged tanker Petro Dolphin on fire, as filmed by the crew on a smaller boat nearby.
The vessel was struck by a drone close to the Sohar Anchorage, Oman, more than 250km (150 miles) from the strait, according to the maritime intelligence firm Vanguard.
Eleven Indian seafarers were rescued but two are still missing, the Forward Seamen's Union of India said.
Attacks have continued this week with the container ship GFS Pride sinking after a strike by an unknown projectile in the strait on Tuesday. Twenty-one crew were safely evacuated.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) published footage of what appeared to be the same ship sinking. It said the vessel was carrying "2,500 containers of contraband" and had taken an "unauthorised route".
Oil shipments stall
Middle East oil exports have slowed as the number of ship strikes has risen.
About 12.6 million barrels per day went through the strait on 13 October, below the 15 million reported at the end of September, data from trade intelligence firm Kpler shows. This compares with a pre-war baseline of some 17 million barrels per day.
The recent increase in attacks comes as US Navy data indicates the number of vessels given assistance to navigate the Strait of Hormuz during the first 10 days of October was up 85% compared with the same period in August.
Most of the oil being shipped from Gulf Arab states recently has been carried using a "shuttle" system where a fleet of tankers load up and sail through the strait before transferring their cargo to larger tankers in the Gulf of Oman.
These shuttle ships use a route close to Oman's coastline. Iran says this is "unauthorised" and insist vessels take an alternative route closer to its own shore.
So-called assisted transits were a key factor in helping drive oil flows from the Middle East back towards pre-war levels in September. This does not include Iranian exports which have completely stalled as a result of the US blockade of Iranian ports and ships.
Martin Kelly, CEO of Orbital Risk Intelligence, said Iran has "evolved its strategy" in response to this loosening of its control over the strait and has been carrying out "near daily or multiple attacks every single day".
"The aim here is to stop the ships going through and to deter others," he added.
The IRGC's navy has said strikes would not be "limited to the Strait of Hormuz" and later announced a "new deployment formation" across the region, according to state media.
Martin Kelly told BBC Verify that Iran is widening its attacks and targeting ships near the coast of Gulf Arab states and in the Gulf of Oman.
A tanker was struck by multiple projectiles north of Qatar on Thursday 8 October, more than 500km (310 miles) from the strait, resulting in multiple reported casualties, according to Vanguard.
Another tanker was attacked close to the UAE town of Al-Jazirah al-Hamra on Friday 9 October, Vanguard said.
Verified footage shows crew members running across the deck and putting on lifejackets as a large cloud of black smoke rises over the ship.
Additional reporting by Becky Dale
Graphics by Tom Shiel and Mark Edwards

Russian security services were waiting when the flight landed in Moscow in December. On board were Russians the US had deported, including activists denied political asylum.
"It was unbelievably frightening. My knees were shaking with fear," says Katya, one of the deportees. We have changed her name to protect her identity, as she remains in Russia.
Katya had left Russia and claimed asylum in the US two years earlier.
When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, many countries publicly welcomed fleeing Russians. But more than four years later, attitudes have hardened. The numbers of anti-war Russians forcibly returned from Western countries is rising, and Katya's experience highlights the potential risks they face.
US authorities rejected her application for asylum, after she said she had provided evidence that she had taken part in protests and was a member of an opposition movement.
In Moscow, Katya says officers from the FSB security service handed all the male deportees military papers, requiring them to register with the local enlistment office, from where men are often sent to the war in Ukraine. Another passenger on the flight and an activist confirmed her account.
The officers interrogated her, and many others, for several hours.
"At one point, they found incriminating information on my phone," says Katya, "Their faces changed in a second. I was very afraid that they would simply bundle me off somewhere."
Katya was eventually released and allowed to stay with relatives. But she says police continue to call her and visit her at home.
"I feel as if I'm in a cage, like in a zoo," she says, "Whenever I see a police car, I feel terrified and start thinking, "What if they're coming for me?"
Katya showed the BBC documents and photographs confirming her story, which matches accounts from other deportees.
Removals from the US rose from 222 in 2023 to more than 1,200 in 2025, amid a wider increase in deportations under President Donald Trump's second term. Activists say Russian deportees included dissidents and Russian army deserters, some of whom were imprisoned or sent to war after returning to Russia.
One such case is Leonid Melekhin, an anti-war activist who sought asylum in the US after being arrested at protests in Russia. He had posted photographs of Russian President Vladimir Putin online with the message "Putin: murderer, fascist, usurper". After being deported back home last year, Melekhin was charged with "justifying terrorism" and sentenced to six years in prison.
"We have several examples of people who got eight years in prison when they crossed the [Russian] border," says Andrei Pivovarov, from Russia's exiled opposition Anti-War Committee.
And deportations are taking place from Europe too. His organisation has changed its advice to dissidents escaping Russia: the EU is no longer safe, it is better to seek refuge elsewhere.
Germany has sharply increased the number of Russian nationals it deports. Seven were sent back in 2023, rising to more than 110 in 2025, according to German government figures. More than 21,000 Russians sought asylum in Germany between 2022 and 2025, but the proportion of positive decisions fell from 29% in 2023 to just 6.8% in the first eleven months of 2025.
"Protection is only granted if there is an actual, well-founded fear of persecution," Germany's migration and asylum agency, BAMF, told the BBC.
Last year, Berlin suspended its humanitarian visa programme for Russians, and across the EU, the proportion of Russian applicants granted some form of asylum protection fell from 23% in 2024 to around 17% in the first nine months of 2025, according to EU data.
Russian opposition activists fleeing repression have become caught up in a wider crackdown on immigration, as governments across Europe and the US toughen rules amid political pressure over high numbers of irregular migrants and asylum applications, as well as over security concerns.
Western governments are "focused on limiting humanitarian programmes and asylum seekers", says lawyer Anastasia Burakova, founder of rights group Kovcheg (Ark), which helps anti-war Russians leave the country. The clampdown is "in response to public concerns and rising support for right-wing populist parties", she adds.
Following a negative asylum decision, Russian nationals are often given the chance to leave independently, but a rising number are being forcibly returned to Russia, usually escorted via third countries.
Several Russian activists in exile told the BBC that immigration officials had told them they faced "no danger" in Russia, and that officials often lacked an adequate understanding of the risks that activists face.
"I tried to explain that if they sent me back, I would be put in prison, or sent to war where I'd be killed," explains former soldier Artyom, who deserted from the Russian Army in 2022 after officers threatened to send him to Ukraine. "They just didn't believe me."
He says he provided US authorities with proof that a criminal investigation had been opened against him back in Russia for desertion. But he was put on a deportation flight back to Moscow via Egypt.
"I was preparing for death," says the former soldier, "I was thinking, 'how can I die without it being painful?'".
Back in Moscow, Artyom was held in a military detention facility but managed to escape. He is now in hiding abroad.
"Another country could investigate me better and give me asylum. Why didn't they give me that chance? Instead they deported me specifically to Russia," says the deserter. "It ruined my life."
The US Department of Homeland Security told the BBC: "All illegal aliens receive due process. If a judge finds an illegal alien has no right to be in this country, we are going to remove them."

A 16-year-old has shot dead three children and a teacher at a primary school in the US state of Oregon before he was killed by a bystander, police said.
The suspect, who has not been named, forced his way into Silver Rail Elementary School in the city of Bend on Thursday afternoon by shooting at locked doors, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said.
The teenager was shot dead by a community member who "pursued him into the school and engaged him", Krantz said. Police arrived three minutes later.
The three children killed were aged five, eight and 11. A seven-year-old and a 54-year-old teacher were taken to a hospital in a critical condition, Krantz said. It is unclear if the attacker had any links to the school.
"We are stunned and heartbroken by this senseless tragedy," Steven Cook, the top administrative official of the local school district, said in a statement.
"No words can adequately express the grief our community is experiencing."
Police said the attacker was a local 16-year-old boy, but they did not release any further details on him or the identity of the victims.
Police were alerted to an active shooter at Silver Rail Elementary at 12:59 local time (19:59 GMT), Bend Police Department spokeswoman Sheila Miller told reporters.
The first call came from a person who said that an unknown suspect was shooting into their car with a long gun, police said. Photos released from the scene show a red truck with bullet holes.
Minutes later, the local county dispatch received 911 calls reporting that the attacker had entered the school.
Police said he shot at locks on the doors in order to force his way inside.
Local media reports suggested the school received new classroom doors in 2022 which can be locked with the flip of a switch.
A bystander saw the shooting begin to unfold, pursued the attacker into the school and shot him dead, police said.
Three minutes later, officers first arrived at the scene. They confirmed that the attacker had been killed, and then searched the school.
Oregon Governor Tina Kotek praised the bystander who "heroically intervened" to stop further loss of life.
"Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well," she told a media briefing alongside other officials.
A local newspaper reporter told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that the school was in lockdown during the shooting and that students were able to communicate with parents outside with their Apple watches.
Michael Kohn, a reporter with Bulletin newspaper, said the incident had left the parents stunned.
"This is a neighbourhood school. Parents are stunned. It's just something you don't expect to happen in Bend, Oregon. It's a mountain town," he said.
Schools in Bend have been closed on Friday. Officials said the community needed time to heal.
Around 450 children attend Silver Rail Elementary School, which has more than 40 adult staff members, police said.
According to the K-12 School Shooting Database, there were 235 shooting incidents at American schools last year and at least 140 so far this year.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has urged Albertans to vote to remain in Canada ahead of an independence referendum on Monday, warning that the "stakes are high".
Speaking at a pro-unity rally on Thursday in Calgary, Carney said the referendum is taking place "at the worst possible time" and called on voters to deliver a "decisive result" against separation.
More than 450,000 Albertans have already voted early or by mail on a question asking if they wish the province to remain part of Canada, or start the process of holding a binding referendum to separate.
Campaigners on both sides are making their final pitches, though polls indicate most Albertans appear supportive of remaining in Canada.
Still, Carney said Albertans should not assume that the result is decided based on the polling alone.
"Turnout will determine the outcome," he told a crowd of more than 7,000 in Calgary.
Thursday's rally is one of two back-to-back pro-unity events that the prime minister is scheduled to attend in Alberta, with another one set for tomorrow in Edmonton, his hometown.
Earlier in the day, Carney toured several businesses in Calgary and spoke to pro-unity volunteers in a get-out-the-vote push.
The 19 October referendum was called by the province's premier Danielle Smith earlier this year after a grassroots group gathered around 300,000 petition signatures asking for a binding referendum on separation.
Smith, a Conservative whose political base includes supporters of independence, has advocated for Alberta to remain in Canada but has said the referendum is a chance to hear directly from Albertans on the issue.
Supporters of separation say the oil-rich, landlocked province has been overlooked by federal politicians in Ottawa despite the wealth it contributes to Canada.
Successive Liberal governments of the last 10 years, they argue, have put environmental policies above helping Alberta develop its oil and gas sector, and that Alberta would get to keep more of its wealth if it splits from Canada.
Those who oppose separation say a newly-independent Alberta would be left responsible for billions of dollars in debt, and warn that the uncertainty would drive thousands of jobs and investment out of the province.
Some, including Prime Minister Carney, have likened the Alberta referendum to "Brexit" when the UK voted to leave the European Union in 2016, warning that a vote to leave may come with unintended economic consequences.
In his speech on Thursday, Carney acknowledged that "the frustrations that many Albertans have felt are real".
But he said that his government is willing to support Alberta and its energy industry.
In the weeks leading up to the referendum, Carney announced his plans to fast-track approval of a new oil pipeline from Alberta to Canada's Pacific coast.
He has described the project as "a demonstration of the power of Canada" and argued it would help the country diversify its markets as it deals with US tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump.
Premier Smith is set to speak at a separate pro-unity event in Calgary on Friday alongside Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre, who has also advocated for Alberta to remain in Canada.
Meanwhile, advocates for Alberta separation are planning a rally in Edmonton on Saturday in their own last-minute push to turn out voters.
Early figures suggest a high voter turn-out, with the number of ballots cast already higher than Alberta's last provincial general election.

After a years-long investigation, police in Nevada have identified the remains of the person found stuffed in a corroded barrel near Las Vegas.
Police identified the man as Edward "Buddy" Lelburian Jackson. He was found in May 2022 with a gunshot wound to the head. The corroded barrel was exposed in Lake Mead after a severe drought caused water levels to drop.
His remains went unidentified until recently, when investigators found his family using DNA, according to the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department.
Robert Price, a homicide detective with the department, said there is no evidence that the death was tied to any known criminal group, despite public speculation that it was mob-related.
"At this point in our investigation, we don't have information to support those theories," Price said.
Jackson is believed to have died after being shot in the head in the 1980s, he said, adding that he was probably in his "mid to late 50s" when he died. He was originally from Arkansas, but was known to travel throughout the US West. He had previously lived in California and Utah, officials say.
Authorities have not released new photos of Jackson
He was found with a single gunshot wound to the head. The bullet that killed him has not been found, Price said at a news conference on Thursday, adding that nothing else was found in the barrel besides the clothing that he was wearing.
He had previously been arrested in Salt Lake City, Utah. Price added that he had no known ties to Las Vegas, and had never been reported missing.
His extended relatives in Arkansas told police that he was known to move around frequently.
"He would travel the country. He would show up when he showed up," Price explained.
Police are still working to identify his killer and any motive in the shooting. Jackson was not known to be a "gambler", Price said, adding that it could be challenging to track down any of his living associates.
The largest US reservoir, Lake Mead supplies drinking water to 20 million people from Las Vegas to Los Angeles.
Police had previously warned that more bodies would probably be found as the lake recedes in drought conditions. Three other people have been found inside, and positively identified by authorities. Two are believed to have died from drowning, while a third death remains unexplained.
Police had constructed a 3D rendering of the victim's skull in their effort to identify his remains.
Lake Mead levels have been declining since 2000 - droughts have been getting worse in recent years, with scientists saying climate change is exacerbating the situation.
Droughts have been worsening in recent years, something scientists say is being driven by climate change.
Persistent hot summer weather has been causing water levels to drop in rivers and lakes in several countries â leading to unexpected discoveries.
In Hungary, the bodies of two World War Two German soldiers were recovered from the Danube River in Budapest earlier this year. Alongside the remains was a largely intact German army Wehrmacht motorcycle.
Other remnants of World War Two have appeared in the Danube recently, including a broken-up hull near Prahovo in Serbia.

âJudge me by my actions and my work, but please do not assume that because I might pray differently than anybody whoâs ever held this office, that somehow I am not deeply committed to this Constitution,â El-Sayed said in response to a question from Semafor.
Republicans have recently amplified claims that El-Sayed and his family have ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. Trump posted a video Thursday night that directly called El-Sayed a member of the group, which was founded in Egypt; his administration has designated chapters as terrorist organizations.
El-Sayed, an American of Egyptian descent who would be the first Muslim senator if elected, has rankled at the GOP accusations, including in a recent TV interview. His comments on Thursday are as close as he has come on the campaign trail to alleging Islamophobia by his opponents.
âThey donât want to talk about any of the other issues that people are actually experiencing in their lives. They want to talk about me or point to my mom or my sister,â El-Sayed said. âMy mom and my sister are not running for office. Iâm running for office.â
El-Sayed called it âan insane thing to assumeâ that members of his family were part of the Muslim Brotherhood, saying he didnât âknow what my mother was doing in Egypt in the 1970s.â Republicans have cited social media posts from his half-sister that appear to refer to his motherâs engagement with the group.
âMy parents got divorced when I was very young â 3,â El-Sayed said. âI didnât see my mom for years after I was raised by my dad and my stepmom, and when I asked, [to] the best of my knowledge, nobody in my familyâs been a member of this organization.â
Know More
El-Sayed said insinuating he might not be loyal to the Constitution because of his faith was âthe same thing that was done to JFK when they tried to say that, âOh, well, heâs going to answer to the Pope because heâs Catholic.â Same thing they tried to do to President Obama.â
John F. Kennedy, the first Roman Catholic president, faced some false accusations of âdual loyaltiesâ because of his faith. And the hard right pushed conspiracy theories about the religious practices of Obama, who is a Christian and was the first Black president.

c0989f8802f7.text: The Trump administration is suing California and two election officials over claims that there are suspected ineligible voters who received mail-in ballots for this November's election . Why it matters: The lawsuit is asking the court to prevent about 20,000 voters from having their ballots counted until their citizenship status is confirmed. What they're saying: "State-facilitated voter fraud is unacceptable in the United States of America," Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a press release statement. "If found responsible in a court of law, the State of California will have seriously undermined confidence in our electoral system and violated laws that protect our nation's representative system of government," Blanche said. Zoom in: The Justice Department alleges that California is knowingly allowing noncitizens to vote in the federal elections, according to the lawsuit. The lawsuit says U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and ICE's investigative arm compiled the list of potentially ineligible voters using agency data and records from the Social Security Administration and State Department. But administration-created lists of potential noncitizens on the voter rolls have been found less than accurate before in Nevada , Pennsylvania and New Jersey . Zoom out: California's top election official and Los Angeles County's election chief received letters two days ago threatening "emergency action." The Justice Department gave Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk Dean Logan a password-protected thumb drive listing more than 20,000 voters and instructed him to verify their citizenship within 48 hours, according to the department's letter and statements. "Maintaining accurate voter registration records is a fundamental responsibility of our office. Our response will be grounded in compliance with federal and state voter registration laws and procedures," Logan said in a statement on social media after the initial letter. Friction point: Federal law restricts systematic voter roll maintenance within 90 days of a federal election — in part to prevent eligible voters from being removed shortly before voting. This litigation also follows legal attempts from the federal government to get California's voter rolls, beyond public lists, which have failed in court. The other side: "This is a sad, desperate attempt by Trump to use his politicized Justice Department to try to suppress California voters just three weeks before Election Day," Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) said in a statement. "The courts have made clear that the federal government has no role in how a state carries out its election process, and now, in the middle of Californians voting, they have asked local officials — who do a damn good job defending democracy — to violate federal law."

8990c7e1917a.text: Nine former FBI agents and intelligence personnel sued the Trump administration Thursday, alleging they were unlawfully fired for working on the investigation into President Trump's handling of classified documents . Why it matters: The agents' bid to regain their jobs adds to a growing number of legal challenges accusing the Trump administration of retaliating against FBI personnel who investigated the president. Driving the news: "Plaintiffs were unlawfully terminated not for any cause or any legitimate reason, but only to satisfy the President's personal vendetta," the 70-page lawsuit says. "As a result of their unlawful and hasty firings, Plaintiffs' investigations were not properly transferred to other FBI Special Agents or Analysts. The impact of these heedless actions on America's national security is immeasurable." All nine plaintiffs are seeking their jobs back. FBI Director Kash Patel , Attorney General Todd Blanche and their agencies are named as defendants. The other side: Patel said in February termination letters that the employees had "exercised poor judgment and a lack of impartiality in carrying out duties, leading to the political weaponization of the government," according to the lawsuit. The FBI did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment on the lawsuit. Zoom in: The lawsuit disputes Patel's accusations, saying none of the plaintiffs had any history of "misconduct or poor behavior while employed with the FBI." None had been internally investigated for wrongdoing, nor were they given the opportunity to explain or appeal their terminations. The lawsuit alleges the firings bypassed FBI policy requiring an administrative inquiry before disciplinary action. The complaint also notes that "[i]n many instances, Plaintiffs' immediate supervisors expressed disbelief and regret that Plaintiffs' FBI careers had been ended." What they're saying: "With over a century of experience among them, these former FBI agents and analysts served our country with honor and distinction," Margaret Donovan of Koskoff, Koskoff & Bieder, a firm representing some of the plaintiffs, told Axios in an emailed statement. "[T]hey investigated leaks of national security and defense information, thwarted threats and attacks from our enemies, and responded to critical incidents like the Boston Marathon bombing, the interdiction of Iranian weaponry intended for the Houthis, and the assassination attempt against then-candidate Donald Trump." "In return for their service, they were fired because they did their jobs, as they always did, to follow the facts and law without bias or favor." Context: Multiple plaintiffs said they were involved in investigating Iranian intelligence threats when they lost their jobs. One, Jeremy Linton, was managing "several dozen" Iranian counterintelligence cases and was fired three days before the U.S. and Israel launched strikes against Iran, without an opportunity to transfer his work or convey intelligence he had received to colleagues. The suit alleges this process endangered American national security. Zoom out: Other fired FBI agents have also sued the administration, alleging they were punished for investigating alleged wrongdoing by the president. In February 2025, a group sued to prohibit the administration from obtaining a list of agents who investigated the Jan. 6 Capitol riot. Agents who investigated Trump's conduct during the 2020 election sued over their firings in March. Three former FBI officials filed a separate lawsuit in September 2025. Go deeper: Kash Patel's FBI loses another top official
